Precise Listeners Learn Languages Easier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:09:13 UTC
15:09:13 KST

Study suggests developing a ‘good ear’ for sounds instead of practice alone
People who are better at noticing fine details in sound—known as auditory precision—can master the pronunciation of new languages faster and more accurately than other learners, a new study finds.
Even when hearing a human voice, some people’s brains do not immediately treat new sounds as language, instead they understand them as unfamiliar acoustic signals. This ability may be one of the keys to successfully mastering pronunciation of a new language.
Researchers from UK’s University College London and Japan’s Tohoku University measured the auditory precision of 67 Japanese learners of English by measuring their ability to detect slight acoustic differences, such as changes in pitch, length, and tone, in non-speech sounds.
They then used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) technology to measure the participants’ brain activity as they tried to distinguish between the English vowels /æ/ (like the ‘a’ in ‘cat’) and /ʌ/ (like the ‘uh’ in ‘cup’). Neither of these sounds map directly on to Japanese vowels.
In a second task, the participants distinguished similar subtle differences in non-speech sounds.
The results, published in The Journal of Experimental Psychology: General showed that learners with higher auditory precision relied less on the brain’s left sensorimotor system (involved in language processing) when processing foreign-language sounds. Their brain activity patterns were similar to those that occur when the brain processes non-speech sounds. With less interference from pre-existing patterns of their native language, it was simpler for these learners to accurately process new sounds.
In contrast, the fMRI results showed learners with lower auditory precision relied more on the brain’s left sensorimotor network when listening to foreign-language sounds. They used the pronunciation patterns of their native-language when processing unfamiliar foreign language sounds.
Lead author Dr Kazuya Saito-van Poeteren (UCL Institute of Education) said: “Learners with a ‘good ear’ for auditory differences can hear a new foreign-language sound objectively, without immediately processing it as ‘language’. Instead, their brains analyze the acoustic information itself, and this may be the key to why some people grasp new languages with more ease than others.
“Most people approach foreign language learning by memorizing vocabulary and listening to speech, but our study indicated that language learners might also benefit from training the auditory abilities that underpin language learning itself.
The research team aim to develop a new form of combined language and auditory training designed to improve the ability to detect fine differences in pitch and other acoustic properties.

With less than a fortnight before Healey’s tax and spending announcement, the reading is a surprise boost amid the Middle East rattling the global economy and hitting British households and businesses with a surge in energy costs.
After petrol and diesel prices rose last month and as higher energy bills hit household spending, the ONS said the consumer-facing services sector fell by 0.3% on the month, following a decline of 0.1% in July.
The largest negative contribution came from sports, amusement and recreation activities, alongside a slump in food and drink services. Analysts said the fall could be a sign of a reversal from an earlier boost from the World Cup and unusually hot weather, or reflect households trimming their spending.
Despite the overall services sector showing no growth in August, the surprise headline improvement was driven by strength in manufacturing with 0.8% growth in the wider production sector, which includes manufacturing, mining and energy generation. Construction output fell by 0.2%.
Sanjay Raja, chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said: “Undoubtedly, there may be some hiccups to come in the run up to year end, especially as energy prices continue to bite household incomes, and higher rates continue to drag on spending and investment.
“The good news? The UK’s resilience story continues. It’s hard to overstate how strong the UK performance has been all year.”
Against a volatile backdrop, the chancellor is under pressure to use his tax and spending address to the Commons on 28 October to announce a package of support to soften the blow including energy help for poorer households. However, he will face a delicate balancing act amid a sharp increase in government borrowing costs.
In recent months, Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.
Jake Finney, senior economist at PwC, said: “The UK’s growth performance has been a bright spot amid a less impressive run of economic news following events in the Middle East. Business investment has been an important driver, particularly spending on ICT hardware, likely linked to the build-out of AI infrastructure.”
In a fillip for the chancellor, the International Monetary Fund this week upgraded its UK growth forecastsfor this year, but warned that it expected a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.
The latest figures from the ONS showed GDP over the wider three months to the end of August rose by 0.7%. On an annual basis it said the economy had grown by 2.1%, the strongest growth rate since August 2022.
However, economists said momentum was likely to falter at the end of the year as households come under pressure from rising inflation. Healey would also face a challenging balancing act to support households with the cost of living within tight constraints on the public finances.
Financial markets currently anticipate the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month from the current level of 3.75% to 4%, before four more quarter-point rate increases in 2027.
Matt Swannell, the chief economic adviser to the Item Club, said: “We’re sceptical this strength can last … Some pullback looks inevitable. The impact of the conflict in the Middle East is also starting to be felt. Higher energy bills and petrol prices are pushing up inflation and hitting consumers’ spending power.”

China’s economic model relies on state subsidies and nonmarket practices rather than international trade rules, Lin said. He argued that Beijing seeks to make Europe dependent on China rather than pursue mutually beneficial trade.

He pointed to growing Taiwan-Europe industrial cooperation, citing TSMC’s investment in Germany, GlobalWafers’ investment in Italy, and Foxconn’s advanced packaging operations in France. He said such projects aim to create jobs, transfer expertise, and strengthen Europe’s industrial ecosystem.
Taiwan is also promoting plans to establish a Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association technology park in Poland, Lin said. The initiative aims to bring Taiwan’s industrial capabilities and integrated supply chain ecosystem to Europe while fostering cooperation in electric vehicles, smart cities, and AI.
Having visited Europe eight times since becoming foreign minister 18 months ago, Lin said he had witnessed the deepening of Taiwan-Europe ties. He described AI as an industrial revolution of historic proportions, with Taiwan playing a central role.

‘I introduce myself to anyone who looks a bit jumpy’: a security guard’s take on anti-shoplifting fixes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

I’ve run into volatile thieves for years – from opportunistic phone snatchers to people ripping computers off desks and biofuel bandits trying to steal vats of used cooking oil – and every time I file an incident report, I try to make a recommendation for preventive measures.
It’s safer to try to avoid a situation where things get physical with a suspected criminal. I don’t want to let my employers down, but I also don’t want anyone to have to go to hospital – myself included.
Greggs seems to be following a similar train of thought: earlier this year the chain phased out self-service cabinets in areas where shoplifting is rife and has installed safe pod “robocops” with 120-decibel sirens in some stores.
But snatch thefts seem to be on the rise everywhere, from “steaming” (large groups overwhelming a store) in city centres to machinery being swiped from rural farm shops. The cost of this crime – in terms of lost merchandise and measures to tackle it – further erodes margins at a time when retailers are battling higher employment costs and increases to business rates.
Customers, ever squeezed by rising energy bills, are becoming doubly impatient: those who are not tempted by grabbable goods are rightly affronted by measures such as sliding shields that seem to imply that everyone is a criminal.
But is it possible to make a store thief proof and welcoming to law-abiding clientele?
Discreet high technology is a happy medium. PTZ cameras (pan/tilt/zoom, which can be adjusted to track and focus on a single suspect) are one of the most-effective choices. They’re more efficient than fixed-camera CCTV, less controversial than AI surveillance and a serious upgrade on the convex mirror mounted at the end of the aisle in your local corner shop.
PTZ camera manoeuvrability means high-quality facial images, a must-have when trying to build evidence. Freeze-frames can also be used to generate stills that some premises owners choose to turn into warning posters, or share on a chat group with other local businesses.
My advice here is to be wary of GDPR regulations and remember that an incorrect time signature can render recordings inadmissible.
As useful as movable cameras are, they still require a human operator. Hiring guards can feel like a tax on businesses – but one that goes unpaid at considerable risk.
Ask anyone who lives in a village whether they’d prefer a CCTV camera or a “bobby on the beat” and the answer would be probably unanimously the latter.
The sight of a uniformed officer can be a strong deterrent. However, it comes with an upper limit. For example: if a 3,000 sq metre supermarket can accommodate 40,000 goods and 4,000 daily customers, one guard will not be able to cover it all.
It is also hard to identify which customers might be preparing to swipe something, especially given the rise of “middle-class shoplifting”. As someone whose job pays just above minimum wage, this is an interesting phenomenon.
I get that inflation presses down on all of us, but people further up the pyramid than me should know it won’t be shareholders or bonus-receiving bosses taking the hit for goods being pinched: it will be prices. Higher costs will further imperil the most vulnerable people who walk on site, the ones who already cannot afford bread or baby formula.
My best approach in these cases is empathy. I try to introduce myself to anyone who hangs around but looks jumpy; explain that every tap of my bank card makes me sweat too.
I also try to build local knowledge of repeat offenders: insight that made the bobbies on the beat so valuable. I know it won’t work against content creators who film me for “lols” while I’m administering first aid, and who half of all young Brits apparently want to emulate. I honestly fear them more than I do getting punched, stabbed or spat on.
But doing your revision pays off, especially when encountering an unsettled local resident with a penchant for threatening people with kitchen utensils. As the resident in question strode towards the premises one morning, my shiftmate quickly asked me whether I knew his name and address (I did).
“Morning, Mr Beddlington,” said my colleague as the resident got level with us and before he could grab his first frying pan. “Everything OK at Thorn Court today? Anything we can help with?”
The resident did an about-face and left the site. Loss prevention done low-cost and painlessly.
Names and addresses have been changed
What the Bouncer Saw: Life on the Front Line of the Security Business by George Bass is published by Hachette. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

The government has refused to say when the public will be able to freely access information about who owns large plots of land across England and Wales.
Emma Reynolds, the previous secretary of state for the environment, announced in March that the paywall protecting large amounts of the Land Registry would be partly lifted.
Campaigners called for this change in order to make large landowners more accountable, particularly for key areas such as river catchments, grouse moors and peatland.
But Reynolds did not put a date on when the paywall would be lifted, and the Land Registry is an “arm’s length body”, a non-ministerial government department that falls under the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
In setting out the land use framework in March, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) pledged only that it would “work with HM Land Registry this year to provide access to free, spatial land ownership data for larger properties covering the vast majority of England and Wales, excluding almost all homeowners”.
This may require a further public consultation, in addition to the consultation that preceded the land use framework. In July, a spokesperson for the Land Registry said: “HM Land Registry is supportive of initiatives that promote the more effective use of land. However, our plans with regard to this are still at a very early stage, and a number of aspects will be subject to consultation before any firm decisions are made. As such, we are currently unable to comment on timelines, what may be released, the format, or any associated attributes. We anticipate being in a position to provide more of an update early next year.”
In August, a Land Registry spokesperson said it was not clear which parts of the Land Registry data would be made public, nor who might be allowed to access the data and by what means.
Guy Shrubsole, the environmental campaigner and author of Who Owns England?, said: “It’s ridiculous that in the 21st century the public are kept in the dark about who owns the land beneath our feet. This is data that will help councils build more homes, expose who’s polluting our rivers and help communities restore nature.”
Andy Burnham, who took over as prime minister from Keir Starmer this summer, has made localism a key priority of his premiership. Shrubsole said allowing people to see data on the ownership of land should be part of that agenda. “Burnham has come to power promising place-first politics, and to bring unaccountable government agencies to heel,” he said. “Who owns our land underpins any politics of place, and it’s high time the Land Registry was made to reveal this profoundly important information.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “We are improving the transparency of land ownership data, and will provide free access to land ownership data for the vast majority of England, as we committed to in our land use framework. We are taking forward this commitment and will share further details as this work continues.”

====================================================================================================

The Welsh mountain inn that helped conquer Everest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:00:24 UTC
15:00:24 KST

In the early hours of 2 June 1953, guests at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel in the heart of Eryri (Snowdonia) were woken from their sleep by the sound of footsteps running down the corridor outside their rooms. The commotion was followed by gleeful shouting and the sound of champagne corks popping. A late-night telephone call to the hotel’s owner had moments earlier confirmed that Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay had successfully summited Mount Everest. It had taken two days for the news to travel from the Himalayas to London. Serendipitously, news of the historic achievement coincided with the coronation of Queen Elizabeth II later that day.
In the days and weeks that followed, the two mountaineers were feted across the front pages of newspapers around the world. Posing awkwardly for the cameras, their beaming smiles shone out of frost-burnt faces. In the decades that followed, Tenzing Norgay’s role in the expedition was increasingly marginalised – he was a Sherpa, indigenous to the area, and the load-carrying guide, while Hillary firmly planted his ice axe in the history books.
A new film, set for release this week on Apple TV, aims to set that record straight. Tenzing, starring Genden Phuntsok and Tom Hiddleston, tracks Tenzing Norgay’s life from a young boy growing up in the Khumbu Valley to his rise as one of the most accomplished climbers within the Sherpa community, and his eventual recruitment to the 1953 British expedition to Mount Everest (known locally as Chomolungma) led by Colonel John Hunt.
The film opened the Zurich film festival last month, where its director, Australian film-maker Jennifer Peedom, told audiences: “It’s often reduced to a familiar shorthand: Hillary conquered Everest, assisted by a Sherpa. But Tenzing had more experience on Everest than anyone else on that 1953 expedition. He wasn’t just helping another man achieve his dream. He had his own dream.”
In the spring of 1952, a full year before the British expedition, Tenzing, alongside Swiss climber Raymond Lambert, came agonisingly close to reaching the summit – less than 250 metres stood between them and glory. After a storm-lashed night on the south-east ridge, and with little oxygen, they were forced to retreat, albeit having set a new altitude record.
Meanwhile, back in the UK, Hunt, having been assigned by the Joint Himalayan Committee to assemble a team of climbers, set up base camp at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel at the foot of the Llanberis Pass. It was here they would practise their technical climbing skills and test the state-of-the-art equipment that had been designed specifically for this adventure, in particular the closed-circuit oxygen tanks that would be critical in keeping them alive in the “death zone” above 8,000m. The teams spent weeks on Yr Wyddfa’s (Snowdon) notorious Crib Goch ridge and on Yr Lliwedd mountain, testing the revolutionary new high-altitude boots that would replace the old leather and hobnail ones, which offered little to no protection from the freezing temperatures of Everest.
Artefacts from those pioneering days can be seen at the hotel today. A glass cabinet contains some of the summit team’s original equipment and mementoes: goggles, an ice axe, a ledger of Sherpas’ fingerprints as most could not read or write, a compass and a battered tin mug. Little has changed in the 73 years since Christopher Briggs woke his guests with those glasses of champagne. The Pen-Y-Gwryd is a time capsule; it remains in family hands, now run by Briggs’s grandsons, Nick and Rupert Pullee, who are determined to maintain the hotel’s legacy and the traditions that have made it a beloved destination for those with a penchant for adventure and late-night conversations in front of roaring fires.
“My grandfather was originally from Scarborough,” Nick says. “He was a chemist, but his shop was bombed during the war, so [in 1947] he persuaded a friend to lend him the money to buy a hotel in Wales. The building had been used to home children during the blitz and had fallen into terrible disrepair, but he somehow managed to turn it into a success.”
Briggs also started the Snowdon Club, where guests under the age of 16 who have successfully climbed the mountain take part in a small ceremony in which they are quizzed on their mountain knowledge. Those who answer correctly get to drink (lemonade) from Hillary’s pewter tankard and are awarded a sterling silver ice-axe brooch, with their name added to a book of members – a ritual that still happens today.
The Smoke Room serves as the residents’ bar, a tiny wood-panelled snug whose walls are adorned with photos of the Everest team, with Tenzing featuring prominently. In one, he’s perched in the bar drinking tea with George Band, the youngest climber on the 1953 expedition. In another, he’s on a rocky outcrop of Tryfan, another famous Snowdonia peak, with team leader Hunt.
“I was only a toddler when Tenzing last visited the hotel,” says Nick. “I remember he was incredibly kind and was constantly smiling. He used to give Rupert and myself piggybacks up the stairs. He was great friends with my grandfather, who visited him in Nepal often.”
Built in 1810 on the bedrock that makes up the Glyderau range, the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel is also the original starting point of the Pyg track, one of the most iconic routes to the summit of Yr Wyddfa, and today guests can walk directly from the hotel’s door to the path that snakes upwards towards Pen y Pass. The timeless interior of the hotel is devoid of TV screens or piped music, and the only concession to the 21st century appears to be the wifi.
This summer’s endless heatwaves saw sun-scorched hillwalkers cool their limbs in the natural outdoor pool in the grounds of the hotel. Fed by mountain streams, it offers unparalleled views of the hills and sweeping valley towards the mountain village of Capel Curig. The addition of an outdoor sauna and the popularity of cold-water swimming mean it’s now a year-round proposition.
The 20 rooms are all named evocatively after local peaks: Pen yr Ole Wen, Elidir Fawr, Crib Goch, Y Garn. Each is as cosy as one would expect from a rain-lashed mountain hotel: softly lit and with comfy mattresses wrapped in vintage Welsh wool blankets. In the labyrinthine corridors upstairs, you’ll discover bathrooms with Victorian roll-top tubs and Heath Robinson-esque showers. The bathroom doors are adorned with illustrations in the style of Aubrey Beardsley, and photos and artworks capturing the surrounding landscape and its mountaineering history adorn virtually every wall.
Dining at the Pen-Y-Gwryd is an event in itself: mealtimes are announced by the banging of a gong, the dining room is an unapologetic whirlwind of Axminster and silverware, and the menu features roast Welsh lamb and Welsh steak and ale pies, sticky toffee puddings or rhubarb crumble – everything you’ll need to replenish after a long mountain trek.
The ceiling of the Everest Room in the public bar has been signed by pretty much every big-name mountaineer of the past 100 years, and each corner of the building appears to have a story and artefact attached. It’s this authenticity that Nick believes gives the hotel its charm.
“I think our greatest attraction may be that things remain unchanged,” says Nick. “We have a lot of regular guests from all over the world, and for many people the opportunity to step back from the world in the wilds of Snowdonia is extremely enticing. It’s something we aim to protect and cherish.”
Rooms at the Pen-Y-Gwryd hotel range from £114 to £172 B&B; three-course dinner £49. Tenzing is on Apple TV from 16 October

He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died.
“I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel. Utterly determined to prove him wrong.”
Beyond ruling out a second independence referendum, recent British prime ministers have often paid little attention to Scottish internal affairs. Burnham has already said there is “no clear consensus” for another vote. But unlike his predecessors, he has decided to take on the SNP by loudly make the case for the union on Scottish soil.
Burnham presents a new challenge for the SNP as they seek to re-energise the case for Scottish independence. Swinney has said he wants a new vote before 2031. The separatists have grown used to facing off against rightwing, pro-Brexit governments in London during two decades in power in Holyrood, making it easier to argue that Scotland’s interests have been dismissed. Burnham’s devolution agenda, openness to exploring a return to the European Union and £2 bus fares are harder to confront.
Even among SNP voters, he is popular. Polling by PF Global found that 46% of Scots have a favourable view of Burnham, far higher than the Labour party itself, and double Keir Starmer’s when he left power. Only Swinney is more popular than the prime minister among SNP voters who supported yes in 2014, reaching a level not seen for a Labour leader since Jeremy Corbyn. Despite this, SNP figures have sought to capitalise on Burnham’s stance on the EU in their quest for a second independence vote.
“We are in a situation where Andy Burnham is actively and unilaterally opening up the conversation about whether we are able to go back to results of referendums and relitigate those decisions while saying that that same democratic principle does not apply to the people of Scotland,” said Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry. “The idea that the union can continue to exist in its current form is absolutely farcical.”
In Aberdeen, the SNP is hoping to draw a line under a bruising few years after Nicola Sturgeon’s resignation and the subsequent fraud conviction of her estranged husband and former SNP chair Peter Murrell, who is serving a five-year prison sentence for embezzling £400,000 from the party. A proceeds of crime case against Murrell is scheduled for early December.
In May, the SNP won a fifth successive election, but only enough to form a minority government in Holyrood. Despite the victory, Sturgeon criticised a “lack of vision or big picture thinking” in the campaign in the opening to her memoir. Swinney has said they were still good friends. Some SNP figures wonder how much they owe to the unpopularity of Starmer. The party also faces challenges on multiple fronts: Reform has as many MSPs as Labour in Holyrood with 17, while the Scottish Greens won a record 15 seats. The Tories have showed that they can still win seats, defeating the SNP in Aberdeen South in June.
Despite the potential for a standoff between Swinney and Burnham, there is growing appetite in Scotland for collaboration between Westminster and Holyrood. Since the May elections, there has been a sharp rise in Scots who support a closer working relationship between the UK and Scottish governments. Polling by Ipsos has found that 42% of Scots would feel happy about the SNP-led Scottish government working with London, up 12 points since Starmer was in charge in May. Just over half of Scots believe that the country is going in the wrong direction, up six points in the same time period.
This conference, the SNP has invited speakers from other separatist and pro-independence parties. Sioned Williams, deputy first minister of Wales, will give a fraternal address on Friday. Gillian Mackay, a Scottish Green party MSP, will speak at a panel about the right pathway to independence on Saturday.
“We understand, and members of the SNP know, that this is bigger than the SNP. Obviously, I fundamentally believe that the SNP will be the party who secures independence for Scotland. But that runs so much deeper throughout the Scottish population than just those who vote for the SNP. I do think that it is important at this moment to harness and to build on that support as broadly as we can,” said Bird.

For Gaza's chronically ill, every missed dose carries a risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
06:00:23 UTC
15:00:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's healthcare collapse leaves chronic patients facing life-threatening complications
Three years into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, people living with chronic illnesses are struggling to access the medicines, tests and routine treatment they need to stay alive. For patients with diabetes, heart disease, kidney failure and cancer, shortages of essential drugs, medical equipment and fuel have turned the management of everyday conditions into a daily struggle for survival.
Across Gaza, disrupted medical care means patients are increasingly unable to monitor their conditions, attend follow-up appointments or complete essential treatment.
The consequences can be life-threatening: uncontrolled blood sugar, untreated heart problems, interrupted dialysis and cancer patients left uncertain about whether their disease is progressing.
The World Health Organisation says noncommunicable diseases, which accounted for the largest burden of disease in Gaza before the war, are now being underdiagnosed and undertreated because of limited access to diagnostic tests and treatment services.
According to 2026 figures, more than 18,500 people with injuries or chronic illnesses were in need of treatment unavailable inside Gaza and were awaiting medical evacuation.
'Diabetes has become a ghost'
Khalil al-Turk, 59, displaced from northern Gaza, once understood his illness well. Before the genocide, diabetes was something he could measure and manage: a tablet in the morning, an HbA1c test every three months, and regular medical follow-up.
Today, he says, diabetes has become "a ghost I cannot see."
"There are no glucose testing strips, and the insulin that is available is either constantly running out or spoils because there is no proper refrigeration. Sometimes I feel extremely dizzy, and I don’t know whether my blood sugar is too high or too low."
In those moments, even the decision to eat becomes frightening. "I eat a date and risk pushing my sugar higher, or I avoid eating because I’m afraid I might die."
Then came a small wound on his foot. Two months ago, Khalil developed a wound that, he says, did not receive the follow-up care it needed. It eventually developed into a deep infection threatening his foot.
Diabetes is not simply a temporary rise in blood glucose. Persistently high blood sugar can damage blood vessels, nerves, kidneys, eyes and the heart, making regular monitoring an essential part of treatment rather than a medical luxury.
In stable conditions, doctors can detect deteriorating blood-sugar control or the early signs of complications before they develop into a crisis. But when laboratory tests, monitoring equipment and follow-up appointments disappear, patients may not realise that their illness is no longer under control until their bodies begin sending far more serious warning signs.
'I don’t know how many attacks my heart has endured'
In Deir al-Balah, Aisha Juha, 62, lives with high blood pressure and heart disease. She used to attend a cardiology clinic every two months and took her blood-pressure medication regularly.
Now, she says, everything has changed. "For a year and a half, I have not stood in front of a single blood-pressure monitor," Aisha shares.
Her medication is no longer consistent either. "The medicine available at medical points changes from one week to another depending on whatever aid happens to arrive. Sometimes they give me an alternative; other times they simply tell me, ‘You’ll have to manage somehow.’"
Then came a night when she felt a heavy pressure in her chest and numbness spreading through her left arm. She knew the symptoms could be serious, but she could not find an ambulance or reach a nearby hospital equipped with an ECG machine.
"I took a patience pill, so to speak, and waited until morning. I don’t know how many attacks, or small heart events, my heart has gone through without any of them ever being recorded in a medical file," she says.
High blood pressure and heart disease require long-term monitoring and treatment. In Gaza, however, care for chronic conditions remains constrained by shortages of medication and equipment, as well as difficulties in reaching healthcare facilities.
The problem is not simply the absence of medication. It is also the absence of medical information.
Four hours became two
For Yousef Hammad, 41, a dialysis patient from Khan Younis, routine healthcare isn't an occasional visit to the doctor. It means staying alive. Under normal circumstances, he says, each dialysis session lasted four hours, three times a week.
"Today, a session lasts only two hours, twice a week — or sometimes just once, if we are lucky and there is enough diesel and treated water," Yousef tells The New Arab.
He describes reaching a dialysis machine as though competing for the chance to breathe. "I arrive at the machine competing with hundreds of other patients, our bodies full of toxins and fluid that are suffocating us," he adds.
The World Health Organisation says dialysis services in Gaza remain under intense pressure, with shortages of dialysis machines and essential medicines. Gaza’s Ministry of Health has estimated that as many as 1,100 patients require regular dialysis to stay alive.
For someone with kidney failure, treatment cannot simply be postponed until "conditions improve." When the kidneys stop functioning, they can no longer remove waste products and excess fluid from the body. In end-stage kidney failure, patients depend on dialysis or a kidney transplant to survive.
"A delay of just one day means I cannot sleep lying down because my lungs fill with fluid," Yousef says. "We are not waiting to recover. We are simply waiting to leave the dialysis session able to breathe."
When epilepsy medication runs out
For the mother of eight-year-old Karim, epilepsy was not an emergency before the genocide. Her son had lived with well-controlled epilepsy for years, and regular medication helped keep his seizures under control.
But when supplies of his medication began disappearing from pharmacies, she was unable to obtain it for three consecutive days.
Then the seizures began.
She says Karim suffered repeated, prolonged convulsions, and that she watched him struggling to breathe without knowing what to do.
The family tried replacing his medication with another drug they managed to find, but she says the seizures became worse.
With chronic illnesses, an "alternative medication" is not always a simple substitution that families can safely make on their own.
Some anti-epileptic drugs require careful selection, precise dosing and medical follow-up, because uncontrolled changes can result in a loss of seizure control.
Epilepsy also reveals something fundamental about routine healthcare: patients do not need doctors only when a seizure occurs. They need medical care to prevent that seizure from happening in the first place.
The cancer Khadija cannot see
Khadija Ahmed, 52, a breast cancer patient, has been displaced twice. Before Israel's war on the besieged enclave, she underwent surgery and was expected to begin adjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy at the Turkish-Palestinian Friendship Hospital.
Then the treatment plan stopped. She says the closure of the hospital, the destruction of medical equipment and the interruption of patients’ ability to leave Gaza for treatment brought everything to a halt.
Today, she can no longer undergo the tests that were meant to help her and her doctors monitor her condition.
"I cannot get tumour-marker tests. I don’t know whether the cancer has returned or whether it is spreading through my body," she tells The New Arab.
Sometimes, she feels pain in her bones. "I ask myself: is this simply exhaustion from displacement, or has the cancer reached my bones without me knowing?" she adds.
This is one of the less visible faces of war: not only living with illness, but living with medical uncertainty.
The World Health Organisation has confirmed that cancer patients in Gaza continue to face serious difficulties accessing treatment because of shortages of medicines, equipment and specialised services.
From chronic illness to emergency
Modern medicine does not treat chronic illnesses as conditions that patients can simply “put up with” indefinitely.
Diabetes requires monitoring, follow-up and treatment.
High blood pressure requires regular checks and medication adjustments when necessary.
Heart disease requires assessment and continuing care.
Kidney failure requires regular dialysis.
Epilepsy requires medication and medical follow-up to prevent or reduce seizures.
Cancer requires completion of a treatment plan and continued monitoring for response to treatment or recurrence.
When this system functions, patients may appear to be "well." But that apparent stability does not mean their illness has disappeared. It means the healthcare system is doing its job: keeping the disease under control.
When that system collapses, diseases that once remained silent can return as medical emergencies.
That is what makes routine healthcare part of the humanitarian response to war — not a secondary concern that can simply be postponed until the fighting stops.
According to the World Health Organisation, only 19 of Gaza’s 36 hospitals were functioning in September 2026, even partially, and none was operating at full capacity. Severe shortages of essential medicines, diagnostic tools, medical equipment and fuel persisted.
The care that disappeared
Nearly three years into the war, the problem may be more than just patients losing access to hospitals.
They have also lost the daily rhythm that once separated chronic illness from medical crisis: the scheduled blood test, the doctor’s appointment, the blood-pressure reading, the dialysis session, the prescription refill, the scan that reassured a patient that what was happening inside their body was still being watched.
When these seemingly small details disappear, chronic diseases do not.
They accumulate quietly, until some eventually emerge as emergencies that may be far more difficult to treat.
In Gaza, many patients are no longer waiting to be cured of their illnesses. They are simply waiting for their bodies to keep holding on.
Images of war tend to show injuries, explosions and destroyed hospitals. But another war is unfolding inside bodies we cannot see: people whose blood sugar rises without their knowing it, hearts functioning without medical monitoring, kidneys waiting for the next dialysis session, children waiting for medication that will prevent another seizure, and cancer patients waiting for a test that might finally tell them what is happening inside their bodies.
These illnesses may not appear in photographs of war. But every day, their patients continue to pay its price.
Dr Haya Hijazi is a gynaecologist and obstetrician from Gaza

Panama City's international airport was temporarily closed, and several flights were diverted. A tsunami warning for the eastern Pacific was later lifted, while the Panama Canal Authority said shipping through the waterway continued normally.
More than 400 aftershocks have been reported since the initial quake. Earthquakes are relatively rare in Panama and more commonly occur in the western province of Chiriqui, which borders Costa Rica.

Manosphere experts warn if we lecture boys 'we lose them'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:54:54 UTC
14:54:54 KST

What is the manosphere? How can you help someone drawn in? Your questions answered
If you're worried about the pull of the manosphere, but don't know how to help someone in your life who has been drawn in, you're not alone.
We asked a panel of experts to answer your common questions about the manosphere, masculinity and how to approach conversations about it.
Read what developmental paediatrician Dr Billy Garvey, psychologist Dr Zac Seidler from Movember and Genevieve Sheppard from Our Watch had to say below.
If you or someone you know needs help, you can click here to find a full list of resources at the end of this article.
What is the manosphere?
There's no single definition of the manosphere, but generally, it's the term used to describe online communities that promote narrow definitions of masculinity that oppose feminism and the gains of the gender-equality movement.
As UN Women describes, "these communities promote the idea that emotional control, material wealth, physical appearance and dominance, especially over women, are markers of male worth".
The ideas in the manosphere are nothing new. Misogyny has been prevalent for a very long time. What’s different today is the reach and business model. Online platforms connect these groups, algorithms amplify their messages, and influencers can profit from attention and outrage.
A recurring tactic of those who promote messages on the manosphere is to take real difficulties — loneliness, financial insecurity or uncertainty about relationships — and blame women and feminism.
That offers a simple, yet inaccurate explanation, which also reinforces male entitlement and resentment. This is a harmful message for all young people to believe and absorb.
To counter this, we need to address the challenges boys and men face while challenging the idea that women owe them sex, attention or obedience. That means well-resourced respectful relationships education in every school across Australia, supportive communities and opportunities to build belonging and connection without dominance.
What are the signs someone is in the manosphere and how can I help?
Watching out for this stuff early and discussing it in an open and curious way is the best solution to staying connected with someone skirting around the edges of this content, as it pulls you in very quickly if you are in a certain headspace.
Some things to look out for:
New language: Terms like "alpha", "high value", "red pill", "simp" or "the matrix", or talking about women in transactional or contemptuous ways.
One-source thinking: Constantly quoting the same few influencers, and treating them as the only people telling "the truth".
Rising grievance: A growing sense that the world is rigged against men, or that women, feminism or "the system" are to blame for how they feel.
Pulling back: Withdrawing from friends or family who disagree, or becoming dismissive and defensive when challenged (this can also be a sign of broader mental health challenges or a change in character).
Rigid self-improvement: Gym, money and discipline aren't bad things. It's a flag when they come with shame, contempt for "weak" men, or the idea that your worth depends on dominance.
Some recommendations for what to do:
Stay close! Your relationship is the best antidote, but it's key to avoid shocking or shaming them.
Get curious, not combative. What does he like about this guy? What does that video tell him about what it means to be successful and what it is giving him? Usually there's a real need underneath: loneliness, rejection, feeling lost or unseen.
Don't try to win in one conversation. You won't argue your way to victory. Be consistent and caring.
Offer an alternative. Take him out, show him the world, and help him interact with other people.
How can we challenge misogynistic views without alienating boys?
This can be tough, and I fail at it too. Start with curiosity because correction often leads to conflict. "What makes you feel like that, mate?" If we lecture them, we lose them.
Separate the belief from who they are. "You've got such a big heart mate, you're better than saying those things about girls and women". We hold the line while also keeping our belief in them as good people.
Look for the underlying need. Many boys are lost and unhealthy messages hook them with the promise of confidence, power and success. Once we understand that, we can offer better pathways for them to meet these needs, and help them see those voices are chasing their own money, status and control.
We can also share our own story, the traps we've fallen into, the hurt we've experienced and caused, and most importantly how we repaired and found a better way ourselves.
How can I approach this with my younger kids?
These conversations can be scary but they are already happening for our kids without us there to guide them. Our best chance is to start with low pressure, when our kids feel safe, like during a walk around the block with just us or while playing together with no-one else around.
We know body language, tone of voice and lack of judgement are just as important as what we actually say, if not more. Getting down to their eye level, sitting side by side facing the same direction, and keeping the conversation slow and casual helps. We also want to explore their experiences. "What do you think boys are like? What about girls?" is a gentle way to understand their beliefs without pressure or shame.
We can also go first as a way for them to be safe too. "When I'm scared, sometimes I get angry. It doesn't help much so I try to work on asking others for help instead." It's also important this never feels like a single conversation we need to deliver perfectly. The most important part is that over time our children feel more safe to come to us for support in understanding their world.
Is the manosphere a 'passing wave' or something bigger?
Honestly, I don't think it's either/or yet. It's going to take time to understand how the moment we are in potentially differs from the gender reckonings that have come before, but it would be remiss of me not to say that this is in no way a 'passing wave', given the volume and ferocity of online misogyny fuelled by tech platforms. The underpinning themes have not changed, their reach has.
What I see clinically is that the content itself is a symptom. Our research at Movember has told us that young men aren't drawn in by misogyny. They're drawn in by someone finally speaking to their loneliness, their sense of purpose and their worries about the future. The misogyny comes bundled with that, and therefore can probably be purposefully decoupled.
What are young men searching for in these spaces?
Many young men are lonely, often more than they'd admit, and these spaces offer an instant sense of brotherhood. You're part of something, you share a language and someone's on your side.
Then there's direction. Plenty of boys feel lost about who they're meant to be and where their life is heading. The manosphere gives them a clear script: Here's what a man is, here are the rules, here's the plan. When everything feels uncertain, that clarity is very attractive.
Respect and status matter too. Young men want to feel they count and that people see them as capable. When that isn't happening at school, at work or in relationships, someone promising to make them "high value" is hard to ignore.
Underneath many of these is a need to make sense of pain. Rejection, failure, anxiety and feeling invisible all hurt, and most boys haven't been given the words or the space to talk about that. These spaces give them an explanation and often someone to blame. That can feel better than sitting with the hurt.
None of these needs are the problem. They're completely normal, healthy human needs. The problem is that the manosphere offers a distorted way of meeting them. If we want boys to walk away, we have to offer them real belonging, purpose and respect in their everyday lives.
Resources
For immediate help:
- Lifeline on 13 11 14

- Respect.gov.au features a collection of resources, including culturally specific and translated articles, posters and guides.
- Body image and eating disorders charity Butterfly has an info page on how to discuss looksmaxxing and appearance pressures with young men and boys.
For boys and men:

- The Man Cave has created videos and podcast episodes on consent, bullying, healthy masculinity and more.
- Anti-racism charity All Together Now has a suite of resources about healthy masculinity in their Unplug Hate campaign, in partnership with Headspace and Multicultural NSW.

For educators:

- Monash University has a guide for educators, including advice for how to handle misogyny in the classroom.
- OurWatch has developed a detailed publication for practitioners working with men in the prevention of men's violence against women.
- VicHealth has a messaging guide with advice about how to frame conversations about men and masculinity.

One of the ships is registered to Guinea-Bissau but the other one, the Chelsea-3, is Ukrainian-owned, registered in Odesa and sails under the flag of Malta, a European Union member.
“There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favours Russia and indeed, the logic points in that direction. The problem is that we cannot prove it,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told Parliament.
On Tuesday, Radev summoned the Russian ambassador to Sofia, who said she does not have any information from the Russian defence ministry but she did not rule out the possibility that “these attacks represent a provocation by a third party.”
The Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo ship Dignity sank on Tuesday after it was hit by a military strike. Four sailors, three Syrian nationals and one Egyptian, were rescued and arrived in the port of Varna, district Gov. Mario Smarkov said.
“All four appeared to be in relatively good condition and had sustained no injuries,” he said. A fifth sailor is expected to arrive later on Wednesday.
Smarkov said the search for the 11 missing crew members continues.
Bulgaria has requested international assistance for the investigation into attacks on commercial vessels, as well as NATO support to strengthen surveillance and control systems and response capabilities against drone attacks.
Black Sea security
The incidents have renewed scrutiny of Europe's ability to protect shipping and critical infrastructure in the Black Sea, more than a year after the EU launched a strategy to strengthen security in the region.
When the Black Sea Security Strategy was unveiled in May 2025, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that the region was bearing the spillover effects of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"The Black Sea region is the prime target for hybrid actions. The European Union aims to boost cooperation to combat cyberattacks, disinformation, and other hostile actions," she said.
“Recurring airspace violations and attacks on ports and shipping lanes highlight this reality."
The policy was aimed at ensuring the security of this maritime corridor, as well as protecting critical infrastructure and assets, such as offshore installations and subsea cables.
It also promised the development of a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub aimed at coordinating support and boosting coast-guard cooperation, among other activities.
The hub would also analyse seabed sensor data and alert allies to potential dangers and incoming threats.

A major Russian business association has proposed sweeping away tax breaks for small businesses. Here’s what would change — and why the Kremlin might agree.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:51:12 UTC
14:51:12 KST

A major Russian business association has proposed sweeping away tax breaks for small businesses. Here’s what would change — and why the Kremlin might agree.
What happened?
Delovaya Rossiya, one of Russia’s largest and most influential business associations, has proposed more than 50 economic reforms to the authorities, RBC reported. Many clearly run counter to small businesses’ interests.
The association wants to scrap tax regimes that benefit small businesses and sole proprietors, bar regional governments from lowering taxes at their discretion, eliminate the patent tax system, and tax gifts and inheritances.
- The organization proposes eliminating the “income” option under the simplified tax system (USN) and the automated simplified tax system (AvtoUSN) as early as 2027. Businesses using these options pay tax on their total revenue at a rate of 6% under USN or 8% under AvtoUSN. Yevgeniya Memruk, head of the Union of Accountants and Tax Consultants, told RBC that these options are used by smaller businesses with high profit margins — meaning their expenses are low relative to their income — and revenues of 10 million to 20 million rubles. Their success depends largely on their owners’ labor and expertise. Switching to other tax regimes would leave them with a tax base at least two and a half times as large, making many businesses unprofitable and forcing them to close, she warned.
- Another proposal would set a uniform revenue threshold for value-added tax (VAT) across all special tax regimes, including AvtoUSN, starting that same year. Businesses would have to pay VAT if their revenue exceeded 20 million rubles in the previous calendar year. Under AvtoUSN, businesses can still avoid paying VAT up to a threshold of 60 million rubles. This has already prompted a mass shift to that system: Sberbank said early this year, for example, that the number of its individual entrepreneur and corporate clients using AvtoUSN had jumped sixfold in a single month — just as the threshold for businesses using “regular” USN was lowered to 20 million rubles. The proposal would effectively defeat the purpose of AvtoUSN. Nearly 3.5 million entrepreneurs in Russia still use the simplified tax system.
- Also starting in 2027, Delovaya Rossiya proposes stripping regional governments of the right to lower USN tax rates at their discretion. Regional authorities can currently cut the rate from 6% to as little as 1% under the “income” option discussed above, and from 15% to as little as 5% under the “income minus expenses” option. Removing that power could make regions that attract businesses through favorable tax terms less attractive to investors.
- The association also advocates abolishing the patent tax system (PSN). Under this system, sole proprietors pay a fixed amount of tax, calculated by the state based on assumed income, to operate their businesses. The benefit of paying a fixed amount is that higher actual earnings do not increase a business’s tax burden. In 2026, the annual revenue threshold for eligibility was also cut to 20 million rubles. By 2028, it will fall to 10 million. This has already made the system less popular, but eliminating it altogether would affect a substantial number of entrepreneurs in trucking, independent retail, and personal and household services, Memruk told RBC. Nearly 1.5 million entrepreneurs across the country still use PSN. Abolishing it would also reduce regional budget revenues.
- Other major proposals include requiring social insurance contributions from people who earn most of their income from interest and dividends, as well as taxing inheritances and gifts. Shares in publicly traded companies would be exempt from both inheritance and gift taxes.
Those are some strange proposals… But why is Delovaya Rossiya working against the interests of Russia’s businesses?
The association offers a simple rationale for these unpopular proposals, one also advanced by officials responsible for tax policy: Unscrupulous entrepreneurs exploit special tax regimes by, for example, artificially splitting up their businesses or posing as self-employed workers to reduce their tax burden. “Companies posing as small businesses” distort market competition, the organization’s chairman, Alexey Repik, said.
Repik’s own background also helps explain the association’s lobbying. The founder of pharmaceutical corporation R-Pharm, he is known as a businessman loyal to the state and close to Vladimir Putin’s family. As The Bell reported, Putin received Repik at the Kremlin just a day before Delovaya Rossiya presented its proposals, and the businessman made clear his desire to be useful to the authorities. He said that “higher taxes today are better than sky-high rates forever” and that “a Russian entrepreneur isn’t someone out to make a quick profit, but a patriot.”
Experts acknowledge that abuse of special tax regimes is a real problem. But rather than targeting individual offenders, Delovaya Rossiya’s proposals target “the regimes themselves, which most small businesses use in good faith” across Russia, Memruk told RBC.
Still, these are only proposals for now, right? Maybe they won’t be adopted at all…
That’s true. So far, all we know is that the reform program will be presented at Delovaya Rossiya’s forum on October 15, which Vladimir Putin is also expected to attend, and that the proposals have been sent to the relevant government agencies for review. Russia’s Finance Ministry, for one, has already considered them. A ministry representative told RBC that they still “require further comprehensive study.”
We don’t know whether the proposals will be adopted. Delovaya Rossiya’s proposals have become law on several previous occasions. The authorities have an incentive to agree to the plan this time, too: The government needs additional revenue to keep the war going while preventing the federal budget deficit from growing. The government plans to limit the deficit to 2.2% of GDP in 2027 (5.5 trillion rubles) and an average of 2% in 2028–2029. In 2026, however, it has already reached 3.2% of GDP (7.3 trillion rubles).
“Adjustments” that would force businesses to pay more tax could help meet those targets. Exactly how much Delovaya Rossiya’s proposals would bring in is unknown. But the amount would be at least tens of billions of rubles: United Russia lawmakers estimated that abandoning further cuts to the revenue threshold above which businesses must pay VAT — a decision made at Putin’s insistence — would cost 51 billion rubles in 2027 and 100 billion rubles a year in 2028–2029.
For the changes to take effect at the start of 2027, as Delovaya Rossiya proposes, the law would have to be published by the end of November 2026. That would leave entrepreneurs only about a month to switch tax regimes.
After RBC’s report was published, Delovaya Rossiya issued a press release in which Repik said the tax proposals had “only a very tenuous connection to the agenda” and that the organization was not proposing to end experimental tax regimes ahead of schedule. In response to this denial, Pyotr Kanayev, head of RBC’s integrated newsroom, published the text of the proposals, which RBC had obtained, on his Telegram channel.

Türkiye, Italy seek to expand archaeological cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:49:23 UTC
14:49:23 KST

The Göbeklitepe show at Rome’s Colosseum draws 6 million visitors.
Türkiye and Italy are seeking to expand archaeological cooperation through joint excavations, conservation projects and exhibitions, Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy said on Oct. 14 at the opening of the 17th Symposium of Italian Archaeological Missions in the ancient city of Hierapolis in Denizli.
Noting that Italian excavations at Hierapolis began 70 years ago, Ersoy said scientists from Pamukkale University were also contributing to the work under the Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Legacy to the Future Project.
Archaeology today extends beyond uncovering ancient structures to include conservation, restoration, visitor management, museum work and scientific research, Ersoy said, stressing the importance of preserving archaeological sites for future generations.
Türkiye has expanded archaeological research in recent years while strengthening cooperation between Turkish and foreign research teams, he said. Italian scientists are working at sites including Aslantepe, Hierapolis, Uşaklı Höyük, Karkamış Höyük and Yumuktepe, with Turkish academics participating in the excavations.
Denizli is also home to ongoing research at ancient sites including Laodicea, Hierapolis, Tripolis, Kolossai and Attouda. Conservation and visitor-management projects are being carried out alongside excavations, Ersoy said.
Ersoy highlighted cultural initiatives between the two countries, including the exhibition “Göbeklitepe: The Mystery of a Sacred Place” at Rome’s Colosseum, which attracted approximately six million visitors.
A subsequent exhibition, “Troy and Rome: Myths, Legends and Stories of the Ancient Mediterranean,” features 221 artifacts from Turkish museums and explores the historical and mythological connections between the two civilizations.
Plans are also underway to develop scientific and cultural cooperation between the ancient city of Ephesus and the Pompeii Archaeological Park. A joint project at the ancient city of Elaiussa Sebaste in Mersin, in cooperation with Italy’s Central Institute for Archaeology, is targeted for launch in 2027.
Turkish and Italian specialists are also collaborating on cultural heritage conservation in Cappadocia, particularly the preservation of wall paintings.
Ersoy said the return of cultural artifacts seized in Italy demonstrated the countries’ cooperation in combating illicit trafficking.
A concert featuring Italian violinist Riccardo Zamuner and the İzmir State Symphony Orchestra, scheduled to take place at Hierapolis’ ancient theater following the ceremony, was canceled due to rain.

US weighs using 'Mother of All Bombs' in potential strikes on Iran: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:45 UTC
14:48:45 KST

The US military has developed new strike plans that include the potential use of the “Mother of All Bombs” against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders a resumption of combat operations, CNN reported on Wednesday, citing multiple US officials familiar with the plans.
The proposed use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast (MOAB) bomb, the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal, would mark a significant escalation in the conflict with Iran.
However, officials have questioned whether the weapon could achieve Washington’s military objectives.
According to CNN, Trump has directed the military to prepare additional strike options against Iranian targets, including energy infrastructure and facilities linked to the country’s nuclear programme.
The plans could be activated before or after the upcoming US midterm elections if the president decides to resume major combat operations.
One source familiar with the planning told CNN that strikes could take place before US forces withdraw from the US Central Command area of responsibility, potentially allowing the administration to launch further attacks before declaring victory and pulling out its forces.
A second source said plans targeting Iranian nuclear sites explicitly included the possible deployment of the MOAB, including against a suspected underground facility at Pickaxe Mountain.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to target Pickaxe Mountain in the Isfahan province, where Washington and Israel believe Iran has stored components of its nuclear programme.
The president has maintained that preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon remains a central objective of the US campaign.
Doubts over effectiveness
A US official told CNN that military planners routinely prepare a range of options for policymakers, from lower-intensity operations to more powerful strikes against heavily fortified targets.
However, the MOAB's effectiveness against deeply buried nuclear facilities remains uncertain.
The GPS-guided bomb can devastate a surface area equivalent to about nine city blocks, but it is not designed to penetrate deep underground.
Sources cited by CNN said it would likely struggle to destroy facilities protected by thick layers of granite and other fortifications.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” a source familiar with the planning discussions told CNN, describing it as unsuitable for deep penetration.
If deployed, the bomb could cause extensive destruction at the point of impact. Its large blast radius could also raise serious concerns about civilian casualties, particularly if energy infrastructure near populated areas or other civilian facilities were targeted.
The MOAB was previously used only once in combat, in 2017, against a Daesh terror group hideout in a cave complex in Afghanistan’s Nangarhar province.
Psychological pressure
Despite its limitations, US officials have reportedly considered the weapon’s potential psychological impact as part of the administration’s broader military options.
One source told CNN that Trump could face pressure to take further action against Iran despite uncertainty over whether additional strikes would force Tehran to accept Washington’s demands.
The source suggested the MOAB could be used to exert psychological pressure, particularly given the limitations of available munitions against deeply buried targets.

New artifacts unearthed at Ordu’s ancient Kurul Castle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:44 UTC
14:48:44 KST

Finds include a statue of Cybele, a figure of the child Dionysus and a representation of Pan, along with animal-shaped composite vessels. (AA Photo)
Archaeological excavations at Ordu’s Kurul Castle, which began in 2010, are continuing to uncover new artifacts at the ancient site.
According to a statement from Ordu Municipality, the 2,300-year-old Kurul Castle, located in the Bayadı neighborhood of the Altınordu district, stands out as the first scientific archaeological excavation site in the Eastern Black Sea region.
The excavations are being conducted under the leadership of Professor Süleyman Yücel Şenyurt, a faculty member in the Department of Archaeology at Ankara Hacı Bayram Veli University, with support from Ordu Metropolitan Municipality.
Finds unearthed at the site to date include a statue of Cybele estimated to be 2,150 years old, a figure of the child Dionysus, a representation of Pan, who raised him, and animal-shaped composite vessels associated with the cult of Dionysus and Pan.
Ordu Metropolitan Municipality Mayor Mehmet Hilmi Güler visited the ongoing excavation site and received information about the work from Şenyurt.
Güler said the site was an archaeological and historical treasure where discoveries were shedding light on the past.
Describing Kurul Castle as a source of cultural and historical wealth, Güler said approximately 40 percent of the excavation work had been completed and that academics were working intensively at the site.
“We have made important discoveries here dating to the period associated with Dionysus. These artifacts will both shed light on the past and add significant value to this region,” Güler said.
He added that the finds indicated that Kurul Castle was not merely a fortress but also a settlement.
Important discoveries
Şenyurt said the team had uncovered significant finds in the region, particularly the statue of Cybele.
Noting that Kurul Castle had attracted attention with discoveries that surprised the scientific community, he said the latest finds would introduce two divine figures from Anatolia to the scientific and cultural worlds in connection with the cult of Dionysus.
“With this year’s finds, we will introduce two god and goddess figures from Anatolia to the scientific community and the cultural world, alongside the cult of Dionysus,” Şenyurt said.
He thanked the relevant ministry and Ordu Metropolitan Municipality for their support, adding that the discoveries at Kurul Castle could serve as a model for future archaeological research.
Şenyurt noted that the Eastern Black Sea region contained cultural heritage sites hidden beneath dense vegetation.
“Kurul Castle has had the opportunity to make these discoveries, but it has also set an example for us. There is cultural heritage hidden beneath the vegetation in the Eastern Black Sea region. Kurul Castle has ignited the spark for future work,” he said.

Istanbul union’s call to pause bonito fishing sparks public backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:33 UTC
14:48:33 KST

AA Photo
An Istanbul fisheries union has sparked consumer outrage after calling for a fishing pause when a surge in bonito catches drove prices down, leading to accusations of price gouging.
The Istanbul Provincial Union of Seafood Fishers and Producers (Istanbul DEMBİR) set the requested pause from midnight until 8 a.m. on Oct. 12, saying a short break would help fishers earn a fair return without amounting to a ban.
Some social media users called the appeal opportunistic and urged authorities to investigate. One wrote fishers resented earning from one bonito what they had previously made from two.
Central Union of Seafood Fishers and Producers (DEM-BİR) Deputy Board Chairman Mehmet Aksoy opposed a ban, citing rising personnel wages and fuel costs. “Conditions have become harder. When we catch too much, fish sells cheaply. We do everything we can to provide people with affordable fish. No boat should catch 3,000 to 5,000 crates a day,” he said.
Aksoy said bonito is a migratory fish and could move to Georgia and return, making it harder to catch in November. He urged fishers to limit catches, saying excess fish loses value and can be crushed and spoil aboard boats. He said the goal was to balance supply with demand, not make consumers pay more.
The Istanbul DEMBİR notice said lower prices led fishers to catch more to offset losses, adding to supply and driving prices down further. It called the cycle economically unsustainable.
Türkiye’s commercial fishing season reopened on Sept. 1 after an annual ban from April 15 to Sept. 1 to protect fish stocks during spawning. Fishermen along Türkiye’s Black Sea coast had forecast an abundant bonito harvest, expecting larger catches to lower prices for consumers.

3D models recreate 7.7-million-year-old fauna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:23 UTC
14:48:23 KST

DHA Photo
Anthropologists in Türkiye’s central province of Kayseri are creating 3D miniatures of 10 animals whose fossils date back 7.5 to 7.7 million years, giving visitors a glimpse of the region’s prehistoric fauna.
The figures, made from polymer clay and based on fossils found near Yamula Dam, include four elephant models, two rhinoceroses, a giraffe, a three-toed horse, a bovid similar to a modern antelope and a saber-toothed tiger. The miniatures will be displayed at Kayseri Science Center.
“We created this display to satisfy visitors’ curiosity and show what 10 different creatures from that period looked like, both morphologically and physically,” Expert Anthropologist Ömer Dağ said.
The team sculpted the figures in clay, scanned them in 3D and reproduced them with resin printers.
Kayseri Metropolitan Municipality supplied a resin printer and the models will be painted before being placed in a miniature habitat exhibit.
Rising water levels at the dam delayed fieldwork in 2026, so the team split in two, with one group continuing excavations and the other working in the laboratory. The display will show two of the elephant models in a forest setting and two in open terrain, allowing visitors to compare their physical differences.
Shepherd Murat Adıyaman found a bone fragment near the dam in the Taşhan area of Kocasinan district in 2017. Initial tests dated the fragments to between 6 million and 7.5 million years ago. The Culture and Tourism Ministry’s General Directorate of Cultural Heritage and Museums authorized excavations in 2018.

Divers have begun exploring shipwrecks off the coast of the western province of Muğla’s Bodrum district following a campaign opening the protected underwater site.
The Culture and Tourism Ministry granted special permission for the dives in coordination with the Bodrum Chamber of Shipping and local centers. The treacherous shallows around Yassıada hold 11 sunken ships on ancient routes, including five overlapping Roman and Byzantine vessels. Divers reported seeing ancient amphoras preserving their original glory on the seabed.
Documentary producer Tahsin Ceylan filmed the artifacts alongside Bodrum Coast Guard dive teams, specialist instructor Ahmet Yaşar and underwater photographer Mehtap Akbaş Çiftci. Underwater Archaeologist Aşkın Canbazoğlu said he worked at the site between 1981 and 1983 for the Culture Ministry.
“We have always tried to open the area to tourism because it is one of the most important places in the archaeology world,” he said.
Crews excavated a Roman wreck from 1961 to 1964, while operations resumed in 1974, leading to the recovery of an Ottoman vessel in the 1980s. Experts completed excavations on three ships in total, with the site now needing international promotion. The Yassıada shallows gained international fame in the 1960s when scientists pioneered modern underwater excavation techniques on its ancient shipwrecks.

Tallinn food bank takes on 43,000 canned wild boar from state after ASF cull
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:48:00 UTC
14:48:00 KST

Tallinn food bank takes on 43,000 canned wild boar from state after ASF cull
The state handed over more than 43,776 canned wild boar to a food bank this week, to be distributed to those in need, Maaleht reported.
The project uses meat from wild boar culled to halt the spread of African swine fever (ASF).
Over 625,000 cans were produced in total, of which the 43,776 delivered to the Tallinn Food Bank (Toidupank) — 19 pallets' worth — form part of a wider distribution and delivered by Regional and Agricultural Minister Hendrik Johannes Terras (Eesti 200).
The rest has been allocated or is being allocated to the State Defense Investment Center, the Estonian Large Families Association and local government welfare institutions across the country.
The Ministry of Regional Affairs and Agriculture organised two procurements to produce the canned meat — €1.7 million in 2025 and €959,000 for the second
The cans contain 80 percent meat, and will be distributed by social workers, and Toidupank CEO Piet Boerefijn and project manager Kerttu Olõkainen noted they give "much greater flexibility in planning food parcels, as they don't have to be packed as quickly" – the cans can keep for up to a couple of years.
To keep aid consistent, the Food Bank must hold reserves and, where needed, buy basic foodstuffs, as around 4,000 food parcels of 7-12 kilograms are needed each week; contents depend on donations and food rescued from going to waste.
"The aim of a food parcel is not to provide a four-person family with a week's food, but to help them save on food costs and use the money saved for other necessities, such as winter clothes or school supplies," Boerefijn explained.
In addition to aid to those in need in normal times, Toidupank has set up a nationwide network which could provide up to 10,000 crisis aid parcels, pending agreements with the state and local governments.
The original Maaleht piece is here.
ASF reached epidemic proportions in Estonia last year with 11 outbreaks on pig farms, which to the culling of around 60,000 domestic pigs as well as close to 17,000 wild boar. The outbreak led to the closure of several meat businesses and an estimated €22 million in economic damage .

DHA Photo
Turkish television dramas, which reach an estimated 1 billion people worldwide, are helping popularize the Turkish language and promote the country’s culture abroad, according to Murat Yancı, head of the television group at Demirören Media, who spoke at MIPCOM 2026, a major international television content market in Cannes, France.
“Turkish series reach 1 billion people worldwide,” Yancı said, noting that viewers in different countries increasingly report learning Turkish by watching the programs.
“When we ask them, ‘Where did you learn Turkish?’ they say, ‘From Turkish series,’” he said, describing the productions as a form of cultural influence that extends beyond entertainment.
Yancı said Turkish-language television dramas ranked second globally in terms of international reach, behind English-language productions. He added that international sales of Turkish series amounted to approximately $1 billion last year.
“On the one hand, we export Turkish culture and the Turkish language. Turkish series are, in a sense, a power that conducts diplomacy on our behalf,” he said, describing the productions as an important instrument of Türkiye’s soft power.
Running through Oct. 15 at the Palais des Festivals et des Congrès in Cannes, MIPCOM 2026 brings together more than 10,000 industry professionals from over 100 countries to showcase television content, negotiate distribution agreements and explore international partnerships.
Kanal D, owned by Demirören Media, is attending through its international distribution arm, Kanal D International, presenting its latest dramas to prospective buyers. The broadcaster is promoting titles including “Daha 17,” “Haysiyet” and “Güller ve Günahlar,” alongside established productions such as “İnci Taneleri” (Secret of Pearls), “Veda Mektubu” (Farewell Letter), “Üç Kız Kardeş” (Three Sisters), “Yalan” (The Family Burden), “Zalim İstanbul” (Ruthless City) and “Siyah Beyaz Aşk” (Price of Passion).
Its catalog also features internationally recognized series such as “Aşk-ı Memnu” (Forbidden Love) and “Fatmagül’ün Suçu Ne?” (What is Fatmagül’s Fault?)
Promotional posters and digital advertisements for the broadcaster’s productions have appeared across Cannes as it seeks to expand its international distribution network.
Turkish dramas have developed audiences across the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, the Balkans and Latin America, giving distributors opportunities to reach new markets and negotiate additional licensing agreements at the event.

Fund repayment bill clears parliamentary committee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:42:01 UTC
14:42:01 KST

Parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee approved a bill on Oct. 14 that would allow interim payments of up to 1 million Turkish Liras to eligible investors in funds under liquidation.
The nine-article proposal concerns unfinished liquidations among 131 funds ordered wound up by the Capital Markets Board (SPK). It still requires approval by parliament’s general assembly.
AK Party lawmaker Ersan Aksu, one of the bill’s sponsors, said around 350,000 investors were expected to recover their net investment through interim payments while retaining their rights to a final settlement.
Interim payments would be calculated from investors’ actual cash deposits and withdrawals, without inflation adjustment, and deducted from the final amount payable.
If available cash is insufficient, the SPK could prioritize investors with the smallest net investments or set a minimum interim payment for all eligible investors.
Where fund assets fall short, final entitlement calculations would include inflation adjustments through the liquidation date, based on the average change in consumer and domestic producer price indices.
Aksu said payments would come from fund assets and money recovered from those responsible for losses, with no public funds used.
Committee amendments clarified how eligible investors would be identified and revised calculations for the voluntary return of gains above an inflation-adjusted benchmark.
Some repayments have already been made. The Communications Directorate said on Oct. 13 that 43,643 investors in funds managed by A1, Bulls and Pardus received 6.4 billion liras the previous week.
Separately, Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Şimşek authorized an investigation into former SPK chairman İbrahim Ömer Gönül following a preliminary ministry review.
Istanbul prosecutors had sought permission on Sept. 30 to investigate alleged abuse of office in connection with the fund inquiry. Gönül gave a statement as a suspect that day.
