New Zealand regulators unveil supervisory expectations on AI-related cyber risks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:19 CST
14:37:19 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's central bank and financial markets regulator on Thursday outlined supervisory expectations for financial institutions to manage cyber risks associated with frontier artificial intelligence (AI).
The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) and the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) said their expectations focus on three key risks, namely increased cyber threats, evolving governance and oversight challenges, and growing third-party and concentration risks, according to an RBNZ statement.
The expectations build on existing prudential, conduct, cyber and operational resilience obligations, aiming to support resilience of regulated entities and the broader financial system, RBNZ Assistant Governor for Financial Stability Angus McGregor said at an industry roundtable.
Regulators expect financial institutions to maintain cybersecurity strategies and frameworks that adequately address the threats they face, as well as strong foundational cyber controls and security measures, McGregor said.
FMA Executive Director of Response and Enforcement Louise Unger said advances in AI are changing the cyber threat environment, highlighting the importance of strong governance, effective oversight, operational resilience and the management of third-party dependencies as entities adapt to emerging risks.
While AI can bring benefits to financial institutions and their customers, it also changes the risks they face, Unger said, adding that boards and senior management need to understand where AI is being used, the risks involved and who is accountable for managing them.
The regulators will continue engaging with regulated entities to ensure AI-related risks are managed appropriately, McGregor said. ■

S. Korea's money supply rises for 10th month in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
13:37:04 CST
14:37:04 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's money supply rose for the 10th straight month, driven by the fund influx into short-term fixed-income products, especially from semiconductor companies and households, central bank data showed Thursday.
The seasonally adjusted M2, called broad money, grew 0.9 percent from a month earlier to 4,266.8 trillion won (about 3.16 trillion U.S. dollars) in August, keeping an upward trajectory since November 2025, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The BOK delivered its back-to-back rate hikes in July and August to 3 percent, prompting an inflow of funds into short-term fixed-income products such as time deposits, money trusts, and money market funds.
Affected by the monetary tightening, the M1, called narrow money, fell 1.1 percent in August on a monthly basis.
The M1 refers to currency in circulation, demand deposits and transferable savings deposits equivalent to cash. The M2 adds money market funds, time deposits and financial products that mature in less than two years.
The liquidity of financial institutions, called Lf, increased 0.6 percent in the cited month, while the liquidity aggregate, the broadest measure of money supply, gained 0.2 percent.
The Lf includes financial products with a maturity of over two years and liquidity at insurers and brokerages along with M2. The liquidity aggregate adds state and corporate bonds to the Lf. ■

Egyptian villager helps unearth colossal Ramses II statue head

Egyptian villager helps unearth colossal Ramses II statue head
An Egyptian villager’s chance discovery of an inscribed stone near his home has led archaeologists to uncover a colossal statue head of Pharaoh Ramses II and several other ancient artifacts in the Nile Delta, Qazinform News Agency cites Anadolu Agency.
According to Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities, Khaled El-Shahat Khalil found the stone while working on his land in Behbeit el-Hagar village in Gharbia Province. Recognizing its potential significance, he notified local antiquities authorities.
Subsequent excavations revealed a massive 1.6-meter-tall stone head depicting Ramses II wearing the double crown that symbolized the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt.
Archaeologists also uncovered much of a second royal statue, measuring 2.4 meters in height and believed to represent Ramses II. The statue’s head retains well-preserved facial features beneath a traditional royal headdress.
In addition, researchers discovered a 1.3-meter block of pink granite bearing hieroglyphic inscriptions, including two royal titles associated with the ancient pharaoh.
Tourism and Antiquities Minister Sherif Fathy and Gharbia Governor Alaa Abdel Moaty visited Khalil on Wednesday to recognize his role in the discovery. Khalil and his wife received a certificate of appreciation and were awarded an Umrah pilgrimage to Mecca in recognition of his honesty and civic responsibility.
Officials said Khalil’s decision to report the find enabled archaeologists to properly investigate the site and preserve its historical treasures.
Behbeit el-Hagar, located in Egypt’s Nile Delta, is known for the remains of an ancient temple dedicated to the goddess Isis.
Earlier reports highlighted, archaeologists from the Al-Farabi Kazakh National University unearthed a settlement dating back to the first Turkic Khaganate during extensive fieldwork in the Zaisan basin of East Kazakhstan.

S. Arabia advances neurodegenerative disease research through space mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:34:56 UTC
14:34:56 KST

S. Arabia advances neurodegenerative disease research through space mission
Saudi Arabia has launched the first biological samples from the Middle East into space, marking a major milestone in the Kingdom’s growing space and life sciences programs, Qazinform News Agency cites SPA.
The mission, known as BioGravity-1, was launched aboard the SpaceX CRS-35 resupply flight to the International Space Station in cooperation with NASA. The initiative is being led by the Saudi Space Agency (SSA) and King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) as part of a long-term research effort focused on Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis.
During the mission’s first phase, researchers sent biological samples from healthy human donors into space to establish a scientific baseline for future studies. Scientists will use the microgravity environment aboard the ISS to examine cellular changes linked to aging and neurodegenerative disorders.
The research program includes two experiments, SSA-1 and SSA-2, developed by KAUST. It is being conducted in partnership with the U.S.-based National Stem Cell Foundation (NSCF) and Axiom Space, with NASA support.
Saudi astronaut and SSA microgravity research supervisor Rayyanah Barnawi described the mission as an important step toward leveraging the space environment to advance human health research and strengthen national scientific capabilities.
KAUST bioscience professor and project lead Imed Gallouzi said the mission allows researchers to investigate disease models under conditions that cannot be replicated on Earth, potentially contributing to future medical discoveries.
According to Pinar Mesci, scientific adviser to the NSCF and global head of biomanufacturing and biotechnology at Axiom Space, the mission will also test the “Brain Organoid Village” concept in microgravity for the first time, enabling population-scale studies using multiple cell lines within a single organoid.
The BioGravity program consists of three phases. The first focuses on healthy reference samples, the second will examine models derived from patients with Alzheimer’s disease and multiple sclerosis, and the third will explore therapeutic responses and potential drug targets in microgravity.
Saudi officials say the initiative supports efforts to expand scientific research, strengthen international partnerships, and harness space technologies to improve healthcare outcomes in line with Vision 2030.

Who controls Latvia’s critical data? Next week, Techritory 2026 will focus on digital sovereignty and communications security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:33:50 UTC
14:33:50 KST

How can Latvia keep its critical services running if foreign technologies or infrastructure suddenly become unavailable? How can satellite communications strengthen communications security, and how can Latvian companies contribute to the development of Europe’s digital infrastructure? These questions will take centre stage next week, on 21–22 October, when the ninth Techritory digitalisation and connectivity forum takes place at the ATTA Centre in Riga.
Digital sovereignty is becoming a practical issue of national security and business competitiveness. Latvia needs to know where its critical data is stored, who controls access to it and how essential services will continue operating if a technology provider or communications link becomes unavailable. This requires both transparent data governance and arrangements prepared in advance to restore services and switch to alternative solutions.
“Digital sovereignty begins with the ability to keep critical services running even when familiar technologies or communications routes become unavailable. At Techritory, we will discuss how to combine global technologies with local and regional infrastructure, and how Latvia can become a provider of digital infrastructure and security solutions for Europe,” says Neils Kalniņš, Director of the Techritory Ecosystem.
The forum’s discussions will also focus on the development of European data centres, the adoption of artificial intelligence and the resilience of digital infrastructure. These areas offer Latvian companies opportunities to develop secure cloud services, computing capacity and other solutions for European customers.
“Businesses and public institutions must first identify which data and systems are critical, where they are located and how quickly they can be restored or migrated. Alongside global services, we need primary and backup infrastructure managed in Europe. For Latvian data centre companies, this is an opportunity to offer customers both greater control over their data and continuity of service,” says Andris Gailītis, CEO of DELSKA.
Satellite Communications: An Additional Communications Route and Economic Opportunities
Satellite connectivity is becoming an important part of Europe’s infrastructure for everyday communications, crisis management and defence. It can complement terrestrial networks in areas where connections are limited or damaged. Latvia’s security depends on having multiple communications routes available and being able to switch between them. Using satellite communications as a backup connection requires equipment, power supplies and service access to be arranged in advance.
The core constellation of Europe’s secure satellite connectivity system, IRIS², is planned to comprise 348 satellites, with the first launches scheduled for 2029. The system is also intended to serve public administration, defence and emergency services, with deployment and service availability developing in stages.
Space technologies also create opportunities for Latvian companies and researchers to develop new services and secure international contracts. One practical example is a satellite data solution developed jointly by Sadales tīkls and Baltic Satellite Service to identify trees and shrubs within power line protection zones. It demonstrates how satellite data can help monitor infrastructure and detect potential threats at an early stage.
LIAA Panel Discussion: From Pilot Projects to Measurable Business Results
On 22 October, from 14:30 to 15:20, the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) will host a panel discussion entitled “Scaling Business Digitalisation: Investment and European Partnerships”.
The discussion will explore what distinguishes digitalisation projects that deliver measurable results from isolated pilot projects, and which business processes benefit most quickly from digitalisation and artificial intelligence. Participants will also examine the availability of EU and national funding, the role of public policy, and opportunities to use European Digital Innovation Hubs and the Horizon Europe programme to help Latvian companies deploy solutions at scale and compete internationally.
“The value of digitalisation in a business is determined by measurable results: more efficient processes, higher productivity and new market opportunities. European funding and partnerships can help turn a successful pilot project into a widely adopted solution, provided that support is clear, accessible and aligned with the company’s development needs,” says panel moderator Egita Aizsilniece-Ibema, Head of LIAA’s Representative Office in Brussels.
The discussion will feature Aiga Irmeja from the Latvian IT Cluster, Ģirts Slaviņš, CEO of Mobilly, Artūrs Vasiļevskis, CEO of Tilde, and Andris Kuznieks from the European Commission Representation in Latvia.
The main theme of Techritory 2026 is “Security and Prosperity Through Digitalization and Connectivity”. The forum is organised by Elektroniskie sakari, with LMT Group, the Nordic Council of Ministers, DELSKA and the Ministry of Smart Administration and Regional Development as strategic partners. Participation is free of charge, and the working language is English. The programme and registration are available at techritory.com.

Estonia's EE-ALARM test sets SMS record but sheltering gaps remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:33:00 UTC
14:33:00 KST

Estonia's EE-ALARM test sets SMS record but sheltering gaps remain
The Rescue Board tested the nationwide EE-ALARM warning system again on Wednesday, setting a delivery record but finding many residents still don't know what the sirens mean.
SMS messages reached one million phone users in 17 minutes, down from 27 minutes in the previous test. Shelter drills ran in Tallinn, Tartu and Haapsalu, but home sheltering options are found to still be inadequate.
Between 3 p.m. and 3.10 p.m., EE-ALARM warning sirens sounded across the country and alert messages were sent to people's phones. A ticker in English ran along ERR News' front page at the same time.
"We also set a speed record for SMS delivery, with messages reaching one million phone users in 17 minutes. During the previous test, it took 27 minutes," said Viktor Saaremets, deputy director general of the Rescue Board (Päästeamet).
The Rescue Board says it plans to introduce an even faster emergency notification system in the future, allowing messages to reach all phones within seconds.
Shelter drills were also held in Tallinn, Tartu and Haapsalu. Most participants in the 15-minute drill in Tallinn, where the exercise was held in the Rotermanni Quarter, reached the designated shelter, in an underground parking garage, within five minutes.
"Since everyone responded to the warning siren by heading underground and, as far as I know, there were no bottlenecks or other problems arising from a lack of awareness, we can say the result was good," Sergo Kohal, a crisis preparedness specialist with Tallinn Municipal Police (Mupo), told "Aktuaalne kaamera".
However, Anu Vaikjärv, a shelter adviser at the Rescue Board's Northern Rescue Center, said more public awareness campaigns are needed.
"The response could have been better in the sense that the sirens were sounding, but many people didn't know what they meant. We still have a lot of work ahead of us to raise awareness," Vaikjärv said.
Participants who reached the shelter said they considered the drill a success, though many lack suitable conditions for sheltering at home.
"I think there have been drills here before, and everyone seems to know pretty well what to do — drop everything and head downstairs," said Henri, who took part.
"Last time, I was walking around town and didn't know where to go, but now I know where to go here. Unfortunately, I haven't made any preparations at home. I have nowhere to shelter there because I don't have a basement," said another participant, Andres.
"We've discussed where we could shelter. Our apartment building doesn't have a basement, but there are rooms without windows," added Piret, who also took part.
According to Kohal, Estonia has fallen behind in its sheltering capacity.
"One option is to create sheltering capacity in existing buildings and basements, but another possibility is to install modular shelters in urban areas, which would provide additional safety for city residents. We've discussed approximately 50 modules," Kohal said of possible solutions.
"A great many apartment associations are contacting us. We visit them to provide guidance and advice, and various grants will also become available to help them. Interest is continuing to grow," Vaikjärv went on.
Starting in July 2027, the law will require apartment associations managing buildings larger than 1,200 square meters to have a sheltering plan and to adapt a suitable space for sheltering by 2028.
More information on crisis preparedness in Estonia is here.

A little bipartisan bromance as Schwarzenegger, Newsom laud California’s climate-change wins
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and Gov. Gavin Newsom marked 20 years of California’s landmark climate law, celebrating a rare show of bipartisan unity amid deepening political polarization.
- The 2006 law helped cut greenhouse gas emissions to 1990 levels and fueled clean-energy growth, but California is falling behind its next targets.
- Schwarzenegger said the state’s climate policies show what cooperation can accomplish; California’s cap-and-invest program, extended through 2045, is now moving toward a link with Washington state’s market.
Former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, celebrated the 20-year anniversary of landmark climate legislation he signed while in office alongside Democrats including Gov. Gavin Newsom on Wednesday.
“California is the perfect example of what can be done when people work together and when we don’t look at this as a Republican or as a Democratic issue,” Schwarzenegger said at an economic conference in Long Beach, noting that Assembly Bill 32, the Global Warming Solutions Act had significantly reduced greenhouse gas emissions while creating more than a half a million clean-energy jobs.
“This is the message that is so important for the world,” he said, because the state’s policies have become a model for other states and nations.
Newsom noted that the state had met “audacious” goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions, touting 39,000 megawatts of clean energy that have been installed in the last seven years, 23,000 megawatts of battery storage created, and that no flex alert has been issued in the state in four years.
“So we’re not in the goal-setting business; we’re in the how business,” he said.
He added that the clean energy transition is “the most critical national security issue in the United States of America,” with economic and supply chain leadership at stake as China surpasses the U.S. in electric vehicles, clean-energy manufacturing and the deployment of renewables.
The state already met the climate change legislation’s ambitious target — returning emissions to 1990 levels by 2020 — four years ahead of schedule. However, recent analyses indicate California is not on track to meet its future targets of cutting emissions 40% by 2030 and 85% by 2045.
The legislation paved the way for the creation of California’s nation-leading carbon market, cap-and-invest, which launched in 2013. The Legislature extended cap-and-invest’s life to 2045 last year, and the state is now initiating the process of linking its market with Washington state.
The event as well as a luncheon the prior day in Santa Monica were rare displays of bipartisan unity at a time of heightened political polarization in the United States. Schwarzenegger and Newsom piled praise upon each other during the Wednesday afternoon discussion, hugging at the end.
At the luncheon, former Gov. Gray Davis, whom Schwarzenegger ousted from office in the 2003 recall election, as well as billionaire hedge-fund founder turned environmental warrior Tom Steyer, who unsuccessfully ran for governor this year, were among the Democrats in attendance, as well as former state Assembly Speaker Fabien Nunez and former state Sen. Fran Pavley, who were both pivotal in the passage of the climate-change legislation.
In addition to remarks highlighting the foundation of some of the nation’s bedrock environmental policies, such as former GOP President Richard Nixon creating the Environmental Protection Agency and signing the Endangered Species Act, there were moments of levity.
Schwarzenegger said he told fellow Republicans “f— you” when they balked at him naming Susan Kennedy, a Democrat, as his chief of staff, he said Tuesday.
During a breakout session at the Wednesday conference, he referenced his former wife, Maria Shriver, a scion of the Kennedy family, as he described his desire to hear from people on both sides of the aisle.
“So I had Democrats in my administration, and of course the Republican Party went nuts,” he said. “I didn’t care because, to me, I thought I wanted to hear what the Democrats were thinking. Plus, I was sleeping with one every night anyway.”

Two people died as heavy rain flooded Istanbul, sweeping away vehicles and stranding workers overnight, while authorities closed schools for Oct. 15 and warned of further downpours.
In Fatih, a 14-year-old died after stepping into a puddle and receiving an electric shock in Çukurbostan Park, the governor’s office said. An investigation was opened.
A 34-year-old also died in hospital after slipping while crossing a flooded street in Sarıyer’s Ayazağa neighborhood and hitting their head on the curb.
Rescue crews used trucks and minibuses to evacuate about 200 night-shift workers trapped in workplaces on Ayazağa’s Kemerburgaz Street.
Floodwaters swept away parked cars and stranded a municipal bus, while residents used ropes to help people reach safety.
Homes and businesses were flooded in several districts. Crews also worked to pump water out of Şişli Hamidiye Etfal Hospital in Sarıyer.
Rainfall reached 242 millimeters in Beykoz, 190.5 millimeters in Eyüpsultan and 187.9 millimeters in Sarıyer, the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality said.
It described the totals as among the highest recorded since 1985.
Municipal services received 6,937 incident reports. The governor’s office said 8,000 personnel and 2,000 vehicles and pieces of equipment had been deployed.
The governor’s office suspended in-person classes at public and private educational institutions for one day.
Motorcycles and other two-wheeled vehicles were barred from roads from 9 p.m. on Oct. 14 until further notice.
Schools were also closed for Oct. 15 in Kocaeli, Sakarya, Yalova, Düzce and Zonguldak.
The Transport and Infrastructure Ministry said 43 flights bound for Istanbul Airport were diverted to other airports in Türkiye and abroad. Three flights bound for Sabiha Gökçen Airport were diverted to Ankara.
Sabiha Gökçen resumed arrivals and departures late on Oct. 14 after strong winds and wind shear temporarily disrupted operations.
The municipality’s Disaster Coordination Center, AKOM, forecast further rain, particularly on the Asian side and along the Bosphorus. Residents were urged to avoid unnecessary travel and stay away from stream beds and areas at risk of flooding.

'Mother of all bombs': US potential Iran strike plans include largest non-nuclear weapon - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:29:06 UTC
14:29:06 KST

The United States military has developed strike plans against Iran that include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), colloquially known as the "mother of all bombs," the largest non-nuclear weapon in the US arsenal, CNN reported on Thursday.
According to CNN, multiple US officials said that the plans called for the MOAB to be used against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites, including Pickaxe Mountain.
Another source said that the phrasing used in the plan was that the attack would come “prior to US retrograde in CENTCOM AOR (area of responsibility),” meaning that the US might strike Iran and then immediately pull its forces out of the region.
Several of US President Donald Trump's advisors have also told CNN that, despite Trump's claims that he would not take further action against Iran before the US midterms, it remains unclear whether he will change his mind before Election Day.
The potential deployment of the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal would mark a significant escalation in the conflict, although officials familiar with military planning discussions told CNN that questions remain over its effectiveness in achieving Washington's strategic objectives.
MOAB unlikely to penetrate Iranian nuclear sites
According to several sources, the MOAB likely would be unable to penetrate deep below the ground, where Iranian nuclear facilities, such as Pickaxe Mountain, are believed to be.
“The MOAB is a massive information operation type weapon that is great for huge area clearance but not much else,” one source familiar with military planning discussions around Iran told CNN. “It is definitely not designed as a deep penetration warhead.”
The source said the MOAB's main tactical advantage in this scenario would be its psychological effect on Iran.
“POTUS has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level… you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped,” the source said.
When asked about the plan, a White House official told CNN that “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” adding that they do not comment on sensitive military plans.
A Pentagon official told CNN that it "plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary‑level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment.”
Reuters contributed to this report.

'Completely reversed': Why more Australian households are feeling miserable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:26:24 UTC
14:26:24 KST

In Brief
- Inflation, high interest rates and rising unemployment are keeping pressure on households.
- Economic misery is expected to remain above historical averages until at least 2028.
Australians are feeling increasingly miserable about the economy, with financial pressures unlikely to ease anytime soon, according to new analysis.
New research from the Committee for Economic Development of Australia (CEDA) found economic "misery" has returned to post-pandemic highs, wiping out improvements made since 2023 and leaving the country on track for several more years of elevated financial strain.
The think tank expects misery levels to remain well above recent historical averages through to at least the end of 2028, as households continue to grapple with inflation, high interest rates and a gradually weakening labour market.
Fresh data released on Thursday added to those concerns, showing Australia's unemployment rate climbed to 4.7 per cent in September — its highest level since October 2021.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
CEDA's misery index combines inflation, unemployment and interest rates to provide a broad measure of the economic pressures facing households.
"When those things go up, there's more of a financial pinch for households and there's a little bit more pressure on the pocketbook," CEDA head of economics Liam Dillon told SBS News.
Progress 'completely reversed'
CEDA says higher prices and borrowing costs have been the main contributors to the recent rise in economic misery.
"What we found is that since 2023, the misery index had been coming down as inflation was trending lower and the Reserve Bank was able to lower interest rates accordingly," Dillon said.
"Since then though, inflation's been a little bit more persistent than we had hoped. That's led the Reserve Bank to increase interest rates to 15-year highs."
"The combination of those things means that the progress on lowering that economic misery has now been completely reversed and we're back at 2023 levels."
After briefly returning to the Reserve Bank's two to three per cent target range in 2025, annual inflation rose to four per cent over the year to August.
The Reserve Bank has raised interest rates four times this year, taking the official cash rate to its highest level in 15 years, with some economists expecting another increase before the end of 2026.
The report also points to broader signs of economic pessimism, with consumer confidence remaining at levels comparable to those seen during the pandemic.
Unemployment exceeding forecasts
While inflation and interest rates have driven the latest increase in the misery index, the labour market has helped cushion the impact on many households.
But that source of support is beginning to weaken.
In the decade before the pandemic, unemployment was the largest contributor to Australia's economic misery, averaging 5.5 per cent of the population and peaking at 6.3 per cent in late 2014.
Since the pandemic, unemployment has remained comparatively low, averaging around four per cent.
But fresh figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday suggest labour market conditions are continuing to soften.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics said on Thursday Australia's unemployment rate for Australia in September was 4.7 per cent — the highest it's been since October 2021.
The August rate was initially flagged as 4.6 but revised up to 4.7.
Employment fell by 39,300 people over the month, while the number of unemployed Australians increased by 8,900.
The result also exceeded the Reserve Bank's forecast for unemployment to reach 4.5 per cent by the December quarter.
Despite the deterioration, Dillon said the jobs market remained a relative source of strength for the economy.
"What we've seen is that even though unemployment has been rising, the labour market is still showing signs of resilience and that's really helping to support households," he said.
About 177,000 jobs have been added since the start of the year, according to CEDA.
Dillon said that had helped insulate households from some of the effects of higher inflation and interest rates, while household savings remain above the decade average in the years before the pandemic.
The remedy to misery
The report argues reducing economic misery remains difficult because efforts to bring down inflation can often come at the expense of employment and economic activity.
To return inflation to the Reserve Bank's target range, it has largely relied on higher interest rates, increasing pressure on households already facing elevated living costs.
Minutes from the Reserve Bank's September meeting, released this week, showed staff were increasingly concerned weak productivity growth may mean unemployment needs to be higher than previously thought to keep inflation stable.
Dillon said stronger productivity growth offered the best long-term solution because it could ease pressure across all three parts of the misery index.
"What we suggest and what we argue through this is that really the only way to get at all three drivers of misery is to boost productivity growth," he said.
"That's a challenge and a long-term one at that, but really this index shows why that's so important."
CEDA expects misery levels to remain above recent historical averages through to the end of 2028 based on current trends.

Israel’s voters seem more tired than engaged by crucial election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:25:00 UTC
14:25:00 KST

Israel’s voters seem more tired than engaged by crucial election
- Israel’s Oct 27 election is seen as highly important, but voters look tired after three years of war, hostage fears and repeated fighting in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon and Syria.
- Campaigning is unusually quiet, with fewer rallies and posters. Many voters seem fixed in their choices, while polls suggest no clear majority and a possible repeat election.
- Opposition hopes centre on Gadi Eisenkot, who promises a more transparent government. Likely changes include an inquiry into Oct 7, prime minister term limits and action on ultra-Orthodox conscription.
AI generated
JERUSALEM – Two weeks before what is widely considered Israel’s most consequential election in decades, its streets are surprisingly empty of rallies and campaign posters, with voters seemingly more exhausted than engaged.
For a society that a few years ago saw hundreds of thousands pack central squares weekly to protest the policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the listlessness is noteworthy.
“It’s the most significant election since 1949 and the most lacklustre existential moment that I can recall,” said Yossi Klein Halevi, author of several books on Israel and a senior fellow at the Shalom Hartman Institute, a Jerusalem think-tank.
“Israelis are tired after three years of war,” he said. “They also know that the war isn’t over, that whoever wins will have to fight its next stage. It makes it hard to generate excitement for the future.”
The Oct 27 election will be the first since Hamas militants attacked Israel three years ago, killing 1,200, abducting 250 and triggering a brutal war in Gaza that the territory’s health ministry says killed at least 70,000 Palestinians.
Israel has since waged further battles against Iran and groups it backs in Lebanon and Syria.
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis have been called up for military service and many have spent months in uniform, away from family and work.
The Oct 7, 2023 attack inspired patriotic unity, but as Hamas held on to hostages in Gaza, fissures opened, with some blaming the government for not prioritising their freedom over combat.
In addition, Netanyahu’s ruling coalition includes ultra-Orthodox parties who have traded their votes for keeping their young men out of military service, an issue that has infuriated most of the rest of the country.
This combination of issues could be expected to inspire an impassioned opposition to make its case and get out the vote.
But that is happening far less than many expected, although pollsters say opposition supporters will vote in large – perhaps record – numbers.
While a Channel 12 poll on Oct 12 had the opposition bloc winning 54 seats to Netanyahu’s 49, other surveys have been much closer and neither side is expected to secure a clear majority to form a government.
That is another possible factor in keeping enthusiasm low, since it could require complex negotiations or even another election to deliver a decisive outcome.
The opposition’s main candidate is Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who has pledged to lead a more transparent government.
He is positioning himself as a self-effacing contrast to the high-profile Netanyahu, a global figure who has been in office longer than anyone in Israeli history.
“You’d expect to see Eisenkot in the centre of Tel Aviv with tens of thousands of people expressing a desperate desire for change,” said Yoel Esteron, who founded business daily Calcalist. “But he’s not a charismatic candidate and does small events.”
He also noted that a lot more campaigning is done on social media than in previous eras.
Shmuel Rosner, who produces analysis and polling for Channel 13, said the low-key campaigns may be a result of most people having long ago deciding which bloc they support, with little movement between them.
While cars lack bumper stickers and billboards are fewer, television and radio debate has been vigorous and intense.
Oded Ben Ami, who anchors an evening news broadcast on Channel 12, said he believes some things will change if Eisenkot wins: a commission of inquiry for Oct 7, term limits for prime ministers and an attempt to address the ultra-Orthodox conscription issue.
But Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Gaza and the West Bank, not to mention education and transportation – add up to a mountain of challenges.
Amalia Rosenblum, a Tel Aviv psychologist, when asked why the opposition energy seemed so low, referred to a concept known as learnt helplessness – when people stop trying to escape an unpleasant situation because past experiences have taught them their actions have no impact.
“Those who packed the streets a few years ago feel increasingly that they can’t move the needle,” she said.
“Even if they win, it’s like having a disease and being prescribed medicine. You take it, but it doesn’t exactly make you excited.” BLOOMBERG

Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:24:40 UTC
14:24:40 KST

Restoring nature is key to a more resilient future
At COP17 and COP31, governments must accelerate positive tipping points in energy, food and finance.
Nature is humanity’s life-support system, but it is being depleted at an alarming rate, leaving our world increasingly vulnerable. From deadly heatwaves and raging wildfires to catastrophic floods and prolonged droughts, the effects of environmental change have been impossible to ignore this year. With El Nino forecast to intensify, the risks to people, nature and economies are only increasing.
These shocks are unfolding against the backdrop of widespread nature loss, with WWF’s Living Planet Report 2026 finding that the average size of monitored wildlife populations declined by 73 percent between 1970 and 2022. Nature loss is increasingly a question of economic and national resilience – affecting food and water security, health, supply chains and geopolitical stability.
The situation is serious, but science shows there are still grounds for hope.
The economic systems driving nature’s decline can be transformed, and change can accelerate much faster than many may expect. Evidence shows that under the right conditions, positive change can cross a tipping point threshold and become self-reinforcing, making a safer, more resilient future not just possible, but inevitable.
The question is: How can we accelerate the actions needed to trigger those tipping points and accelerate the transition?
Positive tipping points and the opportunity for transformational change
In environmental terms, we often think about tipping points in terms of the threats they pose to vital ecosystems, such as coral reefs or the Amazon rainforest, where constant damage risks compounding and becoming increasingly impossible to reverse. These dangers are real and urgent. However, these tipping point dynamics can also work in our favour.
Three economic systems are driving most of nature’s decline: the energy system that fuels climate change; the global food system that leads to habitat loss and climate change; and the finance system that bankrolls it all. Triggering tipping points in those systems would see them rapidly transform for the better and reduce harm to the climate and nature. Once that threshold is passed, change can happen quickly as knowledge and technology advance, with solutions becoming cheaper and more accessible and as people learn from others. Encouragingly, progress is already under way – not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required – but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.
The world does not lack goals for 2030. What it lacks is the pace of implementation. With the Global Biodiversity Framework, the UN Sustainable Development Goals and the Paris Agreement in place, governments have already agreed on a pathway. Focusing on implementing these agreements in full will create the conditions for rapid systemic change.
The global energy system has already passed a tipping point, with the transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy now accelerating. While far from complete, this transition demonstrates how rapid systemic change is possible, offering valuable lessons for the equally urgent transformation of our food and financial systems.
Twenty years ago, solar power was used mostly in satellites and pocket calculators. Now, it is the cheapest option for new electricity generation in most countries. Affordable solar panels are electrifying rural households and improving the resilience of food and medical supply chains. Renewable technologies are displacing fossil fuels at a pace few people predicted even a decade ago.
Changing the food and finance systems is proving slower but is no less urgent.
To progress towards a food systems tipping point, we need to hit major milestones in the uptake of nature-positive food production and see wider shifts in consumer demand for healthier, more sustainable foods to reinforce and reward this shift. Some progress is under way with efforts to tackle commodity-driven deforestation, and more than 130 countries have national strategic plans for food system transformation, but commitments have not yet translated into the policies and incentives needed to accelerate the transition.
Tipping the finance system so that more finance flows to activities that protect and restore nature than activities that harm it is a fundamental challenge. Reaching this tipping point will require a combination of regulatory change, subsidy reform, and a shift in how the sector values climate and nature as material financial risks. If even a portion of the money currently directed towards harmful activities is redirected to environmental recovery, it could shift the economics of the entire transformation.
Governments meeting at the COP17 biodiversity and COP31 climate conferences have before them a vital opportunity to work together to accelerate the actions needed to trigger positive tipping points and to build resilience into societies and the global economy.
Learning from conservation success
Hidden within the broader picture of global biodiversity decline are inspiring stories of species recovery. Populations of green sea turtles and tigers are rebounding due to dedicated conservation work bringing together governments, communities and organisations.
Creating systemic change will similarly take action from all of us, from governments to businesses, financial institutions, local communities, and individuals. We know where we need to get to and the hurdles we need to overcome together; the task now is to create the conditions in which positive change gathers momentum and starts reinforcing itself.
Building strength and resilience into our natural support system will require the courage to shift from extractive, wasteful economies focused on short-term gain to systems that are sustainable and regenerative for the long-term benefit of all. We have the goals, the solutions and pathways to get there. Yes, there might be setbacks along the way, but science shows nature and the climate can still recover and that change can happen faster than we might think.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

New four-lane bridge between China and North Korea opens after a decade of delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:23:28 UTC
14:23:28 KST

The new bridge's opening comes about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations.
A new four-lane road bridge linking China and North Korea finally opened on Thursday, 12 years late, enabling the Asian giant and its isolated nuclear-armed neighbour to substantially step up cross-border trade.
China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a vital diplomatic and political backer, although relations have not always been smooth with the ruling Kim dynasty.
Hundreds of people gathered on Thursday in the northern Chinese border town of Dandong, taking selfies in front of the 3,026-metre New Yalu River vehicle bridge before it opened.
Trucks bearing the nations' flags began moving in both directions late in the morning, with some of the North Korean vehicles decorated with flowers.
"It's great," one woman who came to watch told the AFP news agency in the town dotted with Chinese as well as Korean shops and restaurants, where residents were relieved the bridge had finally open.
"It's already been over 10 years. It's certainly going to be good for business," she said, without wishing to be named, accompanied by her friend and her dog.
"I hope the standard of living in North Korea can rise to the level we have here," Dandong local Yu Shuyan, who before the pandemic had visited North Korea, said.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang said that the bridge symbolised Beijing's friendship with Pyongyang and that relations were "entering a new stage and opening a new chapter".
"Thanks to the joint efforts of both sides, the successful opening of the bridge will not only strongly boost economic and trade cooperation between the two countries, but will also further facilitate people-to-people exchanges and tighten the bonds of affection between the two peoples," Li said by video link at the opening ceremony, China’s Xinhua news agency reported.
The structure was completed in 2014 but its opening was delayed due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side, South Korea's Yonhap news agency reported.
North Korea also sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic and train journeys between the East Asian neighbours only restarted in March after a six-year halt.
The new bridge is not the only border crossing between the two countries.
But the new structure will supersede the "extremely narrow" rail-and-road Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge downstream on the Yalu River, said Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University.
"Previously, transporting heavy cargo such as industrial machinery, raw materials, construction materials and energy-related supplies required extreme caution because of safety concerns surrounding the ageing bridge," Lim told AFP.
"The new crossing will make such shipments much easier and more efficient," he said, calling it a "groundbreaking development" that will substantially increase cargo traffic.
Russia-North Korea bridge
The new bridge's launch came about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a road bridge as part of their efforts to cement relations.
Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about its opening.
China has long been North Korea’s biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in recent years, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has prioritised Moscow, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance.
But Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve his country's economy and build a front against the United States.
China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China.
North Korea has not yet resumed issuing tourism visas to Chinese citizens, who once made up the bulk of its overseas visitors.
South Korea's unification ministry said that Seoul is "closely monitoring" the situation regarding the new bridge.

Home Affairs 'unlawfully' jailed Australian citizen for 945 days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:20:23 UTC
14:20:23 KST

Home Affairs 'unlawfully' jailed Australian citizen for 945 days, ombudsman reports
In short:
An ombudsman report has set out a litany of errors spanning four decades that led to a citizen's unlawful detention.
Another non-citizen was wrongfully detained for 304 days.
What's next?
The report has made three recommendations to the government, including better communication between the Home Affairs Department and the minister.
An Australian citizen is among 30 people unlawfully held in immigration detention in the last financial year, according to a Commonwealth Ombudsman report.
The person, named as Mx B, was wrongfully detained by Home Affairs for 945 days — two and a half years — due to incorrect reading of Australia's citizenship laws.
Mx B was born in Australia in 1989 to New Zealand parents, briefly left, then returned in 1992, and should have been granted automatic citizenship on their 10th birthday in accordance with the Citizenship Act. But this did not occur due to "poor record keeping".
The ombudsman report sets out a litany of departmental errors, incorrect assumptions and failed checks spanning four decades.
Three incorrect citizenship assessments
After growing up in Australia, Mx B was convicted of criminal offences and sentenced to prison in 2010 at the age of 21.
In 2018, while in jail, Home Affairs carried out a citizenship status assessment and incorrectly found Mx B was not an Australian citizen, due to their brief departure from the country as a baby.
"They [Mx B] were assessed as not having been ordinarily resident [in Australia] for the first 10 years of their life," the ombudsman report said.
"Officers failed to consider relevant case law about absences from Australia."
In 2019, the department, acting on the mistaken understanding that Mx B was a New Zealand citizen in Australia on a special category visa, considered whether to cancel Mx B's visa on character grounds, but found their visa had ended in the 1990s.
A second citizenship assessment again determined Mx B was not a citizen, which the ombudsman described as another "failure to consider all available information and relevant case law".
Upon Mx B's release from jail in 2022, the department placed them into immigration detention.
"Mx B claimed to be an Australian citizen on multiple occasions throughout their detention," the ombudsman report stated.
In 2024, Mx B's legal representative sent the department correspondence regarding Mx B's claimed Australian citizenship.
"The Department completed a further citizenship status assessment for Mx B based on existing information in its systems," the report states.
For the third time, the department determined Mx B was not an Australian citizen, "failing to take into account the new information indicated by Mx B's legal representative".
Eventual release after High Court NZYQ ruling
In November 2023, the High Court's NZYQ ruling found the indefinite detention of non-citizens where there was no reasonable prospect of removal was illegal.
That triggered the release of more than 300 people from immigration detention.
Mx B was not one of them, remaining in detention until April 2025, when the New Zealand government told the Home Affairs department that Mx B was not a New Zealand citizen.
"The Department subsequently found Mx B to be affected by the outcome in NZYQ because their removal from Australia was not reasonably practicable in the foreseeable future," the ombudsman report said.
"On the same day, the Department granted Mx B a Removal Pending bridging visa on strict conditions and released them from held detention."
A fourth and final citizenship assessment found that Mx B was an Australian citizen.
'Mx A' wrongfully detained for 304 days
Mx B is not alone. The ombudsman report found 30 out of the 4,247 people placed into immigration detention between July 2024 and June 2025 were unlawfully detained.
Of those, 60 per cent of cases were due to a delay in communicating a ministerial visa approval to the department, leaving 18 people in unlawful detention for one day.
One individual, known as Mx A, was wrongfully detained for 304 days due to a decision maker's "incorrect understanding of the law".
Of those affected, none have filed compensation claims against the government.
The report has made three recommendations, including that the department work with the Home Affairs minister to "formalise policies and procedures relating to the communication of Ministerial intervention decision".
It also recommended Home Affairs apologise to those impacted.
The Home Affairs department has been contacted for comment.

Both nations participate in the Jordan-led Aqaba Process, established in 2015 to bring governments and security experts together to address terrorism, violent extremism and emerging security threats.

The administration of US President Donald Trump is considering easing sanctions on shadow fleet tankers to lower shipping costs and increase oil supplies from the Persian Gulf, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing people familiar with the discussions.
The proposal would allow sanctioned vessels to transport “legitimate” fuel, excluding Russian and Iranian oil subject to sanctions, the sources said. Companies seeking to use the vessels would have to obtain authorization from the US Treasury Department.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The move could make a small number of additional tankers available for short-haul trips through the Strait of Hormuz, but is unlikely to lead to a widespread drop in freight rates, maritime industry sources told Reuters. Insurers would still have to comply with European Union and UK regulations.
The US Energy Department said any easing of restrictions on the shadow fleet would not help Russia transport oil or petroleum products.
Trump lifts sanctions on Russian diesel, blames Zelensky for high prices
The latest proposal comes days after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports following an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets.
The US Treasury Department authorized the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
Trump said lower fuel prices for Americans were his top priority ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, when Republicans hope to retain control of both chambers of Congress.
Musk Says US Government Controls Ukraine’s Starshield Limits as Zelensky Accuses Russia of Exploiting Outage
The US president has repeatedly blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure for driving up fuel prices.
On Oct. 10, he called for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky, saying Kyiv needed a leader willing to reach a deal with Moscow.
“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals, but for some reason he never does,” Trump said.
Zelensky condemned the diesel agreement, arguing that easing sanctions would provide Moscow with additional revenue to continue its war against Ukraine.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world,” Zelensky wrote on X on Oct. 9. “Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged.”
In an interview with Axios, Zelensky described Trump’s decision to lift sanctions as “not fair and not honest,” adding that it looked like a “happy birthday present” for Putin.
The Ukrainian president also argued that any halt to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure should be reciprocal, with Moscow stopping its attacks on Ukraine’s energy facilities.
The diesel agreement drew criticism from US lawmakers, including some Republicans, who argued that allowing Russian fuel sales would undermine sanctions intended to restrict Moscow’s ability to finance its war against Ukraine.
Russia seeks relief from energy restrictions
The US also temporarily exempted some Russian oil and petroleum product shipments from sanctions in the spring amid the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
The Kremlin argued at the time that stabilizing global oil markets was impossible without significant volumes of Russian oil. Putin also warned that attempts to damage Russia’s oil fleet would create problems for everyone, particularly those seeking to harm Moscow.
The latest discussions on easing shadow fleet restrictions come as the Trump administration seeks to contain fuel prices amid disruptions to global energy supplies. However, any broader reduction in shipping costs could be limited by insurance restrictions and the continued enforcement of European and British sanctions.

Finnish households to receive paper emergency preparedness guide in January
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
08:16:35 EEST
14:16:35 KST

The Finnish Interior Ministry will distribute around 3.5 million printed emergency preparedness guides to households and businesses across mainland Finland in January.
The guide will explain how people should prepare for disruptions and crisis situations. It will also cover the increasingly topical threat posed by drones.
Such a guide is essential in case electricity and internet connections are disrupted.
"It is not enough for guidance on preparing for disruptions and crises to be available to the public only through the Suomi.fi online service," says Ira Pasi, a project manager at the Interior Ministry.
The ministry has previously noted that an online guide is a cheaper option and easier to update.
"Reading the online version is particularly easy for the groups that are least prepared. Those who are least prepared are young adults and urban residents," Pasi says.
In May, Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) said preparations were under way for a guidebook to be distributed to households. Finland's Parliamentary Ombudsman has also commented that the current method of communicating preparedness advice is lacking.
Concise guide, not a weighty handbook
The guide sent to households will be a brief summary rather than a comprehensive information package. It will consolidate essential advice from various authorities and organisations.
The material draws on sources including the Suomi.fi preparedness guide and the 72 hours website. Advice on the threat posed by drones comes from the rescue services' website.
"The aim is for everyone to be able to read it from cover to cover. It will not be a guide running dozens of pages that people would have to memorise," Pasi added.
He further noted that the advice is intended as guidance rather than a set of requirements. People can adapt it to their own resources and circumstances.
The guide's preparation and distribution will cost around two million euros. In addition to Finnish and Swedish, versions will also be produced in Sámi.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Defense and transportation officials have raised concerns about Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an’s (蔣萬安) proposal to convert Songshan Airport into an AI park, citing military, transportation, and emergency medical needs.
Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) told the Legislative Yuan’s Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee on Wednesday that Songshan Airport plays an important role in Taiwan’s defense in peacetime and during war, per UDN.
When KMT Legislator Huang Jen (黃仁問) asked whether the airport could be targeted in a decapitation strike, Koo said it was possible and that Taiwan Taoyuan International Airport could face the same threat.
Koo added that closing Songshan would make Taoyuan Airport even more difficult to defend. He also agreed with KMT Legislator Huang Chien-pin (黃建賓) that the risks of abandoning an airport should not be overlooked.
Koo said legislators representing outlying islands and eastern Taiwan had opposed phasing out Songshan, which provides an important transportation link for residents seeking medical treatment in Taipei. Those areas have fewer medical resources, making access to the capital’s hospitals especially important.
Deputy Civil Aviation Administration Director Yang Kuo-feng (楊國峯) told the committee that the Taipei City Government had not submitted proposals or applied for budget subsidies related to planning or research on relocating or closing Songshan Airport in the past four years, per LTN.
DPP Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) asked whether the city had raised the issue during that period. Yang said former Taipei Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) had proposed relocating the airport, but the current Chiang administration had not. Yang added that the airport’s overall plan, approved in November 2023, designates Songshan as an international business airport and a hub for domestic air transport.
Deputy Transportation Minister Lin Kuo-hsien (林國顯) said the planned third terminal and third runway at Taoyuan Airport were intended to expand capacity, not accommodate flights currently using Songshan. After the third runway is completed, Taoyuan’s existing second runway will also need to be taken out of service temporarily for maintenance, Lin said.
Lin said Taoyuan primarily serves international routes and medium- and large-sized jet aircraft, while Songshan handles domestic and regional services, including flights by slower aircraft such as ATR turboprops.
Transferring Songshan’s flights to Taoyuan would require changes to terminal and apron arrangements and could be costly, Lin said. A Ministry of Transportation report estimated that passengers traveling on ATR-72 aircraft would add about an hour to their journeys compared with flying from Songshan.
Taoyuan Airport handled about 47.8 million passengers in 2025, exceeding its stated annual capacity of 42.8 million, according to the report. Terminal 3 is scheduled for completion by the end of 2027.
Songshan handled about 2.39 million passengers traveling to and from Kinmen, Matsu, and Penghu in 2025, the report said. It also cited 38,651 outlying-island residents who traveled to Taiwan for medical treatment and noted that nine major emergency hospitals are within a 10- to 15-minute drive of Songshan, per Liberty Times.
The two airports can also serve as alternate landing sites for each other during bad weather or other exceptional circumstances. Lin said the Songshan Airport proposal remained open for public discussion but would be considered in the next five-year plan only after its consequences and necessary supporting infrastructure had been adequately assessed.

Chinese and DPRK flags also lined the cable-stayed bridge with towering pylons that had been completed in 2014 but remained unused, while approach roads and a customs compound on the North Korea end remained unfinished.
The opening signals progress in bilateral relations between Beijing and Pyongyang, marked by two summit meetings between their leaders in the past year.
China is by far Pyongyang's largest trading partner, even after a series of UN sanctions banned the flow of goods and workers to and from the DPRK.
China and Russia, two UN Security Council permanent member states that voted to approve sanctions resolutions until 2017, have since questioned  the legitimacy and efficacy of such bans.
The bridge will help move heavy equipment, raw materials and energy products needed for DPRK's development projects, said Lim Eul-chul at Kyungnam University's Institute for Far Eastern Studies.
China's exports to the DPRK rose to a six-year high of US$2.3 billion last year, a 25 percent increase, That was still well below levels before UN sanctions were tightened in 2017. (Reuters)

Rahul Gandhi's key petition on mass voter deletions listed in Supreme Court today
The Supreme Court is slated to hear a petition filed by India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and several other opposition lawmakers over a sweeping exercise which has so far purged over 130 million names from the country's electoral rolls.
A list of cases to be taken up on Thursday by a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kanta shows the petition named "Rahul Gandhi and others versus Election Commission of India and others."
The plea was filed on Monday at the end of a protest march to the Supreme Court that saw Congress' Gandhi rallying thousands, including members of the opposition INDIA bloc, student leaders, activists and civil society, through a heavily barricaded part of the capital.
The protest was the latest in a series of demonstrations calling for India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to step down over alleged manipulation of voter rolls to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The poll body, whose neutrality has come under scrutiny, rejects the allegations and says the exercise, called Special Intensive Revision (SIR), removes deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and also prevents the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants."
Modi's party has also dismissed the accusations and deems the protests as attempts to "create anarchy."
Meanwhile, neither Modi nor Kumar have publicly addressed the issue.
Gandhi's petition seeks an interim suspension of the nationwide revision of voter rolls, along with an audit of voter deletions and safeguards against deletions without prior notice.

- Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao called the Leidos Seahawk a “force multiplier” and said it shows the Pentagon’s growing use of autonomous systems in modern warfare.

AI generated
WASHINGTON – An uncrewed surface vessel has deployed with a US aircraft carrier strike group for the first time in the US Navy’s history.
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao mentioned the presence of the large autonomous vessel in a panel discussion about the Pentagon’s use of such systems at an Army conference in Washington on Oct 14.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group left its San Diego home port in late September headed for the Middle East.
“This is the first carrier strike group to ever deploy with a large-sized unmanned surface vessel,” Cao told the audience. “This is a force multiplier. Imagine having more guns out there.”
The uncrewed vessel was a Leidos Seahawk, a 145-ton, 42m-long surface vessel designed to operate over extended distances for months, according to a person familiar with the ship.
The Seahawk is sailing from the West Coast with the carrier and its escort vessels, said the person.
The presence of the large autonomous vessel in a carrier strike group – possibly the most potent symbol of global US military power projection – underscores the Pentagon’s increased reliance on uncrewed platforms as modern warfare evolves.
Cao referred to US forces in the Middle East already having used a Corsair II autonomous vessel built by Saronic Technologies to rescue two Apache helicopter pilots.
He also said unmanned underwater vessels were deployed to remove sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
The strike group is en route to the Middle East to give US commanders more options if President Donald Trump chooses to restart military strikes against Iran, a US official told Bloomberg News.
USS Roosevelt personnel operated the autonomous Seahawk vessel during 2026’s annual Rim of the Pacific naval exercises near Hawaii, Leidos said in a release in September. BLOOMBERG

Russia turns to new tactics to destroy Ukraine’s energy grid this winter for good
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:06:27 UTC
14:06:27 KST

Russia turns to new tactics to destroy Ukraine’s energy grid this winter for good
Employees work at a power plant of Ukrainian energy provider DTEK, which was damaged by constant Russian air attacks, at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, on Nov. 13, 2025. (Roman Pilipey / AFP via Getty Images)
Volleys of explosions deafened Kyiv in the early hours of Oct. 14, as Russia targeted multiple energy facilities powering the embattled capital amid a new campaign to isolate and disconnect the city following a brutal summer of relentless strikes on businesses and critical infrastructure.
While Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy system have been ongoing throughout the year at a low level, Moscow has recently ramped up mass attacks to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure for its fifth winter offensive during the full-scale invasion.
The latest attack on Oct. 14 alone targeted 26 power facilities, President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media.
There’s also been a recent uptick in Russian drones and missiles flying near nuclear plants, one energy official with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent under the condition of anonymity.
The drones are likely monitoring the plants and their infrastructure, with the official warning that Russia may be preparing to strike them — something Moscow has largely refrained from throughout its invasion.
Ukraine is in a vulnerable position. In just the week of Oct. 5-11, there were around 200 hits on power sector facilities and 17 on the oil and gas sector, the Energy Ministry’s press department told the Kyiv Independent. And Ukraine lacks critical air defense against Moscow’s expanding arsenal, energy specialists told the Kyiv Independent.
As the winter draws closer, Russia will likely expand its campaign to other major cities to sow panic.
Meanwhile, Russia’s tactics and weapons technology have changed since last winter. In addition to ballistic missiles, Moscow overwhelms Ukraine’s air defense by launching jet-powered drones and AI-powered loitering munitions en masse, attacking during the day as well as at night, and hitting infrastructure that power plants rely on, like railways for coal deliveries, energy experts said.
The recent attacks have already left hundreds of thousands of citizens in Kyiv and front-line regions suffering power and water outages. The situation has deteriorated so much in Kyiv that power to the metro was even temporarily cut off following attacks on Oct. 8 and 14.
"The overall pattern is systematic: the strikes damage the network, force emergency restrictions, and slow down repairs, especially when crews cannot work safely during air-raid alerts," Viktoria Gryb, a lawmaker and head of the parliament’s subcommittee on energy security, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The methods and targets can change, so I would not call this a simple repeat of last winter. But the goal remains the same: to destabilize the energy system."
read also
New tactics
The first few weeks of Russia’s latest campaign have primarily targeted Kyiv, continuing Russia’s months-long offensive on the capital’s economic centers that has made life in the city increasingly harder and more dangerous.
For now, Moscow is picking up where it left off last winter — focusing on disconnecting Kyiv by targeting power plants in and around the capital, as well as key substations, Olena Pavlenko, president of the Kyiv-based energy-focused think tank DiXi Group, told the Kyiv Independent.
The capital is particularly vulnerable as it is reliant on thermal and cogeneration plants that are exposed to enemy strikes, while substations that connect it to generation sources, including nuclear plants in western Ukraine, are protected against drones but not against ballistic missiles.
Meanwhile, the city hasn’t prepared enough backup generation supplies for when its power plants are inevitably taken offline. Despite experiencing a humanitarian crisis last winter when residents lacked heating and power in minus 25 degrees Celsius, political infighting and funding shortages mean the city will likely experience the same difficulties again.
Kyiv and other cities are also frequently attacked by jet-powered drones, which weren’t widespread last winter. They are faster and more precise than the older propeller-powered drones, making them harder for Ukraine’s limited air defenses to shoot down.
"Jet-powered drones changed the game to some extent. They are cheaper than missiles and can destroy more distributed generation infrastructure," Pavlenko said.
"It’s easier for jet-powered drones to attack transformers, smaller transformers, and infrastructure for cities. This has a huge impact on cities in terms of heating supply, water supply, and sewage."
In addition to striking power plants and substations, Russia has also increasingly hit power lines around big cities over the last few weeks to cut power supplies to consumers. While not a new target, Russia’s tactics have improved, including attaching a new type of warhead to a jet-powered drone designed to destroy high-voltage electricity pylons.
Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants, which generate around 60% of the country’s electricity, will likely be the country’s lifeline again once other power plants are taken offline.
Unlike substations, which are largely protected against jet-powered drones via massive concrete fortifications, power lines and pylons are more exposed since they can’t be easily shielded. But damaged power lines can be restored in 24 hours, in contrast to substations, which require complex repairs, the anonymous energy official said.
The problem with pylons could surface in the long run, as Ukraine’s steel industry has shut down amid debilitating strikes on factories. Stockpiles of products to reconstruct pylons will gradually deplete until steel firms can safely resume production, the press service of Metinvest, Ukraine’s largest steel company, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The situation regarding future supplies is becoming critical," Metinvest’s press service wrote in a statement to the Kyiv Independent.
What’s next?
After the last autumn and winter period, which saw Russia wipe out more than half of Ukraine’s gas production and 9 gigawatts of energy generation, the energy sector expects the same challenges again this year.
There’s little else that Russia can target, said Volodymyr Kudritsky, former head of Ukraine's state-grid operator Ukrenergo and co-founder of energy firm Nedzhen.
"We’ve already seen 95% of the menu. The Russians have left themselves with very little room to surprise us more," Kudritskyi told the Kyiv Independent.
The key issue for the energy sector is the air defense situation, as Ukraine struggles to down the jet-powered drones, said Kudritskyi. In recent months, Ukraine has developed interceptors that are showing increasingly positive results, but more time is needed to scale production.
At the same time, Ukraine continues to upgrade and reinforce protection at its energy facilities, including concrete fortifications, electronic warfare, early threat detection systems, and critical equipment reserves, the Energy Ministry said.
As the winter draws closer, Russia will likely expand its campaign to other major cities to sow panic, said Pavlenko. While attacks so far this autumn have largely impacted cities like Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia, Russian drones and ballistic missiles can reach deep into western Ukraine.
There’s also a heightened threat to nuclear infrastructure, like substations, this winter, said Pavlenko. Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants, which generate around 60% of the country’s electricity, will likely be the country’s lifeline again once other power plants are taken offline.
The risks to nuclear plants were majorly tested last winter, as Moscow targeted substations connected to the plants. One of the worst Russian attacks in February halved the output of nuclear plants, with Ukraine stabilizing the situation before it could worsen.
In a worst-case scenario, a big attack on substations could disconnect nuclear plants from the grid, forcing the plants to shut down, said the anonymous energy official. The consequences would be "extremely serious," they added.

‘They’re not dead yet’: Bleached corals recover in record time after touching healthy clones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:02:27 UTC
14:02:27 KST

In the lab, bleached corals recovered within just seven weeks of being put in brief contact with healthy corals.
Dying corals may have found an unexpected lifeline: their neighbours.
Scientists at Stanford University have discovered a way to bring corals back from the brink of death by placing them in contact with healthy corals for just a few days.
Published in Science Advances, the study presents a promising new approach to restoring coral reefs as rising sea temperatures cause more frequent and severe coral bleaching events.
When water becomes too hot, corals expel the microscopic algae that provide much of their energy, an event known as bleaching, which leaves them vulnerable to starvation.
After bleaching events, it can take months or years for surviving corals to recover – but the scientists contend hope is not lost for them.
“While bleached corals may be dying, they are not dead yet,” says lead author Danny Collins, a PhD student at Stanford. “The question we wanted to answer is, once a coral has bleached, what can we do?”
How scientists brought bleached corals back to full strength
The discovery happened by accident in 2025, when Steve Palumbi, a professor of oceans and marine biologist at Stanford’s Doerr School of Sustainability, noticed two pieces of coral that had fallen against each other in a laboratory tank. One was healthy while the other was bleached. But where the two touched, the bleached coral was beginning to regain its colour.
Collins then arranged 10 pairs of coral fragments, each containing a healthy and bleached piece from the same colony. Five pairs were placed in contact with one another, and the others were kept a few millimetres apart.
Within seven weeks, all five bleached fragments put in contact with their healthy clones had recovered. The ones that were kept apart had died.
Under a microscope, the scientists discovered the corals had fused together, creating tiny channels that allowed algae and nutrients to pass from one to the other. Within three days, beneficial algae had begun moving from the healthy corals into the bleached ones. After about a week, some had received enough algae to recover on their own.
Once inside the damaged corals, the beneficial algae began multiplying rapidly. “They flood in and start dividing at the fastest rates seen in corals,” says Palumbi.
During the second week, the algae doubled in number every four days – about 10 times faster than in wild corals – allowing the damaged corals to continue recovering even after they were separated from the healthy ones.
The finding marked a breakthrough in the lab. “Bleached corals are often considered a lost cause because recovery after a heatwave is very slow, if it happens at all,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a Stanford professor and one of Collins’ faculty advisors.
But the scientists say the technique isn’t ready for wide-scale application in the oceans.
The corals must be genetically identical for their tissues to fuse. In other words, every damaged coral would need a healthy copy of itself – an impractical solution for restoring whole reefs. But the researchers hope to find ways to deliver the beneficial algae without requiring direct contact or identical twins.
Coral reefs may be running out of recovery time
The revelation comes at a crucial time for coral reefs.
According to the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network’s latest assessment, the world's reefs have lost nearly 10 per cent of their living coral over the past four decades. Between 2023 and 2024 alone, it fell almost 9 per cent during a global bleaching event – the largest single-year decline ever recorded.
Global bleaching now occurs roughly every five to six years, leaving reefs less time to recover between bouts of extreme heat. The report warns that reefs will continue declining unless man-made emissions fall and threats such as overfishing, water pollution and coastal developments are curbed.
And while combining coral to help them recover from bleaching might save some of them, Palumbi stresses that it can’t protect them from rising sea temperatures.
“This is a recovery story. It doesn’t blunt heatwaves; it just helps the aftermath. There is still a huge need to reduce heatwaves and protect all of Earth’s life from rapid climate stress,” he says.
“Eventually, it can hopefully help the huge effort being put into restoration succeed better by helping those coral gardens survive heatwaves more completely.”
