Embryo gene editing is getting more precise, but how safe and ethical is the practice? | Euronews Tech Talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:26 UTC
14:00:26 KST

The use of a precise gene editing technique to edit human embryos has caught the attention of academics and society, yet doubts over its safety and ethics remain.
In the summer of 2026, two studies revived the debate on embryo gene editing, a technique that consists of manipulating the DNA of a human embryo for reasons ranging from better understanding human development to preventing children from developing certain diseases.
One study was led by Kathy Niakan at Cambridge University in the United Kingdom, and the other by Dieter Egli at Columbia University in the United States.
Both researchers employed base editing, a technique developed in 2016 to alter genetic material with greater precision than earlier methods. Both conducted their research on human embryos instead of mice, and both delivered results which caught the attention of many around the world.
Embryo gene editing is not yet a medical reality. Scientifically, modifying the genes of a human embryo is extremely challenging. In addition, no country allows the modification of cells that can be passed on to offspring.
With these studies, is society closer to the possibility of safely creating gene-edited babies? What are the ethical concerns surrounding this practice?
The studies
Using base editing, the Cambridge study targeted NANOG, a specific gene which was found to be essential for the formation of future bodies from an embryo.
“Base editing represents a significant advance on conventional CRISPR-Cas9 because it carries a far lower risk of causing unintended chromosome errors,” Kathy Niakan said in a press release.
On the other side of the Atlantic, Columbia’s research group tried base editing in three genes: one linked to high cholesterol and cardiovascular disease, and the other two related to haemoglobin production.
“By introducing such damage using editors, we are starting to understand how human embryos handle damage in their genomes. Long term, we hope to learn how to prevent genetic and developmental abnormalities during IVF to create more efficient, safer, and more affordable fertility treatments,” said Dieter Egli in a press release.
According to Robin Lovell-Badge, principal group leader and head of the laboratory of stem cell biology and developmental genetics at the Francis Crick Institute in London, the two studies are on the right path, but there’s room for improvement.
“The methods look much safer. But there's still work to do,” he told Euronews Next. “It looks like the levels of mosaicism are low, but not zero. So there's going to have to be more work done there,” he added.
Mosaicism is one of the main obstacles of gene editing. It happens when base-editor molecules fail to find and modify certain cells. This phenomenon could potentially cause the development of certain diseases.
The ethical debate
Although research on embryo gene editing might be advancing, several ethical questions remain unanswered.
“A question that very often pops up in regard to that is the tension between therapy versus enhancement,” Pascal Borry, professor of bioethics at the University of Leuven, in Belgium, told Euronews Next. “Where do we put the line? What is therapeutic? What is an improvement?” he added.
Borry also highlighted other ethical puzzles, ranging from the issue of consent to the problem of stigmatising a community already living with a certain disease.
In addition, he underlined that embryo gene editing might not be necessary: “There are many other alternatives to this technology, and I think it’s important to reflect upon that. And I’m thinking about the pre-implantation genetic testing,” he said.
Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is a medical test that takes place during in vitro fertilisation treatment to detect any abnormalities in the embryos.
Björn Heindryckx, professor at Ghent University in Belgium and principal investigator coordinating research in the infertility department, agrees with Borry on the non-necessity of using embryo gene editing to prevent certain genetic conditions.
Yet, he argues that this technique could still have benefits: “If we understand, and with this tool we can really test it much better, if we can get more insight into embryo development, it will give us more insight into certain forms of infertility.”
Badge, on the other hand, is less worried about the ethical implications of this technique. “I don't have a problem with doing it if it's safe and there's a good ethical reason for doing it. I think it's unethical to allow people to have children that have a genetic disorder if you can avoid it,” he explained.
According to Badge, countries should regulate the practice; however, they should not adopt a restrictive ban. “Let's say you want to fly to Mars. You're going to be in space for a long time; you're going to have an environment with very high levels of radiation. So you may want to be modified to deal with high levels of radiation,” he told Euronews Next.
Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

Rachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with Marmite | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

Here is a simple, practical recipe that I trust will be useful to many who don’t have the time for lengthy kitchen preparations. Boil the spaghetti as usual, drain it, and toss it with a little butter and parmesan. Then, for four, take a spoonful of meat extract and dissolve it in a small saucepan with just a few drops of boiling water. Pour the meat extract over the pasta, stir and serve. You will be pleasantly surprised by the exquisite flavour the pasta acquires – achieved with such a negligible investment of time.
This is a roughly word-for-word translation of an Italian recipe for spaghetti con l’estratto di carne (spaghetti with meat extract). It is another dish from Ada Boni’s Il Talismano della Felicità (The Talisman of Happiness), which was published in English for the first time last month and, according to the food writer and editor Angela Frenda, is “still considered one of the most precise and accurate of all cookbooks”.
I was alerted to spaghetti con l’estratto di carne by the food historian and author of A Brief History of Pasta, Luca Cesari. I recently met Luca for dinner at St John in London and, over bone marrow on toast, kidneys on toast, welsh rarebit and fried tripe, we talked about many things, including recipe outrage. Spaghetti with Marmite came up as an example, and Luca pointed out that, in terms of approach, taste and spirit, it was more or less identical to Ada’s iconic and “exquisite” recipe.
He also noted that using a spoonful of meat extract as a pasta sauce is in the spirit – and a short-cut version – of pasta al sugo d’arrosto (pasta with sauce of the roast). That is, the pan juices, and those fat and tasty, crusty bits left at the bottom of the tin when you’ve roasted a joint of meat, are lengthened with a bit of water or wine, maybe more rosemary (or whatever you fancy) added, before being used as a pasta sauce. Pasta with gravy, if you like. (When I make braised chicken with rosemary, garlic and wine, I particularly like the last of the congealed pan juices as a pasta sauce.)
It was the great Anna del Conte, who was born in Milan in 1925 and moved to London in 1949, who first wrote about spaghetti with butter, cheese and Marmite, noting in her autobiography Risotto and Nettles that this was a dish she herself made (and that was loved by her children). I wonder if Anna knew Ada’s version? She certainly mentions pasta al sugo d’arrosto in her writing. And Anna inspired Nigella Lawson to make her own version of spaghetti with Marmite, which is the recipe I followed, although it is hardly a recipe.
Marmite is, of course, a dark, sticky, salty-savoury spread made from concentrated yeast extract. What yeast extract and meat extract have in common is glutamic acid or free glutamates, an amino acid that provides a savoury, lip-smacking umami flavour. Tomatoes, mushrooms and cheese are high in free glutamates, too, so in the Ada-Anna-Nigella recipes all provide a double dose of umami by adding parmesan; butter is vital for adding fat, flavour and slippiness to the final dish. I hope you will be pleasantly surprised by the exquisite flavour this pasta acquires, and all achieved with such a negligible investment of time.
Spaghetti with Marmite, Bovril or Vegemite
Serves 4
400-500g spaghetti
Salt
1-2 tsp Marmite, or Bovril or Vegemite
60g unsalted butter, cubed 
2-4 tsp grated parmesan, or grana padano
Boil the spaghetti in plenty of lightly salted water, because both the Marmite and the cheese are already salty.
Meanwhile, in a very small saucepan on a low heat, warm two tablespoons of water with the Marmite until it has dissolved.
Once the pasta is cooked but al dente, lift it into a warm bowl (reserve some of the pasta cooking water), then add the cubed butter and cheese, and toss well. Pour the dissolved Marmite over the spaghetti and stir again, adding a little of the reserved cooking water, if you think it needs it, until the sauce is soft and slippery. Serve immediately.

The day bad weather brought half a million birds to England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:24 UTC
14:00:24 KST

My birding mentor, the late Derek Moore, was also a keen cricketer. But one autumn day in 1965 he was unable to concentrate while fielding because many hundreds of songbirds were landing around him on the pitch at Lowestoft.
The arrival of hundreds of thousands of birds along the Suffolk coast that day became known as the “Great Fall”, and it was caused by a weather system bringing cloud, winds and heavy rain.
The conditions caused migrating songbirds heading south across the North Sea from Scandinavia to become exhausted, with many falling into the waves and drowning. But an estimated half a million survived and made landfall along a 24-mile stretch of English coastline. Having rested and fed, they then continued their long journey south to sub-Saharan Africa.
When I began birding in the 1970s, older birders waxed lyrical about the autumn falls from their youth. Yet today they are few and far between. Not because the weather patterns have changed, but simply because there are now far fewer songbirds breeding in northern Europe and migrating through Britain to Africa.
One place they do still occur – though with smaller numbers of birds – is Spurn Head on the East Yorkshire coast. Last month, birders gathered there for the annual MigFest, which, since 2013, has celebrated the wonders of bird migration – with attenders ever hopeful of witnessing one of these extraordinary falls.

Parents of Chloe Moffat want Treasury staff held to account over her death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

The parents of a woman who killed herself after facing disciplinary proceedings at the Treasury will call for anyone found to have contributed to their daughter’s death to be held to account.
A coroner found in August that the Treasury had “materially contributed” to Chloe Moffat’s death after the 26-year-old personal assistant was called into a surprise disciplinary meeting about anonymous complaints alleging she had disclosed sensitive information at work, which she denied.
The Treasury’s response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report, seen by the Guardian, acknowledges the department’s role in her death and commits to safeguards so this does not happen again. A review of the civil service by the Cabinet Office found that the conditions Moffat was subjected to had been replicated in other disciplinary meetings.
“We have some tough questions to ask,” David Moffat, Chloe’s father, told the Guardian before a meeting with the Treasury’s permanent secretary, James Bowler. “We do want to know that staff have been held to account. The coroner didn’t ask for that, but obviously that is very important. Chloe was held to account; we need to know that the managers and HR staff are being held to account.”
Moffat’s managers declined to allow her to bring a colleague to the meeting, did not give her any advance notice of it, and refused to tell her whether she was likely to lose her job. They also removed access to her director’s email and changed her work responsibilities. This was despite the meeting being described as “informal”.
Moffat left the meeting “devastated” and convinced she would lose her job, the coroner found, and the next morning she took her own life.
She had worked at the Treasury as a personal assistant for almost three years, “loved her job” and had an “exemplary employment record”, the coroner heard.
During the inquest, Moffat’s line manager was asked if she would have done anything differently and told the court: “No, I think we did all we could at the time with the information and advice we were given.”
Moffat’s parents have spent the year since she died fighting to get answers from the Treasury, which initially did not take any responsibility.
“It has taken us a long time to get to this point, and they have not helped us in any form,” said Anne Moffat, Chloe’s mother. “Now we are also trying to think how we want lessons to be learned so no other young person suffers in the same way as Chloe suffered. So we are looking at Chloe’s legacy, to ensure that there is learning across all organisations in HR departments.”
They say they have not had the chance to grieve properly yet and are thinking about holding a second celebration of life for Chloe. David said: “The funeral was in some ways uplifting as so many people chose to join us, but we didn’t really know what we knew now. We want to revisit it and have a more joyful time and celebrate Chloe as the person she was.”
The prevention of future deaths report issued by the coroner found there was still a risk at the civil service due to its disciplinary procedures. The civil service has put in place multiple safeguards to address these issues.
Documents seen by the Guardian read: “HM Treasury has accepted the findings in the report in full. In direct response to the inquest findings, HM Treasury immediately stopped using informal fact-finding meetings for allegations of potential serious or gross misconduct, introduced strengthened procedural and wellbeing safeguards, and issued urgent interim guidance.”
This guidance includes allowing staff to have a supporter in disciplinary meetings, giving proper notice of any such meeting, and informing staff if a dismissal is not likely. The Treasury is also hiring an on-site occupational therapist to support staff wellbeing.
Of this, David Moffat said: “We feel a lot better than we did about it going through the inquest. This is a step forward, but we still have some difficult questions to ask the permanent secretary.”
The coroner heard that during the disciplinary meeting, Moffat repeatedly asked for her best friend at work to be allowed to come in for support. This was not felt by her managers to be “appropriate”, the court heard, despite the obvious distress the young woman was in.
The department has now changed its policy. An email sent to staff at the Treasury last week, seen by the Guardian, reads: “Where concerns may amount to minor misconduct, these will continue to be handled informally. You will be able to ask to bring a colleague with you for personal support if you would like.”
Anne Moffat hopes other young people will not be put in the same position as Chloe. “It is so avoidable what happened, and such a waste. I wish we had known the risks. As parents we are still taking a bit responsibility that we could have done things differently. And if we had, the result wouldn’t have been so catastrophic.”
Chloe’s friends have been keeping her memory alive by running marathons for Shooting Stars Children’s Hospice, a charity for which her mother used to work, and volunteering for Samaritans.
Her parents hope their experience can stop other families from going through the same tragic event.
“We are hoping when we see the Treasury they will give us more reassurance and work with us on how Chloe is remembered,” Anne said. “We so miss having Chloe now. Our lives will never be the same again as we have lost her through something that was so preventable.”
A HM Treasury spokesperson said: “The Treasury’s deepest sympathies continue to be with Chloe’s friends and family, and the department continues to mourn our colleague. Our response to the coroner’s prevention of future deaths report sets out the action we have taken following this tragic case. An independent review found staff acted in good faith and with a duty of care throughout.”
- In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

UK households have paid extra £13,961 on bills since 2021 amid soaring inflation, TUC says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:23 UTC
14:00:23 KST

UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills over the past five years, according to a report urging the chancellor to tackle soaring living costs at the budget.
With less than a fortnight before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) said the cost of living crisis was weighing on the economy as hard-pressed households held back on spending.
Urging the chancellor to support households through a series of measures in the budget, it said the UK had recorded the weakest growth in consumer spending in the G7 since before the pandemic.
According to analysis of official figures by the union umbrella body, British households have forked out an additional £13,961 on bills on average since 2021 – an extra £2,792 a year – amid soaring inflation triggered by the exit from the Covid pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said: “From austerity to the pandemic to energy shocks and Trumpflation, working people have borne the brunt of crisis after crisis. When the crackpots in the White House or the Kremlin launch an illegal war, everyone pays the price in their bills.”
In his speech at Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Healey pledged to use his 28 October budget to give households “breathing space”. However, he warned that the government had limited resources to soften the global economic shock hitting Britain.
Against a volatile backdrop, the Treasury has been preparing for a “tightly focused” budget to limit the potential for a market backlash provoked by large tax and spending measures. The International Monetary Fund this week urged Healey to “stay the course” to cut the budget deficit amid rising borrowing costs in global financial markets.
The chancellor is however under growing pressure to take action to support households and businesses before the winter amid predictions that consumer energy bills could reach £2,000 a year from January for the typical household.
After retail industry bosses pressed Healey for support in Downing Street meetings on Tuesday, the Confederation of British Industry said he should listen to calls for a cut in employer national insurance contributions to encourage firms to take on younger workers.
The lobby group also called for cuts to business electricity costs, changes to business rates and measures to support private investment.
In a separate report, the centre-left IPPR thinktank urged Healey to raise £16bn, mostly through a rise in capital gains tax that would be softened by a new entrepreneur “super exemption”.
It was reported on Tuesday that Healey had rejected calls from Labour MPs and thinktanks to use the budget to equalise the rates at which capital gains and income from work are taxed.
However, the IPPR said headroom against the chancellor’s fiscal rule was likely to have shrunk by between £7bn and £15bn since the spring amid the impact on government finances from the Middle East war.
Calling for a cost of living package funded largely by higher taxes on wealth, it urged Healey to introduce a “rent stabilisation mechanism” to cap private rent increases, alongside a £2,000 cap on consumer energy bills, a freeze in fuel duty, and an increase in housing allowance benefits for households on universal credit.
The TUC said Healey should launch a social energy tariff and take action to help poorer households and young people with rising living costs. It also called for a rise in capital gains tax and higher taxes on banks.
Highlighting the costs from sticky inflation and higher interest rates, the analysis showed households with mortgages had spent on average £9,034 extra on repayments (£1,806 extra a year) since 2021. Those with loans had paid £1,911 extra in total (£382 extra a year).
Average rental costs have risen at a higher rate than mortgages, suggesting mortgage costs are being passed on to renters.
In the study of Office for National Statistics figures, it found households had spent on average £2,644 extra on electricity and gas bills since 2021 (£529 extra a year), and £372 extra on water bills (£74 extra a year).
Meanwhile, growth figures show that consumer spending remains behind pre-pandemic levels, after a period of broadly flatlining growth in household disposable incomes since the 2008 financial crisis.
Nowak said: “Eye-watering bill rises have hammered household budgets, squeezing consumer spending. That’s being felt on high streets up and down the country, holding our economy back.
“The chancellor needs a serious plan to put working people at the heart of growth, raising living standards so Britain can afford to spend. That means shielding households from punishing energy spikes and putting more money in workers’ pockets.”
The Treasury has been approached for comment.

Poland looks to economic heights in a country transformed since Soviet days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

Above the rain-soaked streets of Warsaw, the observation deck of the Varso tower overlooks Joseph Stalin’s gift to Poland that has divided opinion for decades.
For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.
For the managers of the Varso – completed four years ago, as the tallest building in the EU – with its 310m-high spire rising symbolically above its Stalinist neighbour, it is a waypoint on Poland’s rapid path to economic prosperity.
“We look down on it,” says Cezary Błaszczyk, the managing director of HB Reavis in Poland, which owns the tower, gesturing at the palace opposite. A few months ago a slackline walker traversed the 500m gap between the buildings. “It was a symbolic walk from the past to the future,” says his colleague Natalia Kasperska.
“Since we are higher and taller than the Palace of Culture, we treat it as: ‘We got over communism, and now we are a country with a strong economy,’” Błaszczyk says.
Over the four decades since regaining its independence from Soviet-dominated rule, Poland has been transformed. Excluding oil-exporting states and financial hubs, incomes have converged with western levels at the fastest rate in the world; from 40% of the EU average in the mid-1990s to 81% last year.
National income surpassed $1tn (£755bn) last year, ranking Poland among the world’s 20 largest economies. International Monetary Fund projections show income per capita will soon overtake Japan and Spain.
“Four decades ago, we were in – excuse my English – deep, deep shit,” says Marcin Bosacki, the Polish deputy foreign minister.
Stirring a cup of tea and lemon in his opulent Warsaw office, he recalls queueing after school in the 1980s for up to five hours to buy butter and meat as the communist government imposed martial law.
However, the Gdańsk shipworkers’ Solidarność movement and Pope John Paul II’s 1979 pilgrimage to his home country paved the way for Poland’s transition to democracy in 1990 and an “economic miracle”. Integration with western institutions, including Nato in 1999 and EU accession in 2004, also helped.
For years, many Poles chose to emigrate to earn more abroad, in a brain drain accelerated by EU membership. Polish plumbers became shorthand in Britain for foreign labour amid the political battles over EU freedom of movement before the Brexit vote.
Now Britons are increasingly likely to have their taps fixed by Romanians and Bulgarians, after a surge in the number of Polish nationals leaving. In each year since 2021, when Brexit was enacted after a year-long transition period, twice as many Poles left the UK than arrived.
Meanwhile, Germany recorded more non-Germans moving to Poland in 2024 than heading in the opposite direction for the first time on record.
On the Varso’s 44th floor, in the Warsaw practice of Foster + Partners, Jedrzej Kolesinski and Krzysztof Gornicki are among those returnees. Both moved to London in their 20s to work in the British architecture firm’s head office – where they led the design team behind the tower they now occupy.
Gornicki says Poland has changed dramatically in the years he was away. He always wanted to return to contribute to the country, and raising a family near his parents in a safe, green city that is more affordable than London also has its plus points. Now the pair are working to design Warsaw’s new airport – the biggest greenfield infrastructure project in Europe.
“You can work globally from one location. In London we worked on projects from North America to Asia … right now, we’re doing the same thing, just from Warsaw.”
On the streets below the Varso, the sights and sounds of progress are unmistakable. Modern electric trams glide past skyscrapers, there are cranes and construction work, giant advertising boards, and dockless e-scooters.
The traditional working-class bar mleczny (milk bars) still do a roaring trade serving beetroot soup and Polish dumplings. But at the oldest, Prasowy, orders are taken on a digital touchscreen.
Once an asphalt desert designed for columns of Soviet tanks, the old Parade Square surrounding the palace has had a green makeover. Further development is planned to bolster Warsaw’s bid for the 2040 summer Olympics.
There are also growing pains. Just as the facades of Warsaw’s medieval old town – rebuilt from the rubble of the second world war – conceal 20th-century concrete, Poland’s stellar growth obscures tensions. The influx of global capital has driven up living costs, squeezing out poor Varsovians. Income inequality is among the highest in Europe, while growing political divisions set the stage for a fractious general election next year.
Convergence with the west also presents a novel challenge for a country with a reputation as a low-cost hub within the EU.
For years Poland’s cheap, skilled workforce attracted companies such as Volkswagen to build cars, Cadbury to make chocolate and banks such as JP Morgan to open global support centres. At €19.10 (£16.10) an hour, average labour costs (wages, taxes and other costs) are still half the level of Germany and France, but the gap is closing.
Since 2004, the average monthly wage has more than tripled in nominal terms to 8,904 złoty (£1,723) last year. The net monthly salary in Warsaw has risen by 120% since 2016, according to Deutsche Bank, lifting it above Rome and Lisbon. A meal for two in the capital now costs more than in Tokyo and the price of a cappuccino has doubled.
Rafał Brzoska, the billionaire founder of InPost, the pan-European parcel locker company started in Kraków, says Poles deserve their reputation as hard workers. But now the country must focus on working smarter, in higher-value-added manufacturing and knowledge-intensive services.
“The next phase will depend less on catching up, and more on productivity. We don’t have labour cost advantage at all. We need to focus on productivity, technology, cheaper energy and better regulation.”
He is, however, concerned about the tensions in Polish politics. Divisions between the nationalist president, Karol Nawrocki, and Donald Tusk’s liberal government have grown increasingly acrimonious. Meanwhile, fringe far-right parties together hold a fifth of public support. Poland is also investing heavily in defence and energy security – aiming to boost economic growth in the process – amid Europe’s response to Russian aggression and US disengagement.
“People may put trust in someone else that has a magic remedy. [But] there is no magic remedy. We need to be super careful in terms of believing there is a secret sauce that will magically change things,” Brzoska says.
“In my opinion – unfortunately for all of us – we still need to work hard.”
As part of its growth plans, Poland is pushing to become a regional tech hub, bolstered by a $1bn investment fund backed by public and private capital to support tech startups and AI companies. The number of high-growth firms is rising, including ElevenLabs, an $11bn AI audio generation and voice cloning company named after 11 November – Poland’s national independence day.
There are strong foundations for its ambition. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s annual programme for international student assessment (Pisa) scores ranks Poland equal to the UK among the top countries in Europe and globally for maths, while a greater share of adults have higher education qualifications than in Germany.
On the eastern side of the Vistula River in the gritty and creative working-class district of Praga, the campus of the games company CD Projekt Red shows the progress being made.
As the developer behind the smash hit games series The Witcher and Cyberpunk 2077, the company started life in the 1990s as an importer of CD games made by US publishers.
Michał Nowakowski, its co-chief executive, says this was about the limit of Polish ambition in the early days. Now he competes globally to attract coders, games developers and graphic designers.
“In the late 90s and early 2000s I feel there was a massive inferiority complex. Among everybody who was young, you wanted to catch up with the west.”
Growing up in the 1980s, his family were expelled from Poland in the period of martial law. He recalls visiting London aged 15 and being “blown away” by the Virgin megastore and British culture. “I could never imagine Poland being like it.”
Within a generation, though, he says this attitude would be alien to his own children. “For young people now they have no inferiority complex. They don’t stop and think: ‘Can we be as good as Brits, French, Spanish?’ It’s not holding them back.
“We have really good universities and skills teaching people. I think that can take us to unprecedented heights as a country.
“We’re a proper-sized country. Not too small, not too big; no inferiority complex any more. There’s nothing holding us back.”

The global economy is muddling through against the odds. But a storm is coming | Larry Elliott
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:22 UTC
14:00:22 KST

Not much has gone right for the global economy this year, and plenty has gone wrong. Two big regional wars are destabilising prices and supply chains everywhere. Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts. China and the US are at loggerheads over trade.
Yet, so far, the impact has been modest. It is something of a miracle that the finance ministers and central bank governors gathered for this year’s annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok are not having to deal with a full-blown crisis. This is not like the autumn of 2008, when the meetings took place during the worst of the global banking meltdown.
The IMF is right when it says countries have shown resilience when having to cope with so many headwinds. It could have been worse. A lot worse. There was even some good news for the UK, with the IMF upgrading its growth forecast for this year and praising the government for its deficit-reduction plan.
The better-than-expected performance of the global economy breaks with historical precedent. In the past, oil shocks of the magnitude witnessed since the start of Iran war have had a marked and immediate impact, but there are three key reasons why growth has remained robust and inflationary pressure has been muted this time.
The first is the massive amount of investment in the development of artificial intelligence. This has been particularly important in the US, which is comfortably the fastest growing member of the G7 group of major developed economies year on year. The second is that countries have drawn on inventories of oil, and that has helped to alleviate the loss of crude from the Middle East. Had stockpiles not been run down, oil prices would have risen even more sharply. The third is that China’s economic strategy relies on exporting cheap goods to the rest of the world, and this is bearing down on the prices of imports elsewhere.
All that said, the potential flashpoints for trouble are everywhere. The situation in the Middle East is deteriorating, with the conflict spreading to Saudi Arabia. Oil stocks are running low and Donald Trump has got the US into just the sort of forever war that he used to rail against. The downside to cheap Chinese goods is that they are threatening manufacturing jobs in the west, with Germany especially vulnerable.
Meanwhile, massive US investment in AI has pushed up the cost of borrowing and resulted in shortages of capital for non-AI sectors. Governments are coming under pressure to rein in spending or raise taxes in the hope that bond markets will be impressed by their efforts to cut budget deficits.
Warnings from (among others) the head of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva, and the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, of the need to run a tighter fiscal ship come at a time when voters want politicians to do more, not less. There is little appetite for a new era of austerity, and finance ministers know it. If they follow through on the tough talk and actually deliver painful measures, the backlash is likely to be brutal.
Just as big a problem for governments is the need – at a time when global supply chains are stretched and fragile – to boost national self-sufficiency. The student protests in India and France highlight the pressures on states to intervene. Yet the capacity of states to act effectively is much weaker than they care to admit.
At a time when globalisation is in retreat, there is a need for a strong system of multilateral cooperation to cope with the strains. That is not currently the case. The World Trade Organization is moribund in this new age of protectionism, and the IMF and the World Bank are reluctant to call Trump out for his erratic behaviour.
Yet the idea that a new era of partnership will flower when there is a new US president is for the birds. The problems of multilateralism run far deeper than that. The liberal world order that the IMF and World Bank have presided over since the end of the second world war was dysfunctional long before Trump arrived in office.
As the former UN official Richard Kozul-Wright points out in a paper published next month, the IMF and World Bank – created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference – may still be operational but they have lost their connection to the New Deal principles laid out 82 years ago: state intervention in the running of economies, active industrial policy, the pursuit of full employment and help for poor countries to develop. “Instead, they have in recent decades pursued an agenda which encourages footloose capital, bolsters (and protects) private profit, and reduces the policy space available to governments. As a result, they have acted as hand maidens to an age of rising inequality, debt distress and heightened anxiety.”
The IMF’s own programmes for countries that come looking for financial assistance illustrate Kozul-Wright’s point about the lack of policy space. Help comes with strings attached: an insistence on tax increases and spending cuts that are frontloaded so that half the measures are implemented in the first year and two-thirds within two years.
The IMF argues that this “tough love” has a higher chance of success, although its view of what constitutes success is limited, and primarily means that a borrowing country doesn’t need another IMF programme in the next three years. It doesn’t mean living standards are improving or that fewer people are in poverty.
Clearly it would help to return to New Deal principles. It would mean governments had more policy space to develop strategies tailored to their own needs. It would mean a boost to public investment. It would mean a new Marshall plan to help poorer countries cope with the climate crisis. It would mean a serious attempt to tackle debt distress. But, in all honesty, none of that has a chance of happening any time soon. As a result, the world will become hotter, more fractured, more prone to conflict, less equal and a lot angrier.
The IMF is worried that the limits of this resilience may soon be tested, and it is right to be worried. Peace in the Middle East would bring oil prices tumbling down, but unless that happens quickly a long winter lies ahead. This looks more like a crisis postponed than a crisis permanently avoided. A lull before the storm, in all probability.
- Larry Elliott is a Guardian columnist

Next year, travellers will “humble everyone who thought they had them figured out” and surprise themselves in the process with “a trip nobody saw coming”, said the online travel platform. And according to the data, 77% are interested in choosing a holiday specifically to do something "completely out of character”.
Booking.com said the reaction from others will be “part of the appeal”, with 36% actively wanting to surprise their friends and family with their holiday choices. “These trips are designed to disrupt the status quo, rewrite the story everyone thought they knew, and deliver the twist nobody predicted.”
In fact, nearly a third of respondents (29%) have deleted or avoided posting about a holiday “because it felt too predictable or ordinary”.
So, will 2027 finally be the year that they have something worth sharing on their socials? As Booking.com puts it: “The best souvenir? The look on everyone else’s face.”
From all-exclusives to a hotel in the sky
Beyond the plot twist trips, Booking.com’s predictions suggest that travellers want holidays tailored to their lifestyles and budgets.
Its “all-exclusive” trend sees 66% of respondents wanting packages that let them remove services they won’t use. "Moving forward, the most appealing travel package isn't the one that includes everything."
Meanwhile, “vibe check(in)” finds 81% of travellers would choose a destination primarily based on how they want to feel, rather than where they want to go.
Under “social currency”, money could shape the holiday guest list. Half of travellers have reconsidered who to invite on a trip because of spending differences and 38% have removed people from a travel group entirely. The kids may not make the cut either as 61% of parents are keen to travel child-free so they can spend more on themselves.
Venturing into the supernatural, 65% are interested in paranormal experiences and a “trip to the beyond”. Nearly half (48%) would seek an experience with the hope of speaking to someone on the “other side”.
While back in the working world, the “PTO: powered by AI” trend finds that 64% are interested in having AI cover their work while they’re away.
“Hotel in the sky” reflects demand for wellness in the air, with 89% of respondents saying they would take a long-haul journey if it guaranteed they would arrive rested and refreshed.
For “sweat synergy”, 66% of respondents who have travelled alone say a shared physical activity or challenge has led to a lasting connection or friendship.
Under “trailside therapy”, the new romantic getaway may be more about tough talks with your partner, rather than candlelit dinners. The data found that 47% would consider a trip to resolve conflicts or arguments, with walking and hiking among the activities that help couples tackle difficult conversations.
Top trending destinations for 2027
Alongside its predictions report, Booking.com has revealed 10 trending destinations for 2027, including three in Europe: Reims in France, Bratislava in Slovakia, and Pescara in Italy.
- Reims, France
- Monterey, California, USA
- Sendai, Japan

====================================================================================================

Lithuania risks losing more citizens abroad after years of positive migration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

After six years in which more Lithuanian citizens returned home than left the country, preliminary figures suggest the trend may be reversing, raising concerns about the country’s workforce, economic growth and ability to attract its diaspora back home.
In September, 1,642 Lithuanian citizens emigrated, while 1,300 returned, according to the State Data Agency. The figures show a turning point after months in which the numbers of people leaving and returning had remained relatively close.
From January through September, 12,294 Lithuanian citizens returned to the country, compared with 11,753 who emigrated – a difference of just 541.
The figures are preliminary and may be revised, the agency said.
Žygimantas Mauricas, chief economist at Luminor Bank, said the trend was concerning because Lithuania had hoped to attract more citizens living abroad to help develop the economy and bring back experience gained overseas.
“I would view this with a certain degree of concern, because Lithuania very much hoped that a significant number of Lithuanian citizens living in other countries would return to Lithuania, contribute to the country’s economy and share the experience they have gained abroad,” Mauricas said.
He warned that Lithuania could record a negative migration balance among its citizens this year for the first time in years if the trend continues.
Wages, prices and security concerns
More men than women are emigrating, and most are of working age. The main destinations remain the United Kingdom, Norway and Germany, according to Vaiva Randytė, a specialist at the State Data Agency.
The reasons for leaving are varied, but economic factors remain important. High housing costs, rising prices for consumer goods and services, and competition in the labour market are among the concerns facing people considering a move abroad.
Mauricas said some Lithuanians see little reason to remain in the country if they can perform similar work abroad for significantly higher pay.
“What difference does it make whether you work in Lithuania and speak a language other than the state language in certain sectors, or work with almost the same people in Sweden, Finland or Norway and earn twice as much?” he said.
Geopolitical uncertainty is another factor, Mauricas said, with fears of war potentially influencing decisions to leave.
He also warned that the longer people remain abroad, the less likely they are to return. Migrants establish social networks, start families and enrol their children in local schools, making a move back to Lithuania increasingly difficult.
“Returning becomes, in a way, a second emigration,” he said.
A 2024 survey found that six in 10 Lithuanians who had emigrated did not rule out returning in the future. However, many did not expect to do so within the next five years.
Keeping ties with the diaspora
As the government seeks to maintain connections with Lithuanians abroad, officials are promoting Lithuanian-language schools to help younger generations preserve their language and links to their ancestral country.
Deputy Foreign Minister Kristupas Vaitiekūnas said the schools offer educational and practical benefits while helping children maintain ties with Lithuania. In the United States, for example, completing such a school can provide an additional point in some higher education admissions processes.
Vaitiekūnas said stronger cultural connections could eventually translate into economic ties, whether through a return to Lithuania, investment or tourism.
“Once that stronger connection with Lithuania is established, an economic connection follows,” he said.
The government is also considering financial incentives to encourage emigrants to return.
Social Security and Labour Minister Inga Ruginienė has proposed a family support package offering between 2,000 and 5,000 euros to returning emigrants. An additional 1,000 euros would be allocated for certain integration needs, recognising that returning families may include children born abroad who need to learn Lithuanian and adjust to life in the country.
Mauricas said such measures would need to form part of a broader strategy to address the reasons people leave.
He argued that Lithuania also needs a clear immigration policy defining how many foreign nationals the country should admit, what skills they should bring and how they should be integrated into society.

The Kremlin is fabricating an offensive against Sloviansk and Kramatorsk: ISW exposed Russia’s information operation
Kyiv • UNN
Russia is exaggerating its advances in Donetsk Oblast to create the impression that Ukraine’s defenses are collapsing. ISW has not confirmed any gains near Sloviansk and Kostiantynivka.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense is spreading exaggerated claims about the advance of its forces in Donetsk Oblast, particularly near Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, attempting to create the impression that Ukrainian defenses are allegedly collapsing. However, the actual situation on the front does not confirm reports by the Russian command. This is stated in a report by the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), UNN writes.
Details
Analysts noted that Russia’s Ministry of Defense claims offensive operations near Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, and Semenivka. At the same time, these settlements are located far beyond the furthest confirmed advance of the occupying forces.
According to the ISW assessment, such reports are part of the kremlin’s systematic information campaign aimed at exaggerating Russia’s gains and creating a false impression of the situation on the battlefield.
Russians claim to have advanced dozens of kilometers
Analysts recorded similar manipulations in other areas as well. In particular, the Russian command claimed an advance near Tarasivka and Havrylivka, although these settlements are located approximately 16 and 15 km, respectively, from the furthest positions to which, according to ISW assessments, Russian forces have advanced.
In the Hulyaipole direction, the occupiers also reported combat operations near settlements located approximately 14–19 km from the confirmed boundary of Russia’s advance.
Analysts noted that Russia’s Ministry of Defense publishes some of these claims on the Russian messenger Max rather than on Telegram. In ISW’s view, this may indicate an attempt to impose an exaggerated picture of successes primarily on a domestic Russian audience.
At the same time, on October 13–14, Russian forces continued attacks on the approaches to Sloviansk and in the Kostiantynivka area, but analysts did not record any confirmed advance in these areas.
Thus, according to the ISW assessment, the kremlin is attempting to portray the Ukrainian defensive line as allegedly collapsing, although the available evidence does not support such claims.

He was released after around 22 hours.The detention took place amid protests in Delhi led by the CJP, which has been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Ebola outbreak spreads to new health zone in DRC: WHO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:46:49 UTC
13:46:49 KST

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to evolve, expanding geographically and in terms of infections and fatalities, the World Health Organization (WHO) Africa regional bureau said on Wednesday as the virus spread to a new health zone.
The number of confirmed cases in DRC has reached 9,066, including 4,381 deaths, since the outbreak declaration in May, according to the latest WHO situation report.
The epidemic has affected seven provinces — Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele, Tshopo and South-Ubangi.
The WHO said the Dakwa health zone in Bas-Uele province has become the latest health zone affected by the Bundibugyo virus strain, bringing the number of affected health zones to 65 since the start of the outbreak.
The report indicated that transmission rates vary widely across the affected regions.
Ituri remains the principal focus of the outbreak, while substantial transmission persists in North Kivu and Haut-Uele.
Catherine Swallwood, incident manager at the WHO in the country, said there is still concern about the high number of deaths in communities, which stands at about 60 percent.
She said in recent weeks, about one-third of all new cases have still been community deaths, meaning health authorities are not detecting cases before the patients die.
The outbreak has become the largest and deadliest-ever recorded in DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 epidemic in West Africa.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has urged enhanced regional preparedness to avert additional spread of Ebola after Kenya reported its first imported case from DRC last week.
Kenyan authorities on Wednesday confirmed a second case of Ebola of the Bundibugyo strain, involving a 39-year-old man who is a close family member of the country’s first confirmed case.

S. Korea's fiscal deficit narrows to 8-year low through August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:46:32 CST
13:46:32 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's fiscal deficit through August narrowed to its lowest in eight years, boosted by a surge in corporate tax revenue from semiconductor giants, government data showed Thursday.
The consolidated fiscal balance, or gross revenue minus gross expenditure, posted a surplus of 5.0 trillion won (3.7 billion U.S. dollars) in the January-August period, turning black from a deficit of 53.7 trillion won in the same period last year, according to the Ministry of Planning and Budget.
The managed fiscal balance, which excludes social security funds to offer a more precise picture of the fiscal health, logged a deficit of 43.0 trillion won in the first eight months of 2026, marking the lowest deficit for the period since 2018.
Gross revenue, including tax and non-tax revenues, jumped 98.0 trillion won from a year earlier to 529.7 trillion won in the eight-month period.
Tax revenue surged 69.1 trillion won to 329.9 trillion won amid skyrocketing corporate tax collections, caused by an unprecedented artificial intelligence (AI) boom leading to soaring global demand for locally-made memory chips.
Corporate tax collections expanded by 28.2 trillion won, and those for income tax and value-added tax (VAT) climbed by 14.4 trillion won and 7.4 trillion won each.
Securities transaction tax mounted by 7.0 trillion won on the back of higher stock trading volume.
Gross expenditure through August reached 524.7 trillion won, up 39.3 trillion won from a year earlier.
As a result of the cumulative fiscal spending, the central government debt stood at 1,372.1 trillion won at the end of August, up 17.9 trillion won compared to the previous month. ■

The trading halts, known as circuit breakers, were triggered on both the KOSPI and KOSDAQ markets on the same day for the first time in about two and a half months since July 29.
Before the full trading halts, the bourse operator already issued consecutive sidecars, or program trading curbs, on both the KOSPI and KOSDAQ markets.
The severe market meltdown was attributed to harder-than-expected inflation data in the United States that renewed fears over the possible prolongation of high interest rates.
Memory chip heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK hynix faced intense selling pressure, dropping 9.7 percent and 11.35 percent each.
The tech sell-off was fueled by growing market skepticism over the long-term payoff of massive artificial intelligence expenditures.
Foreign investors dumped domestic stocks, causing a cascading effect across the overall stock markets. ■

Interview: German business leader urges pragmatic approach to China-EU economic ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
12:46:17 CST
13:46:17 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- Germany and the European Union should address their own structural economic challenges rather than rely primarily on protectionism in response to growing competition from China, a German business leader has said.
As debate over China policy intensifies in Europe, Michael Schumann, chairman of the Board of the German Federal Association for Economic Development and Foreign Trade, stressed the need to distinguish between competitive pressures and the underlying causes of Europe's industrial difficulties.
"Chinese competition is real; it is not, however, the principal explanation for Europe's and Germany's structural difficulties," he said in an interview with Xinhua.
Germany and other European economies face long-standing structural problems, including underinvestment in infrastructure, excessive bureaucracy, high energy and labor costs, and an overreliance on technological advantages that were once taken for granted, he said, noting that competition from China has exposed some of these weaknesses and accelerated the need for change, but it did not create them.
Europe would make a serious strategic mistake if it responded to its competitiveness challenges primarily through protectionism, Schumann said.
The aim should be to rebalance economic ties with China, not sever them, he said, adding that concerns over reciprocity, market access and trade imbalances need to be addressed through dialogue and consultation.
Schumann deems it a priority for Germany to restore industrial competitiveness while remaining open to one of the world's most important markets and innovation centers.
Trade policy may give industries some breathing space, but it cannot replace the structural transformation needed to strengthen their long-term competitiveness, he said.
"China has become a formidable industrial competitor, but competition should not be confused with hostility," Schumann said, describing competition as a potential driver of innovation and renewal.
He argued that Europe's competitiveness ultimately depends on its own efforts to lower energy costs, accelerate planning procedures, improve infrastructure and invest more in education and research. "China cannot do that work for us, and tariffs cannot do it for us either," he said.
Despite increasingly prominent calls for "de-risking" in European political discourse, German companies have continued to invest in China, highlighting a gap between political rhetoric and business decisions, Schumann said.
According to the German Economic Institute, German companies invested more than 7 billion euros (7.8 billion U.S. dollars) in China in 2025, the highest annual figure in four years. A recent survey by the German Chamber of Commerce in China found that 61 percent of German companies planned to increase their investment in China over the following two years, the highest proportion since 2023, Schumann said.
The investment pattern is also changing. German companies already established in China are reinvesting locally, expanding research and development capabilities and localizing supply chains under an "in China, for China" strategy. German headquarters are increasingly learning from their Chinese operations, reflecting a more reciprocal flow of knowledge and innovation, Schumann said.
Having made several trips to China in a year, Schumann said he has witnessed firsthand the dynamism of the Chinese economy.
A visit to Chinese technology company Xiaomi's electric-vehicle factory in Beijing left a deep impression on him. "The level of automation and production efficiency was truly impressive," he said, adding that the experience offered a glimpse into the pace and scale of China's industrial innovation.
"China's dynamic innovation environment is like a 'fitness room' for foreign companies, allowing them to test their capabilities, adapt to new developments and strengthen their competitiveness," Schumann said. He added that German companies are expanding their presence in China not only to access its market but also to remain connected to global manufacturing networks and emerging technologies.
Rather than viewing China solely as a competitor, German companies should seek opportunities to build on their complementary strengths, Schumann said. The future of Germany's automotive industry will depend not only on its ability to compete with Chinese manufacturers, but also on how effectively it adapts to the technological changes reshaping the global market.
"Maintaining an open and pragmatic economic relationship with China is essential to safeguarding Germany's industrial base and securing its future growth," Schumann said, adding that cooperation between the two countries could help their companies strengthen competitiveness and navigate the transformation of the global automotive industry. ■

====================================================================================================

Expert says trust use to avoid tax 'bordering on a joke'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:45:25 UTC
13:45:25 KST

Proposed discretionary trust tax changes divide advocates and experts
In short:
Small business advocates say tax reforms that would see a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts are a "kick in the gut" and another cost for tradies.
One expert says the way discretionary trusts are being used to offset tax bills is "bordering on a joke".
What's next?
If the bill passes, the reforms would come into effect in July 2028.
Small business advocates say it is a misconception that trusts are only used by wealthy families to minimise tax, but one expert says the current system is "bordering on a joke" and in urgent need of reform.
On Wednesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers introduced a bill that would impose a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts starting July 2028 to try to discourage people and businesses from using the arrangement to minimise taxable income.
Discretionary trusts differ from other types of trusts as they allow the trustees to change beneficiaries and how much they receive each year.
Associate Professor Dale Boccabella from the University of New South Wales's Business School of Accounting, Auditing and Taxation told The Business some trusts were being used to distribute income in a way to offset tax bills.
"It's bordering on a joke,"
he said.
"A 17-year-old beneficiary of a discretionary trust, not allocated anything for years and years, and all of a sudden they turn 18, this is a child of the parents, and they get $22,500. Now why do they get $22,500 allocated? It's tax-free. It's under the effective tax-free threshold.
"In a discretionary trust, you can have a two-day-old baby born on the 28th of June being allocated $22,500. I mean, you can see how silly it is."
He said in some cases, the income allocated did not get paid to the children and stayed with the parents.
The treasurer said the reforms would affect less than 10 per cent of small businesses; however, Housing Industry Association managing director Jocelyn Martin said there were costs beyond the tax changes.
"Even before they know whether that structure is going to impact them, they have to seek advice from their lawyer or their accountant, and our members are saying that that could cost anywhere between $10,000 and $25,000," she said.
"It's not enough to say that these changes just impact a small proportion; they impact a large proportion.
"Maybe the result might be that they don't have to restructure, but they need to do the work to find out whether that's what's going to happen or not."
Growing number of trusts
More than 1 million trusts are operating in Australia, with about 84 per cent of them discretionary.
The number of discretionary trusts has doubled since 2001–02.
About one in six small businesses used discretionary trusts in 2022-23, the last year of available data, with Treasury analysis suggesting 140,000 businesses of an estimated 350,000 would not need to pay the new tax.
Ms Martin said about three in five small businesses in the housing industry used a trust structure.
"I think there's an assumption that a trust structure is just something that wealthy people use to avoid or minimise taxes," she said.
"What we see are small businesses that are using the legitimate structure of a trust to manage their business, manage the cycles, the cash flow cycles, to actually pay themselves in a lot of instances as well, because some of our members have said they will pay themselves in good times and not necessarily be able to in bad times," she said.
Questioned on how much tax tradies currently pay, given that the proposed change introduces a 30 per cent minimum, Ms Martin said the HIA's concern was that the change was an additional cost to residential construction.
"Already we know that the tax that is paid by our residential businesses is extremely high," she said.
"But not just that, the cost that they pay to comply with some of these business measures is also escalating all the time.
"So I think our concern really when we say there's another tax on tradies is really it's just another kick in the gut."
Asset protection or 'economic injustice'?
Dr Boccabella said other features promoted by accountants such as asset protection, flexibility and succession planning were not being changed as part of the government's plan, although he believed they probably should be overhauled.
"The other thing with discretionary trusts is that you can set them up so that they have limited liability, a bit like a company," he said.
"If the small business and discretionary trust fails, you might actually end up with creditors not getting their payment.
"You can call that asset protection if you want, but a lot of people would turn around and say, 'Well, isn't that economic injustice, someone not getting paid for their services and goods supplied?'"
Property Council executive director of capital markets, Torie Brown, said the government had ignored the legitimate concerns raised by industry during an expedited consultation process.
"Industry was given almost no time to consider how these radical changes will affect their businesses. Despite the warnings from industry, the government had decided to push ahead and introduce this legislation anyway," he said.
"Changes to trusts is incredibly complex — pulling one thread unravels another. The government announced these changes without considering the impacts they would have on small business and housing supply."
There are also concerns that restructuring trusts would incur stamp duty at a state or territory level, something the New South Wales government has promised to waive if re-elected next year.
The Australian Council of Social Services (ACOSS) welcomed the changes, with CEO Cassandra Goldie saying the current system was being exploited.
"It is not fair that someone earning $200,000 or more, who would usually pay 47 per cent tax on extra income, can bring that rate down to 30 per cent or less by passing income through a discretionary trust to their adult children or a private company, while an average worker pays tax at a rate of 30 per cent of the next dollar earned," Dr Goldie said.
"This reform helps fix this severe unfairness in the system so people on higher incomes contribute according to their ability to pay."

Israel has detained more than 2,000 Palestinian children since 2023: report
At least 350 Palestinian children currently face “harsh conditions” in Israeli prisons.
Israeli forces have detained more than 2,000 Palestinian children since October 2023, the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society said.
In a report released on Wednesday, the Palestinian rights group said Israeli authorities continue to escalate their targeting of Palestinian children. At least 350 Palestinian children are currently facing “harsh conditions” in Israeli prisons.
On Tuesday, Israeli forces arrested at least six children from Hebron in the occupied West Bank, the report said.
The organisation said information regarding the number of children arrested in Gaza is unclear, given the thousands of missing persons in the besieged Gaza Strip, including children, and the ongoing policy of enforced disappearance.
The group said Israel’s policy of detention without charges or a release date constitutes “an additional violation and crime that leaves children facing the unknown and deprives them of family and educational stability”.
Cases of Palestinian children in prison
The report described Israeli practices that begin with “intimidation and arrest” and extend to “torture, starvation and denial of healthcare”.
The group highlighted the case of 15-year-old Mohammed Hamid, who contracted scabies, a contagious skin infestation, while he was detained in Ofer Prison, where rights groups have long documented abuses. He suffered severe infections, underwent heart surgery and was admitted to intensive care in critical condition. He subsequently had one of his legs amputated.
The organisation also highlighted the case of 17-year-old Walid Ahmed, who died in March 2025 after six months in Megiddo Prison. In December, an Israeli judge halted the investigation into his death, stating that although there was evidence of starvation, no definitive cause of death had been established.
American children in Israeli prisons
Ahmed was imprisoned in Megiddo with his friend Mohammed Ibrahim, a teenager from Florida. Ibrahim was released after months of advocacy from US-based organisations and appeals from high-ranking lawmakers.
Mohammed Ibrahim was not the only young American held in Israeli prison without charge – Israeli forces reportedly took Abdalkareem Issa Ahmed Safi from his West Bank home in a late-night raid in June. He turned 18 in detention, and authorities subsequently moved him from a youth holding area into an adult section at Ofer Prison.
Similarly, Israeli forces arrested 16-year-old Adam Wajeh Abdelfattah Karakrah, also an American, in July. Although he was set for release in August after his family secured bail, Israeli authorities abruptly reversed the decision to free him.
The Palestinian Prisoner’s Society called for “real international action” to ensure the release of arbitrarily detained children, enforce investigations and end torture, starvation and the denial of treatment in Israeli prisons.
Israeli forces have detained more than 25,000 Palestinians in the West Bank, and thousands more in Gaza, since Israel’s genocidal war began in October 2023.

What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade Starlink system, and how will its restriction affect Ukraine?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:43:04 UTC
13:43:04 KST

The development – and its dire consequences for Ukraine – has put the spotlight on Starlink -SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a powerful military version developed by Elon Musk’s company for the Pentagon.
Here’s what we know about the two SpaceX systems, how they are controlled and why Zelenskyy has framed the shift as a betrayal by Donald Trump and the US.
What has happened to Ukraine’s connection?
On Tuesday night, Ukraine’s military reported the Starlink satellite communications system, produced by SpaceX but managed by the US government, was no longer working on terminals moving at speeds greater than 100mph (160km/h).
Kyiv installs SpaceX Starlink receptors in many of its drones as part of an onboard guidance system. Kyiv said the change was imposed without any explanation from the US.
How does the restriction affect Ukraine?
The restriction had two immediate consequences: It effectively rendered most of the drones used by Ukraine to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and it hampered air defence systems that stop Russian drones bombarding Kyiv.
Ukraine uses Starlink systems to direct many mid-range drones towards their targets – a critical frontline offensive capability. Russian Shaheds fly at speeds close to 200mph, so the new restriction means Ukrainian interceptor drones have no chance to chase them down.
Starlink is not used for long-range Ukrainian missions that have successfully targeted Russian oil refineries in recent months.
A Ukrainian air defence unit intercepts a Shahed drone during an attack on Kyiv. Photograph: Evgeniy Maloletka/AP
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon. Starshield’s service is separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, but the distinction is sometimes blurry.
Starlink cannot be used for offensive military action, SpaceX says, only defensive activities or for use by civilian clients.
Starshield, however, allows those capabilities and uses enhanced encryption to transmit sensitive information. In addition, Starshield provides users with the ability to integrate sensors on object like drones. Starshield’s secure communications rely on Starlink, the vast network of 11,000 satellites that Musk and SpaceX have sent into space since 2019.
Who made the decision to restrict access, Musk or the Pentagon?
Musk said the Ukrainian military was linked to Starshield, because Starlink is not licensed to clients who are using weapons. He added that any Starshield disruptions being experienced by Ukraine would be the responsibility of the US government, not SpaceX. “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” Musk said, referring to Donald Trump.
A Ukrainian serviceman prepares a Starlink satellite at his positions at the frontline. Photograph: Reuters
The White House has not confirmed or denied Musk’s assertion. But the Trump administration has been pressuring Ukraine to limit its strikes on energy targets inside Russia.
What has the reaction been?
Zelenskyy said he felt personally betrayed by Trump, in an interview with Piers Morgan, saying Kyiv was “losing a strong partner”. As for what it meant for Ukraine and its people, Zelenskyy said: “This decision will bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die.”
In the US, Democrats denounced the Trump administration. “Trump’s making a choice – and it directly aids Putin’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Democrats said in a post on X, describing the restrictions as “unconscionable”.
Republican senator Tom Tillis voiced his concern on X: “Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a gray area for the US government or for American corporations.”

Kazakhstan exports wheatgrass juice to Russia and UAE

The White House denies involvement in restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine – Axios

The White House denies involvement in restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine – Axios
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine contacted the United States over problems with Starlink. The White House said it does not control SpaceX but will look into the situation.
The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump denies any involvement in the alleged restrictions on the operation of Starlink satellite communications in Ukraine. Ukrainian authorities contacted the White House, the CIA, and the Pentagon to determine the causes of the problems with the service. Axios reports this, citing its own sources, writes UNN.
Details
According to the publication, on October 14, senior advisers to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held talks with representatives of the White House. They sought to determine whether Washington had made a decision to restrict Starlink and how the system’s full operation could be restored.
A senior Trump administration official assured them that the White House was not involved in the alleged restrictions and did not control SpaceX. At the same time, the American side plans to contact the company to clarify the circumstances of the situation.
Musk explained who controls Starlink and Starshield
Earlier, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk commented on the situation on the social network X, emphasizing the differences between the commercial Starlink system and the military Starshield.
According to him, Starshield belongs to the U.S. government, and any restrictions on the speed or use of this system are determined by the U.S. military and ultimately by the president.
Starshield systems belong to the U.S. government and are under its control. Any restrictions on speed or use are determined by the U.S. armed forces and, ultimately, by the president of the United States
At the same time, Starlink remains a commercial service under SpaceX’s control. Musk noted that the company allows it to be used for civilian and defensive purposes, but not for offensive military operations.

====================================================================================================

Country diary: Thrilled by Darwin, and the wonder of worms | Lev Parikian
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
04:30:21 UTC
13:30:21 KST

The garden beds are moistened by steady rain, but the ground is still unyielding. A blackbird hops across bare soil. A dart, a jab, and up it comes – a wriggling tube of pink flesh. A simple catch. But when I rummage in the dirt, my only reward is loam under the fingernails. Perhaps I should have brought a bassoon.
I’ve come to Down House. Here, Charles Darwin changed the world. And here he wrote his last book, its title usually shortened for convenience: Earthworms.
“I know not whether it will interest any readers, but it has interested me,” he said. Quite the understatement. When a subject interested Darwin, no aspect of it escaped scrutiny, and earthworms had occupied his mind for decades. They were regarded by many as lowly creatures of the dirt, but he understood their worth.
He tested their potential for intelligence, their sensitivity to atmospheric variations, their senses of taste, smell and hearing. The latter involved his son Frank attempting to stimulate them by tootling his bassoon. It’s no small wonder to stand in Darwin’s study, surrounded by his paraphernalia. All those years of painstaking labour and rigorous observation in the quest for truth… Crikey!
Outside, a circular stone slab sits embedded in the grass. It’s the base for a “wormstone” – a wood-and-copper apparatus that measured the amount and rate of their soil displacement. A layer of about 2mm a year, it turned out. Darwin concluded that few animals “have played so important a part in the history of the world”. He wasn’t wrong – a modern estimate reckons that every 10 years, earthworms turn over the equivalent of all the soil on earth to a depth of one inch.
I prod the ground. Still too hard. Away from the damp loam of the kitchen garden, they’ll be hard at work, aerating and mixing, grinding and digesting organic matter, their excretions converting unpromising clumps into fertile humus. Custodians of the soil.
As I consider those worms, going about their business under my feet, I’m struck by a fanciful thought. Their ancestors were participants in the great man’s final project. Just for a moment, absurd though it is, the connection with something so special feels thrillingly tangible.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Digital Affairs has asked supermarket chains to check their systems for cybersecurity vulnerabilities following reports of a cyberattack on grocery stores in France, the ministry said Wednesday.
The attack was discussed at a Legislative Yuan committee meeting, where lawmakers warned that a similar incident could cause significant damage in Taiwan, per Yahoo News.
In France, hackers remotely accessed refrigeration systems and raised temperatures to as high as 50 C, resulting in major food losses and fires at several stores, Al Jazeera reported.
Legislator Hsu Chih-chieh (許智傑) said a similar attack in Taiwan could lead to significant economic losses, given the country’s high density of convenience stores and supermarkets.

It asked them to inspect connected devices and update their firmware.
TWCERT/CC operates under the Ministry of Digital Affairs and helps address cybersecurity incidents in the private sector.
Digital Affairs Minister Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) said many companies had overlooked cybersecurity when they connected their systems to the public internet a decade ago.
The global trend is now to disconnect systems from the internet unless necessary, he added. Companies can instead connect devices to an intranet and monitor access through a whitelist.

House prices are falling. So why are first-home buyers disappearing?

Unknown Publisher
