Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:08:58 UTC
09:08:58 KST

Mexican court closes case against official over 2023 detention centre fire
Victims’ groups, however, have denounced the ruling as ‘selective’ justice that exonerates a former government head.
A Mexican judge has closed the case against Francisco Garduno, former head of the country’s immigration agency, for crimes related to the 2023 fire at a Ciudad Juarez detention centre that killed 40 migrants and injured 30 others.
The incident was the deadliest event ever to occur at a Mexican immigration centre, and critics said it exposed the shortcomings and irregularities in the country’s detention system.
Garduno faced trial for the crimes of abuse of public office and dereliction of duty after footage from the fire showed guards had failed to respond to cries for help.
On Tuesday, Judge Victor Manlio Hernandez Calderon ruled that Garduno had fulfilled the court-mandated measures required to address the damage. But victims rejected that decision and announced they would appeal.
“Yesterday, corruption and the impunity of politicians protected by power won again,” the Foundation for Justice, one of the NGOs representing some of the victims, wrote on social media on Wednesday.
The victims have also compared the judge’s decision to close the criminal case to a de facto exoneration for Garduno.
In their view, the ruling “confirms that justice in Mexico is selective” and denies the victims “full reparations” and concrete guarantees that such an event will not be repeated.
Miguel Zenteno, one of the foundation’s lawyers, noted that the ruling is not yet final because it will be appealed and because another injunction is pending against the court-mandated reparations, which critics say failed to meet the standards for serious events.
On March 27, 2023, some 70 men were crammed into a locked dormitory with no ventilation and barely any water at the Ciudad Juarez immigration detention centre, on the border with El Paso, Texas.
As night fell, a small group set fire to some mattresses in protest, and within seconds, smoke engulfed the entire area.
Security cameras recorded the guards leaving the area despite cries for help. They made no attempt to open the gates of the dormitory. Only the women, held in another cell, were released. Most of the victims were Central Americans and Venezuelans.
Garduno, a former prison guard and current official at the Ministry of Education, led the National Migration Institute (INM) starting in 2019 and continued in the role until 2025 despite the fire.
The judge had previously ordered Garduno to compensate the families, provide them with free specialised medical care, issue a public apology, provide human rights training to migration personnel and guarantee that the events would not be repeated.
Zenteno acknowledged that the measures were implemented only partially because Garduno did not pay the damages as stipulated by the legal process.
Instead, Zenteno pointed out that the funds came from the INM, and the payments did not fully compensate the families. Furthermore, he added, the victims were not even informed how to access free medical services, and the apology “was a mere formality, not substantive”.
In addition to Garduno, prosecutors accused another former director of the institute of the same crimes.
Six immigration agents – including a military officer and a private security guard – and the two migrants accused of starting the fire are charged with homicide and assault. Most of the officials remain free pending trial.

Russia-US diesel deal already having positive effect – Putin aide to RT (VIDEO)

Russia-US diesel deal already having positive effect – Putin aide to RT (VIDEO)
The Russia-US diesel deal has already helped lower American fuel prices and could pave the way for broader economic cooperation between Moscow and Washington, Russian presidential aide Kirill Dmitriev has said.
Speaking to RT on Wednesday, Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, described the agreement as a win-win for both countries and a “great help to global markets.”
“Diesel futures in New York fell by 5% on the announcement of this cooperation between Russia and the US,” he said.
The agreement was announced on Friday following a phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The US Treasury subsequently issued a temporary sanctions waiver allowing Russian diesel to be sold, delivered and imported into the US until April 7, 2027.
Trump said Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and one million tons shortly thereafter. Up to three million additional tons could become available “within a short period of time,” he added.
The arrangement is aimed at easing soaring fuel prices amid global supply disruptions caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran.
Dmitriev argued that the immediate market response demonstrated the economic benefits of cooperation and the costs of maintaining sanctions against Moscow.
“We are seeing that lifting [US] sanctions on Russian diesel is having an immediate positive effect, including for American farmers [and] the American economy,” he said.
The presidential aide also accused the EU of hypocrisy for criticizing Washington’s decision while continuing to purchase Russian energy.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak recently estimated that the bloc had spent more than $320 billion on Russian energy since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, despite claiming to have sharply reduced its imports.
Trump similarly lashed out at Brussels in a Truth Social post on Monday, insisting that he had “made the right choice for the American People.”
Novak has welcomed Washington’s decision as a step toward stabilizing global energy markets and restoring normal trade. He also announced that Moscow would begin immediately lifting its own restrictions on diesel exports.

Israeli guards shoot Palestinian prisoners with rubber bullets, causing severe wounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:07:21 UTC
09:07:21 KST

Israeli prison guards have shot Palestinian detainees with rubber bullets in confined spaces, leaving one prisoner requiring surgery and another undergoing an operation for a fractured shin, Israeli daily Haaretz reported, citing medical records and inmate testimonies.
According to Physicians for Human Rights Israel and the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, at least 21 shooting incidents have been documented across five Israeli prisons since October 2023.
Rights investigators noted that most cases occurred in late 2025 and the first half of 2026, often at point-blank range and without any preceding unrest or security disturbance.
The most severe incident occurred in June at Ketziot Prison in southern Israel.
Hospital records from Soroka Medical Centre confirmed that an inmate's organ was completely destroyed by rubber-coated ammunition, necessitating immediate surgical excision.
In formal legal testimony, the prisoner stated that guards initially kicked him during a strip search a week earlier before members of the prison service's specialised Masada unit discharged rubber rounds directly into his cell, striking his previously injured groin and knee before dragging him roughly 50 metres while bleeding heavily.
Systemic abuse
Further records from Ketziot revealed that another prisoner underwent emergency surgery in July after sustaining a fractured left shin from a rubber bullet.
A former detainee told Haaretz he was shot at close range in April and denied medical care for 15 days, receiving surgery only upon release.
Rights organisations confirmed that shootings occurred inside sleeping cells, exercise yards, and legal consultation waiting areas.
Although rights monitors formally petitioned authorities in August to prohibit the use of rubber and plastic ammunition in confined settings, the Israeli Prison Service rejected a blanket ban.
Meirav Ben Zeev, a lawyer with the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, emphasised that detainees remain fearful of reporting abuse due to potential retaliation, noting that previous complaints failed to produce prosecutions.
Around 9,350 Palestinians, including 350 children and 90 women, remain incarcerated in Israeli facilities amid widespread reports of torture, starvation, and severe medical neglect.

AfD and BSW deputies voted in favor of the document; together, they hold 44 of the 83 seats in the regional parliament. Representatives of the CDU, SPD, the Greens and the Left Party opposed it.
Berlin rejected the demands of pro-Russian politicians

At the same time, AfD co-chair Alice Weidel called on the German authorities to reach an agreement with Moscow on the supply of diesel fuel, following the example of the United States.

“Every little boat here, every fisherman… is an act of resistance”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Meet Alexandre Anderson – a water defender from Brazil
For Alexandre Anderson de Souza and other artisanal fishers, Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, is a source of livelihood, identity and culture.
But pollution from multiple sources, including the oil and gas industry, industrial waste and untreated sewage has turned the bay into a sacrifice zone. Artisanal fishers face contaminated water, declining fish stocks, eroded mangrove, shrinking fishing areas and increasingly dangerous routes, while polluters profit without paying for the environmental degradation they cause.
Alexandre co-founded Associação Homens e Mulheres do Mar (Association of Men and Women of the Sea – AHOMAR), a network of artisanal fishers that has spent nearly two decades defending the bay and their traditional way of life from the impacts of oil and gas infrastructure. Several environmental human rights defenders (EHRDs) told Amnesty International that they feared for their safety, some facing intimidation and harassment.
Among them, Alexandre has been repeatedly threatened and has survived several attempts on his life. Here, he shares his story:
My name is Alexandre Anderson. I am 54 years old; I am a fisherman and I have been living and working in Guanabara Bay since 1997.
Artisanal fishing is not just a means of subsistence. It is our culture, a way of life.
In the 1990s, we felt that something was already changing in Guanabara Bay. Our elders say that when the first refinery started to work, the bay suffered a lot. There was a lot of oil around because it was next to two rivers and these rivers were used to illegally discharge sewage.
I’m not the oldest fisherman in the region, but the elders say that fish used to be abundant here, and they disappeared. It wasn’t a natural phenomenon, it was a phenomenon of man’s influence, an industrial phenomenon. Oil is not synonymous with wealth, it’s not synonymous with growth, it’s synonymous with destruction.
“No one warned us”
I remember that I used to sail, on a rudimentary boat… always built by us. With the disappearance of fish, we had to go further into the sea, and I had to buy an engine for the boat. The fish kept moving away, because the shore was increasingly polluted.
The fishermen were then forced to leave the region or change profession. Some say that this is environmental racism. Some say that this is a ‘sacrifice zone’. There has been no public communication… no consultation in our community. No one warned us. When we came to know about the industry, the infrastructure was already being built in the middle of the sea, or in the middle of a beach. (With growing industry presence) there was violence, physical violence, even personal violence against some leaders. Unfortunately, at dawn on 18 January 2000, there was a big (oil) leak in the water caused by an oil pipeline. This whole area was contaminated, and we were pushed away from artisanal fishing. We were pushed to leave everything that we understand – cultural, religious, traditional – and even leaving the place where we were raised, where we were born.
“We are successful in what we do because we work with the truth”
We revolted against everything that was happening and started to look for actions we could take. In 2003 we started to search for answers as a group, and we founded the Associação Homens e Mulheres do Mar (Association of Men and Women of the Sea – AHOMAR).
Soon after in 2009, through our monitoring efforts, we were able to remove two oil sites which were illegally occupying our space and contaminating our region. We are successful in what we do because we work with the truth and we do not work alone. We’re supported by many well-known organizations, such as Amnesty International and observers have even accompanied us to these sites.
In 2009, we lost a treasurer and our founder was shot. In 2012, we had two more deaths of artisanal fishers monitoring the bay. But we are resilient, history will remember us as a resistance and as heroes, and the oil giants will be remembered as destroyers and polluters.
… History will remember us as a resistance and as heroes,
… and the oil giants will be remembered as destroyers and polluters.
Alexandre Anderson
The killings came after sustained threats against Alexandre Anderson de Souza and other members of AHOMAR. The threats relate to complaints the group have made against the construction of a gas pipeline in the bay, and environmental damage that is threatening artisanal fishers’ livelihoods.
On 22 May 2009, the treasurer of AHOMAR, Paulo César dos Santos Souza, was beaten and shot in the head in front of his wife and children; the following year Márcio Amaro, a founding member of the association, was also shot dead in his house.
Both cases remain unresolved.
“We are resilient, but we didn’t ask for this”
Every little boat here, every artisanal fisher who still bravely wakes up early or arrives late from the sea, is an act of resistance. As long as there are boats like these, they cannot take over Guanabara Bay. Protecting artisanal fishing territories means ensuring that rivers and seas continue to be a source of life and dignity, and not just profit.
Guanabara Bay represents everything. It’s our livelihood and our struggle is against large companies. Sometimes we don’t have any more space to fish, it’s something we always tell them. We are not after money, we only want what is ours, we just want to fish in Guanabara Bay, it’s our right and they are taking away our rights.
We are resilient, but we didn’t ask for this. We must resist or we die. We transformed our tears into struggle. This revolt, this sadness that is part of our history, (but) we transformed it into action.
We transformed our tears into struggle.
This revolt, this sadness that is part of our history, (but) we transformed it into action.
Alexandre Anderson
The struggle in Guanabara Bay reflects a reality observed all over the world: fossil fuel and other extractive projects benefit a few at the expense of nearby individuals and groups. But it also tells the story of community power: artisanal fishers leading the fight for environmental and climate justice.
Their stories cannot be erased.

Vishal Prasad, Fiji
Antonia Burke, Australia
Chief Dsta’hyl, Canada
Knowledge is power

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
00:00:00 UTC
09:00:00 KST

Florida can enforce state law barring young kids from social media, appeals court rules
- Florida can enforce H.B. 3, a law barring under-14s from social media with addictive features, after the 11th Circuit said it does not breach free speech rights.
- Tech groups NetChoice and the CCIA, backed by Meta, TikTok and Snap, sued to block the law. NetChoice said it is “currently evaluating all of our options”.
- The court also sent Florida’s case against Snap back to state court. Florida says the law protects children’s mental health, while critics say it limits teens’ online speech.
AI generated
ATLANTA – A federal appeals court on Oct 14 allowed Florida to enforce a state law barring children under 14 from accessing social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok or Snapchat, rejecting tech industry groups’ claims that the law violates the US Constitution’s free speech protections.
In a unanimous ruling, a three-judge panel on the Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals vacated a lower court’s preliminary injunction blocking the law, known as H.B. 3.
The court said the law does not regulate the content hosted by social media sites and therefore does not run afoul of the First Amendment.
“HB3 applies to platforms wholly without regard to the topics discussed or the ideas or messages conveyed on them,” wrote Circuit Judge Kevin Newsom, an appointee of President Donald Trump.
“Truth Social is just as likely as Instagram to be affected by HB3.”
Representatives for Florida Attorney-General James Uthmeier, who defended the law, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The law bars social media platforms that have so-called addictive features, which include things like video autoplay and infinite scroll, from allowing children under the age of 14 to create accounts.
Tech industry groups NetChoice and the Computer & Communications Industry Association, which count Meta Platforms, TikTok and Snap as members, had sued in 2024 to block the law.
In a statement after the ruling on Oct 14, Paul Taske, director of the NetChoice Litigation Center, said the group is “currently evaluating all of our options as we continue the fight to ensure Floridians’ rights to free expression online are protected, and parents remain in the driver’s seat when it comes to making decisions for their families”.
Snap sued
Florida was among the first of several states to pass a law regulating social media use for children amid a broader reckoning over the apps’ role in young people’s mental health.
After H.B. 3 took effect, Uthmeier sued Snapchat owner Snap in April 2025, accusing it of illegally employing features that addict children and opening accounts for children aged 13 and younger. S
nap said H.B. 3 and the lawsuit sought to restrict teens’ speech online in violation of the US Constitution.
A few months later, the judge overseeing the industry groups’ lawsuit granted their request for a preliminary injunction blocking the law’s enforcement, saying H.B. 3 was likely unconstitutional.
Uthmeier appealed that ruling to the 11th Circuit, and the court had stayed the injunction while it weighed the case.
Separately, a lower court overseeing Florida’s case against Snap had rejected the state’s request in August 2025 to order Snap to comply with H.B. 3, also finding the law likely violated constitutional rights.
But in a second ruling on Oct 14, the 11th Circuit vacated that decision and said the case should move forward in state court, not federal.
A representative for Snap declined to comment. REUTERS

Zhuozhuo Community / WEI+ Design
Unknown

Architects: WEI+ Design
- Area: 9532 m²
- Year: 2026

Photographs:Wei Wei
- 
Manufacturers: Minimaist (vases)
- 
            
            Lead Architect: Shi Jianwei
Text description provided by the architects. Located in the heart of the Taoyangli Historic District in Jingdezhen, Zhuozhuo Community is an urban regeneration project that transforms a collection of existing buildings, residential structures, and traditional alleyways into an open, multifunctional cultural community. Situated between Zhongshan North Road, a historic commercial street dating back approximately 600 years, and the Imperial Kiln archaeological site, Taoyangli preserves the layered urban fabric of Jingdezhen's ceramic heritage. Former workshops, residences, guild halls, and narrow alleyways form a dense urban environment shaped by centuries of porcelain production, commerce, and everyday life. Rather than preserving individual buildings as isolated objects, the project explores how historic urban spaces can accommodate contemporary functions while retaining their architectural identity and cultural continuity.

BULLHEAD CITY, Arizona – US President Donald Trump said on Oct 14 that he wants to see Pope Leo XIV “get well” after the pontiff underwent surgery in Rome this week to remove a cancerous tumour.

“His brother’s a friend of mine who’s a great, he’s a fantastic guy, and his wife. You know, they’re big Trump supporters,” Trump said, adding “his brother loves him a lot, loves the Pope a lot, and that’s good. That’s good enough for me”. AFP

Eight U.S. states have sued OpenAI over ChatGPT, accusing the company of having a dangerous impact on users
Kyiv • UNN
Prosecutors from eight states accuse OpenAI of ChatGPT’s dangerous impact on users, particularly teenagers. They are demanding changes, compensation, and fines.
As many as eight U.S. states have filed lawsuits against OpenAI, accusing its ChatGPT chatbot of having a dangerous impact on users, particularly teenagers. Prosecutors believe that artificial intelligence may encourage people to harm themselves and others. Reuters reports, according to UNN.
Details
The lawsuits were filed by the attorneys general of Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska, and West Virginia. They claim that ChatGPT was specifically designed to build users' trust through friendly interaction.
At the same time, according to the plaintiffs, the chatbot may reinforce dangerous beliefs, encourage risky behavior, and even help plan violent acts, including mass attacks.
Prosecutors demand that OpenAI change how ChatGPT operates
The prosecutors accuse the company of violating consumer protection laws and misleading people about the chatbot's safety.
The states are asking courts to order OpenAI to change the principles governing ChatGPT's operation, pay compensation, and pay civil penalties. The demands also include restrictions on developing artificial intelligence models capable of improving themselves independently unless the company guarantees that they align with human values.
As Reuters notes, this is the largest coordinated legal campaign by U.S. states against OpenAI. Florida filed the first similar lawsuit in June.
The company is also involved in dozens of private lawsuits related to ChatGPT's potentially dangerous impact. As of publication, OpenAI had not provided comment on the new allegations.

What is celebrated on October 15 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:43:25 EEST
08:43:25 KST

What is celebrated on October 15 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 15, several international commemorative dates are observed around the world, while believers commemorate saints according to the new and old calendars.
On October 15, the world observes International Rural Women's Day, Global Handwashing Day, and International White Cane Safety Day. According to the new-style church calendar, Saint Euthymius the New is commemorated, while according to the old style, Hieromartyr Cyprian, Holy Martyr Justina, and Venerable Andrew are remembered, UNN writes.
International Day of Rural Women
An official UN international observance proclaimed by the General Assembly in 2007. The event highlights the important role of rural women in ensuring food security, developing the agricultural sector, preserving traditional communities, and overcoming poverty. The day calls on governments to eliminate gender barriers to access to land resources, credit, modern education, and medical services in rural areas.
Global Handwashing Day
Launched in 2008 by the Global Handwashing Partnership with the support of UNICEF and WHO. This educational observance highlights a simple but vitally important hygiene practice — washing hands with soap, which is the cheapest and most effective way to prevent the spread of intestinal and respiratory infections, especially among children in developing countries.
International White Cane Safety Day
Established in the United States in 1964 at the initiative of the National Federation of the Blind and subsequently supported by the World Blind Union. The white cane is an international symbol of blind and visually impaired people. The event aims to draw public attention to the needs of people with visual impairments, ensuring an accessible urban environment, road safety, and equal opportunities in employment and everyday life.
Pregnancy and Infant Loss Remembrance Day
A commemorative observance established in 2002 in the United States and Canada that has since gained international scope. This day gives parents and families who have experienced the loss of a child through miscarriage, pregnancy loss, stillbirth, or sudden infant death syndrome an opportunity to share their grief.
The Day of Remembrance of Venerable Euthymius the New
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate Venerable Euthymius the New of Thessalonica — an outstanding Byzantine ascetic who embraced monasticism on Mount Olympus, pursued asceticism on Mount Athos, and founded a monastery near Thessalonica. On this day, they also remember Saint Venerable Martyr Lucian, presbyter of Antioch — an outstanding theologian and founder of the Antiochian School of Theology, who carried out a detailed translation and editing of the books of Holy Scripture and suffered a martyr's death for his faith during the reign of Emperor Maximian Galerius.
According to the old calendar, believers commemorate Hieromartyr Cyprian and Holy Martyr Justina. According to tradition, Cyprian was a pagan sage and sorcerer in Nicomedia, but after witnessing the steadfastness of the virgin Justina's faith in the face of his magic, he sincerely repented, was baptized, became a bishop, and together with Justina suffered a martyr's death during the reign of Emperor Diocletian.

Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:34:00 UTC
08:34:00 KST

Scientists reveal 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost in just 73 years
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Flinders University
- Summary:
- A groundbreaking study suggests that 2.22 million Indigenous Australians lived on the continent before European colonization, far more than previously believed. Researchers estimate that 93% of this population was lost within 73 years, revealing a demographic catastrophe on a scale that dramatically changes our understanding of Australian history.
- Share:
New research suggests that Australia's Indigenous population before European colonization was far larger than historical estimates have indicated. Scientists now estimate that approximately 2.22 million Indigenous people lived across the continent before the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788, potentially up to seven times the number suggested by some earlier calculations.
The findings also reveal the devastating scale of the population decline that followed colonization. According to the researchers, an estimated 93% of Australia's Indigenous population was lost within less than 80 years of European arrival, a much greater decline than previously recognized.
Professor Corey Bradshaw, a Global Ecology Professor at Flinders University and Chief Investigator at the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CIEHF), contributed to the national research effort. Working alongside Indigenous partners, the team is investigating how Indigenous population numbers have changed throughout Australia's history.
By combining advanced computer models with several sources of historical and scientific evidence, the researchers developed new estimates that substantially challenge previous assumptions.
"Understanding the size of Indigenous populations in Australia before European invasion in 1788 is essential to truth-telling and reconciliation," says Professor Bradshaw.
New Evidence Reveals Millions of Indigenous Australians Before Colonization
To reconstruct Australia's Indigenous population before European settlement, the researchers brought together ethnographic observations, archaeological findings, genetic reconstructions, and computer models. They also examined how many people different environments across the continent could have supported.
Earlier population estimates often relied heavily on calculations made during the 1930s by anthropologist Alfred Radcliffe-Brown. His influential assessment placed Australia's Indigenous population before colonization at approximately 250,000 people.
However, Radcliffe-Brown recognized that his estimate did not fully account for the devastating effects of deadly diseases, violence along colonial frontiers, and broader structural violence. Subsequent research has shown that these forces had a much greater impact than was historically acknowledged, suggesting that many early population figures were already substantial underestimates.
Using modeled and genetics-based estimates (supported by, but not relying on, historical or ethnographic accounts), the team calculated a median Indigenous population of 2.22 million before colonization. This corresponds to approximately 0.29 people per square kilometer across Australia.
The figure is substantially higher than earlier historical estimates, which generally ranged from 250,000 to 1 million people.
Researchers believe those lower estimates were influenced by the widespread population losses caused by disease, frontier violence, and systemic oppression before the earliest Australian censuses were conducted.
A Devastating 93% Population Collapse After 1788
The revised population estimate also allowed scientists to calculate the scale of the demographic catastrophe that followed European colonization.
Using their model alongside early census records, the researchers estimated that approximately 2.06 million excess deaths occurred between 1788 and 1861. That represents an average of roughly 28,200 excess deaths annually over the 73-year period.
By 1861, the Indigenous population had declined to an estimated 7% of its size before colonization, representing a staggering 93% reduction.
"These devastating findings highlight the major impacts of invasion experienced by Indigenous Australians, and demonstrate their remarkable survival, resilience and recovery over the past century," says lead author Associate Professor Alan Williams, a Partner Investigator in CIEHF representing EMM Consulting and who is also an Adjunct Research Fellow at James Cook University.
Although Australia's Indigenous population has increased since the 1950s, it has not yet returned to its estimated size before European arrival.
According to the 2021 Australian census, the Indigenous population was approximately 37% of the study's estimated median population in 1788.
If population growth continues along current trends, the researchers project that Indigenous population numbers may not return to their estimated pre-colonial level until around 2047.
What the Findings Mean for Australia's History
Beyond revising historical population figures, the study highlights the long-lasting consequences of colonization for Indigenous Australians.
The researchers say the scale of the demographic collapse has important implications for understanding intergenerational trauma, persistent disadvantage, and the development of policies that better support Indigenous communities.
"The findings highlight the scale of demographic catastrophe experienced by Indigenous Australians due to colonization, with the implications being a heightened understanding of intergenerational trauma and to inform future policy that assists Indigenous people. In addition to recognizing this intergenerational trauma and disadvantage, it is also time to recognize intergenerational privilege," says co-author Distinguished Professor Lynette Russell of the Monash University Indigenous Studies Centre and CIEHF.
The findings also demonstrate why scientists must draw on several independent methods when reconstructing population histories, particularly when written records are incomplete, unreliable, or shaped by historical biases.
By combining genetic research, archaeological evidence, environmental modeling, and historical information, the team was able to develop a more comprehensive picture of Australia's Indigenous population before and after European colonization.
Distinguished Professor Larissa Behrendt AO, Chair of the CIEHF Centre Advisory Committee, says the findings demand a fundamental reassessment of the country's history while also recognizing the extraordinary endurance of Indigenous Australians.
"These research findings challenge us to rethink the scale of what happened after 1788. We are not talking about a marginal consequence of colonization but a demographic catastrophe at the heart of the Australian story. But the research also tells us something extraordinary. Our survival is one of Australian history's most remarkable stories," said Distinguished Professor Larissa Behrendt AO Chair, CIEHF Centre Advisory Committee.
The study, "Large size of the Australian Indigenous population prior to its massive decline following colonial invasion," was published in Nature Human Behaviour. Its authors are Alan Williams, Raymond Tobler, Billy Griffiths, Sean Ulm, Matthew Nitschke, Michael Bird, Shane Ingrey, Frédérik Saltré, Kirsty Beller, Ian McNiven, Nicholas Pitt, Lynette Russell, Alistair Paterson, Christopher Wilson, and Corey Bradshaw.
The research received joint funding from the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Indigenous and Environmental Histories and Futures (CE230100009) and the Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for Australian Biodiversity and Heritage (CE17010001).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Flinders University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Alan N. Williams, Raymond Tobler, Billy Griffiths, Sean Ulm, Matthew C. Nitschke, Michael I. Bird, Shane Ingrey, Frédérik Saltré, Kirsty Beller, Ian J. McNiven, Nicholas Pitt, Lynette Russell, Alistair Paterson, Christopher Wilson, Corey J. A. Bradshaw. Large estimated size of the Australian Indigenous population before its extensive decline following colonial invasion. Nature Human Behaviour, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41562-026-02571-9

Trump on Oct 14 cited what he cast as a strike against Iran that involved US military assets from Missouri, saying a leak of key details forced him to reschedule that operation.

Trump and his allies have long fulminated against what they see as unfavourable coverage of the war on Iran, a conflict the President once said would take weeks – and often claims will end soon – but is now in its eighth month with no signs of concluding.
Trump’s rallies are often freewheeling affairs, with speeches stretching well over an hour long that often highlight cultural wedge issues to mobilise his base.
While Trump always makes a point to talk up the economy and defend his record including on tariffs, he regularly weaves to incorporate off-topic matters unrelated to the pocketbook issues concerning voters.
Yet Trump’s focus on leakers – as well as other issues like demanding his political adversaries take cognitive tests – threatens to distract from his overall closing message ahead of midterm elections widely expected to centre around affordability and the economy.
Trump’s campaign stop in Arizona and Montana was part of a month-long campaign blitz to boost Republican candidates ahead of the Nov 3 midterm vote.
The rallies marked his third and fourth this week, following stops in Ohio and Alaska, with more events slated later this week and next, including in Georgia, with plans to continue barnstorming right up to Election Day.
The president’s low approval ratings have hampered Republicans across the map as voters lament his handling of the economy and climbing costs for food and fuel, driven in part by the war on Iran.

Trump has called on the Fed to cut rates instead.

Meanwhile, Trump has sought to assuage voter concerns about the economy, the election’s dominant issue.
On multiple occasions on Oct 14, he insisted that high prices at the pump will fall after the war with Iran concludes, despite the lack of a clear off ramp, and touted fresh investment projects.
That economic messaging has struggled to break through with voters more attuned to day-to-day pocketbook concerns and wage growth.
Trump’s busy campaign itinerary, with stops primarily in very conservative areas of the country, underscores how Republicans are playing defence even in states that are traditional strongholds or that he carried in the 2024 election.
Trump has long clashed with the press, assailing critical reports as “fake news”, but has escalated his efforts to target the media in his second term, including barring reporters from MS Now, Politico and CNN from the White House due to what he described as unfavourable coverage.
Those outlets sued Trump, alleging that he violated their First Amendment rights and winning temporary relief.

Türkiye's Foreign Minister Fidan arrives in Baku for Asian security summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:30:28 UTC
08:30:28 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has arrived in Azerbaijan's capital, Baku, ahead of the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA).
Hosted by Azerbaijan as the current CICA chair, the summit convenes representatives from member states, observer nations, and international organisations to bolster regional connectivity, digitalisation, and sustainable development.
The gathering is expected to adopt the Baku Declaration alongside a formal framework on occupational safety and health, whilst announcing Laos' accession as a new member.
Addressing the forum on Thursday, Fidan will stress the need for collective solutions based on consultation, consensus, mutual trust, and regional ownership to tackle global crises and geopolitical challenges, while calling for the preservation of UN-centred multilateral diplomacy.
Fidan is also scheduled to raise Israel's continuing genocide in Gaza, condemning illegal settlement expansions and severe restrictions on humanitarian aid to Palestinians.
Institutional transition
Fidan will also champion deeper economic integration across Asia, highlighting Türkiye-backed infrastructure initiatives such as the Middle Corridor and the Development Road.
He will advocate aligning the Middle Corridor with China’s Belt and Road Initiative to consolidate transcontinental trade routes.
On emerging technologies, Fidan will urge a human-centred approach to artificial intelligence that safeguards digital sovereignty, whilst reaffirming Ankara's climate commitments as future host and president of COP31.
Established as a dialogue platform, CICA brings together 28 member states encompassing roughly 90 percent of Asia's landmass and more than half the global population.
Under its 2024–2026 chairmanship, Azerbaijan is spearheading efforts to accelerate CICA's transformation into a fully fledged international organisation.
Türkiye, a founding member that chaired CICA from 2010 to 2014, coordinates key institutional portfolios spanning military-political cooperation, counterterrorism, and trade.

Roundup: Houthis, Saudi-led coalition trade fresh strikes as Houthis vow further attacks on airports, oil facilities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:28:36 CST
08:28:36 KST

A civil defense worker inspects damaged facilities inside a house damaged by missile debris in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, Oct. 14, 2026. (The Saudi Civil Defense/Handout via Xinhua)
RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen's Houthi group continued on Wednesday, with both sides carrying out fresh attacks and the Houthis vowing to continue targeting airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in the coming days.
In a statement posted on social media platform X, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group's forces targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile, claiming it was a "precise and direct" hit.
The announcement came hours after the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital earlier in the day, while residents received aerial-threat alerts on mobile apps.
The Saudi Civil Defense said later in the day that one Arab resident was injured and a residential building and a vehicle sustained minor damage after debris from an intercepted ballistic missile launched by the Houthis fell in Riyadh.
Earlier in the day, Sarea claimed a large-scale missile and drone attack targeting Saudi energy giant Aramco in Dhahran in the Eastern Province, as well as King Khalid International Airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh. He said the operation was carried out in retaliation for Saudi strikes.
Sarea vowed that the group's attacks "deep inside Saudi Arabia" would continue in the coming days, targeting airports and oil facilities. He also renewed a warning to international airlines, civilians and employees to stay away from airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia that the group had designated as targets.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported Wednesday that an unnamed Houthi military source advised Aramco shareholders to "dispose of their shares" to avoid potential losses in the coming days, without providing further details on the basis for the warning or whether it was linked to possible further Houthi attacks on Aramco.
Meanwhile, fighting and airstrikes continued across Yemen. Sarea said Wednesday evening on X that Saudi-led coalition forces had carried out 42 strikes using warplanes and missiles on what he described as civilian facilities in the capital Sanaa and the provinces of Taiz, Lahj, Marib and Amran, as well as Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Majid Al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for Yemen's government forces, said in a statement that the forces had carried out 2,309 "precise and direct" attacks against Houthi positions using warplanes, drones, field artillery, rocket launchers and sniper units.
The spokesperson claimed the operations had neutralized about 1,250 Houthi fighters and destroyed or damaged more than 460 military vehicles and other equipment.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said they had fired three ballistic missiles at gatherings of government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition in the Ras al-Arah and Al-Mudarabah areas of southern Lahj province, causing a large number of casualties and damage to several military vehicles.
The continued fighting drew fresh regional reactions. During a meeting with Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud in Riyadh on Wednesday, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi condemned the attack targeting King Khalid International Airport and attacks on civilian and vital facilities in Saudi Arabia, describing them as a threat to regional security and stability.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to protecting Saudi Arabia's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity as well as its support for the kingdom's legitimate right to self-defense.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

China calls for end to political deadlock in Libya
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:28:24 CST
08:28:24 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese envoy to the UN on Wednesday called for efforts to break the political deadlock in Libya as soon as possible.
The agreement reached through the UN-facilitated "4+4" smaller convening marked important progress in implementing the political roadmap in Libya. China hopes that the agreement will help unify Libya's state institutions and lay the foundation for national elections and the completion of the political transition, said Sun Lei, China's deputy permanent representative to the United Nations.
At the same time, he said, whether the agreement can be truly implemented depends on whether it can gain broad support from all Libyan parties. In supporting Libya's political process, the international community must uphold the Libyan-led and Libyan-owned principle and avoid imposing external solutions.
The political deadlock must be broken as soon as possible, he told the Security Council.
"Libya's security situation is closely linked to its political process. Any new armed conflict could undermine hard-won mutual trust and render political efforts futile," he said.
Recently, attacks on energy facilities have continued in western Libya, and the resulting tensions are a cause for concern. The parties concerned should stop the attacks and refrain from taking any action that could lead to a deterioration of the situation, Sun said.
The unification of military and security institutions is crucial to maintaining a lasting ceasefire and is also an important condition for ensuring the smooth conduct of elections and the transfer of power. China supports the eastern and western sides in strengthening dialogue, building mutual trust, and accelerating the process, he said.
The international community, on the basis of respecting Libya's sovereignty and ownership, should provide greater support to the country in strengthening border management, combating transnational criminal networks, and curbing the illicit flow of weapons, he added.
Sun also called for efforts to improve economic governance and people's livelihoods in Libya.
The international community should call on all Libyan parties to fully implement the unified budget framework, strengthen fiscal transparency and independent oversight, and make greater efforts to support Libya in combating oil smuggling, to ensure that its oil revenues are used for national development and the well-being of its people. International partners should support Libyan authorities in improving public services and advancing development and reconstruction, to strengthen public confidence in national unity, stability and development, he said.
As a good friend of Libya, China stands ready to continue working with all parties and make greater efforts to help Libya achieve lasting peace and stability and enable its people to live and work in peace and contentment at an early date, Sun said. ■

U.S. stocks close drop as hot CPI revives Fed rate-hike bets
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
07:28:09 CST
08:28:09 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks closed lower on Wednesday after a hotter-than-expected September inflation reading revived bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 48.62 points, or 0.09 percent, to 51,621.48. The S&P 500 fell 86.51 points, or 1.11 percent, to 7,718.94, its first decline of at least 1 percent in more than 50 trading days. The Nasdaq Composite decreased 511.51 points, or 1.88 percent, to 26,692.87.
Three of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors finished higher as investors rotated into defensive names. Health Care rose 2.44 percent and Consumer Staples added 2.38 percent, while Energy edged up 0.8 percent. Technology led declines with a 2.62 percent drop, followed by Communication Services down 1.73 percent.
The U.S. consumer price index (CPI) grew 0.6 percent month on month and 3.7 percent year on year in September, up from 0.4 percent and 3.4 percent in August, respectively, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Wednesday.
"Inflation remains public enemy number one for the market and for the Fed," said Adam Sarhan, CEO of 50 Park Investments.
U.S. Treasury yields were whipsawed by the inflation data. The benchmark 10-year yield spiked above 5.32 percent after the CPI report but later eased to 5.186 percent, ending lower on the day as investors fled to safer assets.
Oil prices gained ground amid Middle East supply concerns. West Texas Intermediate settled at 95 U.S. dollars a barrel, up 1.01 percent, while Brent crude settled at 106.06 dollars, up 0.35 percent.
On the corporate front, Bank of America tumbled 4.76 percent after its profit disappointed, even excluding a 1.2-billion-dollar regulatory fine. Morgan Stanley also declined despite beating estimates, while BlackRock gained after reporting record assets.
AI-linked names were hit hard as fears of higher rates mounted, with Oracle, CoreWeave, Nebius, Marvell and Advanced Micro Devices all tumbling. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 4.3 percent for a sixth straight session.
According to CME FedWatch, traders are pricing in a 37 percent chance of a Fed hike at the Oct. 28 meeting, up from 22 percent on Tuesday, with about a 91 percent chance of at least one hike by December. ■

SC: Tough PMLA bail conditions can't override accused's right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:27:22 UTC
08:27:22 KST

NEW DELHI: SC has said that stringent bail conditions set under special laws such as PMLA cannot override rights granted by the Constitution, holding prolonged incarceration of an undertrial violates the fundamental right to speedy trial.A bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M Pancholi said an accused could not be kept in custody till completion of trial and held that the accused was entitled to bail in case of delay in trial despite the stringent bail conditions under the anti-money laundering law.Section 45 of PMLA prescribes twin conditions for grant of bail.PMLA accused can't be in jail till trial ends, says SCThe PMLA section says no accused shall be released on bail unless the public prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release, and the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. The second condition puts the onus on an accused to convince the court that he is not guilty.The bench, however, said, "The twin conditions under Section 45 of PMLA cannot override the constitutional safeguards under Article 21 of the Constitution, as has been held in the case of Manish Sisodia vs Directorate of Enforcement. Prolonged incarceration, if allowed to continue, will set at naught the constitutional safeguards extended to accused persons."
The court granted bail to an accused who was allegedly involved in money laundering of over Rs 6,210 crore. ED said the accused had created 62 shell companies, 34 people were made dummy directors and 20 companies were manned by his relatives who contributed to the offence. He was arrested in Dec 2024.Granting him relief, the bench said, "We are of the opinion that the culmination of the trial is a time-consuming process, since the trial court will have to go through documents running into thousands of pages and examine around 98 witnesses. The appellant must not be subjected to the rigours of custody as long as the trial is pending. Hence, the appellant must be released on bail, subject to furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it."The bench admitted that economic offences were very serious as they impacted the financial fabric of the country but said the rights of accused too have to be protected."In a bail matter, especially in serious offences, the job of a court is to balance the rights of the state with those of the arrestee. In special laws such as PMLA, the conditions for granting bail are stringent, and the circumstances in which bail can be granted are rare, for the simple reason that economic offences of a large magnitude punch a hole through the financial fabric of the country, causing a top-down ripple effect into the entire ecosystem, resulting in large consequences for most of the population.
That is the justification for making the provisions of PMLA stringent. In the same breath, sight must not be lost of the fact that the institutions have a duty to expeditiously investigate the cases. Process must not be turned into a punishment unto itself," the court said.The bench referred to its earlier verdict in the Manish Sisodia case in which it was held that prolonged incarceration before being pronounced guilty of an offence should not be permitted to become punishment without trial, and keeping the appellant behind bars for an unlimited period of time in the hope of speedy completion of trial would deprive him of his fundamental right to liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

BAKU, October 15. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will take part in the 7th Summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence-Building Measures in Asia (CICA) in Baku.
The top Russian diplomat arrives in Baku on Wednesday and has already held a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi.
According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the event will "address the further development of CICA, including its integration into the broader landscape of cross-platform cooperation across the Eurasian space."
"Discussions are expected to cover a wide range of practical cooperation areas on the CICA agenda, including the spheres overseen by Russia: support for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and the assurance of international information security," it said, adding that the participants will also exchange views on pressing international and regional issues.
One of the summit’s expected outcomes is the accession of Laos to the Conference as a full-fledged member, the ministry said.
The summit’s agenda is expected to focus on issues of ensuring the region’s sustainable development, strengthening connectivity across the broader continent, and addressing new challenges and threats, including in the area of international information security.
The summit is expected to yield a general policy declaration and a document on raising the standards of occupational safety.
CICA is a multilateral dialogue platform for addressing pressing regional issues and deepening cooperation among member states to build confidence in the military-political, economic and humanitarian spheres, as well as in addressing new challenges and threats. The initiative to establish this format was put forward by the then Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev in 1992.
CICA has 28 member countries, namely Russia, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, Egypt, India, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, the Republic of Korea, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan, Thailand, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Uzbekistan, and Vietnam and 15 observers - Belarus, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, the Philippines, Turkmenistan, the United States, Ukraine, Japan, the Arab League, the International Organization for Migration, the OSCE, and the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States.
The CICA Chair is elected for a two-year term, with the possibility of mandate extension. Kazakhstan held presidency in 2020-2024 and was succeeded by Azerbaijan in December 2024. The summits are held every four years.

North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:12:08 UTC
08:12:08 KST

North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.
North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.
The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries".
The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.
Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.
The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.
The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.
Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.
Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts
Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water's surface.
The North's ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries "tactical significance", Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP, as the two launch methods serve different purposes.
"Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range," he said.
"Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept."
North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.
Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.
Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.
North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.
The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.
South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Rivers in Alaska are turning rusty and toxic – scientists have recorded a 70-fold increase in metal concentrations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:12:07 EEST
08:12:07 KST

Rivers in Alaska are turning rusty and toxic – scientists have recorded a 70-fold increase in metal concentrations
Kyiv • UNN
Thawing permafrost is washing metals into Alaska's rivers, changing their color and composition. The pollution threatens ecosystems and salmon.
Due to permafrost thawing, rivers in Alaska are changing color and becoming contaminated with metals, the concentration of which has increased 70-fold in some areas. Scientists warn that this process threatens aquatic ecosystems and local communities. LRT reports this, citing ScienceAlert, writes UNN.
Details
In recent years, researchers have observed an unusual phenomenon in Alaska’s Brooks Range: once-clear rivers and lakes are gradually acquiring a rust-brown hue. The cause may be warming, which is thawing soils that have remained frozen for thousands of years.
Water penetrates thawed rock and leaches iron, aluminum, manganese, zinc, nickel, cadmium, and other elements from it. As a result of chemical reactions, these substances enter rivers, changing their color and composition.
In some rivers, the water has become more acidic than mine drainage
In 2022–2024, scientists studied water in six Alaskan river basins. Some samples were more acidic and contained higher concentrations of metals than mine wastewater.
Particularly alarming levels were recorded in the Salmon River, where one contaminated stream increased metal concentrations 70-fold compared with normal levels.
Researchers link the sharp deterioration in water quality to the record-hot summer of 2019. Afterward, sulfate and zinc concentrations in the rivers rose significantly.
Since 2018, similar phenomena have been recorded in more than 200 rivers and streams across North America. Scientists warn that the contamination may cause vegetation die-offs and declines in populations of salmon, whitefish, and other aquatic animals.

Ballots to be transferred to Israel upon completion of program
Once cast and collected, the physical ballots will be transferred to Israel to be counted as a standard part of the upcoming elections, N12 reported.
The N12 report emphasized the logistical coordination required for the program, with the entire voting process lasting around 30 hours.
The physical polling stations and election materials had to be transported to their respective embassies and consulates ahead of time, and the CEC had to train local polling station teams to ensure a uniform and secure procedure in accordance with israeli election law.

moyo shirt jacket weaves korean hanbok silhouette with east african kitenge textile
the moyo shirt jacket brings together two distinct cultural aesthetics, reinterpreting the traditional korean hanbok's silhouette using kitenge, a signature east african textile.
[FEATURED]
HANBOK SILHOUETTES meet EAST AFRICAN KITENGE TEXTILES in MOYO
The MOYO shirt jacket, developed by design-focused social enterprise Jerrybag in collaboration with designer Hyunah Kim of ili studio, combines the structural silhouette of the Korean Hanbok with East African Kitenge textiles. Named after the Swahili word for ‘heart,’ the garment translates the layered construction, wrapping technique, and relaxed proportions of traditional Korean dress into a modern shirt jacket format.
The design pairs the understated geometry of the Hanbok with the high-contrast colors and dynamic patterns of Kitenge fabric, bridging Asian and African design languages. The familiar shirt jacket format serves as an accessible entry point for consumers in both regions to engage with cross-cultural aesthetic elements.
FROM KAMPALA TO SEOUL: SUSTAINABLE PRODUCTION AND DISTRIBUTION
Production of the MOYO jacket takes place in Kampala, Uganda, through a local women’s cooperative trained at Jerrybag’s Sustainable Design Center, an initiative established in 2024 via the KOICA Inclusive Business Program to support skill-building and entrepreneurship. Hyunah Kim, drawing from her experience living in Rwanda, developed the concept to explore shared design possibilities between Korea and East Africa. The shirt jacket is distributed through AFRO LOOM, a lifestyle design retail platform operating in Seoul and Kampala.

What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:10:00 UTC
08:10:00 KST

What is Starshield, SpaceX’s military version of Starlink?
- Ukraine says SpaceX limited “military-grade” Starlink, raising concern over battlefield drone and air defence support.
- Starlink is SpaceX’s civilian satellite internet service, with more than 11,000 satellites and about 13 million users worldwide.
- Starshield is the Pentagon’s military version, with secure communications, stronger encryption and separate terminals, but it still uses the Starlink satellite backbone.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Ukraine said on Oct 14 that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had restricted “military-grade” Starlink services, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences.
The complaint has drawn renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink, SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service, and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases, they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Oct 14 in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
What is Starlink?
Starlink, the main profit engine of SpaceX, is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier in 2026 when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly US$5,000 (S$6,400) per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about US$25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s Defence Ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters. REUTERS

Denmark pushes back as Trump touts Greenland oil and mineral deals
Recent US-Greenland-Denmark agreement excludes mining or drilling rights while reinforcing Greenland’s sovereignty.
Denmark has demanded that US resource exploration in Greenland respect the island’s laws amid President Donald Trump’s claim that oil, gas and mineral extraction will soon begin there.
The Danish Foreign Ministry reaffirmed on Wednesday that last month’s agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the US did not alter the rules for extraction.
The agreement “does not grant investors from the US any preferential treatment” over investors from other NATO and EU countries when it comes to access to natural resources in Greenland, the ministry said.
In a post on Truth Social, US President Trump called the semi-autonomous Danish territory “our new and beautiful Greenland”.
“Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin,” he wrote, without providing details.
What the deal covers
Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen signed the 10-page agreement on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on September 22, ending months of tensions over Trump’s threats to control Greenland.
The deal allows the US to “modernise and expand” its activities at the Pituffik Space Base, a remote US military installation in northwest Greenland.
It also paved the way for two new military bases and Trump’s “Golden Dome” missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
It did not allocate any rights for mining or drilling.
Greenland’s ban
Greenland banned uranium mining and all future oil exploration in 2021.
Its government is reviewing whether a Texas firm, Greenland Energy, can use permits that predate the ban.
The company said in August it planned to drill for oil in 2027 at an untested basin on Greenland’s east coast, although it lacked its own permit.
Danish security policy adviser Jacob Kaarsbo said Trump’s comments could signal that his desire to control Greenland remains unchanged.
“It is extremely dangerous to view this agreement between the Trump administration and Denmark as something that has altered Trump’s intentions,” he said.
Mikkel Olesen, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told Al Jazeera that details regarding mining and exploration rights remained unclear and that information coming mostly from the US side should be taken “with a grain of salt”.
Richard Weitz, a fellow at the NATO Defense College in Rome, said Trump “backed down and settled for less” than he sought, but still “got pretty much everything he wanted, except formal annexation”.

Stopping Pip for ADHD or autism would not make big savings, says thinktank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
23:01:15 UTC
08:01:15 KST

Banning people with anxiety, ADHD or autism from claiming disability benefits would not deliver major financial savings and would probably make it harder for them to get or stay in a job and participate in society, a leading thinktank has warned.
The Resolution Foundation said any proposals to make certain mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions ineligible for personal independence payments (Pip) would be “crude changes” aimed at hitting unrealistic savings targets.
But it warned that Pip was “failing on several fronts” and called for a major overhaul to keep a lid on costs – currently rising at an “unsustainable” rate – and restore public trust in a benefit widely seen as unfair and dysfunctional.
About £4.4bn a year could be saved if Pip support was better targeted, it said. Cash support could be removed from an estimated one in six working-age Pip claimants (670,000) who report having no extra costs as a result of their disability.
However, it added that any reforms should proceed with caution because of the success of Pip in ensuring high numbers of disabled and ill people were able to participate in “economically valuable” activities, such as work, caring, training or volunteering, that they would not be able to do otherwise.
Official concern over Pip has soared in recent years, in part because of the rapidly rising number of claimants, particularly among young people, with much of that sharp increase linked to claims for mental health, ADHD and autism.
Spending on Pip in England and Wales has risen in real terms by 183% since it was introduced in 2014. This year the bill is expected to be £28bn, rising to £34bn by the end of the decade, according to official forecasts.
Attempts by the previous Labour administration under Keir Starmer to push through £5bn of crude savings to Pip collapsed last year amid a rebellion of backbench MPs. His successor, Andy Burnham, has said renewed attempts to reform benefits would not involve “crude cuts”.
Welfare officials, who are awaiting an official review of Pip by welfare minister Stephen Timms and the Milburn review of the youth jobs crisis, are understood to be considering proposals to exclude under-25s from the Pip system.
Pip has also found itself at the heart of culture war rows, with some, such as the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, arguing it should not be paid to claimants with so-called “mild” conditions that were not disabling or likely to incur higher daily living costs.
The Resolution Foundation said attempting to link Pip awards to particular conditions was simplistic and impractical as most claimants reported multiple conditions – often combining physical, mental and behavioural conditions.
Lindsay Judge, the thinktank’s research director, said: “Pip is a vital benefit for disabled people that enables them to participate in society and live fuller and more active lives. But the current system is failing on several fronts – claimants don’t trust it, awards don’t fully reflect the nature of disability today and spending is rising unsustainably.
“As well as continuing to provide cash awards to help with ongoing additional costs, a reformed Pip system should focus on supporting disabled people to participate in society. A system more attuned to people’s needs would also mean that around one in six current Pip recipients who don’t face significant limitations or additional costs because of their disability would no longer qualify for cash support.
“There is no perfect system of disability support, but one that better reflects the fact that people often have multiple and fluctuating conditions must target greater support and engagement where it’s needed, and avoid waste where it’s not.”
A Department for Work and Pensions spokesperson said: “Pip is awarded based on a functional assessment that determines how a condition impacts a person’s day-to-day needs. But as the Timms Review report made clear, Pip is no longer fit for purpose and the recommendations from its final report will lay the foundation for sustainable reform.”

ICE rejects recommendation for body cameras that automatically record
The immigration agency has rejected a report from a government watchdog, making suggestions for improved body camera policy.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a United States agency that has taken a central role in President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, has rejected a government report calling for its agents to wear body cameras that automatically activate.
On Wednesday, the Government Accountability Office, a nonpartisan agency that provides research to Congress, released a report recommending an update to ICE guidelines for camera usage.
It suggested that “automated camera activation” would be helpful in situations where “unexpected and unplanned incidents, unrelated to sensitive operations, result in use of force by or against personnel”.
“Given the important role of body-worn cameras in law enforcement activities, we maintain that additional controls are needed to help ensure that ICE personnel capture footage in accordance with policy,” the report said.
Automatic activation, it added, would address difficulties ICE agents face in manually turning on their cameras during enforcement operations.
But ICE has rejected the recommendation for automatic activation, which could be triggered by an agent pulling a gun or turning on a car siren. The agency cited privacy concerns.
But the Trump administration faces public pressure to improve transparency during its immigration raids.
Agents from ICE and other agencies such as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) have faced accusations of excessive force and civil liberties violations.
In January, two US citizens – Renee Good and Alex Pretti – were shot to death in separate shootings in Minneapolis, Minnesota, during immigration operations.
The New York Times estimated in July that immigration agents had opened fire on at least 25 people since the start of Trump’s second term. A CBS News review updated this week counts at least 30 shootings, with nine people killed and 13 others wounded.
ICE has often blamed such incidents on aggression against its agents, and it has argued that its officers have opened fire to defend themselves from danger.
But in several cases, that rationale has come under scrutiny.
Critics argued that video footage in Good’s fatal shooting disproved government statements alleging that she had weaponised her vehicle against agents. Her car, according to observers, appeared to be turning away from agents, not towards them.
In another case, ICE agent Christian Castro was accused of making false statements about a shooting that resulted in injury to Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan man living in Minneapolis.
Castro faces federal charges for allegedly lying about being attacked with a snow shovel and broom before the shooting, after video footage contradicted his account. Castro pleaded not guilty last month.
More recently, on October 8, immigration agents shot a man named Oscar Belgal in New York City while his five-year-old son was in the backseat of his car. ICE stated that Belgal appeared to be “going towards officers” in his car when they opened fire.
On Tuesday, a judge rejected the government’s effort to have Belgal deported.
Activists say better recording procedures for body camera footage could help clarify what happened in such incidents.
But the Trump administration has largely refused to implement reforms to ICE protocol.
Earlier this year, Democrats in Congress delayed funding for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, on the basis that significant changes needed to be made to reduce incidents of excessive force.
The department said on Wednesday that automatically recording cameras could result in “the unauthorised recording of sensitive interactions with informants or victims”.
The agency added that all ICE offices had received body cameras as of August 5, but that training in their use was still ongoing and would be finished “soon”.
