Trump Aides Admit the House is a Lost Cause
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Trump White House aides see almost no paths to Republicans keeping control of the House in the midterm elections and are more focused on redoubling their efforts to save the Senate majority.
That has been the takeaway for officials in GOP groups who have been discussing the state of play with White House aides in recent weeks, according to three sources familiar with the situation.
It all comes as the White House moves into damage-control mode after contemplating for the first time earlier this month, as Inner Loop previously reported, that Republicans could possibly lose both chambers of Congress.
The general expectation is that the House has become a lost cause. Races that Republican congressional leadership once thought they could flip in order to offset Democratic gains are no longer considered attainable.
The Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Speaker Mike Johnson, has now pulled ad buys in Democratic districts in Michigan and Ohio they were hoping to flip, as well as in the Republican seat being vacated in Nebraska by the retiring Don Bacon. The fund also started canceling remaining ad reservations in two House races where Republicans are seeking reelection in New Jersey and Iowa.
White House aides have shifted their focus to pushing an all-out defense of the Senate majority, which is also looking problematic but to a lesser degree than the House, the sources say. (Polling models and prediction markets agree.)
The aides see the Senate as still in play in large part because early returns for mail ballots have been relatively strong and comparable to 2024 presidential election levels in key Senate battleground states, sources say.
Trump officials at MAGA Inc. have also privately discussed how if Republicans can win some combination of senate seats in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, that would form a firewall that complicates Democrats' path to snatching control of the Senate.
Still, Trump officials appear to have conceded they are unlikely to win in North Carolina. Senate Republicans’ campaign arm has paused ad spending in North Carolina since the start of October, mirroring pullbacks by other outside groups.
“President Trump is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in both the House and Senate,” says White House spokesperson Liz Huston in a statement.
The state of play—retreating from a state like North Carolina, where Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair is on the ballot—would have been unthinkable just a few months ago.
But it speaks to the torrid political climate for Republicans heading into the last stretch of the midterm cycle, which appears to worsen by the week as high gas and living prices caused by the Iran war remain sticky in voters' minds.
With 20 days until the election, sources say, Trump officials are looking to get maximum turnout from the MAGA base in November, rather than trying to capture swing voters who polls show are not breaking for Republicans.
"Republicans remain laser focused on winning and protecting and expanding President Trump's majorities,” says Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassare in a statement. “We're thinking outside the box to fight the typical midterm precedent.”
The effort has manifested in a direct voter outreach play with the president crisscrossing the country to reach out directly to his supporters, showing up at rallies in states that should have been reliably Republican.
Trump started the week by hitting the trail in Ohio, where Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown has been polling consistently ahead of Republican Jon Husted, who has weathered negative ads branding him as "the face of data centers."
On Tuesday, the president flew to Wasilla, Alaska—once the home of former governor and vice presidential nominee Sarah Palin—to help the Republican Senate incumbent Dan Sullivan, who has been trailing Democrat Mary Peltola.
And after stumping in Arizona and Kentucky later this week, Trump is set to host a $1 million-per-plate fundraiser dinner for MAGA Inc. at his Mar-a-Lago club, replenishing a war chest that is being emptied at an increasing rate.
Trump has remained steadfast in his belief that he can drive his supporters to vote in November if he hits the trail, as he did in the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections, a person familiar with his thinking tells Inner Loop.
But Trump, whose polling continues to be among the worst on record for any president, is not always wanted at rallies. To date, the president has not done a rally in Iowa with Republican candidate Ashley Hinson, who recently began to buck the president and called for measures that would help end the Iran war altogether.
This is an edition of Hugo Lowell’s Inner Loop newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Palantir and London mayor settle lawsuit over UK police contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:59:59 UTC
05:59:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Palantir and London mayor's office settle lawsuit over UK police contract
US tech firm Palantir and London mayor Sadiq Khan's office have settled Palantir's lawsuit over a decision to block a £50 million ($66 million) contract with London police, both parties said on Wednesday.
Palantir had agreed a two-year contract with the Metropolitan Police to use its artificial intelligence systems to automate certain tasks and for analysing evidence.
But the mayor's office refused to approve the deal, telling the Met Police it had failed to have an open competition for the contract, with reports also quoting a spokesperson for Khan citing concerns Palantir did not align with "London's values".
Palantir's supply of software for the US military and immigration services, plus billionaire co-founder Peter Thiel's political views, have drawn scrutiny as European governments grow increasingly wary about dependency on US tech platforms.
The company was challenging the decision to block the Met contract, but Palantir and the Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime said in a joint statement that they had resolved the case and "withdrawn their allegations against each other".
MOPAC's decision not to enter into the contract "was not based on Palantir's values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company", the statement said.
It added that MOPAC "does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir" and that it was welcome to participate in any procurement processes.
The settlement comes as Britain is conducting a review of a £330 million National Health Service contract with Palantir, while a parliamentary committee said the company had a "clear mismatch with UK values" and recommended using a break clause, a suggestion Palantir's British CEO Louis Mosley called "irresponsible".

Eight US states sue OpenAI, claiming ChatGPT harms children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:54:28 UTC
05:54:28 KST

Eight US states sue OpenAI, claiming ChatGPT harms children
WASHINGTON – A bipartisan group of eight states said on Oct 14 they had sued OpenAI in courts across the country over harms they say ChatGPT has caused to their residents, alleging the chatbot has coached its users – including teenagers – to harm themselves or others.
Attorneys-general from the states, which include Iowa, Kansas and Arizona, filed the lawsuits independently in state courts, claiming ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to earn the trust of users.
But the chatbot reinforces delusions, encourages dangerous behaviour and assists users in planning violence like mass shootings, the lawsuits claim.
The lawsuits represent the most significant coordinated state action against an artificial intelligence company, adding to a wave of legal challenges OpenAI faces as it prepares for a public listing. Florida’s attorney-general filed the first such state suit in June.
The lawsuits accuse the company of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about the safety of ChatGPT. The states also allege that the company created a public nuisance by endangering the health of their residents.
The lawsuits seek orders forcing OpenAI to make changes to how ChatGPT works. Among other things, the states want the company barred from developing AI models that can improve themselves unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values.
The states, which also include Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia, are also seeking civil monetary penalties for OpenAI’s violations of state law as well as damages.
A spokesman for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The company is also facing dozens of lawsuits by private plaintiffs, alleging ChatGPT helped users plan mass shootings or other violence. REUTERS

Unknown

UNITED NATIONS, October 14. /TASS/. Ukraine’s intelligence, security and defense operatives are behind the creation of ‘secret prisons,’ where inmates are being tortured, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said.
"What exactly are these ‘secret prisons’? They are basements, zindans, stone pits and even outdoor cages exposed to the rain and scorching sun," he told an unofficial Arria-formula meeting of the UN Security Council. "As a rule, they are hidden within guarded quarters of Ukrainian formations, where no foreign inspectors or human rights monitors are allowed."
"Militants, sadists and operatives from the GUR [the Main Directorate of Intelligence], the SBU [the Security Service of Ukraine] and other Ukrainian security agencies with faces concealed behind masks and balaclavas, hold total sway there," the Russian diplomat continued. "They are tasked with beating the required confessions out of prisoners or coercing them into cooperation under the threat of death, and are allowed to use any means necessary for the purpose."

AFRL Partners with Virgin Galactic to Gather Data on Space Weather Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:44:00 UTC
05:44:00 KST

Space tourism company Virgin Galactic announced a new partnership with the Air Force Research Laboratory’s space warfare directorate to collect and share space weather data from the company’s suborbital spacecraft, due for its first commercial flight next year.
The two-year cooperative research and development agreement, which Virgin announced Oct. 14, will provide AFRL with key information about space weather to help researchers understand its impact on satellites and infrastructure that reside on orbit—all gleaned from planned flights of the company’s SpaceShip vehicle. Virgin noted that as part of the agreement, AFRL will “evaluate the integration of sensor systems with Virgin Galactic’s next-generation SpaceShip to collect space weather data during flight.”
“This cooperative research and development agreement will help expand and identify new and additional opportunities for our growing fleet,” the company said.
Understanding space environmental and weather conditions—like solar flares and winds, coronal mass ejections, and geomagnetic storms—is important for government organizations and commercial firms alike. SpaceShip’s suborbital flights offer a chance for AFRL to get more insight into a region where those conditions are perhaps less understood: the mesosphere and lower thermosphere, or MLT. Situated between 60 and 110 kilometers above the Earth, the MLT is too low for satellites to operate, but space weather there can disrupt GPS signals and communications.
Shaun Ard, a senior research chemist at AFRL, said high-quality data about MLT space weather dynamics is limited, and the collaboration with Virgin will help the lab’s researchers “protect and advance space-based systems essential to modern infrastructure and exploration.”
Like previous Virgin Galactic vehicles, SpaceShip is designed to be launched from an aircraft “mothership.” After it reaches altitude and is released from its launch platform, SpaceShip will ignite its own rocket motor to reach suborbital space. The company will launch and land the vehicles from Spaceport America in New Mexico. SpaceShip can carry six passengers.
SpaceShip has been moving through integrated ground testing in recent months, and company officials expect to start flight testing in New Mexico this month.
Virgin envisions SpaceShip as both a space tourism vehicle and a research platform and has aggressive plans to ramp up its cadence following its first commercial flight in February 2027. Once its second vehicle enters service next year, it expects to hit a rate of at least 10 flights per month by the summer, company officials said during an earnings call in August.
“This flight rate is an unprecedented achievement in human spaceflight, and this is made possible with our highly reusable spaceship design,” Chief Financial Officer Douglas Ahrens said at the time. “It’s a beautiful machine with vast potential and now we are approaching the moment when we bring it all together with the ramp of commercial spaceflight operations.”

Families of Trinidadian men killed in US boat strike demand accountability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:42:59 UTC
05:42:59 KST

Families of Trinidadian men killed in US boat strike demand accountability
The Trump administration has killed at least 239 people in boat strikes that critics denounce as extrajudicial killings.
The families of two missing men from the Caribbean country of Trinidad and Tobago have marked the one-year anniversary of their disappearance by calling for accountability from the United States.
Since September last year, the US military has undertaken a campaign of attacking small boats in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean, on the basis that they were transporting “narco-terrorists”.
But critics have called the boat strikes an illegal campaign of extrajudicial killings.
On Wednesday, the families of Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo issued a statement remembering the two men, who they said were killed in one of the US boat strikes on October 14, 2025.
The families are currently pursuing a wrongful death lawsuit in the state of Massachusetts, supported by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). They have argued that Joseph and Samaroo were fishermen and farm workers, not drug-traffickers.
“The last year has been devastating without Chad in our lives. Chad was the heart of our family. He was loving, generous and caring and always there for us. We all miss him terribly,” said Joseph’s mother, Lenore Burnley.
“A year later, we are still grieving and seeking justice for his death. We will always mourn losing Chad but hope that this lawsuit will be a step towards justice for him and the family.”
Four other people were killed in the attack on October 14, 2025, when a missile struck a vessel returning to Trinidad and Tobago from nearby Venezuela.
The families have said Samaroo and Joseph had been working in Venezuela to support their families.
Both men called their families two days before embarking on the trip home to the islands. They were never heard from again.
The boat strike campaign, launched under US President Donald Trump, has killed at least 239 people since September 2025.
But the US government has provided little evidence to prove its claims that those on board were trafficking drugs. It has also not publicly identified the victims.
In several cases — from Colombia to Ecuador to Trinidad and Tobago — relatives have stepped forward to say that their loved ones were among those killed, and that they were fishermen with no connection to the drug trade.
Separately, the family of Colombian fisherman Alejandro Carranza has filed a complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, accusing the Trump administration of violating his right to life when it allegedly bombed his boat on September 15, 2025.
Samaroo and Joseph’s lawsuit was filed in January and is being heard by a US federal court in the city of Boston, Massachusetts.
“Not a day goes by when our family doesn’t think about our brother Rishi,” said Sallycar Korasingh, Samaroo’s youngest sister.
“Rishi was a good person, loved by his family and community. The last year without him in our lives has been heartbreaking. My brother and family deserve justice. We will continue fighting for answers and the accountability we deserve.”
Legal scholars have noted that, even if those killed were involved in criminal activity, the strikes would still amount to extrajudicial killings.
Under international law, it is generally illegal to use military force for civilian law enforcement. Drug trafficking is not considered an act of war, but rather a civilian crime.
“For a year now, our clients have had to live without their loved ones and without justice in the name of President Trump’s lawless killing campaign,” said Jeff Stein, staff attorney with ACLU’s National Security Project.
The group is representing the families in their lawsuit, along with the Center for Constitutional Rights.
“These illegal strikes at sea have devastated countless families, terrified communities, and made us all less safe,” Stein said. “We won’t stop fighting for accountability. We urge leaders in both Congress and the executive branch to finally end this illegal campaign before anyone else is killed.”

Germany to hit consumers with new energy levy – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:41:40 UTC
05:41:40 KST

Germany to hit consumers with new energy levy – media
Germany plans to make households and businesses pay for a national emergency gas reserve costing more than €3 billion over ten years, German media reported Wednesday, citing draft legislation.
First proposed in July, the 24 TWh reserve would equal 10% of Germany’s storage capacity, or two weeks’ winter consumption, protecting against import disruptions.
The Economy Ministry initially proposed funding it through household and industrial levies rather than the federal budget, but the plan stalled after governing coalition lawmakers rejected this notion, citing already excessive energy costs. Industry associations also demanded state funding. However, media reports claim that despite the backlash, the ministry is pressing ahead with its initial plan.
An October 12 draft leaked to Handelsblatt and other outlets estimates the reserve at €3.08 billion ($3.4 billion) over ten years, enough to replace Germany’s largest gas import facility for 30 days. Unlike seasonal storage, the government-controlled stockpile would be off-limits commercially, reserved for crises including sabotage and infrastructure failures. It would not lower gas prices.
Starting in October 2027, households would pay an extra €3.77–€7.20 ($4–$8) annually through gas bills to fund the reserve. Total yearly costs are estimated at €247 million to €308 million, with households and commercial users covering 40% and industry the remaining 60%, although how much individual industrial consumers would pay remains unclear. Final costs will depend on gas purchases, storage, transport, financing, staffing, and operating expenses. Germany’s state-owned gas market manager, Trading Hub Europe (THE), would set the levy annually rather than the federal government.
Energy Minister Katherina Reiche previously considered budget funding or a hybrid model. However, severe budget constraints reportedly prompted the ministry to stick to its initial plan of 100% consumer funding. Frankfurter Rundschau reported that the draft has already been submitted for interministerial coordination. However, it remains far from becoming law, with government approval, parliamentary scrutiny, and votes still ahead, and discussions in the Bundestag over a possible hybrid financing model ongoing.
Julia Verlinden, deputy parliamentary group leader of the Greens in the Bundestag, has criticized the move, telling DPA that citizens would feel the impact of the ambitious gas plans “directly in their wallets.”
Germany’s post-Russian gas predicament
Germany has faced years of severe energy pressure since abandoning Russian supplies following the Ukraine conflict’s escalation in 2022. Alternative imports have sharply raised costs for energy-intensive manufacturers. Berlin has spent approximately €50 billion ($58 billion) cushioning soaring prices since cutting Russian gas imports, Die Süddeutsche Zeitung and Bild reported last month.
The US war on Iran and disruption of the Strait of Hormuz have intensified pressure. Although most German LNG comes from the US, the strait’s effective closure disrupted nearly 20% of global LNG supply, driving wholesale prices higher and undermining commercial incentives to buy and store gas.
As a result, German electricity bills remain among Europe’s highest, averaging 31.4-39.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in late 2026, or roughly €45-€50 monthly for a single-person household. Berlin ranks fourth among European capitals for residential electricity costs.
Meanwhile, Germany’s conventional gas reserves have been under mounting pressure ahead of winter. Following a sluggish summer refilling season, they are reportedly hovering around 60% capacity, an unusually low level for October. German network operators earlier called the EU’s November 1 target of 80%-90% “virtually unattainable.” In September, Berlin even took the unusual step of ordering state-owned SEFE to purchase and inject 8 TWh to shore up winter supplies.
Soaring bills have deepened political divisions. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has gained traction by calling for a return to cheaper Russian energy, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s increasingly unpopular coalition faces pressure over costly gas-fired backup plants and climate-neutrality commitments.
Nord Stream, drones and the ‘Russian threat’
The proposed reserve’s focus on sabotage is particularly notable given the 2022 Nord Stream bombings, which severed key routes for Russian gas to Germany and compounded the country’s energy crisis. Berlin initially refrained from assigning blame, but in July 2026, German prosecutors charged former Ukrainian military officer Sergey Kuznetsov, alleging the attack was carried out by individuals acting on behalf of Ukrainian state bodies. Kiev denies involvement, while Moscow has blamed the West.
The proposal also comes as Berlin and Brussels increasingly cite the purported Russian threat to push through legislation, including tighter security measures and higher defense spending. Just last month, German officials accused Russia of drone activity near airports and other critical infrastructure. Moscow denies the allegations and insists it poses no threat to Europe, describing such warnings as fearmongering aimed at demonizing Russia and distracting from mounting domestic economic and political problems.
Moscow calls Western energy sanctions illegal and counterproductive, arguing that they redirect Russian exports while forcing Europeans toward costlier supplies. Russia has repeatedly offered to cover shortages and resume deliveries but says it received no response. Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev warned earlier this year that EU countries would “inevitably beg” for Russian gas as prices rise.

Letting Ukraine into EU would be economic suicide – Le Pen
Admitting Ukraine to the EU would amount to “hara-kiri” for the bloc and inflict immense damage on France, right-wing French politician Marine Le Pen has warned, using the Japanese term for ritual suicide.
Le Pen has long criticized military and financial support for Ukraine, repeatedly pledging to end France’s direct aid to Kiev and calling for sharp cuts to EU-wide assistance.
The politician has emerged as the frontrunner in France’s 2027 presidential race, according to the latest opinion polls, and is projected to defeat both left-wing and centrist rivals in potential runoffs.
Le Pen made the remarks in an interview with the Financial Times published on Wednesday, arguing against Kiev’s longstanding ambition to join the bloc. Making Ukraine a member would be tantamount to “committing hara-kiri,” a scenario bound to result in “absolutely huge economic losses” and the effective loss of sovereignty for France, Le Pen stated.
Earlier this month, the EU rejected Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s demand that Ukraine be admitted by January 2027. EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos described the deadline as completely unrealistic, stating Kiev must meet all requirements for “merit-based” membership. A recent survey by the Bertelsmann Foundation indicates support for facilitating Ukraine’s accession has continued to wane, dropping below 50% across the bloc.
Le Pen also reiterated her position on aid to Ukraine, arguing that France, as well as the EU as a whole, could no longer afford to bankroll Kiev.
“The honest thing to do with Zelensky is to tell him, to warn him, in fact, that, listen, we can’t do more, we can’t manage more. [The EU] has already done €90bn of loans; that’s €18bn for France. €18bn is really a lot,” Le Pen told FT.
Separately, she made similar remarks to the Dutch VRT NWS broadcaster, insisting that Paris must tell Zelensky it “can no longer provide this financial assistance” and that the Ukrainian leader should seek monetary help elsewhere. “Perhaps there are other EU countries that are in better financial shape,” Le Pen said, without specifying any candidates for footing France’s bill on Ukraine.

Houthis turn to China for missile parts as threat to Israel and Saudi Arabia grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:38:06 UTC
05:38:06 KST

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
The rebels expand their ambition, an analyst says
The Houthis have tried to acquire key parts from Chinese suppliers that could be used to make a version of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile, according to the report. The Kheibar Shekan has a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
“The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed,” said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, a research outfit specializing in tracing the flow of arms in war zones around the globe. “These types of parts are very specific, and producing them would have required design information related to the missile.”
They’re “not goods that can be used for a variety of civilian applications,” Hinz said.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.
China is a major purchaser of both Iranian and Saudi oil and leveraged its ties with both countries to broker a rapprochement in 2023. It has condemned a series of attacks on Saudi airports by the Houthis and called for a de-escalation in the fighting.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government launched a military campaign last month aimed at driving back the Houthis from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical Middle East trade route for oil and other goods.
Yemen interdicted key components to building missiles
The Conflict Armament report was based on information released by Yemeni government authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments that included suspicious equipment.
The shipments originated from China and were intended to be delivered to Hodeidah, a Yemeni port that Israeli officials say has been commonly used by the Iranians as a weapons transfer point. China accounts for the largest share of seized shipments destined for the Houthis, according to U.N. reports.
Components integral to the functioning of a missile were among the parts found in the cargo. They included stabilizing fin cores, rocket motor aft closures with nozzle attachments, and rocket motor igniters.
The cargo also contained phenolic resin, a material used in creating ablative heat shields. These shields protect ballistic missiles from the intense heat associated with atmospheric flight at high supersonic speeds, the report said.
Hinz said that the combination of materials made clear that the Houthis intended to assemble that specific type of Iranian-designed missile.
“This particular type of system is very difficult to smuggle. And you can’t just disassemble and reassemble them,” he said.
Houthi weaponry has grown more sophisticated over time
The Houthis rose to prominence more than 20 years ago as an insurgent group armed with Soviet-era and North Korean weapons seized from the Yemeni government’s military.
But over the years, the group’s access to advanced weaponry has expanded and so has its ability to menace neighbors.
In the current weekslong conflict with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and utilized maneuverable warheads and long-range drones. They previously have fired scores of drones and missiles at Israel, more than 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away.
Over the past week, they managed to puncture the kingdom’s stout air defense system with strikes on Riyadh’s international airport that killed at least 18 people.
Iran could find value in redundancy
Iran has been an important supplier of blueprints and components for the Houthis. But procuring parts from beyond Tehran could be crucial for the group.
"Redundancy is an asset, not a liability in military planning,” said Benham Ben Taleblu, a senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. “With a blockade of Iran in place, the Houthis are diversifying.”
The rebels had long received weapons and materials smuggled from Iran. But the shipments have changed and now more often contain components rather than intact weapons.
The group’s arms program has been “increasingly backstopped by a hybrid, global supply chain serviced by a web of participants — including tribally connected smugglers across Yemen and businessmen working from export hubs in eastern China,” according to research published earlier this year by The Century Foundation, a Washington think tank.
Security forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government have repeatedly intercepted missile components and launch equipment at the port of Aden, according to Yemen’s Aden Counter Terrorism Unit.
Yemen experts believe that the Houthis still rely on Iran for more sophisticated components needed to manufacture guided missiles, including navigation and control systems. But the group has expanded its capacity to manufacture and assemble weapons domestically at facilities deep inside territory under their control.
“The Houthis cannot yet manufacture highly complex weapons systems, and … they still rely heavily on Iran for technology and many critical items,” The Century Foundation report said. “The group has reached a capability tipping point and can build a significant proportion of some weapons systems using imported components.”
Yehoshua Kalisky, a senior researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, said that the Houthis’ supply chain historically mirrored that of other Iranian proxies, including Hamas and Hezbollah.
Iran is among the world’s most advanced in ballistic missile development. And both in Gaza and Lebanon, Iran-backed militant groups have smuggled in raw materials, and relied on Iran for more sophisticated components and assembled weapons themselves, he said.
Kristian Ulrichsen, a Middle East fellow at the Baker Institute, said that the Houthis’ growing reliance on Chinese components could have broader implications for politics in the Gulf.
“Now that the situation has really escalated and seen these attacks on infrastructure and airports, we could see more pressure from the Saudis,” he said, noting that China is Saudi Arabia’s largest trading partner.

World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkiye
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:33:20 UTC
05:33:20 KST

World’s oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkiye
Culture Minister Ersoy said it sheds light on ancient maritime trade in the eastern Mediterranean.
Turkiye’s Culture Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy has said the country unearthed ancient treasures from what he called “the world’s oldest shipwreck”.
Underwater excavations near Kekova Island in the southern Antalya province uncovered ceramic storage jars dating back 4,700 years to the Early Bronze Age, Ersoy announced in a post on X on Wednesday.
While the vessel’s wooden hull did not survive, archaeologists recovered the ancient storage jars following an underwater excavation project launched earlier this year.
The jars, believed to have transported olive oil or wine, provide concrete evidence of early maritime trade and cultural exchange across the eastern Mediterranean, according to the ministry.
Clay analysis indicated the containers were manufactured in workshops in the Jordan Valley, matching similar styles previously found in Egypt, Turkiye, and Greece that illustrate extensive Bronze Age sea routes.
One vessel was singled out for its unique design, featuring nine markings and two holes in its body that suggest it may have been used to churn butter or cheese.
Researchers believe the ship was sailing from the Levantine coast towards modern-day Hisarlik in Turkiye or the island of Crete in Greece when it capsized and sank.
The excavation was directed by Hakan Oniz, an associate professor of archaeology at Akdeniz University.
Speaking to the BBC, the professor said when his team first found the wreck four years ago, the jars only appeared to be a century or two old.
“However, we later became excited when we saw the same amphora forms in a publication on Egyptian archaeology and returned to the site,” he said. “Indeed, they were similar to those found at the Giza pyramids in Egypt. We were incredibly excited.”
The discovery has “shed light on the deep-rooted history of maritime trade along the Anatolian coasts,” added Ersoy.

Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with Chinese supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:32:45 UTC
05:32:45 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis look to build ballistic missiles with more Chinese supplies, report says
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are attempting to build a new advanced medium-range ballistic missile system with the help of Chinese parts, according to a new report released Wednesday by a group that tracks the use of weapons in conflict zones.
The report by the U.K.-based Conflict Armament Research group came as the Houthis, in their ongoing war with Saudi Arabia, are demonstrating remarkable ability to wreak havoc on one of the Middle East’s best equipped militaries.
The weaponry under development could help the group more precisely target the Saudis and Israel. By turning to China, it also appears to be a sign of increasing independence.
The rebels expand their ambition 
The Houthis have tried to acquire key parts from Chinese suppliers that could be used to make a version of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision-guided missile, according to the report. The Kheibar Shekan has a range of roughly 1,200 miles (2,000 kilometers).
"The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed," said Fabian Hinz, a senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, a research outfit specializing in tracing the flow of arms in war zones around the globe. "These types of parts are very specific, and producing them would have required design information related to the missile."
They're "not goods that can be used for a variety of civilian applications," Hinz said.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington didn't respond to a request for comment.
China is a major purchaser of both Iranian and Saudi oil and leveraged its ties with both countries to broker a rapprochement in 2023. It has condemned a series of attacks on Saudi airports by the Houthis and called for a de-escalation in the fighting.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government launched a military campaign last month aimed at driving back the Houthis from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical Middle East trade route for oil and other goods.
Yemen interdicted key components to building missiles 
The Conflict Armament report was based on information released by Yemeni government authorities in July after officials interdicted two shipments that included suspicious equipment.
The shipments originated from China and were intended to be delivered to Hodeidah, a Yemeni port that Israeli officials say has been commonly used by the Iranians as a weapons transfer point. China accounts for the largest share of seized shipments destined for the Houthis, according to U.N. reports.
Components integral to the functioning of a missile were among the parts found in the cargo. They included stabilizing fin cores, rocket motor aft closures with nozzle attachments, and rocket motor igniters.
The cargo also contained phenolic resin, a material used in creating ablative heat shields. These shields protect ballistic missiles from the intense heat associated with atmospheric flight at high supersonic speeds, the report said.
Hinz said that the combination of materials made clear that the Houthis intended to assemble that specific type of Iranian-designed missile.
"This particular type of system is very difficult to smuggle. And you can’t just disassemble and reassemble them," he said.
Houthi weaponry has grown more sophisticated over time 
The Houthis rose to prominence more than 20 years ago as an insurgent group armed with Soviet-era and North Korean weapons seized from the Yemeni government's military.
But over the years, the group's access to advanced weaponry has expanded and so has its ability to menace neighbors.
In the current weekslong conflict with Saudi Arabia, the Houthis have fired ballistic missiles and utilized maneuverable warheads and long-range drones. They previously have fired scores of drones and missiles at Israel, more than 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) away.
Over the past week, they managed to puncture the kingdom’s stout air defense system with strikes on Riyadh’s international airport that killed at least 18 people.
Iran could find value in redundancy 
Iran has been an important supplier of blueprints and components for the Houthis. But procuring parts from beyond Tehran could be crucial for the group.
"Redundancy is an asset, not a liability in military planning," said Benham Ben Taleblu, a senior director of the Iran Program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a hawkish Washington think tank. "With a blockade of Iran in place, the Houthis are diversifying."
The rebels had long received weapons and materials smuggled from Iran. But the shipments have changed and now more often contain components rather than intact weapons.
The group’s arms program has been "increasingly backstopped by a hybrid, global supply chain serviced by a web of participants — including tribally connected smugglers across Yemen and businessmen working from export hubs in eastern China," according to research published earlier this year by The Century Foundation, a Washington think tank.
Security forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government have repeatedly intercepted missile components and launch equipment at the port of Aden, according to Yemen’s Aden Counter Terrorism Unit.
Yemen experts believe that the Houthis still rely on Iran for more sophisticated components needed to manufacture guided missiles, including navigation and control systems. But the group has expanded its capacity to manufacture and assemble weapons domestically at facilities deep inside territory under their control.
"The Houthis cannot yet manufacture highly complex weapons systems, and … they still rely heavily on Iran for technology and many critical items," The Century Foundation report said. "The group has reached a capability tipping point and can build a significant proportion of some weapons systems using imported components."
Yehoshua Kalisky, a senior researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, said that the Houthis’ supply chain historically mirrored that of other Iranian proxies, including Hamas and Hezbollah.
Iran is among the world’s most advanced in ballistic missile development. And both in Gaza and Lebanon, Iran-backed militant groups have smuggled in raw materials, and relied on Iran for more sophisticated components and assembled weapons themselves, he said.
Kristian Ulrichsen, a Middle East fellow at the Baker Institute, said that the Houthis’ growing reliance on Chinese components could have broader implications for politics in the Gulf.
"Now that the situation has really escalated and seen these attacks on infrastructure and airports, we could see more pressure from the Saudis," he said, noting that China is Saudi Arabia’s largest trading partner.

Meink: Operational Prototypes for MMA Drones Coming in 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:32:08 UTC
05:32:08 KST

The Air Force will field operational prototypes for an autonomous drone to replace its MQ-9 Reaper in 2028, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said Oct. 14.
“We’re going to be fielding operational prototypes by ’28, and we’re just awarding the contract now,” Meink said during a panel discussion with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, other service secretaries, and senior Pentagon officials at the annual AUSA conference in Washington. “That’s the speed of what we’re fielding capability, and into production—large-scale production—starting in ’29. That is the goal.”
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine that Meink was referring to the Massed Modular Aircraft, the planned successor to the Reaper.
“The autonomous fighters are already in production,” Meink said, in reference to the Air Force’s Collaborative Combat Aircraft program. General Atomics’ FQ-42A Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A Fury have been selected for production and are undergoing testing with the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit at Creech Air Force Base, Nev.
“Now we’re looking at essentially the autonomous strike platform, the autonomous bomber,” Meink said, referring to MMA. The aircraft is envisioned as a multimission aircraft, like the MQ-9, that can conduct strike missions as well as intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance. In contrast, CCAs are currently focused on an air-to-air role paired with crewed fighters.
Meink previously announced at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the Air Force would field 100 MMAs by 2029 and 500 by 2032.
Air & Space Forces Magazine reported Sept. 30 that the Air Force and Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit had narrowed the field for MMA down to seven companies. An Air Force spokesperson declined to confirm any selections, but Meink said Oct. 14 that “we just awarded those contracts … in collaboration with DIU.” He did not name the specific companies or say how many finalists there are.
Sources have told Air & Space Force Magazine the seven companies still in contention are Anduril, Chaos Industries, General Atomics, Grid Aero, Otto Aerospace, Shield AI, and Swarm Aero. They will develop their MMA candidates and submit a proposal to build a prototype.
The Air Force and DIU want each MMA drone to cost $10 million for the base aircraft, not counting the sensors, weapons, or other equipment it may carry. That’s half the $20 million target price the Air Force envisions for CCAs. MMAs will also use open architecture so they could be more easily upgraded with new sensor packages or weapons capabilities.
But while MMAs will have some autonomous capabilities, they won’t be built with all the latest cutting-edge technology in a bid to keep their price down below that of CCAs. They will likely be powered by turboprop engines, for example.
MMA drones are intended to be able to fly about 4,000 miles, twice the range of CCAs, and carry a heavier payload than CCAs. But they will be slower than CCAs.
The MMA effort is part of the broader push by the Pentagon and the Air Force to field more autonomous systems at a lower cost than crewed platforms, or even the drones that are in service today. The goal is to build “combat mass” to counter China’s growing military, which Meink said is going through “the largest weapons buildup probably in the history of the world,” and to respond to the proliferation of autonomous systems in conflicts of today, and the Pentagon’s view, tomorrow.
“There’s no question that there’s a shift coming,” Meink said. “It’s adaptability, scalability, and affordability. The only way we’re going to meet the threat is with autonomous systems.”
Meink said the Pentagon will work with Congress to secure the funding needed for MMA. The Trump administration’s $1.5 trillion fiscal 2027 budget request for the Department of Defense is currently stalled on Capitol Hill. With midterm elections approaching next month, Democrats could take control of one or both chambers, which could lead to congressional gridlock, particularly surrounding the Pentagon’s request for a massive budget increase—and plans to continue that—amid the war with Iran. The DOD plans to devote tens of billions to autonomous warfare just this fiscal year.
Meink acknowledged the uncertainty surrounding the Pentagon’s budget, but expressed confidence the Air Force would be able to hit its targets for MMA.
“It is heavily dependent upon the resources we get from the Hill, but I think we are not only going to deliver significant combat capability, but we’re going to deliver quickly and efficiently,” Meink said.
“We’ve got to make sure this stuff is affordable,” Meink added, referring to efforts across the Air Force and Space Force. “We’ve got to make sure we’re buying it efficiently. And depending on how you do the comparisons, we’re talking five to 10 times cheaper to field some combat power with these autonomous systems compared to not. So it’s critically important. The good news is, in my mind, there’s no question that the leadership we have in the Air Force, in the Space Force, both military and civilian, is ready to do that. And you see that with the results already. We are integrating autonomous fighters into experimental ops units out at Creech right now, from a year from when they first flew to when we were integrating them into experimental ops units. That’s unheard of. And it only took two years to build the first one.”
The goal for MMA is similarly ambitious.
“It’s in the scalability and the producibility,” Meink said. “In many ways, cost goes with schedule. If something is super expensive, there’s a reason for it, which means it’s probably going to take a long time to build, so we’re really focusing on rapid production and scalability, which means we have to get the cost down on these systems as well.”
Meink’s comments came during a panel focused on the Pentagon’s Project Agincourt, a drive to accelerate the fielding of autonomous systems and create a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, or AUTOWARCOM, which Hegseth announced during a speech late last month.
“The folks who acquire it need to be right there up with the warfighter at the same time who understand how to iterate it and change on and innovate on it,” Hegseth said.
Adversaries such as Russia and Iran have fielded one-way drone attacks to wreak havoc in Ukraine and across the Middle East. Ukraine has used autonomous systems to great effect to defend against Russia’s invasion. Kyiv’s ongoing and thus far successful Operation Vivaldi offensive has relied heavily on the innovative use of drones, including dropping uncrewed ground vehicles behind enemy lines.
“That’s a different battlefield,” Hegseth said. “We’ve learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can’t use everything that’s in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it. So you’ve got to be able to ensure that we take the best of that and the lessons learned … and then push it through [with] an AUTOWARCOM commander with four stars who has the ability to drive that change. So we’ve done a lot with acquisitions and a lot with industry from day one to modernize, realizing this is the future of warfare.”

An OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account and later made a presentation about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges.
In the filing in US federal court in San Jose, California, OpenAI alleged that the presentation happened months ago and that Apple is now making AI products of its own, citing the release of Apple’s HomeView product this week.
“OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple, where Apple engineers can shape Apple’s upcoming products based on OpenAI’s confidential and innovative work,” OpenAI said in its filing.
The two companies were due to face off in court on Wednesday in an ongoing trade secrets lawsuit, but the new allegation delayed the showdown. OpenAI said it may file a countersuit based on the new claim.
Apple said that it has policies and procedures in place to ensure new employees do not use confidential information from previous employers and that it has found no evidence to support OpenAI’s allegations.
The document, filed on Tuesday, is part of a trade secret dispute filed by Apple earlier this year against OpenAI. The iPhone maker alleged its own employees left and took confidential information to OpenAI’s hardware division. OpenAI has denied those allegations.
Earlier this week, US district court judge Edward Davila granted part of Apple’s request for early access to digital files from OpenAI in the suit.
Davila said Apple could gather data from some of its former employees’ devices and sit three of them for depositions on a sped-up schedule, including the two defendants in the case – Chang Liu, a former senior system electrical engineer, and Tang Yew Tan, a former vice-president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch.
The case is likely to go to trial in October 2027, though OpenAI has said in court filings that it could be ready for trial as soon as June 2027.

Mexico to force Meta, TikTok, and X to better protect minors on platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:27:41 UTC
05:27:41 KST

Mexico to force Meta, TikTok, and X to better protect minors on platform
Mexico will require the digital platforms to protect minors from violent and sexual content.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum signed a presidential decree requiring digital platforms, including TikTok, Meta and X, to protect children from violent, sexual and other harmful content online.
The decree establishes that digital platforms must, by design, restrict exposure to content involving violence, harassment or sexual abuse, as well as immediately remove any risky material from the profiles of minors.
Sheinbaum said on Wednesday that the government would back legislation to penalise companies that fail to implement the decree.
“If no progress is made, it would become a law,” she told a news conference on Tuesday.
“The goal is for digital platforms to take on some of the responsibility and refrain from disseminating, promoting, or spreading content related to this type of information — including criminal acts or violent behaviour,” Sheinbaum had said earlier when she indicated she would introduce the decree.
The decree comes after an attack by two 18-year-olds on their former high school in the northern state of Coahuila in early October that killed one and wounded three others.
Digital platforms will have one month to comply with the decree, government adviser Luisa Maria Alcalde said.
Officials said they had already discussed the matter with representatives of social media outlets and streaming platforms such as Meta, Microsoft, Apple, TikTok, Google, X and Huawei.
Last August, Meta, for example, agreed to pay an $18bn settlement in a major US federal case accusing it of endangering children, and was forced to introduce new safety features to platforms including Instagram and Facebook. The lawsuit alleged Meta had violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act by collecting, retaining, and using personal data from children under 13 without proper parental consent.
Mexico’s move follows a broader global push to protect minors online, with governments in Europe and Australia tightening oversight of digital platforms and US states pursuing a range of child-safety measures.
Brazil has also moved to strengthen protections for children online. Such measures have raised questions over how to protect minors while safeguarding privacy and freedom of expression.

Le Pen lands in Brussels lashing out at the European Commission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:27:09 UTC
05:27:09 KST

The French far-right leader wants to strip powers from the EU and cap France’s net contribution to the bloc’s budget at €5 billion a year. “Being pro-France does not mean being anti-Europe,” she says.
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen is preparing to challenge the EU’s powers if she is elected president next May.
The National Rally leader said the European Commission should stop acting in policy areas she considers outside its remit, including health, security and international diplomacy.
"[The Commission] is like the frog in the fable that puffs itself up to be as big as the ox," she said, referring to La Fontaine’s fable, at a press conference in Brussels on Monday. It was following a meeting with leaders of Patriots for Europe, the far-right group her party belongs to.
Le Pen, who leads the polls ahead of the presidential election, also said France’s net contribution to the EU budget should be capped at €5 billion a year, a sharp cut from the current level of around €8 billion, according to figures published by the French Senate.
"Being pro-France does not mean being anti-Europe," she said, setting out several proposals for EU-wide action.
She called for a "real" carbon border tax on imports from countries with weaker environmental standards, with exemptions for products such as fertilisers and coffee that Europe does not produce. She also proposed harmonised taxes on tobacco and alcohol, as well as a common EU corporate tax for large companies, with a single rate of between 20% and 25%.
Le Pen said these measures would help ease the burden on French taxpayers. Last week, she unveiled a plan to save €140 billion over five years, aiming to bring France’s public deficit below 3% of GDP by 2030.
No more money for Ukraine, sanctions relief for Russia
If elected, Le Pen would halt French funding for Ukraine, arguing that France can no longer afford it given the state of its public finances, while pushing for an end to EU sanctions against Russia.
"This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell [Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy] the truth," she said in response to a question from Euronews.
Her position would put France at odds with other EU leaders, who are expected to reaffirm their support for Ukraine at a summit in Brussels on Thursday and Friday.
In February, EU countries agreed a €90 billion loan to cover Ukraine’s budgetary and military needs, with a first tranche of €45 billion due next year. But Ukraine needs around €70 billion in additional funding, its Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has warned.
Le Pen also broke with the broader EU consensus on the need to step up pressure on Russia to end the war.
As the European Commission prepares its 22nd package of sanctions, Le Pen claimed that the restrictions have hurt European economies more than Russia.
"We were right to say that sanctions would have had no impact on Russia and would have increased the price of the raw materials they sell," she said, arguing that EU countries have continued buying Russian oil and gas, thereby enriching Moscow.

Families of American October 7 victims call for US congressional inquiry into massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:24:21 UTC
05:24:21 KST

WASHINGTON - Three years after Hamas's October 7 massacre, and with Israel yet to establish a state commission of inquiry into the failures surrounding the attack, families of American victims are calling for a separate investigation by the United States Congress.
The demand emerged Wednesday during a memorial ceremony at the US State Department in Washington honoring American citizens killed in the attack and its aftermath.
Speaking to The Jerusalem Post following the event, Ruby Chen, father of Israeli-American soldier Itay Chen, said the families could no longer wait for Israel to investigate the circumstances that allowed the massacre to happen.
"Unfortunately, the Israeli government has not seen fit to establish a state commission of inquiry," Chen said.
"Maybe the time has come for the United States, for the US Congress, to establish an investigative commission for the American victims."
Itay Chen was a 19-year-old IDF soldier when he was murdered during the October 7 massacre. His remains were taken to Gaza and returned to Israel in November 2025.
For Chen, the demand goes beyond determining what happened during the attack. He wants an examination of the failures that made it possible.
"For a thousand days now, the families have been waiting to understand not just what happened, but how it happened," he said.
Chen pointed to previous American investigations following terrorist attacks that killed US citizens abroad, arguing that the deaths of Americans on October 7 justify an independent congressional inquiry.
The proposal has not been formally adopted by Congress or the Trump administration. For now, it remains a demand from bereaved families seeking answers and accountability.
During his remarks at the ceremony, Chen also called for legal action against those he said had financed or helped prepare Hamas's terror attack.
He criticized the fact that individuals he believes bear responsibility remain free in countries including Qatar and Turkey, and called on Washington to help bring them to justice on behalf of the American victims.
At least 46 American citizens were murdered in the October 7 attacks, including Israeli-Americans with dual citizenship.
For their families, the effort to secure recognition for their loved ones is increasingly accompanied by another demand: that commemoration be followed by accountability.
Inside the Benjamin Franklin Room: Itay Chen's dog tag returns to Washington
The demand for an investigation formed part of a deeply personal gathering at the State Department's Benjamin Franklin Room on Wednesday morning.
Israeli-American bereaved families came together for a memorial honoring the American victims of October 7, hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his wife, Allison, also participating.
The formal invitation, obtained by the Post, bore the Great Seal of the United States and identified Rubio, Lutnick, and Allison Lutnick as the hosts.
Under the heading "A Memorial for the US Victims of October 7, 2023," guests were invited to attend the ceremony at 10:30 a.m. at the State Department headquarters in Washington.
The invitation was personal and explicitly stated that it was non-transferable.
The event was closed to press coverage, but two family members who participated described its emotional moments in interviews afterward.
For Ruby Chen, one of the most powerful moments came not from a Cabinet secretary, but from a senior American military commander.
Adm. Brad Cooper, head of US Central Command (CENTCOM), attended Itay Chen's funeral in Israel in November 2025.
At the funeral, Ruby gave Cooper his son's military dog tag.
Nearly a year later, as Cooper addressed the bereaved families in Washington, he revealed that he was still wearing it.
"At Itay's funeral, I gave him Itay's dog tag," Chen recalled.
"And today, while he was speaking, he took out the dog tag he was wearing."
Chen said Cooper explained that Itay remained close to him.
For the grieving father, the gesture reflected a personal bond that had developed between the families of the slain Americans and senior US military and administration officials, one that continued well after the return and burial of their loved ones.
'Today, we had a small comfort'
Chen said the idea for Wednesday's ceremony began taking shape about a year earlier, when President Donald Trump hosted a group of living hostages who had returned from Gaza at the White House.
Families of deceased hostages whose remains had been returned were not included in that gathering.
Chen recalled approaching Trump's special envoy, Steve Witkoff, to ask why the families of the dead had not been invited.
According to Chen, Witkoff acknowledged the oversight and said that a separate event should be arranged to honor the murdered Americans and their families.
The families then waited for an appropriate opportunity, eventually settling on a memorial around the third anniversary of the massacre.
Chen credited Allison Lutnick, the commerce secretary's wife, with playing a significant role in making the event happen.
He said she worked extensively to ensure the families received the recognition they sought.
For Howard Lutnick, the ceremony also carried a deeply personal meaning.
The commerce secretary lost his brother, Gary, in the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. The attacks also killed 658 employees of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services company he led.
During the memorial, Lutnick reflected on his own experience of loss and his connection to families whose lives had been devastated by terrorism.
Chen said the ceremony reminded him of a recent conversation with a rabbi about the long recovery process after tragedy.
He recalled the rabbi explaining that healing does not happen all at once. Instead, it is built through a long series of small moments of consolation.
"I think today we can say that we had a small comfort," Chen said.
'I thought it would be very formal, it really came from the heart'
Another participant was Abbey Onn, an American-Israeli whose relatives Carmela Dan and her granddaughter Noya Dan were murdered in Kibbutz Nir Oz on October 7.
Speaking to the Post after the ceremony, Onn said she was surprised by the depth of emotion the American officials expressed.
"It was really exciting. I didn't know what to expect, and I thought it would be very formal, and it really came from the heart of Secretary Lutnick and his wife," she said.
Onn emphasized that Lutnick's personal history made his participation especially significant.
"He lost his brother, and more than 600 people in his company, in 9/11," she said.
For Onn, that experience meant Lutnick understood what it was like to lose loved ones and to return, year after year, to ceremonies of remembrance.
She also praised Allison Lutnick for her involvement with hostage families and her efforts to ensure that their suffering was not forgotten.
According to Onn, Allison had remained supportive of the families and had pushed for continued recognition of the victims.
"They say it's important that we remember everyone, every name, every person, every soul," Onn said.
"And that's our job now, to remember and to live."
She added that the gathering was far more than a routine official ceremony.
"It wasn't standard. It was really from the bottom of their hearts."
Family members addressed the audience during the memorial, including Chen and Onn, as well as another family that had lost both of its daughters.
Rubio, Howard Lutnick, and Allison Lutnick also delivered remarks.
A memorial video displayed the faces of American victims killed on October 7 and in the events that followed.
Onn said the ceremony underscored the shared experiences of Israel and the United States, both of which had endured devastating terrorist attacks over the past 25 years.
"Mainly it was the understanding that we, as Israel and America, have faced two of the worst terror attacks in the last 25 years," she said.
"Our fight is against terror, and our fight is for life."
According to Onn, Rubio drew a connection between the September 11 attacks and the October 7 massacre.
She said the secretary spoke about terrorism's purpose: To make people fear for their lives, their children's safety, and their future.
"What Hamas did on October 7 was to try to make us fear for our lives, to fear raising our children in safety and security, and to fear for our futures," Onn recalled Rubio's remarks.
She added that Americans had experienced the same on September 11.
For Onn, the shared experience of terrorism transcended nationality.
It was a struggle, she said, that united people regardless of which country's citizenship they held.
'There was no siren, we went to school, we went to work'
But the ceremony in Washington also prompted Onn to reflect critically on the way Israel had marked the third anniversary of the massacre.
Despite the commemorations and memorial initiatives held in Israel, she said she had not experienced the same sense of national recognition that accompanies other major days of remembrance.
"I think it's something that we've been missing in Israel," Onn said.
"Look, we just had October 7. There was not a national acknowledgment of the day. There was a civic acknowledgment of the day. It wasn't national."
Onn said the absence of a nationwide memorial siren was particularly striking.
"There was no siren. There was no siren. We went to school. We went to work," she said.
In her view, ordinary life continued without the collective atmosphere of mourning she believed the anniversary deserved.
"It wasn't the appropriate level of respect for the day, in my opinion," she added.
Onn acknowledged that ceremonies and civic initiatives had taken place, but argued that Israel still had work to do in recognizing the significance of the tragedy.
"I think that we have to work harder as a country to accept that this was an awful tragedy that we can't forget," she said.
Her criticism was not limited to remembrance.
Onn also supported calls for an investigation that would establish how October 7 happened and how another catastrophe could be prevented.
"They want a state inquiry. They want a memorial in DC," she said, referring to the bereaved families.
She stressed that 46 Americans had been killed in the October 7 attacks and that the US government had a responsibility to examine what had happened.
"The US government [needs] to understand how October 7 happened and how to make sure that it never happens again," she said.
For Onn, Wednesday's ceremony was an important beginning, but not a conclusion.
She described the memorial as a chance for families to connect, honor those they lost, and ensure their names remained part of the public memory.
But she also insisted that recognition must eventually give way to the harder work of examining responsibility.
"The next step is to do the hard work of understanding what happened," she said.
Three years after the massacre, the families are still navigating grief, the return and burial of loved ones, and the struggle to preserve their memories.
Wednesday's ceremony offered them a moment of recognition from the highest levels of the American government.
Yet for Chen, Onn and other bereaved families, the message emerging from Washington was that remembrance alone is not enough.
With an Israeli state commission of inquiry still absent, they are looking to the United States, and potentially Congress, to help provide the answers they have spent three years seeking.

Yemeni Houthis are attempting to create ballistic missiles with a range of up to 2,000 km using Chinese parts – AP
Kyiv • UNN
The Houthis are procuring components from China for analogues of Iranian missiles with a range of up to 2,000 km. This could intensify their strikes on Saudi Arabia and Israel.
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are attempting to establish production of advanced medium-range ballistic missiles by purchasing the necessary components from Chinese suppliers. The Associated Press reports this, citing research by the British organization Conflict Armament Research, UNN writes.
Details
According to the researchers, the Houthis are seeking components that could be used to create an analogue of Iran’s precision-guided ballistic missile, the "Khorramshahr-4 (Kheibar Shekan)." Its range is approximately 2,000 km, which could potentially allow the group to carry out more precise strikes against targets in Saudi Arabia and Israel.
Analysts note that these are not ordinary dual-use goods, but specific components whose manufacture requires knowledge of missile-weapons design.
The Houthis seek to expand their own missile production
The Houthis’ local ambitions regarding production exceed what was previously believed
According to the researchers, the attempts to obtain Chinese components may indicate that the Houthis seek to reduce their dependence on external suppliers of finished weapons and develop their own production capabilities.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not respond to journalists’ request for comment on the findings of the study. At the same time, Beijing had previously condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi airports and called on the parties to de-escalate.
The report appeared amid a new escalation of hostilities in Yemen. Last month, Saudi Arabian forces and the Yemeni government launched a military operation aimed at pushing the Houthis out of the area of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait—one of the key routes for international trade and oil transportation.

The parliament speaker said the goal was to make Iran strong enough that the United States and other regional and international actors could not achieve their objectives through military attacks.
Ghalibaf said Iran must be prepared to defend itself with full force when necessary while using diplomatic opportunities to consolidate military gains and protect national interests.
He argued that military victories should be translated into political and legal gains, while negotiations should provide Iran with the time and resources needed to strengthen its capabilities.
Ghalibaf emphasized that combining war and negotiations did not mean pursuing an endless war or engaging in permanent negotiations. Rather, he said, the objective was to compel the other side to accept Iran’s demands or, if it refused, acknowledge defeat and grant concessions that would allow Iran to strengthen its deterrence capabilities.
He concluded by stressing the need to maintain national unity and strengthen Iran’s military, economic and diplomatic capabilities. He said the country must use its existing resources to ease the economic pressures facing the public and turn current hardships into a more promising future.

Extremist ultra-Orthodox protesters attempted to storm an office building in Bnei Brak on Wednesday evening where soldiers serving in the IDF's Kodkod program, a specialized training track for software and cybersecurity personnel, are based. Police clashed with the protesters, and two suspects were arrested.
The soldiers participating in the program work on one of the building's floors. Although some protesters managed to enter the building, they apparently did not reach the soldiers. During confrontations with police, protesters were heard shouting "Nazis" at officers.
"Two rioters were arrested after attempting to break into an office building in Bnei Brak and were taken to the police station for questioning," police said in a statement. "Police forces are at the scene. The incident has ended."
The Kodkod program is a specialized technology initiative designed for ultra-Orthodox men aged 23 and older who are not eligible for combat service. The program, which has so far been considered successful, recruits hundreds of young ultra-Orthodox men each year into an adapted military service framework that does not require them to wear uniforms.
Organizations opposing ultra-Orthodox military enlistment have made the program a particular target precisely because it appeals to many young men and offers professional training that could benefit them in their future careers.
Opponents of the program have also succeeded in gaining the support of prominent ultra-Orthodox religious leaders. About a month ago, all members of Agudat Israel's Council of Torah Sages, including the leaders of the Gur, Belz, Vizhnitz and Sanz Hasidic movements, issued a strongly worded letter opposing the program.
"Recently, various tracks have been opened for members of faithful Jewry under the guise that soldiers in these units will serve without uniforms," they wrote. "From now on, no one should join any of the tracks intended for the ultra-Orthodox, without exception."
The Hasidic leaders also accused the programs of seeking to "change the character and spirit of the ultra-Orthodox community. Do not follow their path. Keep your feet from their ways," they urged.
Since its launch in 2023, the Kodkod program has expanded rapidly. It currently has approximately 1,000 soldiers, about 20% of whom are still undergoing training, and recruitment continues to increase.
The IDF estimates that participation will reach approximately 1,100 to 1,200 soldiers by the end of 2026, with hundreds of new recruits joining each year.

What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:15:58 UTC
05:15:58 KST

What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
Elon Musk’s SpaceX restricted “military-grade” Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defences, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.
The claims drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink – SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military or the president.
“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
What is Starlink?
Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. It is the main profit engine of SpaceX.
Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military missions.
What is Starshield?
Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.
While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Watch moreStarlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres
Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.
The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.
Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.
Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service costing about $25,000 per terminal.
Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals and separate network gateways, Britain’s defence ministry has told Reuters.
Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)
