What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:36:48 UTC
23:36:48 KST

What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus?
US reliance on Canadian potash, a key fertiliser mineral, adds to farmers’ cost concerns amid trade tensions.
The United States is preparing to receive its first shipment of Belarusian potash in four years, as President Donald Trump seeks cheaper fertiliser for American farmers amid rising costs linked to the Iran war and a trade dispute with Canada.
A 30,000-tonne shipment of potash is expected to arrive at the Port of New Orleans on Wednesday, according to data from Kpler. The shipment follows Washington’s decision to lift sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers in March, opening an avenue for trade to resume.
Although this shipment from Belarus accounts for only a fraction of the 5.6 million tonnes of potash the US imported last year, it signals a tentative opening of relations between Washington and Minsk.
Trump has said the US is working on a larger agreement to buy Belarusian fertiliser at prices substantially below what it pays Canada, its dominant supplier. But analysts have questioned whether Belarus can compete with Canadian producers on price and expand exports enough to significantly change the US market.
What is potash and why does the US need it?
Potash is a potassium-rich mineral that is a primary fertiliser element. Potassium, an essential plant nutrient, has no substitutes, and potash is widely used in agriculture, including in the cultivation of corn and soybeans.
The US depends heavily on imports to meet its potash needs. Canada accounts for almost 80 percent of US potash imports, according to the US Geological Survey’s 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries. Russia accounts for 12 percent, the second-largest share of US potash imports.
That reliance has made fertiliser supply an economic and political concern, particularly as farmers face rising production costs. In recent months, US farmers have reported higher fuel and fertiliser costs, putting pressure on already tight profit margins.
Trump has reportedly been concerned that financial strain may cost Republicans some of the US farmer vote in this year’s midterms. In 2024, Trump won 78 percent of the vote in farming-dependent counties. At an agriculture roundtable in Wisconsin in June, Trump promised fertiliser prices would “go way down” as the US emerged from the Iran conflict.
Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have added to pressure on global fertiliser markets, particularly for nitrogen-based products. Potash, however, is less directly exposed to the crisis, with the US relying heavily on supplies from Canada.
Trump has argued that buying Belarusian potash could reduce those costs. An additional supplier could also give US buyers more options in a market dominated by Canadian imports.
For farmers, the immediate benefits remain uncertain. Fertiliser is one of several major expenses facing agricultural businesses, alongside diesel fuel and machinery. Even a reduction in potash prices would not necessarily offset increases elsewhere.
Can Belarus offer cheaper fertiliser?
In September, Trump boasted on social media about striking a potential potash deal with Belarus.
“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said in the post. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”
Trump promoted Belarusian potash as a less expensive alternative to Canadian supplies, but the economics of delivering it to American buyers complicates that plan.
Belarus is landlocked, and EU restrictions are affecting its export routes, forcing potash shipments to take a more circuitous path through Russia. The incoming cargo was loaded at the Russian port of Bronka near St Petersburg, according to reporting by the Financial Times.
Those logistical challenges could raise transportation costs and make Belarusian supplies less competitive, even if the product itself is cheaper.
The scale of the exports also matters. A single shipment shows that trade between the US and Belarus has resumed, but it does not mean Belarus can replace a substantial share of Canadian potash or drive down prices across the US market.
However, access to an alternative supplier could give Washington greater leverage in negotiations with Canadian producers, potentially helping US buyers secure more competitive potash prices.
Could Belarus replace Canada as the main potash supplier in the US?
Relations between the US and Canada have been strained since Trump’s second term began, when he unleashed a volley of tariffs on most trading partners, including Canada. His administration initially imposed a 25 percent tariff on many Canadian imports in March 2025, including potash, but reduced that to 10 percent following pushback from agricultural groups and lawmakers. Potash that meets the requirements of the USMCA trade agreement – the trade deal between the US, Mexico and Canada – is exempted. Most Canadian potash imports qualify under the USMCA and remain duty-free.
Trump has maintained that Washington would continue buying from Canada, even as Belarus offered to sell potash at a lower price.
But the viability of Belarus as a major supplier remains unlikely. In September, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said the country could not supply large volumes of potash fertiliser to the US.
“Even if we wanted to supply [potash] to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes – everything is contracted,” Lukashenko said.
Whether this October shipment becomes part of a much larger deal will depend on the ability to sustain exports and the durability of the diplomatic opening between Washington and Minsk.
Why did the US impose sanctions on Belarus, and why are they being lifted?
The planned shipment marks a significant step in the restoration of trade between Washington and Minsk, which have spent years being at odds over Belarus’s human rights record and its support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The US, under former Democratic President Joe Biden, imposed increased sanctions on Belarus in 2021 after Lukashenko’s authoritarian government cracked down on mass protests against its disputed 2020 presidential election. Belarus has also faced Western sanctions for allowing Russian forces to use its territory in the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
But since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, his administration has pursued direct negotiations with Lukashenko. Those talks have led to the release of political prisoners in exchange for lifting US sanctions, creating a pathway towards renewed economic ties.
In March, Belarus released 250 political prisoners under a US-brokered agreement. Washington subsequently lifted sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers and eased restrictions on several financial institutions. In September, US special envoy John Coale announced a further agreement under which Belarus would release 25 prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief.
The rapprochement has opened the door to proposals for deeper commercial cooperation.
On September 29, Lukashenko said he had agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russian state-controlled energy company Gazprom would participate in a project to build a nitrogen fertiliser plant in Belarus. He proposed inviting the US to join the project using American technology, according to the Reuters news agency.
Before this agreement, exiled Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said that a deal with Lukashenko comes with risks.
“Our position is that it is not time to trade with the regime while all the income from potash goes to repression, goes to support of the Russian war machine,” Tsikhanouskaya told AFP in September.
The proposal has not established that Washington will participate in the project. But alongside Trump’s stated interest in buying Belarusian potash, it illustrates how Minsk is seeking to turn improved political relations into broader commercial opportunities.

frame to folly transforms from carnival gateway to neighborhood teahouse in pittsburgh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:35:50 UTC
23:35:50 KST

frame to folly transforms from carnival gateway to neighborhood teahouse in pittsburgh
frame to folly, a collaborativde project between architectural crafts collective, partlab, and neighborhood allies, is a modular timber pavilion developed for different sites and community uses in pittsburgh.
[FEATURED]
modular pavilion shifts from carnival gateway to public furniture
Frame to Folly is a modular timber pavilion designed to be disassembled, transported, and reconfigured for different sites and community uses in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Developed by Carnegie Mellon University’s student-led Architectural Crafts Collective and Pittsburgh-based PARTlab (Laboratory for Radical Participatory Design), the project forms part of a year-long partnership with local nonprofit Neighborhood Allies.
The structure uses a system of vertical timber frames connected by interchangeable infill panels that double as seats, tables, backrests, and awnings. Initially assembled as a gateway for Pittsburgh’s annual Spring Carnival, the pavilion was prefabricated at a shared fabrication space, flat-packed, and transported to the festival site. The frames were joined on the ground and raised into place using a communal technique that required no heavy equipment. Bright orange infill panels were then secured with removable hardware, providing seating, shade, and other amenities for festival visitors.
Reusable timber components adapt to new community setting
After the three-day event, the pavilion was disassembled and moved to the backyard of a neighborhood tea shop, where the same components were reconfigured as flexible public furniture and an open-air teahouse. Built collaboratively by the Architectural Crafts Collective, a student-led design-build collective at Carnegie Mellon University, and Pittsburgh-based PARTlab, the modular system adapts to the new setting while retaining its original components.
At the end of its use at the tea shop, the structure will either be gifted to another community for reconfiguration or disassembled and donated to a material bank operated by the neighboring public library. Through its successive forms and uses, Frame to Folly demonstrates design for disassembly and material reuse, treating architecture as an adaptable system that can respond to changing community needs.
project info:
name: Frame to Folly
architect: Carnegie Mellon University’s Architectural Crafts Collective and PARTlab (Laboratory for Radical Participatory Design)
design team: Sydney Mansavage, Emma Phelps, Tai Le, Gaetan Pelletey, Hazel Buonopane, Jason Asiedu, Neal Lucas Hitch, Kristina Fisher
location: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, US

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia has to build a transparent and clear system for the life and work of foreign specialists, taking into account the needs of all those arriving in the country, CEO of the Agency for Attracting Foreign Talent to Russia Irina Korotkova said.
Earlier, Korotkova said that since the launch of the Time to Live in Russia program, people from 97 countries had submitted 842 applications, with the first seven candidates from China, Jordan, Syria, Canada, Iran, Mexico and Spain already approved.
According to the CEO, interest in the program exceeded the organizers’ expectations. She noted that participants share Russia’s values and are willing to benefit the country.
“Over the past six months, we have observed that the mechanism [of the Time to Live in Russia program] really works and interest in the program has even exceeded our expectations. These are people that share our values and want to benefit our country. For this mechanism to work, we have to create a transparent and clear system for foreign specialists to live and work here. People should consider our country their home, a place where they can realize their potential and where their families will live. Scientists have certain needs, while representatives of creative professions or athletes have others. So each person needs a personalized approach,” the press service of the Agency for Strategic Initiatives (ASI) quoted Korotkova as saying.
Support from day one
Once foreigners receive the special status, they can get a temporary residence permit outside the quota or immediately apply for a residence permit, bypassing the temporary residence stage. The processing of applications will be fast-tracked. The program also helps with relocation, finding a job and settling in Russia.
According to First Deputy Head of the Citizenship and Foreign Citizens Registration Service under the Russian Interior Ministry Konstantin Bukreyev, the ministry helps foreigners who have chosen to move to Russia, including under a decree that streamlines the procedure for obtaining temporary residence permits for those sharing traditional Russian spiritual and moral values. "The Interior Ministry also provides them with advisory and other assistance with paperwork on a priority basis, in a one-stop shop," Bukreyev said.
Program participants’ stories
One participant, Mexico’s Domingo Garcia Martinez Surita, has already been living in Moscow for several years. He worked for big international pharmaceutical companies and is now developing the business for the Russian pharmaceutical firm R-Pharm in Latin America.
"Russia is a wonderful country, it is very safe here. Traditional values resonate with me. I am a Christian, a rather conservative person and I like how Russia values family," he said.
Another participant, Jordanian bioinformatics scientist Tarek Faruni, returned to Russia after working at leading research centers abroad, including Harvard Medical School, McGill University and ETH Zurich. "Russia is a great country. I have lived here before and decided to return, I like Russian culture. My wife is Russian, my son speaks Russian and we want to raise him here," he said.
About program
The Time to Live in Russia program was launched in April 2026, following an initiative to streamline the relocation of foreigners who share traditional Russian values. It is run by the Agency for Attracting Foreign Talent to Russia, a subsidiary of the ASI.
Apart from this program, Russia also has a relocation mechanism under Presidential Decree No. 702, which streamlines the procedure of obtaining temporary residence permits for foreigners who share traditional Russian spiritual and moral values.

Saudi Arabia/Yemen: Civilians must not pay the price of escalation in hostilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:32:28 UTC
23:32:28 KST

Responding to the dramatic escalation of armed hostilities between the Huthi de facto authorities, the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia in recent weeks and the growing toll on civilians amidst ongoing attacks, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Heba Morayef, said:
“The risks to civilians in Yemen and Saudi Arabia are rapidly increasing each day this conflict escalates. All parties to the conflict must ensure civilians are protected and abide by their obligations under international humanitarian law.
“Over the past week, deadly Huthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia have caused significant civilian harm, including a 10 October attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds more- the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in over a decade. The attack came amidst the return of full-blown armed hostilities to Yemen with devastating consequences for civilians there, particularly on the coast and around Ta’iz, Yemen’s third largest city.
Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation.
Heba Morayef, Amnesty International
“Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation. The deliberate targeting of civilians or civilian infrastructure, including civilian airports, is prohibited under international humanitarian law and can amount to a war crime.
“All warring parties must immediately refrain from carrying out direct attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks.
“In Yemen, where civilians are already grappling with a severe humanitarian crisis and the impact of years of sporadic bouts of fighting, the conflict will further compound the suffering of the civilian population. It is critical that parties to the conflict take all feasible precautions to avoid or, in any event, minimize harm to civilians and civilian objects, and provide unfettered access to humanitarian aid for civilians in need.”
Background
Recent weeks have seen a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the Huthi de-facto authorities in Yemen, the internationally recognized Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia. The renewed conflict in Yemen is linked to the regional conflict involving the US, Israel, and Iran. The Huthis are supported by Iran and the Yemeni government by Saudi Arabia.
The escalation in Yemen follows the breakdown of a UN-brokered ceasefire in July 2026, following air strikes on Sana’a airport claimed by the internationally recognized government. Between 2015 and 2022, Amnesty International documented gross human rights violations and serious violations of international humanitarian law, including likely war crimes, committed by parties to the conflict, including the Huthi armed group and Saudi-led coalition.
The escalation has been accompanied by intensified ground fighting between the Huthis and Yemeni government forces inside Yemen, including deadly attacks by Huthi forces on civilian areas. While the real death toll is significantly higher, the UN human rights office reported in late September that it had documented at least 32 civilians, including 15 children, killed since August.
Huthi forces have also carried out attacks targeting airports, military installations and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, as well as ships at sea. Between 5 and 11 October, Huthi attacks on civilian airports across Saudi Arabia damaged passenger terminals and civilian aircraft and killed at least 20 people and injured more than 350 people, according to the National.
Saudi Arabia has also resumed its air strikes in Yemen. According to the Yemen Data Project, at least 66 civilians have been killed and 90 injured.
The latest escalation is exacerbating an already severe humanitarian crisis in Yemen where, according to UN figures, at least 18.3 million people are acutely food insecure and more than 2.2 million children under five and 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are acutely malnourished. Access to food and healthcare have repeatedly worsened due to the conflict, warring party conduct and humanitarian funding cuts.

Starshield Connectivity Begins Dropping on Ukrainian Drones at Speeds Above 72 km/h
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:31:41 UTC
23:31:41 KST

On the night of October 14, SpaceX unilaterally restricted the operation of Starshield terminals in Ukraine.
According to sources in Ukraine’s Defense Ministry who spoke to Militarnyi, the Defense Forces received no advance notice of the changes.
Starshield is a secure satellite communications system SpaceX developed for government, military, and intelligence users.
Across different unmanned platforms and units, connectivity drops at different speed thresholds, ranging from 72 to 161 km/h. The specific threshold depends on the platform on which the terminal is installed.
Once the terminal exceeds the set speed, it loses connectivity. The restriction affects unmanned systems that rely on Starshield for control and data transmission while moving.
In particular, the changes complicate missions involving drones, including interceptor drones and medium-range strike drones, known as mid-strike drones.
The restrictions also complicate frontline logistics, reconnaissance missions, and the use of drones as communications relays.
As of October 14, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was in contact with the United States, SpaceX, and NATO partners to establish the circumstances surrounding the restrictions and identify possible solutions.
The ministry is also collecting information from Defense Forces units on how the changes affect terminal operation. Existing backup communications channels are being reviewed as well.
Volunteer Serhiy Sternenko, who supplies drones to the Defense Forces, suggested that SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.
The restrictions may be part of pressure from the Trump administration on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Burnham careful as he meets Zelensky but promises Ukraine won't leave 'empty handed'
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:30:48 BST
23:30:48 KST

Burnham treads carefully with Zelensky visit, balancing Trump and Ukraine
- Published
President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to London follows a well-trodden diplomatic path in a war now in its fifth year.
For months, US President Donald Trump had been a largely benign presence in the conflict, promising Ukraine greater access to American air defence technology and threatening more sanctions on Russia.
Then last week Trump carried out an abrupt U-turn, lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and calling for Zelensky to be replaced.
Once again Ukraine's leader got on his plane to shore up support among European allies. Today London, tomorrow Brussels.
For the prime minister there was the tricky but now familiar diplomatic task of needing to show solidarity with Zelensky without appearing to criticise Trump.
Burnham's answer was to say and announce as much as he could without exposing himself to questions from journalists asking about Trump's latest betrayal of Kyiv.
So Downing Street issued an embargoed press notice overnight with warm words of support for Zelensky.
It said Burnham would promise to go "further and faster" in helping Ukraine with financial and military aid.
Specifically, the prime minister would pledge to speed up the delivery of lightweight multirole missiles that can help bring down fast jet-powered Russian drones.
There was a military honour guard in Downing Street to greet Ukraine's president, followed by a controlled photo opportunity showing the start of the meeting between the two men.
In No 10, before that meeting, Burnham told Zelensky that Britain stood with him "at this difficult time".
He said it was clear "who the aggressor is" after Russia's attacks on Ukraine's critical national infrastructure. And crucially he praised Zelensky for his "leadership" in being prepared to sit down and discuss Donald Trump's call for an energy ceasefire.
In his reply, Zelensky said it was an "absolutely terrible time" for Ukraine. There was no energy ceasefire, he said, but Russian escalation instead.
He said Ukraine "counted on partnership with the US" but spoke of "some difficulties" and "different surprises" with Ukraine's access to US intelligence and the Starlink satellite network.
Following the meeting, Downing Street said the two men had emphasised how Russia had launched "blatant indiscriminate attacks on civilians and energy infrastructure" after President Trump's call for an energy ceasefire. It was clear, they agreed, "Russia had no interest in peace".
They also discussed how the UK could speed up defensive support for Ukraine ahead of the winter - as well as "retrofitting British capability" on military equipment provided by other allies.
In the House of Commons, at the start of his weekly question time, Burnham used the opportunity to offer what he called his "unwavering" support for Zelensky and promise greater military and financial aid in the future.
But it fell to the Liberal Democrat leader, Sir Ed Davey, to ask the question journalists might have asked if they had the chance.
Sir Ed said the prime minister had studiously avoided commenting on Trump's decision to rip up international sanctions on Russia.
"This House does deserve to know his position, as does frankly President Zelensky and our brave Ukrainian allies," Sir Ed said.
"Doesn't he agree this is yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security?"
In reply, Burnham admitted it was a "very dark and difficult moment" for Zelensky, who was "carrying the heaviest of weights" right now.
But Burnham eschewed the chance to criticise Trump and told MPs this: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."
"That is the role I intend to play - it's the right role for me to play - in this moment. I will listen to President Zelensky carefully but he won't be going away from Britain today empty handed."
In other words, do not expect the prime minister to join in the widespread European criticism of Trump.
After the now infamous falling out between Trump and Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025, the UK played a key role in calming the row and bringing both sides back together.
A key player was national security adviser Jonathan Powell, who shuttled between Washington and Kyiv pouring oil on troubled waters. It seems Burnham hopes the UK can play a similar bridge-building role now.
For millions of Ukrainians facing a grim winter potentially with less US support than before, the task could not be more urgent.

US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:29:42 UTC
23:29:42 KST

Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.
US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.
Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.
Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.
Price increases this year have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record high last month.
September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990.
The economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans more than $1,020 per household, according to Brown University, and a total of $133bn for all US consumers.
Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump.
In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest inflation report.
On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections.
“They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote.
Later on Tuesday, Trump defended his record on the economy during a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, saying that his support for families has been “substantial”. “Every time they want to try and get me, they say ‘affordability’,” he said.
Heightened inflation will put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, its tool to cool prices. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated prices. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%.
“Inflation in the US has come in higher than expected, in a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, in a statement. “The president has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”

Europe injects 50 bln cubic meters of gas into USG for winter, stockpiling pace slows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:29:26 UTC
23:29:26 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Net gas injection (the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes) by EU countries into underground gas storage (UGS) facilities since the start of the summer season in April 2026 has exceeded 50 billion cubic meters (bcm), according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
Consequently, Europe has so far managed to inject only 74% of the volumes required for the upcoming winter into its UGS facilities.
While the average rate of gas injection into EU storage facilities in October remains the highest seen in four years, Europe has already missed the summer months that are most favorable for stockpiling.
As of October 12, European UGS facilities were 73.94% full (14.91 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 83.2% a year earlier. This remains the lowest level for this date since records began in 2011. EU storage facilities hold approximately 80.8 bcm of gas - 11 bcm less than last year's levels and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that gas stocks in European UGS facilities might not even reach 75%, warning that the region faces a difficult autumn-winter season.
Earlier TASS reported that Europe risks starting the heating season with record-low gas stocks. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU countries may fill their storage facilities to only 70-75% capacity, marking an all-time low for the beginning of the heating season.
Under European Commission requirements, EU nations must ensure their gas storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year. A 10% margin of flexibility is permitted in the event of challenging filling conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage facilities must total at least 68 bcm by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter season to meet the filling target. However, anticipating a very mild winter, the European Commission is prepared to lower this threshold to 80% for the current year.

Say what you will about France’s high schools, they still produce world-class slogan writers. Here’s a brief selection spotted during three weeks of blockades and marches over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings:
“Pas d’avenir, pas de calme” (No future, no calm). “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” (Graduates today, insecure tomorrow). “Vous détruisez notre futur, on bloque votre présent” (You destroy our future, we block your present).
A couple more: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” (Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”). “On n’est pas mal éduqués, on n’est pas écoutés” (We’re not badly brought up, we’re just not being listened to).
Spot the common theme? The protests, which continued this week with more than 160,000 on the streets on Tuesday, might be over very material problems – but beneath them there clearly lies an altogether more existential worry.
This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure – the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed.
That was the central theme of a 30-second Instagram post I recorded last week with the Guardian’s social media team and that, at time of writing, had been watched almost 540,000 times – with young people in France the largest single group of viewers.
The same core concerns underlie youth protests elsewhere – notably, ongoing mass housing demonstrations in Spain, where the twentysomethings of Madrid and Barcelona are in revolt at the monthly rental on a one-bed flat costing an entire monthly median salary.
In France, teenagers in Seine-Saint-Denis, a low-income area in the north of Paris, show reporters pictures of broken chairs and desks, holes in walls, leaking ceilings, mould, shattered toilets and defective audiovisual equipment. Some have gone months without key teachers.
The consequence, here, is protest.
As Kitty Sayers, who went to school in France, explained, France’s republic “was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it … The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education.”
This means that in French schools protest is “taught as a legally framed, fundamental right and a civic responsibility”. But the government’s response has also been arguably very French: riot police, teargas, baton charges and stun grenades.
More than 250 pupils have been injured, along with about 100 school staff and 750 police. One teen has lost a hand from a stun grenade, another the sight in one eye, a third his teeth. More than 6,000 people – almost all minors – have been detained.
After a public outcry, the interior minister last week suspended the use of stun grenades. But as Alexander Hurst observed, when pupils complain about the state of their schools “and the response is riot police, the government has lost the plot”.
Wider public support
If the government hoped public opinion would be on its side, it miscalculated. Teachers’ and other unions, parents and university students have marched with the pupils, and a poll this week showed 57% of the public approved of the protests, with 33% opposed.
They come at a particularly delicate time for France’s political establishment. Presidential elections to replace Emmanuel Macron are due next spring, and without a parliamentary majority his government is caught in legislative deadlock.
Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally and the radical-left La France Insoumise of Jean-Luc Mélenchon are weaponising the protests, the former castigating an out-of-control youth, the latter an out-of-control police, and both blaming centrist incompetence.
Above all, the government’s financial room for manoeuvre is all but nonexistent. As Philip Inman pointed out, with a debt-to-GDP ratio and a budget deficit both among the highest in the EU, France has no cash to spare – and the markets are watching.
So while cost-cutting will only provoke more unrest, the absence of it could trigger a boycott of French bonds, or even a default and bailout (although as the economist Paul Krugman says, France “may have crossed from too big to fail to too big to save”).
Ultimately, there seems little doubt France will have to make some of the same painful adjustments to bring its debt back under control that Italy, Spain and Greece made a decade or more ago – and to which French public reaction could be dramatic.
We began with slogans; let’s end with some. The best-known French youth protest – a revolution, more or less – was, of course, May 1968. Comparing its iconic posters with those of today’s demonstrating school pupils is instructive.
In 1968, there was “Sous les pavés, la plage” (Beneath the cobblestones, the beach); “L’imagination au pouvoir” (Put imagination in charge); “L’ennui est contre-révolutionnaire” (Boredom is counter-revolutionary).
Those, you can see, were slogans born out of infinite possibility: a generation that, in overthrowing the old social hierarchies, never doubted its material survival. May 68 was about blowing open the doors of a rigid, outmoded society to grasp a bright future.
Today’s students are fighting to stop the doors slamming shut on them altogether.

EU summit: Leaders tackle energy prices, spar over budget and unite on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:11 UTC
23:28:11 KST

The two-day summit of EU leaders comes with a packed agenda topped by energy prices, the long-term budget and Russia's war on Ukraine. Hybrid warfare, enlargement and migration will also feature prominently.
Spiralling energy prices, the EU's long-term budget and support for Ukraine in the wake of Donald Trump's latest overture to Vladimir Putin will dominate the conversation as the leaders gather for a two-day summit in Brussels.
Enlargement, hybrid warfare, economic stagnation, rising borrowing costs, trade imbalances and irregular migration will also feature in the talks.
The meeting will start early on Thursday with a hotly anticipated discussion on energy prices, which hostilities in the Middle East have sent skyrocketing. Oil remains above $100 per barrel despite a coordinated G7 release, while gas trades at its highest level since winter 2022, with underground storage running below average.
The market shockwaves have rattled EU leaders, who are under mounting pressure to deliver tangible relief for households and industries, especially as temperatures cool down and the heating season begins.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis have led the charge, asking Brussels to relax the bloc's fiscal rules to allow governments to finance "temporary and targeted measures" to cushion the energy crunch.
Other countries, however, worry that excessive flexibility will promote fossil fuel consumption and discourage investments in the green transition.
Meanwhile, six member states (Austria, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal and Spain) have proposed an EU-wide windfall tax to capture excess profits from energy companies amid high prices. But the idea remains divisive and has not gained enough traction.
Energy will be followed by another pressing economic challenge: China.
With a €1 billion trade deficit every day, Brussels threw down the gauntlet by imposing a deadline on Beijing to deliver "tangible results" by October at the latest.
Those results emerged last week in Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's trip to Beijing, where he secured preliminary concessions on hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars, rare earths and permanent magnets, and market access for European companies.
"We're satisfied with the results, but for us, it's only a first step because imbalances are not specific to one sector – there are across the board," a senior diplomat said, cautioning implementation will be key to show whether Beijing is serious.
"Why is China agreeing to something that China has never agreed before? (Because) they're starting to realise they're killing their customers. We're not naïve."
The concessions avert, for now, an all-out trade war. Leaders are expected to call on the Commission to continue "results-oriented dialogue" with China and "urgently enhance" trade tools to retaliate if needed, according to the draft conclusions seen by Euronews.
In a sign of exasperation, Germany and France have pitched a "kill switch" to cut off China's access to the EU market if the deficit remains unsustainable.
Money talks, but does anyone listen?
The summit's most contentious moment will arrive on Thursday afternoon when the next seven-year EU budget is put on the table. The wrangle will take place against the backdrop of steep borrowing costs, particularly alarming in France.
European Council President António Costa has appealed to member states to move away from their red lines and reach an agreement by the end of the year so that the complex legislative work can be fully completed before January 2028.
Ireland, the country holding the rotating presidency, has tabled a proposal that cuts the original draft by €141 billion. But the knife mostly spares agriculture and cohesion funds and falls instead on research, technology, climate action, security and foreign policy.
The Irish "nego-box" has made everyone unhappy.
The so-called "frugals" (Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany) say the cuts need to go much deeper and across the board. The 17 "Friends of Cohesion" say the opposite, that the cuts have gone far too deep. The European Commission warns its vision of a modernised, flexible budget is in real danger.
On top of that, nobody agrees which EU-wide taxes should be approved to collect additional revenue for the common pot.
The clash of opinions and the unwillingness to compromise bode ill for Costa's ambition to have a unanimous deal in December. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's shock decision to call snap elections adds yet another layer of uncertainty.
"I don't think there will be blood on the wall, but it's important in these sorts of negotiations that leaders feel where the contradictions are," another senior diplomat said. "We are not in a hurry. We need a good deal. We don’t feel any time pressure."
The first day will end with a strategic debate on how to prepare the 27-strong bloc for the admission of new member states and reform its internal decision-making. Montenegro, the frontrunner in the accession race, aims to close all chapters this year.
Backing Zelenskyy, rebuking Trump
Friday will be dedicated to Ukraine in the presence of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The peace talks took a dramatic turn after US President Donald Trump blindsided Europeans by cutting a deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to bring tens of thousands of Russian diesel into the US market. Washington issued a sanctions waiver until April 2027 to enable what would until now have been a forbidden sale.
The news jolted Europeans and prompted a scramble to close ranks and rally behind Ukraine to control the fallout from a unilateral, uncoordinated decision that has revived memories from the Trump-Zelenskyy showdown in the White House.
Although the diesel deal is likely to have a limited impact on the prices at the pump, which Trump wants to lower ahead of the midterm elections, there is greater concern over the diplomatic implications of providing relief to Russia at a time when it escalates its attacks to decimate the Ukrainian economy ahead of the winter.
The summit's conclusions have been changed to add a rebuke: "The European Council regrets the United States' decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel."
Trump has spent the last few days calling on Zelenskyy to stop attacks on Russia's oil refineries and abide by his energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy says he is ready for the truce as long as Russia complies, but Russia keeps bombing Ukraine's power facilities.
Europeans are reluctant to endorse Trump's petition because the long-range strikes are Kyiv's greatest leverage over Moscow. Giving it up would further tilt the war.
"It's not the first time that we're going through divergences with the US in what the Ukraine war is concerned, but I would disagree with the idea that we're ignored," a senior EU official said.
"We have seen that dialogue with the US doesn't always lead to full agreement in the way the EU and the US see things, but it's always better than not having dialogue," the official added. "This is what needs to continue to be done. It's the normal thing."
The last item on the summit will be a strategic debate on migration poised to pit Sánchez against the Meloni-led majority in the room. In the aftermath of the Ceuta border crisis, Italy introduced border checks with Spain, and Spain retaliated in kind.
The checks, which are conducted randomly at airports, last to this day.

DeepMind co-founder warns AI hacking incidents are ‘early warning shots’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:03 UTC
23:28:03 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis on Wednesday warned that hacking incidents involving artificial intelligence are “early warning shots,” urging companies and governments to strengthen security as autonomous systems become more powerful.
Speaking at the International AI Summit 2026, Hassabis said AI agents capable of acting on users’ behalf increase both the technology’s usefulness and its risks.
“But also that means that increases also the risks involved with what those systems might do, and we've seen that recently earlier this year with some of these hacking incidents. I think these are early warning shots for us,” he said.
“The systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major,” he added, warning that incidents could become more serious over the next few years without additional security efforts.
Hassabis said ensuring that systems follow their assigned goals and remain within established safeguards becomes harder as they gain autonomy.
“And that gets increasingly difficult the more automation there is in the systems,” he said.
He also warned that AI “can also be repurposed by bad actors for harmful ends.”
Hassabis called for testing systems in secure environments, initially disconnected from the internet, and drawing on containment practices from biology and nuclear technology.
“I think there's a lot of lessons that can be learned about containment systems, and I think we need to start taking that seriously and bring experts in from those areas,” he said.
He advocated giving trusted defenders, including banks and governments, access to advanced AI tools before wider release to identify and repair software vulnerabilities before attackers could exploit them.
“So we've got to kind of asymmetrically power up our defensive side to keep ahead of the attackers,” he said.
Hassabis also called for an international standards body capable of adapting to technological developments.
“It's going to affect everyone in the world,” he said, urging safeguards that reflect emerging risks while preserving innovation.
“If you legislate for something three years ago, it will be out of date today, and actually probably won't even address what the real problems are,” he said.
He also called for “10 times or more resources” for AI safety and security, including research and computing capacity.

French police hit student protesters with ‘violent charge’ – RT reports (VIDEO)
French police have launched violence charges against student protesters in Paris, arresting young demonstrators as security forces crack down on schoolchildren protesting against staff shortages and underfunding in education, RT correspondent Nadege Abderazzak has reported.
The protests began in late September at a high school in Créteil, a Paris suburb, where teachers and students protested severe staff shortages and deteriorating facilities. The movement quickly spread across France, with thousands of students demanding better education funding and an end to cuts in public services. Demonstrators have also challenged government spending priorities, calling for money to be spent on schools rather than weapons.
Reporting from Paris on Wednesday, Abderazzak described police charging at demonstrators and arresting a young protester. “We’re witnessing a very violent charge by the security forces who have just arrested a young individual,” she said, pointing to the detainee lying on the ground.
Abderazzak said that tensions had persisted for two hours, with an estimated 300 to 400 protesters facing three to five times as many police officers and gendarmes. The march had begun at Paris City Hall, she said, noting that two demonstrations had been authorized by the Paris Police Prefecture.
Since the protests erupted last month, the unrest has repeatedly escalated into confrontations, with police deploying tear gas, water cannon, and stun grenades against demonstrators. Thousands have reportedly been detained and hundreds injured nationwide since late September, including minors. A 15-year-old boy reportedly lost a hand after picking up a police grenade.
By early October, protests had disrupted more than 1,000 educational institutions, with over 160,000 demonstrators taking to the streets on Tuesday, according to authorities. Protesters have challenged France’s spending priorities, demanding: “Allocate money to education, not to buying arms,” according to media reports.
The police crackdown has drawn international criticism, including from Iran, which condemned the use of force against students, while French authorities have defended their response and pledged additional school staff.
The protests come as President Emmanuel Macron’s government cuts public spending while pouring billions into militarization and military aid to Ukraine. France has boosted its 2026 defense budget by €6.7 billion to €57.1 billion, with another €36 billion earmarked for military spending through 2030.
Meanwhile, France’s budget deficit is expected to hit 5.4% of GDP this year, with public debt climbing to 119.3%. Despite the mounting financial strain, Paris has pledged to keep supplying Kiev with weapons, including missiles and air defense systems.

Iran's 'soft war': How Tehran turned antisemitism into a weapon against the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:23:36 UTC
23:23:36 KST

Antisemitism and anti-Israel rhetoric across the Western political spectrum are being amplified by a decades-long Iranian campaign designed to erode trust in American institutions and forge alliances across ideological divides, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Simon Wiesenthal Center (SWC).
The report, titled “The War on Western Minds: Iran’s 30-Year Campaign to Divide the West,” said that the Islamic Republic has weaponized antisemitism in its ideological “soft war” against the West, exploiting nationalism, religious narratives, and anti-imperialism to spread anti-American and anti-Israel rhetoric.
Unable to match US military power, particularly under decades of sanctions, Iran has instead focused on undermining Western social cohesion and trust in democratic institutions, the report said.
Antisemitism predates the Islamic Revolution, but the SWC said that it provides Iran with a narrative that crosses ideological boundaries. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has exploited this by presenting the regime as an ally against the “Antichrist,” an anti-imperialist force resisting Western hegemony, or a nationalist partner opposing alleged Jewish and Israeli manipulation.
Iran brought conspiratorial claims to the mainstream
The report said Iran has helped accusations of Jewish control over American foreign policy become mainstream, allowing such narratives to spread without continued Iranian involvement. It compared this strategy to methods first developed in the Soviet Union.
Using narrative intelligence (NARINT) to track Iranian influence campaigns, the SWC found that the objective was not simply to spread false information but also to shape how audiences interpret events, assign blame, and identify enemies. Once established, narratives of Zionist conspiracy, Jewish financial control, or Israeli manipulation of US foreign policy can become resistant to conventional fact-checking, the report said.
Iran tailors these narratives to different audiences.
Among religious Christians, it uses apocalyptic language and biblical prophecy to frame geopolitical conflicts as battles against the Antichrist, hoping to manufacture Christian-Muslim religious convergence, weakening the perceived Judeo-Christian affinity that underpins American support for Israel.
The report cited Russian political philosopher Aleksandr Dugin, who consulted Athonite monks before Russia’s 2012 intervention in Syria. According to the report, the monks encouraged Moscow’s participation in the civil war as part of a “final battle” against the Antichrist. Dugin later credited Russia and Iran with saving Syria from destruction allegedly sought by the West and Dajjal, an Islamic term associated with the Antichrist.
Iran has also sought to exploit grievances in other communities.
The report highlighted the January 1996 World Friendship Tour by Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan, a prominent antisemite who visited countries hostile to the United States. The SWC said Iran recognized an opportunity to capitalize on Pan-African grievances while presenting itself as a defender of the mustad’afin, or oppressed and dispossessed.
In February 2001, Tehran hosted a regional preparatory meeting for the United Nations World Conference against Racism, culminating in the Tehran Declaration. The declaration accused Israel of committing “a new kind of apartheid, a crime against humanity, a form of genocide and a serious threat to international peace and security.”
The report said that these forums enabled Iran to combine anti-imperialism, left-wing anti-Americanism, Black internationalist organizing, and antisemitism under the banner of international legitimacy.
Iranian-linked media apparatus amplified 9/11 conspiracies
Iran also used its media apparatus to amplify conspiracy theories. In the weeks following the September 11, 2001, attacks, the Hezbollah-affiliated Lebanese television network al-Manar promoted the false claim that 4,000 Jewish employees had been warned to stay away from the World Trade Center that day.
Although initially confined to fringe circles, such claims helped attract conspiracy theorists and anti-establishment figures who could carry Iranian narratives into Western media, the report said.
It cited former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke and political writer Michael Collins Piper as examples of Western voices aligned with Tehran’s messaging.
In 2007, Iran launched Press TV to reach Western audiences directly. The report highlighted programming such as Zero Degree Turn, which portrayed Iranians as saviors of Jewish victims of Nazism while comparing Zionism to Nazism and delegitimizing Israel’s founding.
Iranian filmmaker Nader Talebzadeh helped develop programming designed to influence international audiences through polished, emotionally engaging storytelling, the report said.
The SWC also identified MintPress News as an example of an American-facing outlet that presents itself as an independent progressive watchdog but allegedly relays Iranian and Russian narratives.
The outlet’s mix of left- and right-wing contributors, the report said, helps it mimic progressive investigative journalism while promoting positions aligned with Iranian foreign policy. The United Kingdom-based Institute of Contemporary Islamic Thought was cited as another platform promoting Iranian narratives while presenting itself as an intellectual hub for the global Islamic movement.
The report said that this media ecosystem can have real-world consequences. It pointed to the manifesto of Payton Gendron, the perpetrator of the May 2022 Buffalo supermarket massacre, which referenced a 2016 MintPress News article titled “Thousands of Israelis Take to the Streets Calling For Palestinian Genocide.”
By 2026, Iran’s influence operations had expanded to include fake news websites mimicking American media, fabricated online personas posing as American activists, and campaigns designed to simulate grassroots support.
The report said these operations use wire-service material and plagiarized articles to appear credible and embed Iranian narratives within broader coverage. Additionally, they manipulate Wikipedia, which, by extension, manipulates the majority of AI algorithms and allows the network to exploit social media algorithms.
IRGC used cyberattacks to target US institutions
Iran has also conducted hacking operations targeting American institutions. During the 2024 US presidential campaign, an IRGC-linked group sent spear-phishing emails to a senior campaign official using a compromised former adviser’s account, attempting to infiltrate county-level government accounts in swing states, according to Microsoft’s Threat Analysis Center.
OVER THE past year, the SWC identified over 340 influencers, media outlets, organizations, and affiliated entities that it said formed an interconnected influence network with shared amplification channels and consistent information flows.
The report named Dugin, Jackson Hinkle, Max Blumenthal, The Grayzone, and the account GodivaGoddess97 among central figures. It also identified CODEPINK, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), and the Party for Socialism and Liberation.
The SWC outlined a six-stage cycle through which these narratives spread.
First, humanitarian organizations publish legitimate reports with appropriate caveats.
Second, academics and credentialed figures provide intellectual frameworks that, according to the report, delegitimize rather than merely criticize Israel.
Third, alternative media outlets such as The Grayzone and MintPress remove caveats, add inflammatory framing, and cite the original organizations as authorities.
Fourth, commentators, such as Andrew Napolitano, Candace Owens, Jackson Hinkle, and Jimmy Dore, repackage the content for left- and right-wing audiences.
Fifth, activist organizations translate online rhetoric into campus organizing and direct action, creating environments hostile to Jewish students.
Finally, conspiracy theorists cite The Grayzone and MintPress as evidence of alleged Jewish conspiracies.
Jewish-affiliated voices and organizations, including JVP and Norman Finkelstein, are also invoked to deflect accusations of antisemitism, the report said.
Several recommendations were offered to combat this threat: mandatory coordinated-threat disclosure for platforms; mandatory AI-generated-content labeling; a congressional review of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act to remove immunity for content that can be attributed to designated foreign adversaries or their proxies.
“For more than 30 years, Iran has been building an infrastructure designed to exploit the divisions within American society,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “What makes this campaign so dangerous is that Iran doesn't need Americans to support its regime to succeed. It only needs Americans to lose trust in their institutions and in one another. Antisemitism has been central to that strategy, giving a hostile foreign government a way to turn existing grievances into deeper divisions. This is a threat not only to Jewish communities, but to the foundations of American democracy itself.”
“This is not about the Jews. It has never been only about the Jews,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “Antisemitism is the tool. The real target is Western civilization itself: the Judeo-Christian values, democratic institutions, and shared sense of citizenship that hold free societies together. Jewish communities are simply where the attack shows up first. That is why we called our report The War for Western Minds. Iran’s goal is to break the West’s confidence in its own foundations, and every American, whatever their faith, has a stake in stopping it.”
The full Simon Wiesenthal Center report can be found here: https://wiesenthal.org/iran-report

23:23:11 KST

LONDON — The Mayor of London Sadiq Khan and U.S. tech company Palantir have agreed to drop legal proceedings relating to a blocked £50 million police contract.
Palantir brought a claim against the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime in the High Court in June after Khan’s deputy mayor refused to sign off on the £50 million contract with the Metropolitan Police for the provision of an AI and data analysis service.
In July, lawyers working on behalf of MOPAC in turn accused the Met Police and Palantir of coordinating to fix the outcome of the procurement process in breach of the rules. Palantir claimed Khan’s office had unlawfully blocked the contract over the company's “values and ethics,” based on media reporting.
Advertisement
A full trial was expected in January but on Wednesday both sides agreed to “settle their differences” and drop the allegations without admitting liability. They will each cover their own legal costs.
In an agreed statement, the two sides said MOPAC’s decision to block the Palantir contract was “not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company,” though MOPAC said it “recognizes Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the Mayor's spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision.”
“MOPAC’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners and in doing so it focussed on the available information at the time,” the statement said.
The settlement also notes that MOPAC is working with Metropolitan Police Service to re-run a competitive procurement for the relevant service, which Palantir will be eligible to bid for.
“MOPAC does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir,” the statement confirms, while noting the mayor’s duty is to ensure “all procurements are lawful, fair, transparent and deliver value for money.”
“London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organizations across the U.K. and beyond,” Khan said.

Hershko dedicates her win to IDF soldier killed in Oct. 7 massacre
“Representing Israel has always been something that moves me, but at this moment, it carries so much more meaning,” Hershko told JTA. “At the end of the day, I step onto the mat alone, but I feel like I have an entire country behind me.”
Hershko dedicated her victory to the memory of Yonatan Gutin, an Israeli soldier killed on October 7, 2023, as well as his family and the people of Israel.

'I was aiming for gold'

“Before that, I would go into competitions feeling immense pride in representing my country,” she said. “Today, that pride is even stronger. I’m much more aware of what the flag I wear represents, and of the fact that I stand for something far bigger than myself.”
Hershko, however, has little time to dwell on the medal. She told Channel 13 that she would take two days off before returning to training ahead of another competition next week. Asked by JTA how she has managed to stay hungry and focused after achieving so much, the Israeli athlete said she simply enjoys the journey.
“I really love what I do. I love judo, I love competing, I love the challenges, and I think that’s what keeps me hungry,” she said. “Of course, I’m proud of everything I’ve achieved, but I never feel like I’m done or that there’s nothing left to strive for. At the end of the day, the medals are incredible moments, but the journey is what builds me as an athlete, and I’m still enjoying that journey.”

Ethiopian troops mass heavy weapons near Eritrean border amid war fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:22:29 UTC
23:22:29 KST

Andrew Wasike 
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Ethiopian government forces have deployed tanks and heavy weapons toward the Eritrean border after advancing through northern Tigray, according to the latest conflict-monitoring reports on Wednesday.
The move has raised fears that renewed fighting could escalate into a confrontation between the neighboring countries, said the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an independent organization that monitors armed conflicts worldwide.
“Eyewitnesses observed a substantial convoy of tanks and heavy weaponry advancing from Adigrat toward Fatsi and Zalambessa,” according to ACLED, referring to two key strategic towns on the Eritrean frontier.
ACLED reported that the movement began overnight Monday and continued Tuesday, following the capture of the towns by Ethiopian troops and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters.
Eritrea has rejected Ethiopian accusations of military incursions, with Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accusing Addis Ababa of pursuing “an unprovoked war of aggression.”
The Eritrean government has also urged international intervention, with Foreign Minister Osman Saleh urging the UN Security Council to “take the requisite deterrent measures against it in accordance with Chapter VII of the UN Charter.”
The Critical Threats Project, a US-based security research organization, said in its Tuesday assessment that Ethiopian troops had advanced approximately 37 kilometers (23 miles) north from Adigrat to Zalambessa without encountering substantial resistance.
It also reported that Eritrean troops had established defensive positions north of Zalambessa, citing open-source military monitoring, although the extent of Eritrea's deployment could not be independently confirmed.
ACLED said Eritrean forces previously stationed along the Zalambessa-Fatsi corridor withdrew across the border Monday, while rival Tigrayan fighters retreated toward Debre Damo and Irob.
The withdrawal does not establish that all Eritrean troops have left Ethiopian territory, with the situation along other sections of the border remaining unclear.
The military advances are part of an Ethiopian counteroffensive against forces linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), whose renewed campaign has destabilized northern Ethiopia.
The TPF is aligned with Ethiopia's federal government, while the rival Tigray Defense Forces are associated with the TPLF.
The latest fighting has also brought Ethiopia and Eritrea into an increasingly hostile diplomatic confrontation.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of sending troops into Tigray and supporting armed opposition groups, allegations Asmara denies.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos warned that his country had "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea."
Eritrea responded by accusing Ethiopia of threatening its sovereignty and attempting to justify military action against its territory.
The dispute is further complicated by Ethiopia's longstanding demand for access to the Red Sea, which Eritrea views as a potential threat to its territorial integrity, particularly regarding the strategic port of Assab.
Landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, Ethiopia has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to its economic development.
The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Eritrean troops later supported Ethiopia's federal government during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, but relations deteriorated after the Pretoria peace agreement.
The renewed military buildup threatens to undermine that agreement and raises concerns that fighting inside Ethiopia could spread across the border.

Strait of Hormuz traffic plunges once again amid new wave of Houthi attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:21:01 UTC
23:21:01 KST

Nuran Erkul Kaya
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
- Middle East crude oil, petroleum, and LNG exports collapse amid sharp escalation in maritime attacks
- Strait of Hormuz traffic down to 6 vessels on Monday
- Low of 6.7M barrels of crude transited per day this week
Crude oil and petroleum exports from the Middle East sharply dropped over the past week as Iranian-backed Yemeni Houthi militias intensified their attacks on commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting regional shipping lanes.
Maritime transit in the region suffered drastically since the US and Israel’s pre-emptive joint strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, followed by Tehran’s effective closure of the vital waterway and a subsequent American naval blockade.
Attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz reached a new peak this year over the past week.
At least 14 incidents of attacks, attempted strikes, and obstructions were recorded in and around the Strait of Hormuz on Oct. 5-12, while six ships were attacked on Monday alone, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations and global maritime security sources.
Commercial vessel traffic via the strategic chokepoint fell to its lowest since July 22, affecting outward energy flows.
Oil, petroleum, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports from the Middle East plummeted in the wake of the war, and while there have been signs of partial recovery, intensifying security risks sparked concerns.
Houthis increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia, threatening transit through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. 
Vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb, Hormuz hit new low
Middle Eastern crude oil, petroleum, and liquid chemical exports — including shipments from the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea — fell from 21.1 million barrels per day on Oct. 8 to 6.7 million barrels on Oct. 11, 10.4 million barrels on Monday, and 8.3 million barrels on Tuesday, according to Kpler.
The weekly average of 17 million barrels remained below the pre-war volume of around 23.3 million barrels per day.
Only six commercial ships were able to transit the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, while previously 32 ships passed through on Oct. 8, 24 on Oct. 9, 11 on Oct. 10, and 12 on Oct. 11.
Meanwhile, vessel transit through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also dropped, with 35 vessels passing through on Oct. 8, 39 on Oct. 10, 46 on Oct. 11, and 32 on Monday.
The attempts by the Houthis to establish a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia to seize control of the Bab el-Mandeb corridor added a new volatile dimension to the wider conflict.
Large-scale supply disruptions across both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could pressure global energy supplies and market stability even further, analysts say.

In response to repeated questions on the issue, the European Commission said it is "aware of this report" about restrictions on Starlink but declined to comment until it receives "more information".
Another European Commission spokesperson, Thomas Regnier, said talks with Ukraine are ongoing regarding the country's full integration into the Govsatcom system, which pools the existing satellite capacities of EU member states.
Background:
- SpaceX imposed restrictions on Starlink connectivity for terminals being used in moving vehicles overnight on 13-14 October, disrupting Ukrainian military operations.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that US President Donald Trump's administration warned it could halt intelligence-sharing if Ukraine did not stop striking Russian oil refineries.

- Russia is facing more real bear attacks in 2026, with at least 26 deaths since spring. Experts blame larger bear numbers and poor berry and pine nut crops.

AI generated
MOSCOW - A woman in Russia’s Far East was fined this week after an AI-generated image of a bear, created to prank a friend, went viral and triggered a real-life hunt, the regional courts said.
The Russian authorities are on high alert in 2026 due to a spate of deadly attacks in several regions, where growing bear populations and a poor crop of berries and pine nuts have increased the chances of encounters with humans, experts say.
The resident of Magdagachi settlement, in the Amur region, used ChatGPT to generate the picture of a large brown bear seemingly strolling down a local street and sent it to her friend in September.
“The joke quickly got out of control. The photograph of the bear spread through messaging apps, and police began receiving alarmed calls from residents,” the Amur courts’ press service said in a statement, describing how the district head dispatched wildlife rangers to deal with the phantom animal.
The woman called police and confessed to creating the image. A court this week ordered her to pay a fine of 15,000 roubles (S$230), it said.
In mid-September, another woman in the eastern Transbaikal region was fined 30,000 roubles for posting a fake image of a bear in a village, Russian legal news agency RAPSI reported.
In 2026, at least 26 people have been killed in bear attacks since spring, when hungry bears emerge from hibernation, news agency RIA Novosti said on Oct 12.
In response to the attacks, the government said in September that it was drawing up urgent measures to control the brown bear population, which has more than doubled in the last three decades to 308,000, in part due to shorter and milder winters.
Since the start of the year, more than 3,440 bears that were deemed to pose a threat to humans have been killed, according to a tally compiled by state news agency TASS and published on Oct 10. REUTERS
