Copenhagen has far more municipal savings per resident than poorer municipalities
Danish municipalities differ significantly in how much readily available money they hold, according to an analysis by CEPOS, a Danish liberal think tank.
Copenhagen Municipality has the largest liquid holdings per resident, with savings equivalent to 31,685 DKK for each person.
At the other end of the ranking are Hjørring, Sorø, Thisted, Lolland and Aalborg municipalities. Their liquid holdings range from 3,127 DKK to 4,354 DKK per resident.
Liquid holdings can be viewed as municipal savings that have not been allocated to a specific purpose. Municipalities typically use the money to manage ongoing incoming and outgoing payments.
CEPOS said municipalities must always maintain a certain level of liquidity to cover their regular financial obligations.
Local authorities may also build up savings to finance future projects.
More than 500 marine mammals stranded along Danish coasts in 2025
A total of 538 marine mammals were recorded as stranded along Denmark’s coasts in 2025, according to a report from the Danish Environmental Protection Agency’s emergency service for stranded marine mammals.
The animals included 363 harbor seals, 38 grey seals and 137 harbor porpoises.
Most were found dead. Of the harbor seals, 310 were dead when discovered, while 136 of the 137 harbor porpoises were found dead.
The report identified disease, parasites, injuries and weakness as possible reasons for the strandings.
One animal from each of the three groups was recorded as having stranded after becoming caught unintentionally in fishing nets.
More unusual marine mammals were also found along the Danish coastline during 2025. These included a humpback whale and a striped dolphin.
Ambulances get deer whistles to avoid hitting animals
Ambulances and emergency medical vehicles in the North Denmark Region will be equipped with wildlife whistles to reduce the risk of collisions with animals.
The small plastic whistles are mounted outside vehicles and produce a high-frequency sound when air passes through them. The sound is intended to frighten animals away from the road.
“Unfortunately, we have a number of collisions with animals when we drive with emergency signals in forests and natural areas,” the region’s Prehospital Services wrote on Facebook.
“It is dangerous for the people in the car, it delays the driving, and is dangerous for the animals.”
The decision comes as Denmark faces a possible record year for deer collisions.
Dyrenes Beskyttelse, Denmark’s largest animal welfare organization, recorded 8,739 deer collisions during the first nine months of 2026. That compares with 7,994 during the same period in 2025.
The previous annual record was 11,870 collisions in 2025.
The risk of encountering deer is particularly high during autumn and around sunrise and sunset.
However, it remains unclear whether wildlife whistles effectively keep animals away from roads.
Two insurance companies previously gave the devices to motorists as part of separate trials. According to FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ association, the companies could not reach a clear conclusion about whether the whistles reduced collisions.

Apartment prices in Copenhagen fell for the second consecutive month in September, while prices in Aarhus rose sharply.

Prices in Aarhus have increased by 23.3 percent over the past year. Nordea housing economist Lise Nytoft Bergmann called the development “extraordinary” but warned that prices would eventually reach a limit.
Nationwide apartment prices were unchanged in September. Prices for houses and holiday homes increased by 0.3 percent overall.
Suspected hacker says AI created program used in Danish CPR breach
The suspected hacker behind the theft of nearly 8.75 million Danish CPR numbers says artificial intelligence created the computer program used in the attack.
“Any AI model launched within the past year or so would be able to do it,” the anonymous person told Danish newspaper Politiken.
Two experts reviewed the program, which contains more than 40,000 characters, and concluded that its code was generated by artificial intelligence, Politiken reported.
Danish authorities disclosed last week that unauthorized people accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers during approximately 10 days in September. CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The suspected hacker said the program accessed the national CPR register through a website operated by Odense-based company Pays ApS. Login details were allegedly obtained from a former employee’s leaked password.
Politiken reported that at least three Pays accounts used “123456” as their password, including the administrator account. Pays confirmed to Danish broadcaster TV 2 that it was the compromised company.
The suspected hacker denied having advanced technical skills. An error in the AI-generated code reportedly caused the program to search for people born in 1877 instead of 1977. Consequently, data for people born in 1977 was absent from material shared with Politiken.
The person said they did not intend to sell or publish the information. Pays’ director did not respond to Politiken’s inquiries about the company’s security.
Greenland opposition seeks referendum on new US defence agreement
Greenland’s opposition party Naleraq has called for a referendum on the new security and defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the United States.
The agreement received its first reading Monday in Inatsisartut, Greenland’s parliament.
Naleraq chair Pele Broberg said the agreement converts Greenland’s strategic importance into rights for the United States without providing comparable economic benefits for Greenlanders.
“That is the imbalance we see in the agreement. And that is what our criticism concerns,” Broberg said.
He called for a referendum after the public receives detailed information about the agreement.
Greenlandic broadcaster KNR reported that Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen of Demokraatit said the United States had made no financial offers during negotiations.

The agreement also reaffirms the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and recognizes Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. Denmark’s parliament is expected to begin considering it later in October.

Number of disability pensioners under 40 falls for first time since 2020
The number of people under age 40 receiving disability pensions in Denmark has fallen for the first time in more than six years, according to figures from the Jobindsats.dk employment database.
In September, 43,229 people in the age group received disability pensions, 98 fewer than in August. It was the first monthly decline since early 2020.
Jesper Brask Fischer, head of welfare at pension company PFA, said it was too early to celebrate.
“The number of young people on disability pension is far higher than just a few years ago, and the development underlines the need for a strong effort toward prevention and early assistance,” he said.
The number of disability pension recipients under 40 has increased from 29,000 to more than 43,000 over the past decade. PFA has previously identified a possible connection between poor mental health and the increase.
Across all age groups, the number of disability pension recipients has declined for two consecutive months for the first time since late summer 2021.
Denmark had 261,418 disability pension recipients in September, down 487 from August.
Fischer said further consecutive declines could indicate that fewer people are entering the disability pension system. For now, however, he described the figures as only a cautious positive sign after years of significant growth.
Renovating all public concrete shelters could cost up to 3 billion DKK
Renovating Denmark’s 1,694 public concrete trench shelters and preparing them for use could cost between 2 billion and 3 billion DKK.
Public Security and Emergency Preparedness Minister Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of the Socialist People’s Party provided the estimate in a response to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, according to construction trade publication Licitationen.
The estimate remains highly uncertain and requires further assessment.
Renovating only the 831 shelters that already meet basic requirements and could be opened during an immediate emergency would cost between 500 million and 1 billion DKK.
Most of the shelters require treatment for mold and pests because they have not been used for many years, the parliamentary response said.
The Ministry of Public Security and Emergency Preparedness began inspecting Denmark’s shelter capacity and condition in May 2025. The review of concrete trench shelters is complete, while inspections of reinforced shelters are expected to continue until 2027.
Concrete trench shelters are public facilities intended for people away from home, including road users and residents of buildings without shelters.
Most Danish shelter spaces are in reinforced rooms inside residential and other buildings. Denmark also has supplementary shelters that offer some protection but do not meet full shelter requirements.
A 2024 inventory found about 3.4 million shelter spaces nationwide. Concrete trench shelters accounted for 113,018 of them.

Danish inflation rises to 2.2 percent as fuel prices increase
Denmark’s annual inflation rate rose to 2.2 percent in September, up 0.2 percentage points from August, Statistics Denmark reported Monday.
Higher fuel costs were the main reason for the increase, with transportation prices contributing significantly to inflation between August and September.
Mette Hørdum Larsen, chief economist at Lederne, an organization representing managers and executives, said similar developments were visible in neighboring countries.
“But in fact, the rising energy prices do not become quite as visible in Danish inflation because the electricity tax has largely been removed this year and next year,” she wrote in a commentary.
Lower prices for holiday home rentals, package holidays and food helped offset the increase.
Larsen said there was no reason for serious concern because inflation remained close to the two percent level generally associated with stable prices. She added that there were no signs that higher energy costs were spreading throughout the economy.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, reached a similar conclusion.
However, he said the reduced electricity tax was concealing a significant rise in underlying inflation during recent months.
“In fact, in recent quarters there has been a decline in purchasing power for the Danes because precisely during that period prices have run faster than wages,” Kristensen wrote.

Danish business emergency network grows to 223 members
The number of companies and organizations in Virksomhedsberedskabet, Denmark’s business emergency preparedness network, has risen from 63 to 223 in just over 10 months.
Together, its members represent about 350,000 private-sector employees.
The network coordinates resources from private companies so they can help maintain essential services during serious crises.
“It is about having this conversation about what one already has on the shelves, and how it can actually be repurposed for a crisis and support critical infrastructure,” director Maja Broløs said.

Virksomhedsberedskabet is part of a broader effort to strengthen Denmark’s emergency preparedness. In February, the government launched a total defence preparedness initiative and allocated 1.2 billion DKK to the area.
Broløs said more members would be needed to respond effectively to a nationwide crisis.
“If it is a major regional crisis, we are in a pretty good position. But if it is nationwide, then those are completely different numbers we need to reach,” she said.
The network aims to exceed 1,000 members by 2029. By 2028, it plans to be capable of mobilizing members’ resources nationwide within six hours.

`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.

Johansen emphasized that avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol and using sunscreen are more important measures for protecting skin health.
Denmark resumes citizenship and immigration cases after criminal records error
Denmark’s Ministry of Immigration and Integration has resumed processing citizenship applications that were suspended because of errors in the country’s Central Criminal Register.
The ministry announced the decision in a press release after the National Police concluded that the errors had only a very limited impact on the register.
Immigration authorities have also been instructed to restart affected cases involving permanent residence permits and family reunification, according to an update from the Danish Immigration Service.
The applications had been placed on hold September 7 while authorities investigated the problem.
The errors became public in early September when National Police Commissioner Lasse Boje informed politicians at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, that some criminal records had been deleted incorrectly.
Authorities had discovered the problem in June.
The National Police said further investigations would determine whether the errors had affected decisions made by other public authorities.
If problems are identified, police will work with the relevant authorities to determine how those cases should be handled.
The errors also disrupted the issuance of child protection certificates, which are background checks used to identify certain criminal convictions relevant to working with children.
Applications for these certificates were temporarily suspended while police reviewed the affected records.
The National Police reopened applications September 18.
During its review, police restored 43 decisions that had been removed from the Criminal Register earlier than they should have been.
Those decisions were relevant to child protection certificates.
The ministry has not specified how many citizenship, permanent residence or family reunification applications were affected by the suspension.
Danish court rejects detention request for two Kosovo prison officers accused of assault
Two prison officers from Kosovo accused of assaulting an inmate at Copenhagen’s Vestre Prison will remain free while police investigate the allegations.
Denmark’s Eastern High Court rejected prosecutors’ request to hold the two men in pretrial detention Friday afternoon.
The decision upheld a ruling by Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday, which found insufficient grounds to detain them.
Both courts concluded there was no significant reason to believe the men would flee Denmark before a possible criminal trial.
The officers, aged 29 and 24, are undergoing training in Denmark ahead of assignments at Gjilan prison in Kosovo, which Denmark is renting to house prisoners.
According to police allegations, the two officers assaulted an inmate inside a cell at Vestre Prison around 4 p.m. Monday.
The inmate was allegedly pushed onto a bed before being punched in the face and body.
Police arrested the officers Tuesday morning, and prosecutors requested their detention the following day.
Both men deny using violence against the inmate.
During Wednesday’s hearing, a Copenhagen City Court judge found reasonable grounds to suspect the officers had committed the alleged assault.
However, the judge ruled that detention was unnecessary because both men reside in Denmark and are employed by Danmarks Fængsler, the Danish Prison and Probation Service.
Prosecutors challenged that decision, but the Eastern High Court reached the same conclusion Friday.
The investigation remains ongoing, and no decision has been made on whether the officers will face trial.
Once police complete their investigation, prosecutors will determine whether there is sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges before a court.
Fire near Aarup disrupts train services across Denmark throughout Friday
A fire in a railway signaling cabin near Aarup on Funen is causing major train disruptions across Denmark on Friday, with repairs potentially taking several weeks.
Michael Dyrborg, an area manager at Banedanmark, the state-owned company responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, told Ritzau that almost everything inside the cabin had burned.
“It is too early to talk about a timeframe. We are getting an overview of the extent of the damage, but virtually everything inside has burned away,” he said.
A relay cabin is a small technical building along the railway that houses electronics and equipment used by the signaling system.
The fire has caused signal faults on the railway line between Middelfart and Odense. Dyrborg expects train services on the affected routes to remain disrupted for the rest of Friday.
“We are looking into whether it is possible to create some technical solutions so we can increase the speed and make traffic flow more smoothly,” he said.
Banedanmark has not yet said when normal train services are expected to resume.
The disruption is affecting services across Funen and other parts of the country.
According to DSB, Denmark’s national passenger railway operator, all trains between Fredericia and Copenhagen are experiencing delays, while all regional trains between Odense and Fredericia have been canceled.
Intercity trains running between Copenhagen and Fredericia via Roskilde are only operating as far as Odense, DSB said on its website.
Rail replacement buses have been deployed to replace the canceled regional trains on Funen. According to P4 Trafik, six buses were operating between Fredericia and Odense.
Passengers traveling between Jutland, Funen and Zealand can continue their journeys using some of the other trains still running, DSB said.
DSB employees are available at Odense and Fredericia stations to assist and guide passengers.
Both Banedanmark and DSB are urging travelers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s national journey planner, for updates.
Government unveils security-focused budget proposal
The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Iron Dome architect behind new counter swarm system
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:15 BST
23:00:15 KST

A defence technology company founded in Washington and Israel has unveiled what it describes as the world’s first native counter swarm defence system, designed from the outset to engage large numbers of drones at once instead of picking off one target at a time, according to the company.
Skapion said the system has been designed by its founding architect, General (retired) Pini Yungman, who was the architect of Iron Dome and formerly general manager of Rafael’s air and missile defence division. It is built around what the company calls a native many-to-many architecture, allowing multiple interceptors to engage multiple targets at the same time.
The company said the mobile, fully kinetic system is designed to engage more than one hundred targets simultaneously with an interception rate above 97 per cent, at a significantly lower cost per interception than conventional air defence. A vertical launch arrangement gives 360 degree coverage, and the company said it is designed for deployment from ground, airborne and maritime platforms.
Ido Bar-On, co-founder and chief executive, said: “The next generation of threats cannot be defeated by simply stacking yesterday’s air-defense solutions. A swarm is not just a larger number of discrete drones. It changes the dynamics of the engagement, the number of simultaneous decisions, the speed at which they must be made and the economies of every interception. Native Counter-Swarm means designing the entire system from day one for simultaneous mass engagement.”
Most air defence systems were developed to engage single targets or small numbers of them, which creates capacity and cost constraints against simultaneous mass attack. Skapion cited the wars in Ukraine and Iran, where it said legacy air defence is being saturated by swarms built to exhaust the defender’s magazines and budgets.
A Shahed type one-way attack drone costs tens of thousands of dollars. The interceptors fired at it can cost hundreds of thousands or more, and the magazine on any launcher is finite, so an attacker who can generate enough cheap airframes wins on arithmetic even when every shot is defeated. Bringing the cost per interception down, and the number of simultaneous engagements up, is what several companies on both sides of the Atlantic are now chasing.
At the centre of the Skapion system is an AI command and control architecture that fuses data from the company’s own sensors or from third party systems, evaluates and prioritises threats, allocates interceptors and manages engagements in real time. The company said it can run with full end-to-end autonomy or with a single human operator in the loop, depending on customer policy, and that the open, sensor-agnostic design allows integration with existing command and control and other counter-drone systems.

Happiness, not awe, may be the better emotional lever for openness to diversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:14 UTC
23:00:14 KST

Feeling happy might do more to open people’s minds to social diversity than experiencing a sense of awe. New research published in the International Journal of Psychology indicates that a brief burst of joy leads to more positive attitudes toward inclusion, while awe has little effect. The findings challenge the expectation that awe would outperform other positive emotions in fostering acceptance of others.
Awe is an emotional response typically triggered by perceiving something vast and extraordinary that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world, like a starry night sky or a towering mountain range. This feeling tends to diminish attention to oneself and make people view their surroundings as interconnected and meaningful.
Because awe encourages people to feel part of something larger than themselves, researchers have wondered whether it could help foster more positive attitudes toward diversity. The research, led by Jens Agerström, a professor of psychology at Linnaeus University, set out to test whether experiencing awe could encourage greater openness toward different social groups.
“Previous research has shown that people who are exposed to awe-inducing stimuli (e.g., vast and beautiful landscapes, moon landings) are more likely to act more prosocially (e.g., help another person),” Agerström told PsyPost. “We wanted to extend the research literature by examining whether awe can also make people more diversity oriented by, for instance, expressing more positive attitudes toward ethnic minority groups.”
Prior work provided reason to think awe might bridge social divides. For instance, a 2015 study found that awe shifts attention away from the self and promotes generosity: in one experiment, adults who watched an awe-inducing nature clip gave away more raffle tickets than those who watched a happiness-inducing one. Building on this, an experiment covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that experiencing awe, rather than joy, made children more likely to donate to members of an outgroup.
Happiness served as the comparison. Like awe, it is a positive emotion that tends to broaden people’s outlook and encourage helping and cooperation, which made it a solid benchmark. But the researchers expected awe to come out ahead, because awe is more strongly tied to a sense of a smaller self and a connection to others. Happiness also has a more mixed record: a 1994 study found that happy moods can lead people to rely more heavily on social stereotypes.
To test this, the researchers recruited 3,196 adults through the online research platform Prolific. The participants, who averaged about 40 years old, were randomly assigned to one of three groups, and each group watched a 28-second video designed to evoke a specific emotional response.
The awe group viewed majestic images of the universe, vast landscapes, and the Apollo 11 moon landing accompanied by sweeping music. The happiness group watched cheerful scenes of children playing and birthday parties paired with joyful music. A third, neutral control group saw everyday images of people studying or taking a coffee break with ambient background noise.
Immediately after watching the clips, the participants completed three questionnaires assessing their orientation toward diversity. The first survey measured general attitudes toward diversity, asking respondents if they value getting to know people from different racial or cultural backgrounds. The second survey measured diversity fatigue, which captures feelings of weariness or annoyance toward societal inclusion efforts. The third survey assessed social dominance orientation, which captures how much a person believes some social groups are simply inferior to others and that inequality between groups is acceptable.
The researchers found that the awe video did not measurably change how participants answered the surveys. On all three measures, the awe group’s responses did not differ statistically from those of the neutral control group.
Happiness, on the other hand, consistently shifted responses in a more inclusive direction. The neutral group’s average diversity attitude score was about 4.6 on a 6-point scale, and the happiness group scored about 0.08 points higher. The happiness group also scored 0.10 points lower on diversity fatigue (neutral group average: about 2.1 on a 5-point scale) and 0.15 points lower on preference for group hierarchy (neutral group average: about 2.4 on a 6-point scale).
When the two emotions were compared directly, the happiness group reported more positive attitudes toward diversity than the awe group and showed a slightly lower preference for social hierarchy, a difference that fell just short of statistical significance. The two groups did not differ reliably in diversity fatigue. The results held when the researchers excluded participants who finished unusually quickly or slowly and when they accounted for age and gender.
These shifts are small, but the authors note they emerged after a 28-second video and on measures thought to be fairly stable. The researchers suggest that happiness may promote social bonding, cooperation, and concern for others, which could carry over into more welcoming attitudes, though the study did not test this explanation.
“Brief inductions of awe do not seem to make people more diversity oriented,” Agerström noted. “Somewhat unexpectedly we found that happiness, which we used as a contrasting emotion, resulted in more positive diversity-related attitudes. Perhaps most interestingly, happiness seems to reduce social dominance, an individual difference characteristic capturing preferences for inequality and discrimination.”
The team’s biggest surprise, Agerström said, was “that happiness seems to triumph over awe when it comes to diversity.”
The lack of an effect for awe is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that evoking awe through science fiction increased people’s identification with all of humanity. However, that earlier study measured a broad sense of global connection rather than specific attitudes toward demographic diversity and social equality.
“The main takeaway is that even a brief experience of happiness can make people more positive toward diversity and reduce diversity fatigue and social dominance orientation. Interestingly, the researchers did not find similar effects for awe,” said Ewa Palikot of the Institute of Psychology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, who was not involved in the study. “Like the authors, I expected awe to have a positive effect on attitudes toward diversity, especially since previous research suggests that awe can make people feel more connected to others and encourage prosocial behavior.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a very short video clip to spark emotion. A 28-second video can easily lift a person’s mood, but it might not be intense enough to trigger the profound, transformative sense of awe that comes from standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon. It is possible that a stronger, real-world experience of awe would yield different results.
The researchers note, however, that in a pretest with 125 people, the awe video produced about as much awe as the happiness video produced happiness, so a weaker emotional jolt does not obviously explain the difference. The main study itself did not check how participants felt after watching.
The researchers offer a few possible explanations for why awe fell short. Awe is a complex emotion, and although their awe video produced very little fear, it did produce some surprise, which the authors suggest could prompt a disorienting search for order rather than curiosity and openness. It is also possible the video did not create the “small self” feeling thought to drive awe’s social benefits, something the study did not measure.
“The size of the observed effects of happiness was small and it is important to examine whether happiness has the potential to shape diversity-oriented behavior in real-world settings,” Agerström said. “For example, can a more joyful workplace reduce prejudice?”
Palikot cautioned against generalizing the experimental findings to everyday life. “It is important to remember that these findings do not mean that happier people are necessarily more open to diversity in everyday life,” she told PsyPost. “The researchers looked at how a brief feeling of happiness affected people’s reported attitudes right after watching a video. We still don’t know how long these effects last or whether they influence people’s actual behavior.”
The participants in this study also started out with relatively low preferences for social hierarchy, which left less room for their scores to drop, although the happiness effect still emerged.
“As is always the case, findings need to be replicated before strong conclusions are drawn,” Agerström emphasized. “Also, other awe-inducing methods (than those we tested) may have the potential to increase diversity. Future research needs to look into this.”
Looking ahead, Agerström said the team’s long-term plan is “to unobtrusively study effects of awe and happiness on diversity behavior.” Unobtrusive studies observe what people actually do without making the measured behavior obvious, which can reduce the pull to give socially desirable answers.
“From a cross-cultural perspective, I would be curious to see whether happiness and awe have similar effects across cultures,” Palikot said. “Previous research shows that happiness and positive emotions are not viewed in the same way in different cultural contexts. For example, in some East Asian cultures, emotional balance is more valued, and strong positive emotions like happiness can also be associated with negative consequences. This does not necessarily mean that these emotions have different effects on social attitudes, but I think it would be interesting to explore.”
The study, “Happiness, Not Awe, Makes People More Diversity-Oriented,” was authored by Jens Agerström, Magnus Carlsson, and Towe Nilsson.

Climate Change Is Accelerating Faster Than We Can Respond, Scientists Warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

The climate is warming up faster than we can respond. According to a new report published Oct. 14 in the journal BioScience, “Earth’s climate system is moving deeper into uncharted territory.”
The State of the Climate, an annual report that tracks the Earth’s “vital signs,” monitors several climate related indicators—ranging from greenhouse gas concentrations and temperature changes to tree cover loss due to wildfire. The researchers found that, of the 16 planetary vital signs, seven are currently at record extremes. This includes sea levels and greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere. Meanwhile several others, such as areas burned during wildfires and ocean heat levels, show evidence of acceleration or abrupt shifts.
The researchers warn that the rate of global warming appears to have accelerated, from about 0.05°C per decade between 1880 and 1970 to roughly 0.36°C per decade between 2010 and 2024—and the 2°C threshold meant to limit planetary damage could be reached before 2050 they warn. These accelerating and intensifying changes could raise the risk of reinforcing feedback loops and crossing tipping points—critical thresholds that, when crossed, can lead to accelerating and often irreversible environmental changes. In 2025, the Earth passed its first climate tipping point, as rising ocean temperatures, acidification, overfishing, and pollution are combining to cause coral bleaching and mortality.
"Earth’s life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits," the report states, "with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond."
This year, a number of extreme weather events made the impacts of an acceleratingly warming planet impossible to ignore. July 2026 was the hottest month on record for the contiguous United States, with ocean temperatures also reaching a record high that month. Back-to-back heat waves in Europe lead to an estimated 35,000 excess deaths, preliminary reports show. A number of regions—including Utah in the U.S., Ontario, Canada, along with France, Spain, Britain, and Belgium have either experienced their worst wildfire years in history or are on track to do so. While we don’t yet know enough to link these individual weather events to climate change, research shows that it is supercharging extreme weather events.
Concentrations of greenhouse gases—including carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide—all reached record levels in 2026, the researchers say. In May 2026, atmospheric carbon dioxide exceeded 428 parts per million, roughly 50% above pre-industrial levels and generally higher than any time in the last 2 million years.
The authors of today’s report also tracked indicators of the human activities driving these planetary changes, like energy use, food production, and economic growth. Fossil fuel consumption remains the dominant driver of these changes. Fossil fuel consumption rose by 0.9% in 2025, the report found, with oil, coal, and gas all reaching record highs, and annual energy-related carbon dioxide emissions surpassed 41 gigatons for the first time—the equivalent of emissions released by over 10,800 coal-fired power plants in one year.
There have, however, been some signs of progress, the report notes. Low-carbon sources provided roughly 43% of global electricity generation in 2025, and solar and wind energy consumption grew by approximately 18%. That was before the war in Iran laid bare the world’s reliance on fossil fuels, and triggered a global green energy boom.
But cutting carbon emissions will no longer be enough on its own, the report states. Adaptation measures—ranging from shifts towards plant-based diets, to restoring mangroves to better protect against storm surges—will be key to adjusting to a changing climate.
The report underscores an unavoidable truth. "We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth’s climate system,” it states. “This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present.”

She called for ensuring the EU’s full participation in the peace process concerning Ukraine. Meloni proposed that all 27 EU member states designate an authoritative representative with a joint mandate who could represent Europe’s position in negotiations.
As reported, on October 9, U.S. President Donald Trump said that Russia, with U.S. approval, would supply 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the global market and substantially increase its exports in the future.

Earth’s Condition Is ‘Serious and Getting Worse’ as Climate Change Intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The climate just got its annual checkup, and the results aren’t looking so hot.
“If Earth were a patient coming in for an annual physical, I would say its condition is serious and getting worse,” Oregon State University researcher Bill Ripple says.
Ripple is the lead author of a new paper chronicling the state of the climate, published on Wednesday in BioScience. The findings show that seven of the 16 planetary vital signs tracked by the researchers have never been in a more extreme state.
That includes the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which is 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels due to burning fossil fuels, as well as symptoms of burning all that oil, coal, and gas. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have shrunk to record lows, while ocean heat has soared to record highs.
Climate change has already quickened the pace of warming from about 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade from 1880 through 1970 to 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade since 2010, according to the analysis. While the global average temperature, including land, isn’t at a record extreme, that may change by the end of the year as El Niño strengthens. The natural climate pattern is characterized by a hotter-than-normal Pacific Ocean, but it also boosts global heat levels by pouring more energy into the atmosphere. This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be one for the record books.
“A strong El Niño could temporarily push global temperatures even higher, while bringing additional heat and drought to vulnerable regions,” says Ripple. He adds that “El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it's now occurring on top of a much warmer planet. That makes its impacts potentially more dangerous.”
Of particular concern are ecosystems such as coral reefs and tropical forests. The spread of ocean heat is likely to fuel a mass coral die-off, known as coral bleaching. With each successive wave of bleaching, reefs become less resilient. Corals are among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change; if the planet warms beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, most of the world’s coral will be unlikely to survive.
Tropical forests also face pressure from El Niño. This is especially true of the Amazon, which tends to see dry weather during this climate pattern. The timing couldn’t be more dire: The region, dubbed “the world’s lungs,” is already under intense pressure from logging and mining interests and the possible return of a right-wing government in Brazil that prioritizes extraction and land clearing over conservation.
The new report also warns that the Amazon is among the ecosystems at risk of crossing a tipping point—that is, reaching a threshold where it shifts from a tropical rainforest into something more resembling savanna. It’s highly unlikely that crossing that tipping point is imminent, let alone something that will happen this year. But this year’s blast of El Niño–influenced weather will edge it closer.
“Warming, drought, and deforestation could push the Amazon toward widespread forest degradation,” Ripple says. “My concern is that these changes could interact, making them increasingly difficult to stop.”
The report is an avalanche of bad news for the climate, though it does note that carbon-free forms of energy are playing a bigger role in the power grid. The report calls it a sign we’re in the “Age of Electricity.” Despite that, annual greenhouse gas emissions are at record highs. In other words, the world is still smoking a pack a day, even at the risk of losing a lung.
“There are some encouraging signs, especially the growth of renewable energy, but they aren't yet enough to reverse the overall deterioration,” Ripple says. “The climate emergency is not something waiting for us in the future. We are already living through it.”

“The initial versions of Hurjet will be manufactured and delivered by Turkish Aerospace Industries. But with contributions from subcontractors in Spain and additional certification there, we will deliver a version that could become a joint platform for the two countries,” he said.

Defense exports exceed $7.4B
Gorgun said Türkiye's defense industry exports had exceeded $7.4 billion this year, already matching the previous year's total.
He said the sector comprises more than 4,000 companies and nearly 130,000 employees, with an average age of 34.
Highlighting the seasonal pattern of defense exports, Gorgun said shipments in the final two months typically significantly exceed the monthly average, supporting expectations that annual exports would surpass last year's level.
He attributed the industry's progress to Türkiye's industrialization model, which has enabled a transition from direct procurement to indigenous designs and platform exports.
Felipe Javier Carrasco Torres, deputy industry minister of Spain's Valencia region, said cooperation with Türkiye could help expand the region's defense and security industries.
Valencia has industrial clusters spanning traditional manufacturing and emerging technologies, including semiconductors, photonics, aerospace and drones, he said, adding that its companies currently serve mainly civilian markets.
Torres invited Turkish industrialists to a defense and security industry event planned in Valencia next September, emphasizing that cooperation with other countries and institutions would help the region develop capabilities more quickly.

Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:57:03 UTC
22:57:03 KST

Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.
Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.
It is mainly aimed at China, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.
The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December.
Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors.
But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment.
The ACEA is also lobbying for an urgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UK electric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK.
“We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director.
The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car.
Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year.
The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time.
The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently.
Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years.
One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.

Two veterans who each lost a lower leg while defending Ukraine have summited Mera Peak in Nepal, reaching an altitude of 6,476 meters (21,247 feet) and dedicating their ascent to Ukrainian service members fighting Russia’s full-scale invasion and those who have died in the war.
Christopher John Park-Greenwood, a former British soldier who served in Ukraine’s military, and Roman Havryliak, a Ukrainian veteran, completed the climb using prosthetic legs as part of an expedition organized with Second Wind, a Ukrainian community supporting service members and veterans with limb loss through adaptive mountain sports.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The expedition began on Oct. 1, Ukraine’s Defenders Day. The climbers dedicated their ascent to those continuing to defend the country and to the memory of those who have given their lives.
According to Second Wind, the team faced demanding high-altitude conditions, including temperatures below freezing, up to three meters of fresh snow and avalanches in close proximity. The multi-day expedition required gradual altitude gain and acclimatization before the final push to the summit.
For Greenwood and Havryliak, Mera Peak marked another milestone in a mountaineering journey that began after their combat injuries. The climb followed their ascent of Mount Ararat in Turkey, which stands at 5,137 meters (16,854 feet), in the summer of 2026.
From combat injuries to high-altitude mountaineering
Both climbers spent more than a year preparing for the expedition through regular training, climbing-gym sessions and increasingly challenging routes in Ukraine’s Carpathian Mountains.

Greenwood, originally from Yorkshire, England, is a career soldier who previously served in the British Army and the French Foreign Legion.

Havryliak, known by the call sign “Hava,” is from the Lviv region. He volunteered to join the AFU following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion and served as a drone operator with the 80th Separate Air Assault Brigade. He also sustained a severe combat injury that led to the loss of his leg.
After more than a year of treatment and multiple surgeries, Havryliak set himself a new goal: returning to the mountains.
Both veterans subsequently became active members of Second Wind, a charitable foundation and community that brings together Ukrainian service members and veterans who use prostheses, taking part in its training sessions and mountain programs.
The expedition was accompanied by Gennady Gazin, Anna Vozna and Oleksii Aleksieienko, the founders of the organization.
Second Wind grew out of the documentary project Second Wind, which followed five Ukrainian service members who climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest mountain. The foundation currently runs regular adaptive mountain sports programs in Ukraine and organizes mountain expeditions for its community members.
Ukrainian veterans turn to mountain climbing for rehabilitation
Ukrainian veterans are increasingly taking on mountain-climbing challenges at home and abroad as part of their rehabilitation after severe combat injuries.
Many of these expeditions involve service members who have undergone amputations and climb using prosthetic limbs, demonstrating how adaptive mountaineering can help veterans return to physically demanding activities.
In early 2025, five Ukrainian veterans completed a group ascent of Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest peak, at 5,895 meters (19,341 feet). The expedition was described as a world first for a group of veterans with combat-related injuries.
The participants included Roman Kolesnyk, known by the call sign “Dobriak,” a veteran of the 3rd Assault Brigade who underwent an amputation after a severe injury; border guard Vladyslav Shatilo, known as “Shatia,” who lost a limb; and Mykhailo Matviiv, or “Grizzly,” a member of the Omega Special Forces Detachment of the National Guard of Ukraine who was injured by a landmine near Vuhledar.
The group also included Oleksandr Mikhov, known as “Ragnar,” an Omega special forces fighter who uses a prosthesis, and a servicewoman known by the call sign “Vysota” (“Height”), who sustained severe injuries twice while serving at the front.
In May 2025, Ukrainian military intelligence veterans Ivan Taran and Oleksandr Dashko, both of whom had undergone major amputations, reached the Everest Base Camp in Nepal at an altitude of approximately 5,400 meters (17,717 feet), using prosthetic limbs. The expedition was organized by Ukrainian mountaineerc Tetiana Yalovchak.
Veterans have also taken on mountain challenges within Ukraine. Volodymyr Voropai, a veteran of the 73rd Naval Special Operations Centre who lost a leg during the war, helped pioneer climbs of Mount Hoverla (2,061 meters, or 6,762 feet) for veterans with amputations.
In October 2026, service member Maksym Bashynskyi, who was wounded near Huliaipole, climbed Mount Vysokyi Verkh in the Carpathians, which stands at 1,176 meters (3,858 feet), as part of the Travel Therapy project. Volunteers assisted him using a specialized all-terrain mobility cart known as “Julietta.”
Group ascents of Mount Hoverla have also brought together dozens of veterans. Among the initiatives reported in late 2025 and 2026 were a climb involving 50 veterans from the Kyiv region and an ascent by Special Operations Forces (SSO) personnel who carried a fellow veteran with an amputation to the summit of Ukraine’s highest mountain.

EU's new Lebanon security mission explained, and what's next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

Breadcrumb
EU's new security mission to Lebanon explained, and what's next
The European Union has agreed to establish a new security mission in Lebanon as the country faces mounting uncertainty over the future of UN peacekeepers amid continued Israeli attacks and its occupation of parts of the south.
Approved on Monday at the request of Lebanese authorities, the mission will operate under the EU's Common Security and Defence Policy, with an initial mandate of three years.
The move comes as the United States opposes extending the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which expires on 31 December 2026, raising concerns about a potential security vacuum along Lebanon's southern border.
While the European mission is intended to strengthen Lebanon's army and security institutions, it will not replace UNIFIL or carry out peacekeeping operations.
So what exactly will the new mission do, when will it begin, and what does it mean for Lebanon's security?
What is the EU's new mission in Lebanon?
The mission is a European initiative designed to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions, improve border management and support the Lebanese state's ability to exercise authority across its territory.
It was established by the Council of the European Union following a formal request from Lebanese authorities and will operate under a unified political mandate.
Unlike a conventional peacekeeping force, the mission will not deploy troops to patrol Lebanese territory or monitor ceasefire violations.
Instead, it will provide technical assistance, specialised training and strategic advice to the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces.
Its work will extend beyond southern Lebanon, with a broader focus on strengthening state institutions and improving security capabilities nationwide.
EU sources told The New Arab that the initiative is separate from ongoing discussions about UNIFIL's future.
When will the mission begin and how long will it last?
The mission could begin operations in late 2026 or early 2027, according to EU sources who spoke to TNA.
However, no final start date has been agreed, and the number of personnel who will participate remains undecided.
The EU is expected to announce further details as decisions are finalised.
The mission has been granted an initial three-year mandate, although the precise arrangements for its deployment and activities have yet to be confirmed.
Unlike UNIFIL, which operates under UN Security Council resolutions, the European mission does not require Security Council approval because it was established through a bilateral agreement between Lebanon and the EU.
What will the European mission actually do?
The mission will have two main components, military and civilian, working under a single political mandate.
The military component will support the Lebanese army through training and advisory assistance in several areas, including border security, maritime operations, intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance.
It will also help strengthen the army's ability to monitor and control land borders, combat smuggling and improve coordination between security units.
The civilian component will focus on Lebanon's Internal Security Forces, providing specialised training to improve operational capabilities and establish sustainable training programmes.
These will cover areas such as cybercrime investigations, anti-smuggling operations and internal security.
The mission will also help improve security management at Lebanese ports, including the Port of Beirut.
The broader objective is to strengthen Lebanon's state institutions and contribute to long-term stability in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
Will the EU mission replace UNIFIL?
No. European officials have explicitly ruled out the mission replacing UNIFIL or serving as the alternative international force currently under discussion.
The two missions have fundamentally different responsibilities.
UNIFIL was established in 1978 under UN Security Council Resolutions 425 and 426, with its mandate expanded following the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah under Resolution 1701.
Its responsibilities include monitoring the cessation of hostilities, supporting the Lebanese army and helping the government extend its authority across southern Lebanon.
UNIFIL peacekeepers maintain a physical presence throughout the south, including along the Blue Line separating Lebanon and Israel.
They conduct patrols, monitor military activity and work alongside Lebanese forces.
The EU mission, by contrast, will not carry out operational deployments, patrol borders or monitor ceasefire violations.
EU sources said the missions would also have different geographical areas of focus, with the European initiative extending beyond southern Lebanon.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas emphasised the distinction during her visit to Beirut last week, while stressing the importance of avoiding a security vacuum if UNIFIL withdraws.
Why is UNIFIL's future under threat?
UNIFIL's mandate is due to expire on 31 December 2026, amid US opposition to extending the peacekeeping operation.
Washington and Israel have criticised UNIFIL's performance, arguing that it failed to prevent Hezbollah from building its military infrastructure in southern Lebanon.
The United States has also pushed for new security arrangements, including direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies.
Lebanon has resisted such proposals, instead calling for UNIFIL's mandate to be extended or for a replacement international force to operate under UN authority.
Lebanese MP Najat Aoun Saliba told The New Arab that 14 of the Security Council's 15 members were prepared to support extending UNIFIL's mandate, but Washington remained opposed.
Saliba is among 86 Lebanese MPs who submitted a legal memorandum calling on the Security Council to reconsider Resolution 2790, particularly the timing and mechanism of UNIFIL's withdrawal.
She warned that implementing the resolution under current conditions would be extremely difficult because Israeli forces continue occupying Lebanese territory.
One particular concern involves the transfer of UNIFIL positions and facilities to the Lebanese army.
Saliba argued that where these positions remain under Israeli occupation, transferring them to Israeli forces instead would effectively consolidate that occupation.
What happens to southern Lebanon if UNIFIL leaves?
The potential withdrawal has raised serious concerns about border monitoring, civilian protection and the ability of the Lebanese army to fill the gap.
Saliba warned that more than 10,000 residents of three southern Lebanese villages, Debel, Ain Ebel and Rmeish, could become completely isolated without an alternative to UNIFIL.
The peacekeeping force currently helps maintain a humanitarian corridor serving these communities, which have faced increasing pressure as Israeli occupation expands around their villages.
Residents are also dealing with the weakening presence of Lebanese state institutions and limited access to essential services.
Saliba warned that UNIFIL's departure would leave important border positions along the Blue Line without international observers.
"UNIFIL is responsible for the border points demarcated by the Blue Line," she said.
"If it leaves the south, these points that safeguard Lebanon's borders will be left open and unattended."
She stressed that the central concern was the absence of international monitors to help protect Lebanon's borders.
Could another international force replace UNIFIL?
Discussions are continuing over the possibility of establishing an alternative international force, although no agreement has been reached.
Lebanon wants any replacement to operate under the United Nations, maintaining international oversight of the southern border.
Washington has not ruled out an alternative force, according to Saliba, but the negotiations remain complicated by US and Israeli demands for new security arrangements.
Among the proposals is direct coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries, an arrangement Beirut opposes.
The EU mission will operate independently of these negotiations and will not assume the responsibilities of any future international peacekeeping force.
For Lebanon, the European initiative could provide valuable long-term assistance to its military and security institutions.

Who met Egypt's intelligence chief? Israeli security officials all deny receiving pre-Oct. 7 warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:32 UTC
22:55:32 KST

One by one, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the former head of the National Security Council and senior Israeli security officials all denied Wednesday any involvement in a meeting with whoever arrived at Ben Gurion Airport aboard an Egyptian aircraft on September 26, 2023, just 11 days before the October 7 massacre. According to reports, Egypt's then-intelligence chief Abbas Kamel was the man on the plane and he came to warn those he met of "a major attack being planned by Hamas."
In an interview with Channel 14 on Tuesday night, Netanyahu acknowledged, contrary to his previous statements, that Kamel had indeed arrived in Israel. However, he insisted that the Egyptian intelligence chief "did not meet with me because I was at a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers."
Former Mossad chief David Barnea and former Shin Bet director Ronen Bar also said they had not met with Kamel. Both said they believed reports of the visit were fake news, arguing that it would have been unlikely for Kamel to visit Israel without meeting them.
The Mossad said no representative of the agency had met with Kamel.
Ghassan Alian, who was then coordinator of government activities in the territories and was heavily involved in efforts to maintain calm in Gaza, also denied meeting Kamel that day. Former National Security Council head Tzachi Hanegbi similarly said he had not met with the Egyptian official.
Israel's embassy in Egypt, another body that maintains contact with the Egyptian intelligence chief, was excluded from the meeting.
Two days after the October 7 massacre, Ynet journalist Smadar Perry reported, following an Associated Press report about an Egyptian warning, that Kamel had contacted the Prime Minister's Office and conveyed a message warning of "something unusual, a massive operation" expected to originate from Gaza.
The Prime Minister's Office denied the report at the time. Yet, at least as things appear now, it made no urgent effort over the following three years to establish whether any messages had indeed been conveyed by the Egyptian side, even if not directly to Netanyahu.
As for Netanyahu's claim that he could not have met whoever arrived on the aircraft because he was attending a ceremony marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War at Mount Herzl, The Atlantic reported that the ceremony took place about two hours after Kamel's arrival.
Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana suggested Wednesday morning that "it was one of the heads of the security establishment." However, the IDF chief of staff, Mossad director, Shin Bet chief and police commissioner were all seated alongside Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog at the ceremony.
'Reinforcing the deep state narrative'
A former senior Israeli official commenting on the reports Wednesday said: "It is unlikely that Abbas Kamel would come to Israel to meet with anyone below the level of prime minister. Netanyahu has met him before, contrary to what he said on Channel 14. He also met his successor, Hassan Rashad, last year.
"In any case, it is clear that when the Egyptian intelligence chief arrives, a minister and President el-Sissi's No. 2, he meets at the very least with the prime minister and also with the president. It is unlikely that Abbas Kamel did not meet the prime minister. You cannot hide something like that."
The former official continued: "When a senior foreign official arrives, his aircraft enters a special route managed by the Israel Airports Authority. There are cameras and digital location records. Bibi is manipulating things here and laying the groundwork for his continued portrayal of himself as a victim: 'Why wasn't I informed?'
"Netanyahu is reinforcing the deep state narrative. But it is not difficult to check these things. The prime minister is claiming there was a breach of trust. He says a plane arrived. For years, I didn't care. Now I'm saying it happened.
"So the attorney general can order all the digital evidence to be seized, examine the computer records and see who was in a restricted area that day. A plane lands, and its crew is supposed to be registered. Did anyone get off the plane? Did anyone come to meet them?"
Netanyahu's son, Yair Netanyahu, responded with a post on X.
"To all the 'left-wing journalists,' stop your propaganda already! My father was referring to the fact that a prime minister does not meet the intelligence chief of another country 'alone,' as the blood libel against him claimed.
"The meeting they showed from 2021 with the Egyptian intelligence chief also included his Israeli counterparts, such as the head of the National Security Council, Israel's intelligence minister and others.
"During the Egyptian intelligence chief's one-hour visit to Ben Gurion Airport in 2023, 11 days before the massacre, my father was at a ceremony commemorating the Yom Kippur War."
Yair Netanyahu concluded: "Now the question is: Who did meet with the Egyptian intelligence chief at the time? And why has this been concealed from the prime minister and the public for three years? Why are they still refusing the prime minister's request to reveal who met the Egyptian intelligence chief in Israel?"
'We do not dismiss any threat'
Last month, The Atlantic reported that Kamel had arrived in Israel for an exceptionally brief visit on September 26, 2023, during which he "warned that Hamas was preparing a major attack and urged Israel to introduce economic relief measures to prevent escalation."
According to the magazine's investigation, a chartered aircraft linked to Egyptian intelligence services landed at Ben Gurion Airport and remained in Israel for just 67 minutes before departing for Cairo.
A former Israeli official who spoke to the magazine said the Egyptian intelligence chief's decision to make such a short and unusual visit should itself have conveyed the urgency of the warning.
"The messenger was the message," the official said.
Approximately two hours after the Egyptian aircraft landed, Netanyahu attended a ceremony in Jerusalem marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War. "As a central lesson from that war, we do not dismiss any threat," Netanyahu said at the time.
The Wall Street Journal separately reported that Kamel called Netanyahu in early October 2023 to warn him of an impending attack from the Gaza Strip, after two earlier Egyptian warnings had gone unheeded.
"Kamel began to grow concerned," the newspaper reported, lending further support to Smadar Perry's reporting in Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in the days following the massacre about an Egyptian warning.
Netanyahu, however, continues to deny that he spoke with Kamel.

A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:18 UTC
22:55:18 KST

- Category
- World
A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
North Korea launched a KN-30 ballistic missile more than 910 kilometers during an October 12 test, demonstrating substantially greater range than in the weapon’s earliest known trials.
The same missile type has previously been transferred to Russia and could potentially be used in strikes against Ukraine, according to Militarnyi on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
North Korea’s state-run KCNA released images from the launch but did not publicly identify the missile or disclose its range.
Based on photographs of the five-axle mobile launcher, the secretary general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum identified the weapon as the Hwasong-11Da-2.5, also known in Western reporting as the KN-30.
The KN-30 is a solid-fueled short-range ballistic missile and an enlarged member of North Korea’s Hwasong-11 family. Pyongyang has claimed that the weapon can carry a 2.5-ton warhead, although that figure has not been independently confirmed.
At least two ballistic missiles were launched toward the Sea of Japan on October 12. Japan’s Defense Ministry said one traveled roughly 220 kilometers, while the second flew more than 910 kilometers and reached an altitude of about 70 kilometers.
KCNA said the test was intended to verify improvements made to key components of the missile system. North Korea did not specify which components had been upgraded, leaving open the question of whether the longer flight reflected changes to propulsion, guidance, payload configuration, or another part of the weapon.
The reported 910-kilometer flight is particularly notable compared with earlier KN-30 tests. When North Korea first tested the missile in March 2021, Pyongyang claimed a range of 600 kilometers, while Japanese and South Korean military assessments placed the actual distance at roughly 420 to 450 kilometers.
The KN-30 was first publicly displayed during a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021. It is launched from a mobile transporter on a five-axle wheeled chassis and uses a solid-fuel motor, allowing it to be prepared and fired more quickly than liquid-fueled ballistic missiles.
Russia has already received KN-30 missiles from North Korea. Their presence in Russian stocks has raised concern that Moscow could add the weapon to the growing inventory of North Korean ballistic missiles used or available for strikes against Ukraine.
Earlier, reports emerged that more than 50% of the identified electronic components in North Korean Hwasong-11 (KN-23) ballistic missiles recovered in Ukraine were found to be fake.
