A New Report Sheds Light on the Secretive Race to Build Self-Improving AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:01 UTC
22:55:01 KST

For months, Anthropic and OpenAI have warned that AI may be on the verge of improving itself.
This tipping point, known as “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, could mean that new AI capabilities arrive faster than ever. But the advent of RSI might also be highly perilous for humanity, potentially marking the stage at which developers lose control of AI systems entirely.
Even as AI companies warn about the potential dangers of RSI, they have shared remarkably little about how they’re pursuing it. A new report, published Wednesday by the firm Gladstone AI, attempts to change that. It gives one of the most detailed pictures yet of how RSI could work and how AI companies are progressing toward it. The report is based on what the authors say are conversations with half a dozen researchers inside the top AI companies.
The report, exclusively shared with TIME ahead of its publication, emphasizes that AI companies are “actively working on” automating all parts of the AI development pipeline, including generating new ideas, running experiments to test those ideas, and interpreting the results. Most of the insiders Gladstone spoke to “believe RSI will start within the next 3 to 12 months, and possibly sooner, assuming there’s no U.S. government intervention or slowdown,” the report states.
Read More: Inside the Race to Make AI Build Itself
“There's a fair amount of [disaster] prepping and bio-bunker purchasing going on” among these researchers, says Edouard Harris, Gladstone’s chief technology officer.
The aim of the report, Gladstone’s executives tell TIME, is to give lawmakers a better understanding of how RSI works, and, in turn, a greater ability to regulate it.
“Our goal here was to define recursive self-improvement well enough that people can have a sane conversation about it, especially in Washington,” says Jeremie Harris, Gladstone’s CEO. (The pair are brothers.) “There are all these bills proposed to ban superintelligence, which are really interesting attempts to grapple with this problem. But what we're more interested in is: what is the process that needs to be regulated?”
How RSI could work
The report gives a simplified outline of how the AI research pipeline currently operates inside AI companies—and how those companies are beginning to automate the process.
For the first phase of training an AI model, known as pretraining, much of the emphasis is on finding ways to squeeze more intelligence out of a model with less and less computing power, known in the industry as “compute.”
The AI companies take a portfolio approach to testing these ideas. Researchers allocate a small amount of compute to each idea, using it to train a series of models. The models that reliably perform better as they scale up are selected for another round of training, using larger amounts of compute.
Companies don’t have infinite compute, which limits the number of promising ideas they can test at larger scales. This means that even if AI companies can train an AI that is able to generate ideas that seem promising, it matters greatly how many bad ideas it generates simultaneously. If companies need to spend huge amounts of time or compute filtering good AI-generated ideas from bad ones, it might make sense to continue to rely on human researchers with sound intuition.
Conversely, AI companies with access to more compute are able to test more ideas—potentially allowing them to reach RSI first. With more compute to throw at experiments, companies may also be likelier to catch ideas that the Gladstone report describes as the rarest and most desired by AI companies: those that perform better as more compute is thrown at them, even if they appear to be duds at smaller scales.
Being able to tell when those ideas are found—and particularly whether AI is helping find them—“is just such a critical part of this process that right now legislators have essentially zero visibility into,” says Jeremie Harris.
One of the traits that makes regulating RSI tricky is that it is a gradual process. “This is actually one of the reasons why we went to pains to describe it in so much detail,” says Edouard Harris. “So that it is possible to point to a part of this process and say: a human needs to be there.”

Consumer prices rose 3.7% annually in September as gas prices skyrocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:28 UTC
22:53:28 KST

September brought little relief to the accelerating cost of living, as consumer prices increased again and kept the inflation rate well above the Federal Reserve's goal.
The consumer price index, a broad measure of goods and services costs across the U.S. economy, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.6% for the month, putting the 12-month rate at 3.7%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones expected respective gains of 0.6% and 3.6%.
Stripping out volatile food and energy costs, the so-called core CPI rose 0.3% for the month and was up 2.6% on an annual basis, compared with respective estimates for 0.2% and 2.5%.
The annual rate for headline inflation was 3.4% in August while the core rate was 2.4%.
Surging energy costs were again the primary culprit in the inflation picture. The energy index jumped 5.2% as tensions continued between the U.S. and Iran in a war launched in late February that shows no signs of ending anytime soon.
Gasoline prices soared 9.1%, accounting for about half the gain in headline CPI, according to the BLS. Over the past year, gas has posted a 34.2% rise while fuel oil has roared higher by 74.2%.
Food prices were flat on the month and up 2.5% from a year ago. However, shelter prices increased 0.4% and used car and truck prices jumped 0.7%. Apparel prices, which are sensitive to tariffs, increased 0.3% and are up 3.4% on an annual basis.
Stock market futures turned negative following the release while bond yields were sharply higher. Futures traders also raised the odds of a rate hike when the Federal Open Market Committee next meets on Oct. 27-28 to about 54%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds for a rate rise before the end of the year increased to better than 96%, with a near 50-50 chance of the Fed boosting rates by half a percentage point by December.
This is the final CPI reading that FOMC officials will get before that meeting. The BLS on Thursday will release the September reading on the producer price index, a measure of wholesale costs.
"CPI came in hot and it wasn't just fuel prices, as core inflation ran at a 3.7% annualized pace in September and 3.2% over three years," said Sonu Varghese, chief macro strategist at Carson Group. "The only surprise is that investors keep getting surprised by broad-based inflation. And we've yet to see the full impact of higher diesel prices and the AI boom."
Inflation as measured by the CPI has surpassed the Fed's 2% benchmark since March 2021. The gauge had been trending lower at the start of 2026, but then spiked following the strikes the U.S. and Israel launched against Iran.
Over the past few months, the year-over-year trend has moderated but still has held well above target.
Fed officials responded in September by approving their first interest rate hike in more than three years, a quarter percentage point move that took the benchmark funds rate to a target range of 3.75%-4%. Markets expect the Fed to skip an October increase but to hike again in December.
The type of supply shocks that have driven the energy surge generally are considered temporary, and policymakers often will look through them when considering where to set rates. However, Fed officials fear that the longer the war drags on, the higher the likelihood that the spike will make its way through the broader economy and become embedded in consumer and business expectations.
Prices also have faced pressure from President Donald Trump's tariffs as well as demand for goods associated with the artificial intelligence build-out.
In recent days, a number of key policymakers have expressed the belief that the Fed doesn't need to rush to implement another hike. However, most say they expect another increase this year. Market pricing implies the Fed could raise rates at least twice more in 2027.
Fed officials follow the CPI and a host of other metrics but use the Commerce Department's personal consumption expenditures price index as their primary forecast and policymaking metric. The PCE numbers for September won't be released until later this month.

Microsoft, OpenAI executives call for AI safety laws, says warnings alone are not enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:15 UTC
22:53:15 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith on Wednesday called for new artificial intelligence safety laws, saying tech companies must prevent harm rather than simply warn of risks.
Speaking at the International AI Summit 2026 in Ireland, Smith said AI capabilities had advanced faster than protections.
“The world here in Europe or anywhere does not expect our industry simply to warn about what could go wrong. They expect us to prevent it. They expect us to take action,” he said.
“And if we need to slow down, then it is up to each company and each leader to slow down.”
Describing 2026 as “a sobering year for AI safety,” Smith cited reports of rogue AI agents hacking networks and AI worms targeting connected homes.
“There are more safety rules for a carton of milk than for AI. There are more safety rules for your oven than for AI,” he said.
He urged the industry to overcome resistance to regulation and to back incident reporting, notification of victims of AI-enabled breaches, and independent evaluations with findings shared with governments and customers.
“But we need law. We need regulation. It needs to be sensible. It needs to be balanced. It needs to take into account innovation,” Smith said.
“We need to recognize that the power of AI has moved faster than the safety for it. Safety needs to catch up.” 
'We need to make sure the defenders have the tools'
Also speaking at the event, OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar supported cooperation among leading AI developers, saying the company had called for global regulation.
Friar said OpenAI is withholding an unreleased model while doing further safety and alignment work, but cautioned against slowing development so sharply that cyber defenders lose ground.
“So the folks with malicious intent have the tools. So we need to make sure the defenders have the tools,” she said.
She said OpenAI had used AI to identify vulnerabilities in its own infrastructure.
“We found the vulnerabilities, we patched them at machine speed,” Friar said.
“Selling fear is not a good way to come to the world. We have to sell solutions and solutions that feel transparent, open, honest, and so on.”

Ukrainian Il-76 spotted leaving Saudi airport near Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:03 UTC
22:53:03 KST

- A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD flew from Sharurah, near Saudi Arabia’s border with Yemen, toward Istanbul on Oct. 12, flight-tracking data shows.
- Neither Ukraine nor Saudi Arabia has explained the flight, which follows Ukraine’s deployment of counter-drone specialists to Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states.
A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD heavy transport aircraft was tracked on Oct. 12 flying out of Sharurah, a Saudi town in Najran Province near the border with Yemen, in a rare appearance of a Ukrainian military cargo plane in the south of the kingdom.
Flight-tracking data shared by the open-source account Egypt’s Intel Observer shows the four-engine jet, registration 76661, heading north over the Red Sea at about 10,350 m (33,975 feet) at 17:28 UTC on its way from Sharurah to Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen airport, roughly an hour and 48 minutes after takeoff. The account said the aircraft had earlier flown to Sharurah from Lviv in western Ukraine, a leg not visible in the published screenshot.
Neither Kyiv nor Riyadh has said what the aircraft carried or why it landed at Sharurah. The open-source account speculated that it may have delivered Ukrainian interceptor drones or military specialists, possibly to support Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, and described Sharurah as their main supply hub, a claim that has not been confirmed by any government.
Sharurah’s airport serves both civilian and military traffic and sits close to the Yemeni frontier. It was one of seven southern airports Saudi Arabia shut to civilian flights in March 2015, when the kingdom began its air campaign against the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen.
Ukraine already has a documented military footprint in the Gulf. After Iran launched drone and missile strikes on Gulf states during the war that began in March 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had sent more than 200 counter-drone specialists to the region, and later put the number at 228 across five partners, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Jordan. Zelensky signed a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia during a Gulf visit in the spring, and Ukrainian officials have offered partners interceptor drones built to bring down Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones.
According to information obtained by The Defence Blog, Ukrainian specialists are helping Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region defend against hostile drone strikes, and are also training local forces in new tactics for employing attack drones.
That work has drawn threats from Tehran. In March, an Iranian member of parliament said Ukraine’s support to Gulf states made it Iran’s “legitimate war target.”
The Il-76MD is a Soviet-designed strategic airlifter able to carry about 40 tonnes (88,000 pounds) of cargo, and the Ukrainian Air Force operates only a small number of them. Ukrainian military Il-76 flights abroad are usually tied to cargo pickups, equipment deliveries or the movement of personnel.
The routing through Istanbul fits a flight path north over the Red Sea and Turkey back toward Ukraine, though the tracking data does not show the aircraft’s final destination after Sabiha Gökçen or whether it returned empty.
What the aircraft unloaded or picked up at Sharurah, and whether the flight was linked to Ukraine’s counter-drone mission in Saudi Arabia or to the conflict in Yemen, remains unconfirmed.

MK Party spokesperson Sifiso Mahlangu said the party would conduct an urgent and independent investigation into reported discrepancies in the final councillor candidate lists published by the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC).
The party’s 2026 local government election manifesto, referred to as the People’s Mandate, would be distributed electronically to party structures and members on October 15, Mahlangu said.
Zuma was admitted to Netcare St Anne’s Hospital in Pietermaritzburg last week after reportedly falling ill during an MK Party election campaign in uMsinga, KwaZulu-Natal. The party described his hospital visit as a routine medical check-up. However, speculation about his condition continued after reports suggested he had been discharged and returned to his Nkandla home.
On Tuesday, the Jacob Zuma Foundation dismissed the reports, saying he remained under medical care at the hospital. Foundation spokesperson Mzwanele Manyi said the former president was in good spirits, based on information from someone who had spoken to him and spent time with him. The foundation has appealed for Zuma’s privacy and dignity to be respected while he receives medical care.
The party said candidates whose names had been omitted or inadvertently excluded from the IEC’s final councillor candidate list would be prioritised for the first available positions, subject to its processes and requirements. Its leadership would engage directly with affected ward candidates who had been nominated through community meetings. The party also resolved to establish proportional representation (PR) councillor deployment committees at national, provincial and regional levels to finalise the deployment of councillors from its PR lists.
The MK Party announced the launch of its national Molo Makhelwane campaign, which will run until midnight on November 3, the eve of the elections. The campaign would involve party structures, councillor candidates and volunteers visiting households, engaging churches and listening to residents’ concerns across cities, townships, farms and villages.
The party said its candidates and volunteers must be visible in communities as it seeks to strengthen its relationship with residents. “The streets must now be green!” said Mahlangu.

Russia’s internet shutdowns push state firms back to landline phones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:52:44 UTC
22:52:44 KST

State procurement of landline telephones tripled in the first eight months of 2026 as mobile internet outages hit nearly 80% of the country. Rostelecom’s chief urged Russians to keep one at home “like a fire extinguisher".
Russian state-owned companies spent more than three times as much on landline telephones in the first eight months this year as in the same period in 2025, as mobile internet shutdowns affecting nearly 80% of the country push ministries and businesses to seek alternatives to disrupted networks.
Procurement data cited by the Russian business daily Vedomosti show spending at 118 million roubles (€1.26 million) from January through August, with the number of purchase tenders up 12.5%.
Purchases are concentrated in the country’s largest business and infrastructure hubs.
Market participants told Vedomosti that the surge was driven by the restrictions, a shift by Russian ministries and companies to domestically produced software-based PBX systems after Western vendors withdrew from the Russian market following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and demand for secure communications channels.
Russia began systematically shutting down mobile internet access in May 2025, when services went offline in more than 40 regions ahead of Victory Day celebrations. What were initially episodic outages quickly became routine.
An independent monitoring project recorded 655 mobile internet outages in June 2025, rising to 2,099 in July, a figure that exceeded the worldwide total for the entire previous year, according to analysts.
The disruptions have hit banking, taxi services, food delivery and navigation, particularly in rural areas.
The authorities have justified the shutdowns as a defence against Ukrainian drones, which they say are guided via mobile internet signals.
Experts have disputed this, saying drones can fly preset routes without a network connection, and the shutdowns have reached regions far from the front line.
In March, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration “uses landline telephones” when asked how restrictions in central Moscow affect the work of the president’s office.
Shortly after, head of state telecoms company Rostelecom Mikhail Oseyevsky urged Russians to return to fixed lines.
“Like a fire extinguisher, there should be one in every home," Oseyevsky said.
Russia has approximately 12.2 landline telephones per 100 residents. In Moscow, around 2 million households use fixed lines provided by MGTS, the city’s main telephone operator.
Across the country, there are about 17.4 million urban household landline connections.
The Ministry of Economic Development forecasts that the number of all landlines will fall to between 8.2 and 8.5 per 100 residents by 2029.

This is the second major Russian data center operator whose infrastructure has been hit within the past week.

Feature: Global tourists flock to China to see AI-powered future
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:50:31 CST
22:50:31 KST

Tourists watch a robot dog performance at Robot Mall in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 2, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Meiqi)
BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- At Robot Mall in Beijing, when music was playing, Melissa Valarezo and two of her friends raised their phones to record a robot performing Chinese martial arts, amazed by how smoothly it moved.
"This is incredible. I never expected a robot to do kung fu so well, almost like a real person," the university student from Ecuador told Xinhua in an interview.
Valarezo and her friends also planned to have afternoon tea at a nearby restaurant, where nearly 20 robots of different types work together to provide services, from greeting guests to cooking, serving and cleaning up after meals.
"We just couldn't wait to try," Valarezo said. "Everything here feels so futuristic!"
The three were among a growing number of global tourists drawn to China not only by the country's ancient wonders and culinary delights, but also by its futuristic intelligent robots, as the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom turns cutting-edge technology into a new tourist hook.
During the week-long National Day holiday in early October, multiple Chinese cities rolled out robot-themed events and AI-powered experiences that became unexpected hits among visitors.
In east China's Shanghai, a street fair dedicated to embodied AI drew crowds, with foreign tourists seen posing for photos with humanoid robots. In tech hub Shenzhen in south China, the Huaqiangbei electronics market attracted overseas shoppers eager to try AI translation glasses and flying devices. Similar scenes played out in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, where robot shop managers greeted customers and introduced products.
Official data shows that foreign nationals made almost 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period this year, up 19.5 percent from the same period in 2025. Over the National Day holiday week, visits by foreign tourists also maintained an upward trend, increasing 5.4 percent from last year.
For Anna Seferta and Thomas Drayton, a young couple from the United Kingdom aged 24 and 29, Robot Mall in Beijing was a must-stop. Drawn by online clips of humanoid robots running a half marathon in Beijing in April, they decided to see it for themselves.
"We think it's very advanced. We've never seen anything like this in the U.K.," Seferta said, highlighting that she was mostly impressed by the hospital section. "The robot arm helps cut surgery down by five hours, and the exoskeletons for old people would be very good. All these applications are rewarding."
Launched in 2025 in the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, also known as E-Town, the mall is the world's first 4S store for embodied AI robots.
It displays more than 100 of China's most advanced robot products across fields like medical care, elderly care, entertainment, logistics and industry, turning sci-fi fantasy into an experience within arm's reach.
Inside the mall's exhibition hall, visitors can interact with a wide range of robots. They can grab a cup of robot-made latte with their own image printed in the foam, ask a humanoid robot resembling Albert Einstein questions about almost any topic, or join a tabletop drift car race in which speed depends on their brainwaves.
"International visitors are a common sight here," said Yang Song, an on-site technical supporter at the mall. "They enjoy robot boxing and soccer the most. Many find it interesting to control robot players in competitive games."
The mall did not land in E-Town by chance. Home to over 300 leading robotics companies, E-Town has put the whole district to work as a testing ground: self-driving cars, robot restaurants, robot elderly care stations and the world's first humanoid robot half marathon have all taken root there, alongside Beijing's largest public AI computing platform.
The area is working to build a global AI hub, with its core AI industries projected to surpass 200 billion yuan (about 29.74 billion U.S. dollars) in scale by 2030.
E-Town's rise mirrors the country's broader momentum. China's robotics industry has developed a complete industrial chain covering key chips, components and complete machines. By the end of June, China had completed or brought into operation more than 70 robot training facilities, with over 40 others under construction or on the drawing board.
This growing network is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor, and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference.
Among the visitors to E-Town was Phillip Sepulveda, a 34-year-old photographer from New York. The young man has since childhood suffered from a neurological condition caused by a tumor. Touring the exhibition hall in a wheelchair, he was drawn to a hiking exoskeleton on display.
"The exoskeleton is the sort of thing that would help me a lot," he said. "There are many products now, devices for the hips, for the knees, but we are looking for something for the whole leg."
His father, Jorge Sepulveda, a physician, photographed the product information and said the family was interested in further research.
"We came to see medical devices for mobility, like exoskeletons. It seems China is investing a lot in AI," the father noted, stressing the importance of global cooperation in this rising industry. "AI could be dangerous, as agreed by the CEOs of some AI companies. But if governments and the world cooperate, maybe we can prevent the dangers of it and use it to benefit more people."
For the family, the visit was about more than sightseeing. They left the mall hoping that somewhere in China's expanding robotics industry, they might find a device that could help Phillip walk more easily.
It is a hope that speaks to something broader. Technology is ultimately about changing lives for the better. ■

Two scenarios for the Yemen war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:50:28 UTC
22:50:28 KST

Two scenarios for the Yemen war
What comes next is either a retreat for the Houthis or a war of attrition.
The attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia have pushed the war in Yemen to a new level. The targeting of civilian infrastructure, including airports, which has killed at least a dozen people and injured hundreds, has left no room to maintain the “red lines” that previously outlined the limits of escalation.
This is a reckless gamble by the Houthis which is not in their interest. They are aware that the retaliation will be fierce, yet they continue to attack Saudi Arabia to fulfil Iran’s agenda that seeks heightened tensions before the United States midterms.
Given the motivation to escalate, the present situation has the potential to develop into two scenarios: A major region-wide operation against the Houthis or a war of attrition.
Scenario one: A united front against the Houthis
In response to the Houthi escalation, Saudi Arabia is striving to garner maximum international support while deepening its regional and international alliances. The aim is to come up with a united front capable of taking on what has become a regional threat.
Riyadh is certainly looking to its Gulf neighbours who, themselves, are impacted by the continuing conflict in the region. There is a collective realisation that everyone is in grave danger, not just Saudi Arabia.
Therefore, Gulf states – perhaps with the exception of Oman – will support Riyadh both directly and indirectly in the fighting in Yemen.
Pakistan and Turkiye are also likely to join the front, having signed with Saudi Arabia a defence agreement known as the Mecca Pact. The pact is to be ratified by the Turkish parliament in the next few days, opening the way for Turkish military deployment in support of Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, indirect involvement by Turkiye and Pakistan, along with logistical and intelligence support, appears to be already well under way.
A US intervention is also possible, although it seems unlikely before the US midterms, as military engagements in the Middle East remain unpopular among US voters.
A region-wide coalition can help support the counteroffensive of the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government already under way. This could give the necessary push to retake the western coastal region, including areas beyond Bab al-Mandeb and Dhubab.
Such gains could ease pressure on Red Sea shipping and potentially shift the military balance in favour of the government. The opening of additional fronts across other Yemeni cities and governorates could stretch Houthi forces, disperse their resources, and increase the likelihood of further government advances.
Retaking Sanaa could also be on the horizon. The primary obstacle delaying the Yemeni government’s recapture of the city is internal discord among the various factions within the government itself, compounded by negative external interference that exacerbates these rifts and weakens the collective effort to confront the Houthis.
Recent measures taken by the government, specifically efforts to unify its decision-making and consolidate its military operations command, have yielded noticeable progress on the ground. However, achieving the ultimate objective of retaking Sanaa requires sustained effort and focused determination.
If government forces make substantial gains, that could force the Houthis to offer concessions in exchange for a pause in fighting. They have done that before. Their purpose would not be to seek peace but to get enough breathing room to regroup and eventually go back to fighting. Negotiators should keep that in mind when approaching talks with the Houthis.
Scenario two: A war of attrition
If the Saudi-led coalition and the Yemeni government succumb to internal divisions and disagreements, this may slow progress against the Houthis. This would allow the Houthi fighters to hold on to their positions while increasing their pressure on the strategic town of Taiz and maintaining the campaign against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia.
Such a development could further complicate the conflict, increase civilian casualties and displacement, and prolong the war without producing a decisive military outcome.
This will have a significant economic impact on Saudi Arabia and complicate the implementation of its development goals, as it would have to prioritise defence spending.
The rest of the Gulf economies will also be negatively impacted because Saudi Arabia plays such a central role in the region. What is more, losing ground to the Houthis would mean that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would also continue, disrupting energy exports from the region.
In this scenario, there will be “no victor, no vanquished” deadlock in Yemen, but Iran would emerge as winner. A war of attrition along the Red Sea coast would provide Tehran with significant breathing room, allowing it to alleviate pressure on its own war efforts.
This would enable Iran to use the Houthi card as leverage in the intermittent negotiations it conducts with the international community, emboldening it to raise the bar regarding its conditions and demands during those talks.
This means that the only way to resolve the crisis in Yemen is decisive military action led by the Yemeni government and supported by a region-wide coalition. For that to happen, the government has to get its internal affairs and its relations with allies in order.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

The semi-official Tasnim news agency claimed that militants who killed Aqila are linked to the United States and Israel, but did not provide further details.

Batalhadzhin community linked to international terrorist organizations — FSB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:49:20 UTC
22:49:20 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The "Community of Followers of Batal Hajji Belkhoroev - Batalhadzhins," which Russia's Supreme Court tagged as a terrorist organization today, has been linked to international terrorist organizations and illegal armed groups since the 1990s, the FSB and the Interior Ministry said.
On Wednesday, the Supreme Court recognized the community as a terrorist organization and banned its activities in Russia.
"The court took into account the materials indicating that members of the wird, as a closed pseudo-religious movement, have been interacting with participants in illegal armed groups and international terrorist organizations since the 1990s and up to the present day, adopting their methods and providing assistance to terrorist and extremist structures," the FSB noted.
The Interior Ministry said the community members help other international terrorist organizations and illegal armed groups, and participate in terrorist and extremist activities.
Terrorist acts
The Supreme Court ruled to recognize this organization as terroristic based on evidence of its terrorist activities collected by the FSB in coordination with the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Investigative Committee, and the Interior Ministry.
"Within the framework of criminal cases investigated by the Investigative Committee, data was obtained on the involvement of members of this organization in terrorist crimes," the Investigative Committee noted.
According to the FSB, the Interior Ministry, and the Investigative Committee, in 2004, several members of the community participated in an armed attack on government bodies in Ingushetia killing 78 people and wounding more than 100. Sixty·eight defendants in the criminal case were convicted in the crime, while law enforcement continues to try to track down those who were able to flee and escape justice. In 2019, terrorist attacks were carried out in Moscow, resulting in the deaths of Ibragim Yeldzharkiyev, head of the Center for Countering Extremism of the Interior Ministry for the Republic of Ingushetia, his brother, and an employee of the National Guard. The Investigative Committee established that followers from the organization were also involved in these crimes.
In 2009, the Kartoyev brothers, members of the Belkhoroev community, assisted terrorists in the bombing of the Nevsky Express train, which killed 27 people.
As part of the investigation into a criminal case concerning the terrorist attack at the Crocus City Hall, it was established that the individuals who provided weapons to the perpetrators of the crime belong to the religious movement associated with Batal Hajji Belkhoroev, including Dzhabrail Aushev and Husen Medov, who are serving life in prison.
Russian general's death
The Batalhadzhins were involved in a terrorist attack organized by Ukraine’s special services, in which the head of the radiation, chemical and biological protection forces (RCBZ) Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov was killed.
"Wird members Ramazan Padiyev and Batukhan Tochiyev assisted the special services of Ukraine in the terrorist act committed against the head of the RCBZ of the armed forces of the Russian Federation, Lieutenant General I. Kirillov," the FSB said. The Investigative Committee added that Padiyev and Tochiyev helped the perpetrator of this terrorist act. "This crime was prepared for a long time on the territory of Ukraine. The accomplices are serving long prison terms," the Investigative Committee said.
Assistance to Ukrainian militants
The FSB and the Interior Ministry said that the Batalhadzhins actively assisted Ukrainian armed groups engaged in combat operations against the Russian army. "Members of the community participated in supporting terrorist and extremist groups engaged in combat operations against the armed forces of the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine," the FSB said. The Interior Ministry also said that "there is reliable information about the active assistance provided by the organization to the activities of Ukrainian armed groups that oppose the armed forces of the Russian Federation."
Ongoing investigation
The Investigative Committee, the Interior Ministry, and the FSB said that criminal groups belonging to the community continue to commit various crimes, including murders, robberies, and property theft. "Thus, in Moscow, a criminal case is being investigated against several followers of the movement who are involved in murders, extortion, and kidnapping," the Investigative Committee said. In Ingushetia, a local resident supplied forged documents to the wanted members of the community.
"In this regard, law enforcement agencies are carrying out measures to identify, suppress, and solve all crimes committed by members of the ‘Community of Followers of Batal Hajji Belkhoroev -- Batalhadzhins,’" the FSB said.
Warning
The Investigative Committee said that "the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation contains a separate article that establishes liability for participating in the activities of an organization recognized as terrorist under the legislation of the Russian Federation."
The Interior Ministry said this concerns Article 205.5 of the Criminal Code (organizing the activities of a terrorist organization and participating in the activities of such an organization).
Thus, as explained by the Investigative Committee, the Interior Ministry and the FSB actions related to financing, managing, or providing any other assistance to the leaders and participants of the community entail criminal liability and punishment, up to and including life imprisonment.
Batalhadzhins
Batal Hajji is an offshoot of the Qadiri order, one of the influential Sufi brotherhoods. It got its name after its founder, Batal-Hajji Belkhoroev, an (Ingush) Sufi sheikh of the late 19th - early 20th century. It is a closed organization with strict discipline. Although its direct ties to organizations such as Al·Qaeda and the Islamic State (terrorist organizations banned in Russia) were not established, the so·called "combat wing of the Ingush wird (brotherhood) of the Batalhadzhins was put on the federal list of terrorist organizations under a November 28, 2022 decision of the Southern District Military Court. The charges included blood feuds, arms smuggling, extortion, and corruption. According to some legal experts, the community is more reminiscent of a criminal·clan structure with a religious veneer and motives driven by revenge than an ideological jihadist movement.
Several leaders of the Batalhadzhin group were convicted (Yakub Belkhoroev, ten years for embezzlement and misappropriation) or are on the federal wanted list, such as Akhmed Belkhoroev, who, according to law enforcement officials, is one of the leaders of the combat wing. Another active member of the group, Ilyas Belkhoroev, according to open sources, left for Ukraine in 2015, and joined the Dzhokhar Dudayev Volunteer Battalion in 2021. In August 2026, it was reported that he died in prison in Poland, where he was accused of supplying weapons to that country. Poland never confirmed this.

Sally Rooney halts book sales in Britain and even cancelled a trip due to fears of arrest — what happened
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:47:37 EEST
22:47:37 KST

Sally Rooney halts book sales in Britain and even cancelled a trip due to fears of arrest — what happened
Kyiv • UNN
Faber will no longer supply Sally Rooney’s books to Britain because of her support for the banned Palestine Action. The author fears criminal prosecution.
Writer Sally Rooney said she was forced to stop selling her books in the United Kingdom because of her support for the proscribed organisation Palestine Action, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
The Irish writer, author of such works as "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends," said that because of her public support for the direct-action group, she could no longer receive royalties from sales in the United Kingdom.
After Palestine Action was proscribed last year, Rooney said she would direct proceeds from the sale of her books to support it. Supporting organisations proscribed under the Terrorism Act is an offence; the writer later cancelled a trip to the United Kingdom to accept an award, fearing arrest.
In a statement provided to The Guardian, the bestselling author said: "In July 2025, the direct-action group Palestine Action was designated a terrorist organisation in the United Kingdom. The following month, I wrote an article expressing my intention to continue supporting Palestine Action — an organisation that is neither proscribed nor deemed unlawful here in the Republic of Ireland."
"As a result, fulfilling contracts for the publication of my work in the United Kingdom may now be considered a serious criminal offence. Therefore, following consultations and discussions, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has decided that it can no longer supply my work to the United Kingdom market. I have made every effort to be open with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am entirely prepared to accept the consequences."
In a statement to the High Court supporting a legal challenge against the organisation's proscription — and warning of its impact on freedom of expression — Rooney said that her books could disappear from the shelves of British bookshops and that publishing new works in the country could become impossible.
Her books have received critical acclaim (she has been called "the voice of a generation") and achieved huge commercial success in the United Kingdom. Sales of the novel "Normal People" exceeded one million copies, while "Conversations with Friends" and "Beautiful World, Where Are You" each sold more than 500,000 copies. The BBC created television series based on "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends"; the former attracted 62.7 million views, making it the broadcaster's most popular series of 2020.
Last year, Rooney said that the independent producer of the television adaptations had warned her that any payments for the series (both of which had aired before the proscription was introduced) would breach counter-terrorism legislation if the producer knew or suspected that she was using the money received to fund Palestine Action.
Under Section 15 of the Terrorism Act, it is an offence for a person to "provide money or other property, knowing or having reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism." The maximum penalty is 14 years' imprisonment. Faber, which publishes the author's work in the United Kingdom and Ireland, said: "The current law in the United Kingdom has created circumstances in which Faber cannot transfer to Sally Rooney funds earned by her in the country. For a publisher, a situation in which a writer's works are being sold but the resulting income cannot be passed on to her is untenable. Therefore, with Sally's full agreement, we have decided to stop supplying her work to the United Kingdom in any format. We are proud to publish her significant body of work and will continue to sell it in other territories."
We would add
It is believed that more than 3,700 people have been arrested in the United Kingdom for allegedly supporting Palestine Action since it was proscribed last July; most of them were detained over placards reading: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."
Approximately 2,500 people have been charged, but none of them has yet appeared in court, as a legal challenge to the ban is ongoing and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month. Most of the arrests and charges concerned Section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum penalty of six months’ imprisonment.

Berlin can’t deport migrants due to broken police cars – Welt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:47:20 UTC
22:47:20 KST

Berlin can’t deport migrants due to broken police cars – Welt
Berlin police have been unable to carry out planned migrant deportations because of a shortage of functioning vehicles, Welt has reported, citing a police union warning about the German capital’s deteriorating fleet.
Several operations could not proceed as planned because officers simply did not have enough vehicles to collect people scheduled to be returned to their home countries, Frank Teichert, Berlin chairman of the German Police Union, told the newspaper.
The shortages have caused considerable frustration, turning every promised “deportation offensive” into “real-life satire” on the ground, he said.
Some 159 of Berlin’s 3,304 police vehicles have been unavailable because of workshop work, according to a parliamentary inquiry. Teichert also said more than half the fleet meets at least one criterion for replacement.
The problems stem from years of underfunding, Benjamin Jendro, a police union spokesman, said. Officers regularly encounter worn brakes, seat belts, buckles and interiors, while the vehicle budget remains at 2016–17 levels despite higher prices and increased demand.
The problems also extend to the fire service, where vehicle shortages force neighboring stations to cover calls, increasing travel distances and response times, according to the firefighters’ union. External repair costs have also risen from around €4.7 million in 2024 to nearly €8 million last year.
Berlin’s interior administration maintains that reserve vehicles ensure operational readiness, while acknowledging that limited funding and rising procurement costs are hampering efforts to replace aging equipment.
The failures come despite Germany’s promises to tighten migration controls, expand border checks and accelerate deportations. Growing public frustration over immigration, housing shortages, and subsequent pressure on public services has continued to fuel mass protests in recent months both in Germany and across the EU.
European governments have pledged faster removals, but implementation has continued to lag. EU countries issued around 110,000 deportation orders in the second quarter of 2026, while fewer than 37,000 people were actually removed from the bloc, according to Eurostat. Missing documents, legal challenges and receiving countries’ refusal to cooperate have remained obstacles to deportation.

IMF chief warns growth alone cannot bring US debt under control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:47:07 UTC
22:47:07 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Economic growth alone will not bring US public debt under control, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday, urging additional measures to cut fiscal deficits.
Speaking at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva said stronger growth could help improve public finances but would not deliver the necessary adjustment quickly enough.
She said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recognized that federal deficits and debt had become too high and needed to return to a more sustainable path.
US authorities, however, were relying heavily on strong economic growth to reduce those imbalances, she added.
Bessent has argued that sustained growth above 3%, combined with spending restraint, could lower the debt-to-gross domestic product ratio. The administration has pointed to artificial intelligence investment, manufacturing expansion and tax cuts as drivers of economic activity.
Georgieva’s warning underscored the IMF’s broader demand for governments to strengthen public finances as repeated shocks erode their capacities to respond to new crises.
In opening remarks published by the IMF, she said the global economy remained resilient despite frequent shocks and uncertainty, but that resilience was approaching its limits as energy and fiscal buffers were depleted. Inflation also remained persistently high in many economies.
She urged policymakers to increase revenues, rationalize spending and improve public financial management, while ensuring that assistance amid rising energy and food prices protected vulnerable people.
Georgieva said the global outlook was being pulled in opposite directions by an energy supply shock stemming from the Middle East war and stronger demand associated with artificial intelligence.
Economies closely integrated into AI supply chains were generally performing better, while low-income countries and fragile states faced particularly severe pressures, especially those dependent on energy imports or excluded from the technology boom.

How Australia’s Gambling Lobby has Successfully Avoided Any Reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:47:00 UTC
22:47:00 KST

Gambling businesses in Australia have a long history of effectively influencing and controlling government policy and regulation over a national pastime that makes Australians the world’s biggest gamblers per capita. The gambling industry can wield that level of control because it turns over AU$244.3 billion (2022–23) and generates more than AU$10 billion a year in gambling tax revenue to financially stretched state governments. This substantial financial contribution from gambling provides access to government decision-makers.
Meanwhile, gambling businesses have adopted parts of the tobacco industry’s “corporate playbook” to resist regulation. These tactics have allowed the gambling industry to effectively avoid regulation and instead allowed them to expand their highly profitable commercial activities.
Gambling businesses are well resourced because the products they sell are extremely profitable, and they have worked hard over many years to ensure gambling remains deeply embedded in Australian social life. A key development toward that came with the introduction of gambling machines, known as poker or “pokie” machines, into suburban social clubs from 1956 onward, and later into pubs and hotels. This helped make gambling seem like a normal part of community life. In most Australian states and territories (except Western Australia, which restricts poker machines to a single casino), poker machines are widespread and operate largely without question in venues that are also used for family meals and social and sporting activities.
The development of these social clubs in New South Wales was particularly important. They helped provide sporting and recreational facilities in new postwar suburbs at a time when governments were unable to provide enough financial support for community infrastructure. This gave the clubs a strong community image and helped make their gambling activities more acceptable.
This approach continues today. It is not unique to Australia. Gambling businesses around the world use similar strategies, sometimes described as the “alibi model.” Clubs NSW, the largest gambling network in Australia, has carefully maintained this tradition and uses it whenever possible to promote the image of these social clubs as organizations that give generously to their communities. The close connection between local community clubs, sporting organizations, and some of Australia’s largest commercial gambling operators makes it harder to challenge the normalization and influence of the gambling industry.
Gambling operators are also among Australia’s biggest political donors, according to research. Political donations can provide access to decision-makers, which can then give gambling businesses greater influence over policies that affect them. Australia has also developed a strong “revolving door” between politics and the gambling industry.
There are some restrictions on politicians taking jobs after leaving office, but the definition of a “lobbyist” is narrow. It generally excludes people working directly for companies or industry associations to influence government. As a result, many people involved in lobbying are not subject to the same rules. Former senators, premiers, ministers, political advisers, and senior public officials have taken jobs with some of Australia’s largest gambling companies, sometimes soon after leaving public office.
Hospitality is another form of influence. This can range from MPs given private boxes at major sporting events, or the sports minister attending football grand finals and tickets for MPs attending the Melbourne Cup racing carnival, to “policy briefing” lunches and dinners for the minister responsible for oversight of the gambling industry at expensive restaurants.
These benefits may have to be declared, but the conversations that take place are not made public. The access provided by hospitality can be significant. A politician may spend several hours with an industry representative at an event, giving the host much more time and access than they would normally have during a visit to a parliamentary office.
Some states have introduced new rules that limit political donations from certain businesses, including gambling operators. The federal government has weaker rules around political transparency and integrity, with limited enforcement and relatively weak penalties. In practice, this means that Australia has a political system in which powerful interests can influence governments while making that influence difficult for the public to see.
Recent experience suggests they can be extremely effective. In 2010-11, the minority Gillard government sought to introduce a system that would allow poker machine players to set limits on how much they could spend. ClubsNSW, representing clubs with poker machines across New South Wales, launched a highly effective campaign to block the change. It targeted Labor politicians in marginal seats in New South Wales and Queensland.
Although Clubs NSW remained the public face of the campaign, partly because of the positive community image created by the “alibi” of community benefits, it brought much of the gambling industry together behind the campaign and had access to almost unlimited financial resources. Nervous backbenchers became increasingly concerned, and Prime Minister Julia Gillard eventually found a way to abandon the commitment. No major reform followed.
More recently, a 2023 federal parliamentary inquiry into “online gambling and its impacts on those experiencing gambling harm,” chaired by MP Peta Murphy, concluded that “enough is enough.” It recommended major reforms to online gambling in order to reduce its harm to Australians. The recommendations included banning gambling advertising across all media, developing a national strategy for gambling regulation, and establishing a new national gambling regulator. Once again, the gambling industry responded quickly, with wagering companies taking the lead.
Sporting organizations and broadcasters, which now receive significant revenue from gambling, were among those most strongly opposed to the proposed reforms. They successfully stymied the changes. The reforms eventually announced by the government in 2026 fell well short of those recommended by the parliamentary committee.
In both cases, the gambling industry organizations successfully utilized their enormous lobbying powers to influence government. In both cases, those methods worked. And the Murphy inquiry’s important reform proposals were weakened or abandoned.
The gambling industry provides a clear example of how the corporate playbook can be used to prevent reforms that could significantly reduce gambling harm. The reason is simple: the all-powerful gambling industry knows only too well that effective regulation could reduce their revenues and profits.

US blasts case against Lebanon DC envoy over 'Israel contact'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:46:56 UTC
22:46:56 KST

Breadcrumb
US blasts case against Lebanon DC envoy over 'Israel contact'
A legal complaint against Lebanon's ambassador to Washington over an alleged contact with her Israeli counterpart has been referred to the military judiciary, drawing strong criticism from the United States and dividing opinion in Lebanon.
Lawyer Hassan Adel Bazzi filed the complaint against Ambassador Nada Hamadeh Moawad after Lebanese and Israeli media reported that she had contacted Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter following an attack in the occupied West Bank in which his son was injured.
The reports said Moawad expressed sympathy with Leiter and condemned the attack.
Moawad has neither publicly confirmed nor denied that the conversation took place. Lebanese media have cited sources denying the call, while official Lebanese sources told The New Arab they had no comment.
Lebanon's public prosecutor has referred the complaint to Judge Claude Ghanem, the government commissioner at the Military Court, for review.
The step does not itself constitute charges against Moawad or a formal referral for investigation.
The US State Department nevertheless condemned the move.
"It is shameful that a military court is considering a complaint against Lebanon's ambassador in Washington simply for implementing her legitimate government's policy and participating in US-led negotiations," a spokesperson said.
Washington said the military judiciary should instead focus on Hezbollah members it accused of plotting against the Lebanese government and called for an end to laws and practices it said enabled the politically motivated targeting of civilians and diplomats.
The case has also reignited debate over Lebanon's longstanding law banning dealings with Israel, which has faced renewed scrutiny since Beirut began direct US-mediated negotiations with Israel earlier this year.
Several Lebanese politicians opposed to Hezbollah rallied behind Moawad.
Kataeb Party leader Samy Gemayel described the referral as "unacceptable" and "a dangerous precedent".
"Lebanese diplomacy must not be subjected to political calculations," he said. "What is needed is to protect institutions, not intimidate them."
Bazzi, however, told The New Arab that the complaint raised a legitimate issue requiring judicial scrutiny.
"We have no vindictive objective," he said. "There is an incident that requires investigation."
He argued that prosecutors could have dismissed the complaint if they considered it without merit, and said any evidence of contact outside Moawad's authorised negotiating role could raise questions under Lebanon's boycott legislation.
Bazzi also criticised the US response as interference in Lebanon's judiciary and sovereignty.
Moawad is a central member of Lebanon's negotiating delegation with Israel, led by former ambassador Simon Karam.
She and Leiter met at the US State Department in September as part of talks on implementing the framework agreement signed on 26 June.
The negotiations have been politically contentious in Lebanon, particularly as Israel continues military operations and maintains forces in parts of southern Lebanon despite months of diplomacy.

Entire Swedish reality show season lost weeks before premiere amid disputed AI claims

2026-10-14
13:46:12 UTC
22:46:12 KST

The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet.
An AI agent reportedly deleted an entire edited season of a Swedish reality show just five weeks before its planned premiere, forcing the broadcaster to postpone its release until next year.
Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet, citing unnamed sources, reported that the production company behind a reality show named The Challenge Sverige had given an AI agent access to its server, where it deleted the completed season.
The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to the report.
Swedish commercial broadcaster TV4 confirmed to Aftonbladet that a “technical failure” had caused the loss, pushing the planned 22 November premiere back to 2027.
Its news division initially repeated the newspaper’s account of AI involvement, but in an update on Wednesday afternoon, TV4’s head of programmes Mia Lindqvist denied that an AI agent was responsible, saying “that is not true”.
Adapted from the American show The Challenge, the series is billed by TV4 as the world’s toughest reality contest, combining physical challenges, mental endurance and strategic alliances.
How can AI agents go wrong?
Although the Swedish TV channel has rejected the AI explanation in this case, other incidents have exposed the risks of systems that can act on users’ behalf.
AI agents use software tools to carry out tasks, such as drafting and sending emails, rather than simply generating responses. Depending on their permissions, they can make changes to real files, websites and computer systems.
Problems can arise when a system misunderstands instructions, misjudges an action’s consequences or works around an obstacle instead of stopping.
In a report published on Friday, Anthropic said models given impossible tasks could pursue “unintended and sometimes misaligned strategies to achieve their goals”.
In July, its Claude Haiku 4.5 model submitted fabricated information about an unsolved homicide to the US police website while performing example tasks.
TV4 said all the original footage of the show remains available but the season must be edited again from scratch.

The Greek Parliamentary Israel Allies Caucus was inaugurated at the Hellenic Parliament in Athens on Tuesday, followed by the launch of the Cyprus Israel Allies Caucus at the House of Representatives in Nicosia on Wednesday.
The new caucuses aim to build on the existing trilateral partnership between Israel, Greece, and Cyprus, with a particular focus on security challenges in the Eastern Mediterranean, including tensions with Turkey.
“The new Israel Allies Caucuses in Greece and Cyprus will help translate these commitments into parliamentary action,” said Leo van Doesburg, executive director of IAF Europe.

Cyprus, Greece, Israel ties 'more vital than ever'

Tsiaras said the initiative comes amid growing regional security challenges and proves the three countries' shared strategic interests and historical ties.
In Cyprus, the new caucus will be chaired by Democratic Party MP Chrysis Pantelides and will include six lawmakers from three political parties.
The launch followed a meeting between the IAF delegation and Cypriot President Nicos Christodoulides at the Presidential Palace. The delegation was also hosted by House of Representatives President Annita Demetriou.
Pantelides emphasized the importance of strengthening relations between Cyprus and Israel in light of regional security threats.
“The strengthening of relations and the development of alliance ties between Cyprus and Israel is more vital than ever,” he said, citing the security challenges facing both countries.
Israeli ambassadors attended the launches in their respective host countries, while the US ambassador to Cyprus also attended the ceremony in Nicosia.
Reinstein welcomed the establishment of the two caucuses, saying they would help strengthen parliamentary cooperation and support for Israel.
“Through faith-based diplomacy, we are building a bridge between parliamentarians who understand that Israel's security, and the security of the free world, depend on strong alliances rooted in shared Judeo-Christian values,” he said.

Dublin hotel cancels 70 rooms booked for antisemitism conference delegates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:57 UTC
22:45:57 KST

The Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin canceled a reservation for 70 rooms intended for delegates attending an international conference on combating antisemitism after learning the purpose of their visit, according to Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland.
In his speech at the opening event at the Irish Foreign Ministry – sent to The Jerusalem Post – Cohen recalled meeting with hotel management after the booking was completed, and being questioned about whether the gathering was connected to the Israel Defense Forces.
Cohen also remembered the manager’s demeanor changing and becoming tense after he mentioned that the delegates would be Jewish leaders.
“There is an uncomfortable irony in organizing an international conference to discuss antisemitism and finding that, before the conference has even begun, you have already encountered something that forces you to ask exactly the questions the conference was created to address,” he said.
“How quickly does the word ‘Jewish’ change a conversation? How easily does a gathering about antisemitism become associated with the Israeli army?”
He noted that the question about the IDF was not an innocent misunderstanding, as it instead “revealed how quickly Jewish identity can be collapsed into Israel, how quickly Israel can be collapsed into suspicion, and how quickly suspicion can become discrimination because contemporary antisemitism does not always arrive wearing the language of the past.
“It does not always announce itself with a slur, a threat, or a placard. Increasingly, it can present itself as a question, a precaution, a policy, a request for clarification. It begins by treating Jewish identity as evidence of political allegiance,” he said.
Resetting the conversation between Jewish groups and governments
The European Jewish Congress called the incident “deeply disturbing.”
“That a hotel would cancel accommodation for participants in a conference dedicated to combating antisemitism, while raising questions about supposed links to the Israeli military, reflects precisely the kind of prejudice and suspicion that such gatherings seek to confront,” the EJC noted.
“It is profoundly troubling that those working to combat antisemitism should themselves encounter such treatment. Jewish organizations and those standing against hatred must never face exclusion or discrimination because of their work,”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry said. “The Irish government cannot use the fight against antisemitism as a diplomatic PR exercise while failing to confront it at home.”
The conference in question was the 15th meeting of the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Forum, organized by the World Jewish Congress in partnership with the European Commission, and convened as an Associated Event under Ireland’s rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union.
Jewish community leaders from across the world joined government envoys, representatives from international organizations, and technology company executives in Dublin from October 12 to 14.
Leaders representing the J7 Large Communities’ Task Force Against Antisemitism – connecting the Delegación de Asociaciones Israelitas Argentinas, Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Canada’s Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs, the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions, Central Council of Jews in Germany, and Board of Deputies of British Jews, alongside the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations from the United States – also joined the forum following a series of high-level meetings in London earlier in the week.
Statements, condemnations only go so far
The gathering included a meeting with Ireland’s Taoiseach or government leader, Micheál Martin; visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta; and other discussions.
“Our meeting in Dublin is a much-needed opportunity to reset the conversation between Jewish organizations, governments, and technology companies,” Maram Stern, WJC executive vice president, said. “Statements and condemnation of antisemitism only go so far. Practical solutions must urgently be put in place to protect Jewish life globally.”
The delegates were officially welcomed by Irish ministers despite the current Ireland-Israel tensions.
At the start of Tuesday’s agenda, Colm Brophy, a member of the Irish parliament, said he was “very pleased to welcome Jewish community leaders” and was particularly happy to see that the event has a focus on AI and on the regulation of online platforms, given the “troubling increase in antisemitism and other forms of racism online in recent years.”
The incident comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ireland and Israel, with Jerusalem accusing Dublin of fostering an increasingly hostile environment toward the Jewish state.
Tensions have escalated following Ireland’s recognition of a Palestinian state, its legal and diplomatic moves against Israel, and controversy over Dublin City Council’s proposal to remove the name of former Israeli president Chaim Herzog from Herzog Park in Rathgar and replace it with “Free Palestine Park.”
The attempt was eventually condemned by Irish officials, and the J7 representatives visited the park for a photo-op this week during the conference.

INTERVIEW - ‘You’re not alone, the truth will come out’: Nobel winner Navi Pillay on global support for Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:10 UTC
22:45:10 KST

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay said Palestinians seeking justice are not alone and the truth will emerge, urging the international community to draw lessons from the collective action and economic sanctions that helped end apartheid in her native South Africa.
In an exclusive interview on Wednesday, Pillay, judge at the International Court of Justice and a former UN human rights chief, reflected on her experience fighting apartheid and the importance of international support for Palestinians amid continuing concerns over accountability for violations in the Gaza Strip.
"I imagine I'm correct in saying that even though Palestinians are struggling for their freedom for more than 90 years now, attention by the international community and support by the international community would be of great significance for them," she told Anadolu.
"The message being, you're not alone. That with information and correct information, the truth will come out."
Pillay, 85, who was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize for her contributions to international justice, chaired a UN commission of inquiry, which concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Recalling her experience under apartheid, she said South African lawyers fought a lonely struggle with little international attention. "We really had very little relief. And honestly, the rest of the world didn't pay attention to us," she said.
The rights lawyer said a UN commission gathering evidence and presenting its findings internationally would have greatly helped Black South Africans at that time.
Pillay stressed the importance of identifying the root causes of Palestinian suffering, and reiterated her commission's finding that Israel's unlawful occupation was the root cause of the longstanding conflict.
She criticized governments for increasingly prioritizing their political and regional interests over their responsibilities to maintain international peace and justice.
She said the UN Security Council already possessed mechanisms to respond to violations, including peacekeeping operations, investigative commissions, mediation and economic sanctions.
"The principal tool they have is to impose sanctions, economic sanctions against governments that are violating international human rights law, international humanitarian law, they've used this before," she said.
Questioning the international community's response to Gaza, Pillay said: "So, the question that civil society is asking: 'Why are you sitting back and doing nothing in the face of huge violations that we, the people, can see daily? We can see genocide being committed on our television screens'."
"And I am as unhappy as most people that there has been so little action," she added.
Drawing on South Africa's experience, where apartheid ended in 1994, Pillay emphasized the decisive role of international economic pressure.
"Apartheid came to an end mainly because of the economic sanctions imposed by the Security Council, by the United Nations against the apartheid government," she said.
"I never thought apartheid will end in my lifetime, but it's this collective action by governments, by businesses, and civil society all over the world that brought an end to apartheid."
Pillay said she had been hoping for similar international cooperation in response to the situation in Gaza.
"I've been hopefully looking for and calling for that level of cooperation, that level of condemnation of the huge violations and killings of Palestinians," she said.
Asked whether Israel's growing international isolation and sanctions targeting settlers in the occupied West Bank could help end its impunity, Pillay said such developments could contribute to broader collective action.
"The one thing we cannot accept is doing nothing," she said.
Recalling Nelson Mandela's position that South Africans could not fully enjoy freedom while Palestinians remained oppressed and occupied, she said Palestinians were seeking measures similar to those used against apartheid.
"Palestinians are calling for the kind of action that was taken to end apartheid. They see the value of economic boycotts," she said.
She also referred to protests by Israelis against efforts to weaken the country's Supreme Court, urging governments to respect civilians' right to protest and cooperate with international criminal investigations.
She stressed that international legal principles must be applied consistently, without selectivity or bias, particularly when civilians are suffering.
Pillay emphasized that governments, rather than international organizations alone, bear responsibility for preventing genocide.
"The Genocide Convention is very clear. The duty is on every state to prevent genocide," she said. "That's a purpose; it's not to react to genocide and to punish the alleged perpetrators. The main reason is to prevent, because it's an intolerable crime when a whole group is being destroyed in whole or in part."
About the potential legal responsibility of governments supplying weapons, intelligence or political support despite warnings of serious violations, Pillay said the states themselves established international conventions and treaties.
"They set the standards. Now they must implement them without selection," she said, arguing that governments were failing to apply their own commitments because of political interests.
Pillay recalled that her UN commission had urged the General Assembly to seek an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concerning Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory.
She welcomed the court's opinion in 2024, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful, and outlined obligations concerning Palestinian rights.
She, however, acknowledged that legal proceedings offered limited immediate relief to people suffering on the ground.
"I agree; they're not very helpful to relieve their immediate dire situation," she said. "Let's use international law to assert and realize the rights of people who are oppressed everywhere in the world."
On shortcomings of the international system and its eroding credibility, Pillay pointed to the dominance of governments within the UN and the shrinking space for civil society.
"Certainly, the system is very skewed. Who controls the United Nations? It's member states, it's governments," she said, urging UN members to conduct their affairs in closer cooperation with civil society organizations.
Turning to Washington's measures against the International Criminal Court (ICC), Pillay called on governments, including those outside the Rome Statute, to oppose the campaign.
"I would like to see states of the world, the member states, whether they're parties to the Rome Statute or not, to condemn the unlawful measures and sanctions that the United States is imposing on this court," she said.
"We should say roundly that it's unacceptable, and then we all have the responsibility to help the court to overcome these obstacles."
The former ICC judge expressed confidence that the court's staff would continue their work despite mounting political pressure.
"They're not going to stop doing what they are doing because they are working out of commitment. They believe that it is possible to realize justice for all," she said.
Reflecting on receiving the Nobel, Pillay described the recognition as unexpected and deeply meaningful. "This award was a huge surprise to me, but a wonderful surprise," she said.
She expressed gratitude that the Nobel Committee had recognized different aspects of her decades-long career, from challenging apartheid to advancing international justice.
"You don't win a case all the time. You win some. You lose many, especially under apartheid South Africa," she said.
Pillay described the committee's recognition of her work as a "memorable moment," saying she appreciated its efforts to examine her contributions to international peace and justice.
