France’s Mélenchon sees Spain’s Sánchez as inspiration for fixing public finances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:44:43 UTC
22:44:43 KST

Jean-Luc Melenchon attends a press conference on the sidelines of the debates on the draft state budget for 2027 at LFI's headquarters in Paris, France on October 14, 2026. | Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Jean-Luc Mélenchon pointed to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as proof that greater public spending can boost the French economy and repair its strained public finances.
“Ever since Spain adopted a budget focused on ecological and social growth, it has experienced steady growth and a decline in its debt,” said Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s presidential election in France.
In a press conference focused on the budget on Wednesday, the 75-year-old radical doubled down on his calls for a positive demand shock driven by billions in new state spending. He also reiterated his proposal to write off billions of euros in French debt held by the European Central Bank, which has drawn strong criticism, including from ECB President Christine Lagarde.
Advertisement
Polls show Mélenchon neck and neck with center-right candidate Édouard Philippe in the race to qualify for a second-round runoff against Marine Le Pen, the far-right frontrunner who presented her own budget plans last week.
Under Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Spain has significantly reduced its budget deficit, while public debt is projected to fall below 100% of GDP in 2026. His government has raised the minimum wage and supported investment in green energy, alongside other sectors. Although inflation is a major concern and economic growth is expected to moderate in 2027, Spain remains one of Europe’s fastest-growing major economies, with the IMF on Tuesday forecasting 2.5% growth in 2026.
Spanish deficit fell significantly under Sánchez, and became one of the Eurozone’s fastest-growing economies after the pandemic.
Spain’s debt-to-GDP ratio dropped below 100% — while France’s raised to 119% — as the government invested heavily in sectors such as green energy and raised the minimum wage. But the cost of living remains a major concern in the country, particularly housing — one of the issues that led Sánchez to call a snap election earlier this month.
More money, less problems?
Mélenchon wants to boost growth by increasing purchasing power through higher salaries — including a higher minimum wage, a 10% raise for public-sector workers and a nationwide round of collective bargaining — as well as higher benefits for welfare recipients and a monthly payment of €1,337 for every French student intended to lift them above the poverty line.
Together, these measures form what his campaign calls an €82 billion “emergency spending” package.
Advertisement
Eric Coquerel, a Mélenchon ally who heads the French National Assembly’s powerful finance committee, argued in the same press conference that the new spending would drive GDP growth and increase tax revenue.
He also outlined ways to fund it, including a 2% wealth tax on households worth more than €100 million, popularized by French economist Gabriel Zucman, and higher taxes on large inheritances, which would be capped at €12 million under a Mélenchon presidency.
Fiscally conservative think tanks such as Institut Montaigne have argued that Mélenchon significantly underestimated the cost of his proposed spending and the potential tax revenue in previous campaigns. Critics also warn of capital flight if he is elected president, as occurred after his political mentor François Mitterrand was elected in 1981 on a platform of mass nationalizations.
In a statement, Edouard Philippe’s campaign called Mélenchon’s budget proposal “dangerous.”
Mélenchon blamed the current state of France’s finances on President Emmanuel Macron’s decision to cut several taxes early in his presidency, a move Macron said was intended to attract more investment.
“There are no other causes [of the deficit] than the systematic depletion of the state orchestrated by Macronism,” Mélenchon said.
Advertisement
“We are pitting the virtuous cycle of ecological and social recovery … against the vicious cycle of Macronist budgets and the dismantling of the state,” he added.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s government has presented a budget with €43 billion in spending cuts, aiming to reduce France’s deficit to 5% of GDP without raising taxes. This year’s deficit is expected to reach 5.4% of GDP, missing the initial 5% target.
The counter-proposal from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed includes €106.4 billion in additional revenue and €81.7 billion in further spending, according to Coquerel, leaving about €25 billion to reduce the deficit.
France’s current center-right government is expected to pass its budget through the country’s hung parliament either by invoking a constitutional mechanism that allows the executive to pass legislation without a vote or by executive order. Mélenchon said his first order of business if elected in May would be to draft a new budget, which he hopes to pass in summer 2027.
France Unbowed advocates for a reduction of France’s contribution to the European Union, which presidential frontrunner Le Pen also wants to cut by €11 billion, though Coquerel clarified that he had not included a potential rebate in his economic forecasts.
Mélenchon intends to use the contribution as leverage to push for revised EU treaties, including scrapping the 3% deficit target for member countries and allowing national governments to adopt protectionist policies.
Critics, including Lagarde, said Mélenchon’s debt proposal was “dangerous” and potentially illegal because it could amount to direct financing of member countries by the ECB, which is prohibited by European treaties.

Nord Stream trial: Russia used pipelines as ‘weapon’, defence says

A lawyer for a Ukrainian accused of blowing up the Nord Stream pipelines supplying Russian gas to western Europe said on Wednesday that Moscow used the network to exert political and economic pressure, as the former military officer’s trial opened in Germany.
Sergiy Kuznietsov is the first person to go on trial over the 2022 sabotage. The 50-year-old is accused of leading a Ukrainian team of divers and an explosives expert to bomb Nord Stream, seven months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At the start of proceedings in Hamburg, prosecutor Stefan Schmidt said Kuznietsov, acting on behalf of the Ukrainian state, had committed a war crime by “using military means” to hit civilian targets.
He is also charged with attacking civilian infrastructure and causing an explosion.

US judge blocks sanctions against 2 human rights groups engaging with international court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:43:09 UTC
22:43:09 KST

Yasin Gungor
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
A US federal judge blocked the Trump administration from penalizing two human rights organizations communicating with the International Criminal Court (ICC), ruling that the measures unconstitutionally restrict free speech.
US District Judge Jesse Furman granted a preliminary injunction, determining that the federal prohibition against providing services to sanctioned ICC personnel constitutes a content-based regulation of speech that fails strict scrutiny.
The ruling bars federal agencies from enforcing civil fines of up to $377,700 or criminal penalties of up to 20 years in prison under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act against plaintiffs Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN) and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG). DAWN had routinely submitted war crimes evidence filings under Article 15 of the Rome Statute. TAAG was formed to prepare similar submissions but had withheld filing out of fear of prosecution.
The rights groups welcomed the victory and announced they will immediately resume submitting evidentiary documentation to the tribunal, restart formal coordination with UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and re-engage with Palestinian human rights bodies Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights.
ICC measures
The litigation challenged Executive Order 14203, issued in February 2025, which directed federal agencies to impose tangible consequences on entities tied to investigations targeting the US or allies such as Israel that have not consented to ICC jurisdiction.
The order targeted former ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan, six judges and UN personnel.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced last Friday that Washington imposed sanctions on the court, warning that the US would dismantle the tribunal if member nations fail to rein in its authority.
US pressure intensified after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes in the Gaza Strip. The ICC has 125 member states, while neither the US nor Israel is party to the tribunal.

US inflation rises to 3.7 pct as fuel costs climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:41:24 UTC
22:41:24 KST

Higher gasoline prices drove over half of September’s monthly inflation increase.
U.S. annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September, exceeding forecasts as higher fuel prices drove the increase, while core inflation also topped expectations, official data showed on Oct. 14.
The consumer price index climbed 0.6 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis from August, when prices rose 0.4 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said.
The monthly increase matched the average estimate from a broad survey of forecasters. The annual rate, up from 3.4 percent in August, beat the 3.6 percent prediction.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3 percent on the month, matching August’s pace but exceeding the 0.2 percent forecast. The annual rate climbed to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent, above expectations of 2.5 percent.
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1 percent, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase. The broader energy index rose 5.2 percent, accelerating from 2.1 percent in August.
Shelter costs increased 0.4 percent, compared with 0.3 percent the previous month. Food prices were unchanged overall, with grocery prices falling 0.1 percent and the cost of eating out rising 0.2 percent.
Other categories recording increases included used vehicles, airfares, medical care and clothing. Communication prices were among the few major categories to fall.
The figures follow the Federal Reserve’s decision in September to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent.
The central bank said inflation remained elevated and that the move would support a return to its 2 percent goal.

MOD Guard Service

MOD Guard Service
The MGS (MOD Guard Service) plays a vital role in supporting MOD security.
What we do
The Ministry of Defence Guard Service (MGS) has guarded the defence estate since 1992 and provides security services at more than 135 sites across England, Scotland and Wales, including high-profile locations such as MOD Main Building in London and His Majesty’s Naval Bases in Portsmouth, Devonport and the Clyde.
The MGS was formed as a result of a security review of all British military bases following the bombing of the Royal Marines School of Music at Deal Barracks by the Provisional Irish Republican Army in 1989. Over the years, the MGS has evolved into a dynamic organisation that takes great pride in the services it delivers.
The MGS works closely with its security partners: Ministry of Defence Police (MDP), Security Services Group (SSG) and Military Provost Guard Services under Standing Joint Command (SJC) GUARDIAN and the wider MOD to protect the homeland and defend Defence.
The MGS prides itself on delivering a high-quality customer-focused service and will continue its mission to protect Defence from threats including crime, terrorism, espionage and sabotage by providing the highest quality of security services through professionalism and excellence. Working to become a technical authority on security, its vision is to be recognised as an outstanding provider of security services.
It strives to ensure its standards are maintained through external accreditation, holding the National Security Inspectorate (NSI) Gold standard.
The MGS employs more than 2,700 operational and support staff as civil servants. They are managed by a Head Office team, dispersed strategically around the country according to requirements.
MGS officers are often the first point of contact with the MOD for employees, visitors and contractors. They pride themselves on their inclusive, customer-focused culture, working to the Civil Service Code of Conduct and MGS core values of honesty, integrity, professionalism and efficiency.
MGS services
MGS offers a range of services to meet customer needs.
These include:
- control of access and egress
- security searches
- reception management
- event security co-ordination
- incident cordon and control
- control room management including CCTV and alarm monitoring and response
- emergency first aid
- patrolling, including dog patrols
Working for MGS
To achieve our goals, we need dedicated, highly-motivated people with diverse backgrounds, experience and skills, who can adapt to meet a complex range of threats and challenges in a rapidly-changing world.
Our staff come from a variety of backgrounds and professions and bring a wealth of customer service and security experience. We take the time to understand our customers’ values and security needs, and our highly-trained officers must be equipped to deliver services which reflect our culture and underpin the security mission.
We offer a broad range of interesting and challenging jobs, with a variety of working patterns, contributing directly to the UK’s Defence Mission. We enable our people to work at the right place, with the right people, at the right time. We believe that if we look after our people, they will be passionate about delivering great things for our customers.
Training and development
The MGS is committed to investing in its people through structured training and development. All officers receive role‑specific initial training to ensure they are prepared for operational duties, supported by regular continuation and refresher training to maintain skills, confidence and professionalism throughout their career.
We align our training with Defence standards and best practice, supporting both operational effectiveness and personal development. There are opportunities to develop specialist skills, progress into supervisory and management roles, and build long‑term careers while contributing directly to the UK’s Defence Mission.
New entrant requirements
All new entrants will be subject to security vetting and must pass a selection interview.
The MOD Guard Service is currently undertaking a review of grade structures, pay and conditions, aimed at improving employee experience, wellbeing, and career progression. This review may result in future changes to terms and conditions; however, the requirement for this role remains unchanged.
Working hours and leave
Most staff work on average 48 hours per week. Further benefits include:
- day and shift working for operational staff
- flexitime scheme upon completion of 6 months service (dependent on role)
- alternative working practices
- 25 days paid annual leave rising (1 day per year) to 30 days upon completion of 5 years’ service
- in addition to 8 public holidays per year, you will also receive leave for HM The King’s birthday
- generous maternity and paternity package
- highly competitive pension scheme
How to apply
Please visit Civil Service Jobs and look at our for more information.
If you have any questions, please email MGS-RH@mod.gov.uk

The Uyghurs Who Fought in Syria’s Civil War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:41:00 UTC
22:41:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Emily Feng – author of “Our Hearts Burned for Home: Uyghur Militants in Syria’s Civil War” (Columbia Global Reports 2026) and award-winning correspondent for NPR – is the 530th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
What was the impetus behind your reporting on Uyghur militants in Syria’s civil war?
For years, I had been reporting on the ground on the Xinjiang region and the sweeping detention campaign that began in early 2017. And one of the reasons cited in rare official comments from Beijing about why authorities were detaining and arresting hundreds of thousands Uyghur people mentioned the presence of Uyghur “terrorists” in Syria and Afghanistan, but offered no evidence and since these places were nearly impossible to access, no one had done interviews with any of these supposed Uyghur militants.
In late 2024, it suddenly became possible to go to Syria after the surprising collapse of the Assad regime there and the end of a terrible civil war. Coincidentally, I was in nearby Lebanon when the Assads fled to Russia, and I ended up spending much of the beginning of 2025 in Syria.
Imagine my surprise when I saw Uyghur fighters milling about Syria! Indeed, there were thousands of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and I was later to discover, their role in the civil war had been much more impactful than anyone expected.
But I sensed there was much more to the story about these Uyghur fighters than Beijing’s narrative – that these were masterminds behind fatal attacks on Chinese civilians who were now hellbent on destroying China. I wondered what had made them leave their families and livelihoods behind to live in an active war zone, and how they had transformed themselves from hairdressers and engineers and teachers into hardened militant fighters, working in alliance with Arabic-speaking, Syrian rebel groups.
I was also sensitive to the possible implications of reporting on Uyghurs. In no way is their existence in Syria justification for the detention and arrests, mostly without real due process, of so many Uyghur citizens of China. I resolved to find a way to contact the Syrian Uyghurs and interview them – a difficult task, as they had operated as a secretive and highly-disciplined force for more than a decade – and learn more about why they had come to the Middle East.
Analyze the factors propelling Uyghur militants to join the civil war and how they contributed to the overthrow of the Assad regime.
I don’t want to give too much away here! The details are in the book. But in short, many Uyghurs who ended up in Syria had initially hoped to put down roots in Turkey, where a sizeable Uyghur diaspora already exists. However, Turkey does not want these Uyghurs, and it has stymied their ability to get residence documents and even aided in their deportation back to China.
Turkey happens to share a long, mostly unfortified border with northern Syria, however, where a rebel-held swath of territory had been established in a growing civil war. And so that’s where a lot of Uyghurs headed, because Syria was not checking documents or asking for visas, frankly. All of them were also looking for a constructive way to help Uyghurs back in Xinjiang, or East Turkestan as the Uyghurs call it, and they hoped Syria would become a base to fight back politically or militarily against the Chinese Communist Party.
A good number of Uyghurs had also already heard of the possibility of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and they were eager to train militarily. An active war, one Uyghur commander later told me, was free practice.
The Uyghurs’ wholehearted embrace of violence for the sake of establishing an independent Uyghur state is controversial, I should mention, among the Uyghur diaspora globally. But of the five dozen or so interviews I did with Uyghur fighters and their families, all of them described experiences where they felt diplomacy or political activism had failed them, and they felt they had nothing left to lose anymore by taking up arms.
The deadly race riots that began July 5, 2009 in Urumqi, which left scores of both Han Chinese and Uyghur Chinese dead, was a real turning point for many Uyghurs I met. The mob violence they witnessed from all parties that week and the ensuing crackdown and racism Uyghurs experienced in the aftermath convinced the majority of the fighters I spoke to to seek their fortunes in Turkey and later Syria.
What surprised me the most after weeks on the ground in Syria with Uyghur fighters was discovering the reach and breadth of the Uyghurs’ role in the Syrian civil war. The participated in major battles, played a key role in helping rebels with Hayat Tahrir Al-Sham (HTS) take Aleppo, and eventually marched into Damascus to establish the new government. HTS’ Ahmed Al Sharaa, now Syria’s president, privately credits the Uyghurs with being a consistently loyal, effective fighting force, and for that reason, the Uyghurs now have an unusual political purchase in the new Syria.
Explain the difference between the Turkestan Islamic Party (TIP) and East Turkmenistan Islamic Movement (ETIM) and how China views their respective identities.
Both of these entities are part of a broader movement of Uyghurs who have taken up arms and seek to establish an independent Uyghur homeland in the Xinjiang region. I found evidence that members of both groups still maintain communication links, and some of the earliest TIP fighters in Syria initially tried to train with ETIM officials along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
But to call ETIM in particular an organization would be a stretch, based on what I was able to find. The ETIM-linked fighters I met said there were never many Uyghurs along the Af-Pak border, many were killed in American bombings, training was nearly impossible due to the difficult geography of the place, and there were ideological differences between the more relaxed Uyghurs and the more conservative al-Qaida-linked and Taliban fighters there.
TIP, the Syria branch of this nationalist Uyghur militant movement, was much more successful. They became highly disciplined and managed to remain organized, sharing scarce financial resources in self-sustaining communities in Idlib, in northern Syria, and setting up robust social services for a growing Uyghur population that has now reached 20,000 men, women, and children.
While TIP also maintained substantial links to al-Qaida affiliated groups, including with HTS, for years, these links later became problematic and internally divisive as TIP and HTS tried to brand themselves as politically more mainstream and welcoming to Syrians and Uyghurs of all castes. Yet TIP remains controversial within Syria, and also within much of the Uyghur diaspora community, who view their militant past with distaste.
Why are Uyghur militants controversial in Syria?
The Syria Uyghurs find themselves in an awkward position. At home, they were the oppressed. In Syria, they are widely viewed as oppressors, in the eyes of Syria’s many minority communities.
Foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, are viewed with fear and suspicion, as the civil war quickly devolved into a proxy war for various nation states and Islamist groups. Many remain in Syria in peacetime, creating resentments among Syrians who wish for the foreigners to return to their home countries. All the time, Uyghurs are confused with Uzbek fighters, and so many Syrians also do not know why the Uyghurs came to Syria in the first place, and do not understand why they cannot simply return to China.
During the civil war, the Sunni Uyghurs were active in besieging Shiite Syrian villages. They were frequently attacked by Hezbollah proxy forces and retaliated against Shiite populations in response. And for many years, the Uyghurs occupied and lived in several Shiite and Christian villages whose residents had fled in advance of Sunni Islamist groups like TIP arriving, which sowed more distrust and fear among Syrian minority communities who are increasingly on edge under the Sunni HTS-dominated government in Damascus. The Uyghurs maintain they are friendly neighbors and open to Syrians of other faiths and have tried to moderate their religious beliefs somewhat, but there are often significant cultural and linguistic gaps between them and Syrians, which the Uyghurs themselves sometimes do not even fully grasp.
Finally, there were also reports that the Uyghurs were among the perpetrators, alongside Syrian government soldiers, of horrific massacres of mostly Alawi Syrians in 2025. I found no evidence to suggest Uyghurs were involved, and they have no interest in doing so, as involvement would certainly imperil their still uncertain and vulnerable status as stateless refugees in Syria.
Assess the role of Uyghur militants in China-Syria relations and the implications for China-U.S. relations.
In some ways, the Uyghurs are not very important to China-Syria, or broader China-Middle East, relations. Syria has made it clear that it will not let groups on its soil threaten China, even though they also have made it clear they will not send the Uyghurs to China, as Beijing has demanded.
For China however, the Uyghurs are the top issue for them in Syria, and successive diplomatic delegations to Damascus have always mentioned TIP and the Uyghurs as the dominant concern Beijing has for the new government.
The result is that Gulf states, notable Saudi Arabia, have become major investors in Syria’s post-war reconstruction. China was once one of Syria’s top economic partners before the civil war, and it does not look like it will regain that position.
It will be interesting to see how the Uyghurs navigate their future in Syria. Will they buy land and build houses — setting up a much more permanent community in Syria? Will their children born in Syria still maintain strong Uyghur identity links and a commitment to set up a Uyghur state, when they feel more and more wedded to their Syrian upbringing as the years go by?

How much does public transport really cost in Denmark? And is it cheaper than owning a car?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

A few days ago, we broke down how much it costs to own a car in Denmark, and, well, it is not cheap. Nonetheless, public transport is also fairly expensive. And while for a single person living in a city the choice may be clear, for a family the story can be different.
We broke down how much public transport costs in Denmark and what the cheapest option is.
Public transport in the city
Monthly commuter passes are generally cheaper in Denmark’s other major cities than in Copenhagen. In 2026, a 30-day Pendlerkort, or commuter pass in English, in Copenhagen costs DKK 530 for two zones, rising to DKK 600 if Metro access is included. In Aarhus, Odense and Aalborg, the lowest adult commuter fare is DKK 435 for one or two zones, while three zones cost DKK 585 and four zones DKK 810. All four cities use zone-based systems, so the final price depends on how many zones a commuter crosses rather than on the city alone.
Families can reduce public transport costs in Denmark because an adult with a valid ticket or pass can generally bring up to two children under 12 free of charge in Copenhagen, Aarhus, Odense and Aalborg. Children who need their own commuter pass usually pay about half the adult fare, with a 1-2 zone Pendlerkort costing around DKK 218 a month in Aarhus and DKK 217.50 in Odense and Aalborg, while Copenhagen also offers roughly half-price commuter passes for children.
Children aged 12 to 15 must pay for public transport even when travelling with an adult, but they generally qualify for child fares of around half the adult price.
Using trains
For regular train commuters, DSB offers a Pendlerkort covering a specific route or set of zones, with unlimited travel during the validity period. The pass can also be used on buses, metro and light rail within the zones included.
Adults with a valid ticket or commuter pass can generally bring up to two children under 12 for free, while older children can qualify for reduced child fares.
For regular train commuters, the effective cost can be around DKK 1.1 per kilometer when a monthly pass is used five days a week. A Copenhagen-Roskilde Pendlerkort costs about DKK 1,410 for 30 days, which works out at roughly DKK 1.17 per kilometer for someone commuting both ways 20 days a month. A comparable Aarhus-Skanderborg commute costs about DKK 990 for a 30-day pass, or roughly DKK 1.13 per kilometer under the same assumption.
The pass also covers local public transport within the zones included, such as buses and, where relevant, metro or light rail, so commuters can use it for the urban part of their journey as well. Because the passes allow unlimited travel within those zones, the effective cost per kilometer falls further if they are also used outside the daily commute.
Deduction
Denmark’s transport deduction can reduce the cost of commuting for people who travel more than 12 kilometers each way between home and work, meaning more than 24 kilometers in total per working day. In 2026, there is no deduction for the first 24 kilometers, while travel between 25 and 120 kilometers qualifies for a deduction of DKK 3.17 per kilometer, and distances above 120 kilometers qualify for DKK 1.59 per kilometer.
For example, a person travelling 60 kilometers in total each working day can deduct 36 kilometers, which, at the 2026 rate, amounts to about DKK 114 per commuting day. Over 203 commuting days, that would give a deduction of around DKK 23,200, worth roughly DKK 6,000 in lower taxes. The deduction only applies to days when the person actually travels to work, so holidays, sick days and days spent working from home must be excluded, but it applies regardless of whether the journey is made by car, train, bus, bicycle or another form of transport.
Lower-income workers can receive an additional benefit: people earning less than DKK 391,500 before the labour market contribution in 2026 may qualify for an extra transport deduction of up to DKK 30,800, with the additional amount gradually reduced for incomes between DKK 341,500 and DKK 391,500.
The commuting deduction in Denmark is individual rather than family-based. If both partners work and each travels more than 24 kilometers in total between home and work on a working day, both can claim their own deduction based on their personal commute and the number of days they actually travel to work. Having children does not increase the deduction, and extra distance driven to drop off or pick up children cannot be added to the home-to-work journey. If family members share a car, each eligible worker can still claim their own commuting deduction, while lower-income workers may also qualify individually for an additional deduction.
A comparison: car vs. public transport
For a single commuter, public transport is clearly cheaper on both routes. Travelling between Copenhagen and Roskilde 20 days a month costs about DKK 1,410 with a Pendlerkort, compared with around DKK 3,732 in an electric car or DKK 4,200 in a petrol car, using FDM’s total ownership costs. Between Aarhus and Skanderborg, the monthly cost is about DKK 990 by public transport, DKK 2,737 by electric car and DKK 3,080 by petrol car.
For two adults travelling together, the gap narrows because they can share one car, while public transport requires two passes.
Even then, two commuter passes cost about DKK 2,820 on Copenhagen-Roskilde and DKK 1,980 on Aarhus-Skanderborg, still less than sharing either type of car. These figures are before tax deductions, but Denmark’s commuting deduction is calculated in the same way per kilometer regardless of whether someone travels by car, train, bus or bicycle, so applying it would reduce the effective cost of both options rather than giving cars a special advantage.

The Verkhovna Rada approved two decisions to unlock €4 billion from the EU — next in line is a tax on parcels worth up to €150
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:39:32 EEST
22:39:32 KST

The Verkhovna Rada approved two decisions to unlock €4 billion from the EU — next in line is a tax on parcels worth up to €150
Kyiv • UNN
Parliament updated the property valuation system and created a group to select members of the Accounting Chamber. These decisions are needed for an EU loan.
The Verkhovna Rada adopted in the second reading a draft law on updating the property valuation system in Ukraine and also unblocked the competition for the Accounting Chamber. The documents are among the four decisions required to unblock EU macro-financial assistance under the Ukraine Support Loan program. Two more draft laws are still pending—on the taxation of parcels, which are to be considered on Thursday, October 15, UNN writes.
Details
Draft Law No. 13435 "On Property Valuation" was adopted in the second reading and in full with the votes of 271 members of parliament.
The document regulates public relations arising in the course of property valuation, the review of property valuation reports, the professional training and advanced training of valuers, regulation and professional self-government in the field of property valuation, and also establishes rules for determining the amount of property damage, including damage caused by the damage, destruction, or loss of property or other violations concerning such property as a result of an armed conflict.
Property valuation will be carried out by a single professional organization of valuers, which will provide training for specialists, quality control, and protection of their interests, with the aim of forming a professional judgment on the value of property (determining its value) or calculating the value of property.
The types of property value determined through property valuation are:
-  market value; 
-  fair value; 
-  investment value; 
-  other types of value provided for by international valuation standards and other regulatory legal acts in the field of property valuation.  
"Property damage caused by the damage, destruction, or loss of property or other violations concerning property, including as a result of hostilities, terrorist acts, or sabotage caused by an armed conflict, as well as the amount of costs for restoring property, shall be determined through an independent property valuation, and in cases established by the legislation of Ukraine, through a standardized property valuation," the document says.
As Olena Shulyak, Chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on the Organization of State Power, Local Self-Government, Regional Development, and Urban Planning, explained, instead of strict state control and bureaucratic procedures, the draft law strengthens the role of professional self-government. Valuers themselves and their professional associations will receive more powers and responsibility.
Shulyak added that for ordinary citizens and businesses, the valuation of an apartment, house, or enterprise would become more objective and understandable. The results produced by Ukrainian valuers will begin to be recognized by international investors and foreign banks.
Link to EU requirements
The aforementioned draft law is included in the list of conditions for the EU MFA (European Union Macro-Financial Assistance) program—macro-financial assistance from the European Union—and is also one of the structural benchmarks of the International Monetary Fund program.
It should be noted that, under the loan agreement and memorandum with the European Union for attracting a €90 billion loan, Ukraine must fulfill several conditions, including:
-  the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of legislation establishing a property valuation system that defines institutional roles and responsibilities concerning property valuation; 
-  the Verkhovna Rada's approval of the appointment of the three missing experts to the commission for selecting members of the governing board of the Accounting Chamber of Ukraine; 
-  the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of a law abolishing the tax exemption for international parcels, except for goods intended for security and defense purposes; 
-  the Verkhovna Rada's adoption of legislative amendments introducing taxation of income received through digital platforms. 
Rada ratified the attraction of a 90 billion euro loan from the EU28.05.26, 11:15 • 20296 views
What else Parliament approved
At its meeting on Wednesday, October 14, the Verkhovna Rada adopted a resolution establishing an advisory group of experts to conduct the preliminary selection of candidates for positions as members of the Accounting Chamber.
It consists of three representatives from international and foreign organizations, whose candidacies had previously been approved by a Cabinet resolution, including:
-  Lee Summerfield – Director of a department at the National Audit Office of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland (NAO); 
-  Igors Ludboržs – former member and dean of the European Court of Auditors (ECA); 
-  Pascal MUNIER – honorary magistrate of the Cour des comptes (Court of Auditors, the supreme audit institution of the French Republic).  
Three representatives from Ukraine who received the highest number of votes also joined the advisory group:
-  Mykola Marchenko (first deputy head of the secretariat of the parliamentary faction of the political party "Servant of the People") – 265; 
-  Hlib Vyshlinsky (executive director of the NGO "Centre for Economic Strategy") – 204; 
-  Myroslava Masliak (senior lecturer at Kharkiv National University of Economics) – 202. 
As Roksolana Pidlasa, chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Budget, said, the establishment of the advisory group of experts is a condition of the Ukraine Support Loan (the macro-financial component) from the EU, with a deadline of August 2026, while the appointment of the full membership of the Accounting Chamber from among the candidates pre-selected by the group of experts is a structural benchmark of the cooperation program with the IMF, which must be fulfilled by December 2026. The funds from these programs are used to finance the state budget deficit and are disbursed in tranches subject to the fulfillment of the commitments undertaken.
Following the establishment of the group, the submission of documents by candidates will begin within a week of the vote in the Rada and will last 30 days. The advisory group of experts will then conduct testing and interviews and recommend at least two candidates for each position to parliament. The final decision rests with the Verkhovna Rada: it will appoint new members of the Accounting Chamber from among those recommended.
A citizen of Ukraine aged 30 or older may become a member of the Accounting Chamber if they speak Ukrainian and English or French, hold at least a master's degree, have at least seven years of total work experience and at least five years of experience in public control (audit), economics, finance or law, as well as an impeccable business reputation.
Today, two bills on abolishing the exemption for parcels worth up to 150 euros were also on the parliament's agenda, but it was decided to postpone the final vote until Thursday.
"We are now going to hear the amendments to the bills on parcels. Today, the amendments will be considered, while the confirmation, except for one, will take place tomorrow, and the substantive vote will be tomorrow (October 15 – ed.)," First Deputy Speaker of Parliament Oleksandr Korniienko said during the meeting.
It is worth noting that on Tuesday, September 1, the Verkhovna Rada once again failed to vote on bills abolishing the tax exemption for parcels worth up to 150 euros. The bills in question are No. 15460 and No. 15112-d.
On September 7, the Cabinet of Ministers approved and submitted to the Verkhovna Rada two related draft laws on the taxation of small postal and express shipments worth up to 150 euros ordered through marketplaces. The documents provide for the abolition of the tax exemption for parcels worth up to 150 euros.
Bill No. 15460 introduces amendments to the Customs Code of Ukraine (which regulates customs procedures, border-clearance rules and the 150-euro threshold for import duty).
Under the bill, VAT would be imposed on imported goods purchased through marketplaces starting from 0 euros.
Currently, international shipments worth up to 150 euros are not subject to import VAT or import duty. Under the proposed rules, the threshold itself would remain, but its effect would change: goods worth up to 150 euros would be exempt from duty only. Thus, VAT at the basic rate of 20% would already be charged from the first euro of the item's value.
For shipments costing more than 150 euros, the basis for calculating the duty would change. It would be charged at a rate of 10% of the parcel's entire invoice value, rather than only on the amount exceeding 150 euros.
At the same time, private, duty-free gifts worth up to 45 euros were expected to remain exempt from taxation. The new rules would not apply to the distance selling of alcohol and tobacco.
Government Bill No. 16051, which introduces amendments to the Tax Code of Ukraine, establishes rules for the assessment and payment of VAT on e-commerce and parcels; however, the government included provisions bringing the rules concerning politically exposed persons (PEPs) into line with the version agreed with the EU.
Incidentally, on June 9, the Verkhovna Rada adopted in its entirety Bill No. 15111-d on the taxation of digital platforms. On June 11, it was signed by Verkhovna Rada Chairman Ruslan Stefanchuk, and on June 12 it was sent to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for signature, since when the document has been "stuck" with the head of state.
The fact is that, during the second reading, a provision was submitted to the bill envisaging changes to the financial monitoring system for politically exposed persons (PEPs). It was included in the draft by the relevant committee and subsequently supported by the plenary chamber.
PEPs include current and former top officials: from members of parliament, ministers, and the president to heads of law enforcement agencies, members of the NBU Board, and ambassadors.
Bill No. 16051 provides for the exclusion from the list of politically exposed persons of heads of structural units of the central office of the National Bank of Ukraine and employees responsible for conducting financial monitoring at a bank in which the state owns more than 50 percent of the shares.
Under the legislation, banks and other financial companies are required to conduct enhanced financial monitoring of PEPs, their close relatives, and business partners.
PEP status is lifelong. At the same time, enhanced financial monitoring applies throughout a person’s tenure in a top position and for 12 months after their dismissal. However, banks and other financial institutions may continue to subject a PEP to enhanced scrutiny if they consider that the person remains risky.
The amendments introduced to the bill impose penalties on banks that decide to continue enhanced monitoring of a PEP’s transactions after 12 months have passed since the person’s dismissal from a top position.
According to some members of parliament, it is precisely because of this amendment that Zelenskyy has still not signed the aforementioned bill.
However, during its September 16 meeting, the Rada adopted an alternative bill—No. 16051-1—which abolishes the provisions concerning PEPs and stipulates that taxes on parcels will be credited to the special fund of the State Budget of Ukraine and directed toward meeting the needs of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
However, by the second reading, amendments concerning PEPs had also been included in Bill No. 16051-1; they are intended to unblock the signing of Law No. 15111-d on the taxation of income from digital platforms.

African regions record world’s fastest gains in disaster resilience: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:38:36 UTC
22:38:36 KST

Dilara Hamit
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
African regions have recorded the world’s fastest improvements in people’s ability to withstand and recover from disasters since 2023, according to a major global study.
North Africa’s resilience score rose five points, the largest regional increase. In comparison, Southern Africa gained four points, Lloyd’s Register Foundation said in its latest World Risk Poll report, published Tuesday.
Eastern Africa and Central and Western Africa each recorded three-point increases.
The gains were linked to expanding internet access, stronger household preparedness and improved financial resilience in countries including Algeria, Egypt, Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
The findings do not mean Africa is now the world’s most resilient continent. Instead, they show that its regions made the fastest progress during the period examined.
The fourth edition of the World Risk Poll was conducted by Gallup and surveyed more than 143,000 people in 140 countries and territories in 2025.
Its Resilience Index measures people’s capacity to absorb and recover from major shocks on a scale of 0 to 100. It assesses individual resilience, household preparedness, community support and wider societal conditions.
Despite Africa’s progress, the research revealed major inequalities in access to disaster warnings. In Central and Western Africa, only 47% of adults affected by a disaster said they received a warning.
Globally, about 1.1 billion adults experienced a disaster during the five years preceding the survey, but nearly 220 million received no warning, according to the foundation.
Those in low-income countries were almost twice as likely to have experienced a disaster as those in wealthy nations. Nearly one-third of adults in low-income countries reported being affected, compared with 16% in high-income countries.
Only 64% of disaster-affected adults in low-income countries received warnings, compared with 84% in high-income countries.
Receiving a warning also did not necessarily mean people were able to act. Fewer than half of adults warned in low- and lower-middle-income countries took protective action before a disaster, compared with 71% in high-income countries.
The report identified mobile phones as an important opportunity to close the warning gap. Of those who received no warning, 77%, more than 170 million people, owned a mobile phone.
People were also more likely to act when alerts reached them through multiple sources. Just 37% of those warned through a single channel took action. That number rose to 51% for those reached through two channels, and 64% among those receiving warnings through three.
Possible channels included mobile messages, television, social media, radio and direct community communication.
The research found that societal resilience, including trust in national institutions, rose globally from 63 points in 2021 to a record 66 in 2025.
Individual resilience, however, declined from 46 to 42 points, the lowest recorded by the index.
The foundation said the results showed that wider warning coverage must be accompanied by investment in household preparedness and community response capacity, ensuring people have the information, time and resources needed to act before disaster strikes.

Europe’s weak link: The scandals eroding trust in Germany’s BND
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:36:36 UTC
22:36:36 KST

Early this month, German federal prosecutors arrested August Hanning, the 80-year-old former president of the country’s top intelligence agency BND, on charges of treason and espionage for a foreign entity.
A court ordered his pre-trial detention, along with that of his former chief of staff, Manfred D.
Prosecutors say that from 2010 to mid-2022, Manfred D, who remained in a senior BND role until March 2026, supplied Hanning with roughly 2,000 documents – many of them classified – including material originating from foreign partner intelligence services.
Hanning, who led the BND from 1998 to 2005 before becoming a private consultant, is accused of using the material for commercial work and, in at least one instance, preparing an analysis for an officer of an unnamed foreign intelligence service.
The case has prompted partner services to review intelligence previously shared with Berlin.
Analysts point out that the scandal is only the latest in a series of breaches that have repeatedly exposed the BND’s weaknesses.
For example, authorities arrested in December 2022 a man named Carsten L, a German BND employee, on suspicion of treason after he allegedly passed state secrets obtained in the course of his work to a Russian intelligence agency that year.
It is important to note that the tip that helped identify him came from a “friendly Western intelligence agency”. At that time, BND chief Bruno Kahl publicly stressed the need for discretion, noting Russia’s willingness to exploit any detail.
Such episodes have left partner intelligence services wondering whether material they had shared with Berlin remained secure.
Sabir Askeroglu, a Eurasia expert at the Istanbul-based think tank Dunya Siyaseti, sees such cases as more than isolated failures.
“When allegations of espionage emerge within an intelligence service, there are generally two possible explanations: institutional vulnerabilities or a change in the country’s strategic orientation,” he tells TRT World.
In Germany’s case, both dimensions deserve consideration, he adds.
He points to the institutional legacy of German reunification in 1990, saying former East German security officials with residual Moscow ties could possibly carry networks into the unified state.
Secondly, Germany’s increasingly confrontational policy towards Russia, particularly since the beginning of the war in Ukraine, has transformed its domestic political and security environment, Askeroglu adds.
Individuals associated with the more cooperative approach towards Russia from the years of Angela Merkel – Germany’s chancellor from 2005 to 2021 – may find themselves under greater scrutiny, he notes.
“These historical and political factors should be treated as possible explanatory contexts rather than established causes,” Askeroglu says, while stressing that the central question remains whether individual breaches reflect deeper systemic weaknesses.
Intelligence interdependence or a source of friction?
The BND’s analytical shortcomings have been apparent to the world.
In August 2021, as the Taliban prepared to take over Kabul, German intelligence assessments proved overly reassuring.
Internal reporting had flagged the rapid erosion of Afghan security forces, but a key BND assessment presented to the crisis staff concluded that a Taliban takeover before September 11 was “rather unlikely”.
But the Taliban captured Kabul within days, which left critics questioning the BND’s poor intelligence assessments and delays in ordering an evacuation that put German nationals in danger.
The episode reinforced a perception among some partner intelligence agencies that the BND has struggled with independent, timely strategic analysis, even when it possesses substantial raw material.
Germany’s foreign intelligence service has long operated in close partnership with the CIA and the NSA of the US, MI6 of the UK, and intelligence services of other European nations.
Post-World War II arrangements placed the BND within a NATO intelligence architecture heavily influenced by the US.
But that interdependence has also been a source of friction.
For example, the Snowden revelations documented deep BND-NSA collaboration on German soil and, separately, the monitoring of Merkel’s communications.
“The trust has been destroyed by the US when the CIA was listening to Merkel,” said Selcuk Aydin, assistant professor of international relations at Istanbul’s Bogazici University.
“Germany’s defence, specifically its intelligence system, has been organised by the US and NATO after WWII. This causes a problem with the established institutionalised system,” he tells TRT World.
Europe, and Germany in particular, has since sought to revise its defence and intelligence posture, Aydin says, adding that he anticipates a “more dramatic transformation” in defence and intelligence sooner rather than later.
The Hanning case has once again placed that trust under pressure.
European intelligence services are examining whether material previously shared with the BND may have been compromised.
A German security official described the implications for partner relations as “very, very serious”.
MI6 and other agencies have conducted internal reviews of information passed to Berlin, while CIA material was reportedly among the documents later found in Hanning’s possession.
Askeroglu says that repeated breaches can undermine the confidence of partners, such as the US, the UK, and France, especially when sensitive information is involved.
“Intelligence cooperation depends not only on shared interests, but also on confidence that information will remain secure,” he says.
Consequently, Germany’s ambition to assume greater strategic responsibility in Europe must be accompanied by the “credibility and reliability of its intelligence services”.
Aydin framed the problem in structural terms rooted in the post-1945 order.
The institutionalised system built under the US and NATO umbrellas created lasting dependencies, while the Merkel surveillance episode shattered residual assumptions of reciprocity.
As Germany and Europe revise their defence and intelligence arrangements, the Hanning and Carsten L episodes illustrate the gap between aspiration and performance.
Askeroglu says Germany’s intelligence vulnerabilities can’t be fully separated from the country’s “longstanding dilemma between engagement with the East and security cooperation with the West”.
“As long as Germany’s political and strategic orientation remains subject to significant shifts, tensions between strategic priorities, institutional loyalties and intelligence cooperation may continue to emerge,” he says.

The Chamber of Commerce and Industry meets with members of Congress from both parties and asks them to raise this issue before the White House.

And in recent weeks, Trump has blamed Ukraine for strikes on Russian fuel facilities and for rising fuel prices.

EU allocates $188.2M to boost defence production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:33:04 UTC
22:33:04 KST

The European Commission has allocated $188.2 million (€168.2 million) to eight projects aimed at boosting Europe's defence production capacity under the European Defence Industry Programme.
The projects are expected to mobilise $1.41 billion (€1.26 billion) in industrial investments to accelerate and expand the production of energetic components used in missiles, drones, and ammunition, according to a statement on Wednesday.
The projects, which will become operational from 2027, are expected to reduce manufacturing times by up to 90% and enable annual production of more than 20,000 tonnes of energetic materials, 3,500 drone and missile propulsion systems, 200,000 loitering munition warheads, and 60 million rounds of ammunition.
The investments will cover 17 production sites across 14 member states and Norway, while also strengthening their protection against growing physical and cyber threats.
The initiative builds on the EU's Act in Support of Ammunition Production, an emergency instrument introduced to address production bottlenecks and increase ammunition manufacturing capacity following the start of the war in Ukraine.

Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, accelerated to 2.6% annually from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation remained at 0.3%.
The acceleration in both headline and core inflation highlighted persistent price pressures as investors assessed the outlook for Federal Reserve monetary policy.

13:31:55 UTC
22:31:55 KST

Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said.
Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer.
But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India.
When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries.
Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position.
Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%.
But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater.
“In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.”
He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up.
“At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit, you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity.
“We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.”
Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU.
The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses.
“There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.”
Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products.
One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy, which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market.
Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

Archaeologists have discovered a sunken ship off the coast of Turkey that is up to 4,700 years old
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:30:28 EEST
22:30:28 KST

Archaeologists have discovered a sunken ship off the coast of Turkey that is up to 4,700 years old
Kyiv • UNN
Near the island of Kekova, they discovered the remains of an Early Bronze Age vessel with amphorae and anchors. It may be the oldest sunken ship.
Off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists have discovered a sunken Early Bronze Age ship estimated to be 4,400–4,700 years old. The vessel may have transported trade cargo across the Mediterranean Sea. The Independent reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
Although the ship’s wooden structure has not survived, archaeologists dated the storage pottery vessels and stone anchors found near Kekova Island to 2600–2400 BC. This could make the find the oldest known shipwreck in the world.
Previously, this status belonged to a ship that sank near Dokos Island in the Aegean Sea. It is dated to approximately 2200 BC.
Some of the amphorae found—large ceramic vessels with two handles—are similar to Early Bronze Age pottery from the Levant, which includes the territories of modern-day Lebanon, Syria, Israel, and Palestine.
The ceramic vessels were found scattered across the seabed at a depth of about 30 meters. The seabed is partly covered with sand and partly consists of rock.
One of the vessels resembled containers used during the Bronze Age to transport agricultural products, particularly wine and olive oil.
Near the sunken vessel, researchers also found two stone anchors with three holes and one anchor with a single hole. Similar artifacts have been discovered at other Bronze Age archaeological sites.
According to the researchers, anchors with three holes have parallels in Minoan, Cypriot, Anatolian, and Levantine archaeological contexts from the Bronze Age. The single-hole anchor is similar to those found off the coasts of Anatolia and the Levant.
It is not yet known whether these anchors belonged specifically to the discovered ship. At the same time, they may help provide a better understanding of the anchoring technologies used in the region during the Bronze Age.

‘Dune: Part Three’ Cowriter Brian K. Vaughan Has a New Comic on the Way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:30:00 UTC
22:30:00 KST

Brian K. Vaughan would like to apologize. He knows everyone is dying for details about Dune: Part Three, which he cowrote with director Denis Villeneuve, but his lips are pretty sealed until December 18 when the film finally hits theaters.
“Sorry to be coy,” he says as we’re about to leave the New York coffee shop where we’ve been chatting. “I hope the day will come where I’m able to say much, much more. It was truly so awesome. I can’t believe it happened.”
Vaughan is in the city for New York Comic Con, but not to talk about Dune. Ostensibly, he came to the convention to talk about Paper Girls, the comic he created with Cliff Chiang that was turned into a 2022 Amazon Prime Video series. During the Paper Girls panel, however, the pair announced that they’re working on a new comic, Roam, a superhero sci-fi series set to come out in February of next year.
Roam, Vaughan tells me, came from a deep desire to work with Chiang again. They’d considered doing a short eight-page story or maybe a one-shot, but eventually they said “Fuck it. Let’s do an ongoing series.”
Vaughan has the kind of career writers of a certain ilk would kill for. He started working on comics in the 1990s and has been the pen behind favorites like Saga, Y: The Last Man, and Marvel’s Runaways. (Those last two got turned into TV series; the outlier, Saga, is a story people have wanted to see adapted for years.) He also served as a writer on Lost and created CBS’s adaptation of Stephen King’s Under the Dome.
Still, his heart remains in comics. “I think sometimes people are like, ‘Oh, are you just going to sell out, Vaughan? Are you just going to go to Hollywood full-time?’” he says. “But I’m only able to do work in Hollywood because I have comics.”
Here, he speaks about Roam, his worries about AI, and maybe a little bit about Dune: Part Three as well.
On Roam, his forthcoming comic with Cliff Chiang:
It's completely unlike Paper Girls, completely unlike anything I've ever done. It’s set in the distant, distant future. The logline, as it were, is that in the future, everyone will get to be a superhero, but only while they're young. We're trying not to reveal too much more than that.
I remember seeing The Matrix, and having no idea what the fuck it was gonna be about. That was such a delight. So we're trying to do that here. I've been doing this for 31 years. I started when I was a teenager. I have a Spider-Man story here and there. I did a little Batman, and Ex Machina was my sci-fi political comic that sort of deconstructed the superhero. But this is certainly my first true superhero book.
On his fears about AI impacting comics, film, and TV:
It's terrifying. My friends who work in previsualization and as storyboard artists, these jobs are going away. I've heard about editors going away as well. Show business is a business, first and foremost. I’m lucky to sort of have been grandfathered in. I think there will always be people who are interested in bespoke human-made stories. But the future is terrifying and unknowable, and coming at us very, very quickly.
I’m heartened by the fact I've got two teenagers who are so disgusted by AI and grossed out if they ever hear I used it—and I’ve certainly never used it for anything creative. But I do think we're getting pretty close to the day that someone could be like, “I'm tired of waiting for the next issue. Give me the next issue of Saga.” That's when you get to the point of, do you just want content, something that's a distraction?
In Roam there's an element of this as well; AI is a component in the story. So, it's something I guess I need to write about with my human meat machine to process, but I'm in the middle of thinking about it, as you are, every day.
OK, a little bit about Dune: Part Three, which he has seen:
I can't say very much other than it’s a tremendous, insane, ridiculous honor to be involved with it, and my contributions are modest. Denis’ true cowriter on this is Frank Herbert. The novel is the star. And it's obviously the greatest cast and crew ever assembled. It's a fucking beautiful movie. It's my favorite of the three. which I can say with genuine humility. I can't say anything other than it's just as wonderful as you can imagine.
I got special thanks in the first movie. I was doing a tiny amount of consulting. I was working at Legendary [the media company that owns the rights to Dune] at the time, and they just invited me in to see an early cut, which was as fantastic as the finished product. But I just ended up talking to Denis, honestly. Never before has a director been that talented, also that decent and warm as a human being. I wasn't anticipating getting this call at the beginning of three, but it's obviously a call I could not refuse.
I should probably just be discreet at this point. The movie doesn't need me to promote it. I'm reluctant to do anything that makes me sound more important to this process.
On the future of Hollywood:
I am a small worker in the world of Hollywood. It is changing so rapidly that who knows what it's gonna be like tomorrow, six months from now.
But again, I've got teenagers and I see how delighted they were by Backrooms, by Obsession. It feels like Gen X has been force-feeding them a lot of my childhood stories that we have gussied up, and they are clearly hungry for something new.
On why he doesn’t write adaptations of his own comics:
I've taken stabs at it in the past. Richard Price, the novelist, I once heard him say in response to “Why don't you adapt your own stuff more?” that adapting your own work is like being a dentist and giving yourself a root canal. Just because you can do it, doesn't mean you should. Let some other motherfucker handle that. I believe those were Mr. Price's words.
It's been constructive and a thrill to adapt other people, and I like getting to watch other people adapt me, but I've also been doing a lot of it for the last decade, where it feels like I've either been adapting or being adapted. I think that was part of the siren song of Roam. It’s time to break some new ground.
Denis says that to adapt something you love is to do violence to it. When I've been adapted, that has always been what I've told people. It is much more important for this to be good than to be faithful. He's a master of cinema, and cinema is rarely about people sitting in a room having dialog. How do you transliterate this to cinema? That's an alchemy that I don't understand. He's just unparalleled at that.
On Lost and why writing for commercial breaks was a challenge:
I love my prestige drama without commercials, but there was a degree of difficulty working on Lost and having a cliff-hanger five times an episode. To have that was such a challenge and so rewarding when you were able to pull it off. Can you write something where people are like, “OK, I'll just wet my pants. I cannot risk not coming back [before the break is over].”

In Kyiv, an 18-year-old FSB agent attempted to activate 148 Starlink terminals for the Russian Federation; he faces life imprisonment
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU detained an 18-year-old FSB agent who was preparing to register 148 Starlink terminals for Russia. He was notified of suspicion of high treason.
An FSB agent who attempted to activate 148 internet devices for the Russians has been detained in Kyiv. He turned out to be an 18-year-old former student of a college in the capital and faces life imprisonment, UNN reports, citing the Security Service of Ukraine.
Details
The counterintelligence unit of the Security Service of Ukraine prevented the registration of one of the largest batches of Starlink satellite stations for the Russian Federation.
According to available information, the prompt response thwarted the enemy's intention to use the terminals to plan combat operations in Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions.
The investigation established that the enemy's assignment was carried out by an 18-year-old former student of a college in the capital, recruited by the FSB.
He came to the attention of the Russian special service after, having trained as an electric welder, he began looking for "quick" earnings in Telegram channels.
In one of the chats, an FSB officer contacted him and offered cooperation in exchange for a promise of "easy" money.
In Kropyvnytskyi, the SBU detained an FSB agent carrying two knives09.09.26, 10:55 • 6613 views
It was established that within several days of his recruitment, the suspect registered 15 Starlinks using the passport details of his relatives and acquaintances.
The agent then prepared "straw" personal data to register another 133 terminals for the Russian special service.
SBU counterintelligence officers exposed the perpetrator, documented his subversive activities, and detained him "red-handed" near a post office, where he planned to activate a new batch of internet stations.
At the same time, the previously registered Starlinks were blocked; the suspect had sent their details via messenger to his handler from the Russian Federation.
During searches of the detainee, several smartphones containing evidence of his work for the enemy were seized.
Investigators of the Security Service of Ukraine notified him of suspicion under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The perpetrator is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

Holidays remain a ‘spending priority’, but ‘cost-conscious’ travel is on the rise, report reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:26:24 UTC
22:26:24 KST

Travellers are planning on booking cheaper accommodation and eating out less while away, rather than giving up holidays completely.
It has been quite the year for the travel industry, with the Middle East conflict and heatwaves causing major disruption for holidaymakers while the cost of living crisis has seen people tightening their belts.
But that hasn’t stopped people from prioritising their vacations, with 70% of adults planning to travel abroad in the next 12 months, according to ABTA’s Holiday Habits report 2026/27.
Based on polling of more than 2,000 adults based in the UK, the new research shows that holidays are still a “priority”, but that “cost-conscious” travel is on the rise.
Just 7% of people said that the cost of living crisis would mean they would not go on holiday at all next year, but 21% said they would book cheaper accommodation, and 19% would eat out less while away.
Package holidays are proving popular as a result of the cost of living crisis, with 48% of those booking one saying they were doing so as it was the best value option for the price, up from 43% last year.
While the percentage of people who took a cruise in 2026 is stable (13%), the percentage of people planning to do so next year is rising (17%), and the reasons for doing so are reflecting the need for cost-conscious trips.
Some of the main reasons cited for booking a cruise are value for money (52%, up from 49%) and being able to pay for everything up front (40%, up from 38%).
“We continue to love our holidays and the desire to travel remains strong; this looks set to continue despite the ease of getting away, for some, being affected by geopolitical and economic challenges,” Mark Tanzer, chief executive of ABTA – The Travel Association, said.
“When times are uncertain, booking with an expert ABTA member gives holidaymakers added confidence. And, in a ‘value for money’ market, they are excellently placed to find people a fantastic holiday at a budget that works for them.”
City breaks overtake beach escapes
City breaks were the most popular holiday type in the last 12 months for UK travellers, with 53% of those polled going on one, up from 48% last year, while 49% of people went on a beach break.
Of those surveyed, the third most popular type was a countryside break (23%), followed by a multi-destination trip (16%), adventure holiday (14%), cruise (13%), lake and mountains (10%), and wellness (9%).
Europe remained the most popular choice for holidays, with certain destinations seeing an uptick in visitors as people avoided the Middle East or avoided travelling via the region.
For Brits, the top country over the past 12 months was Spain, with 36% of those surveyed having visited.
Portugal overtook Germany as the sixth most visited destination, behind France (24%), Italy (15%), the US (14%) and Greece (12%), with 11% having visited.
The top 10 was rounded out by Türkiye, Australia and Cyprus.

NEW DELHI: The government is set to discuss satellite internet services in the coming days, with a parliamentary panel selecting the subject for a detailed examination amid the ongoing row over Elon Musk's allegations that powerful business interests are obstructing Starlink's entry into India.BJP MP Nishikant Dubey, chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology, said the panel would take up the issue at its upcoming meeting. “We will discuss the satellite net issue at our meeting in the coming days,” Dubey told PTI after a meeting of the panel.A threadbare examination, in parliamentary parlance, refers to a detailed and comprehensive scrutiny of an issue, including its regulatory, commercial and security implications.The panel's decision comes amid a public exchange between Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX, which operates Starlink, and Indian political and business figures over the company's pending approval to launch satellite internet services in the country.In a series of posts on X last week, Musk targeted Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani, with sarcastic jabs. He further argued that financial considerations alone would not determine the government's decision on Starlink, writing: “If our policy were driven by money, we would have rolled out the red carpet welcome for you despite opposition from the security agencies.”Musk, meanwhile, has argued that Starlink's entry would increase competition and expand consumer choice. Responding to arguments against the service, he wrote that competition would benefit ordinary Indians, adding that Ambani's profits might decline but that his business would not cease to exist.

Statement from Bishop Dr. Imad Haddad on the Attack on Starmountain (Sternberg) Support Center by Israeli Settlers
This week we as a church were very disturbed to hear about Israeli settlers trespassing and damaging agricultural facilities at the Starmountain (Sternberg) Support Center for people with disabilities near Ramallah.
The Starmountain Center is operated by our partners from the Moravian Church and serves approximately 100 children and youth with intellectual disabilities. Last Friday, the 9th of October, a large group of Jewish Israeli settlers broke into the facility, damaging the property’s fence. On Monday the 11th, the farmer at the center noticed significant destruction in the greenhouse, including slashed tarpaulins, uprooted plants, and destroyed irrigation pipelines, suggesting the group broke in on Sunday as well and caused additional damage.
The severity and urgency of this situation cannot be overstated. This is illegal violent trespassing and destruction of property that could escalate even further at any time. The current physical damage caused to the facility is compounded by the intense psychological damage to those who attend and work in the center. As the Moravian Church shared in their statement, if Starmountain is no longer seen as a safe place for people with disabilities, this important work will not be able to continue.

In the case concerning medical negligence by Odrex doctors, three court hearings have been postponed at once
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:25:41 EEST
