Preparing for winter: a home checklist to help retain heat and prepare for outages
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:11:29 EEST
20:11:29 KST

Preparing for winter: a home checklist to help retain heat and prepare for outages
Kyiv • UNN
These tips will help retain heat, check the heating system and electrical wiring, and prepare supplies of water, food, and medicine. Fire safety is also highlighted separately.
Against the backdrop of Russia’s aggressive attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, people are trying more actively than last year to prepare for winter, both in cities and in towns. All the more so because domestic and foreign politicians and experts unanimously warn that the winter of 2026–2027 could prove to be the harshest and most difficult in the entire history of our country.
UNN has compiled a practical checklist for residents of apartments and private houses that will help reduce heat loss in advance, make sure equipment is in working order, arrange a water supply, and plan what to do in case of power outages.
How to insulate windows and doors to avoid losing heat
It is worth starting with the simplest things: check whether there are drafts coming through the windows, balcony doors, or entrance doors. Worn-out seals should be replaced, gaps around frames should be sealed, and the fittings adjusted if necessary.
You can take thick-fabric curtains out of the closet or buy some. They help reduce the feeling of cold near the window and eliminate small drafts. However, they should be positioned so that the fabric does not cover the radiators. First, such an artificial barrier between the room and the radiator will inevitably prevent the room from warming up. Second, there is a risk that at some point the curtain could begin to smolder from the high temperatures and cause a fire.
Likewise, radiators should not be blocked by furniture or decorative screens, so as not to impede the distribution of heat throughout the room.
If you live in a private house, in addition to the windows and doors, you should обязательно inspect the roof and take care of insulating the attic. Without this, even continuous gas or stove heating will not create a feeling of warmth in the home, because heat losses will be enormous.
At the same time, you should not resort to the opposite extreme of completely blocking ventilation openings for the sake of warmth. Even in winter, rooms need to be aired, especially if condensation forms on the glass or mold appears. If the house is heated with firewood or food is prepared on a stove powered by a gas cylinder, properly functioning ventilation is an essential condition for safe living. Neglecting safety could ultimately end tragically for all the home's residents, who risk fatal carbon monoxide poisoning.
Why heating should be checked before the first frosts
Residents of apartments with centralized heating should inspect radiators, valves, and pipe connections. Traces of rust, moisture, or leaks are reasons to contact the building manager or a plumber.
Owners of gas boilers need to arrange maintenance in advance: checking the boiler, ventilation, and flue systems to ensure they are working properly. If the house has a stove or fireplace, its structure should be checked for cracks before the season begins, the chimney cleaned, and the dampers and doors checked to make sure they function properly.
A separate issue for apartment buildings is preparing the common property. Through the homeowners’ association or management company, it is worth finding out whether the heating substation has been inspected, pipes in the basement insulated, windows in the entrance stairwell glazed, and doors made to close tightly.
How to prepare the electrical system and backup lighting for the winter months
Before winter, it is also worth inspecting accessible sockets, switches, and cables. Hot sockets or a burning smell are good reasons to call an electrician.
In case of power outages, it is advisable to have flashlights, spare batteries, charged power banks, and cables for phones at home. You should ask your provider whether the internet will work without electricity and how to power the router.
If finances allow, you can purchase a power station. It should be selected according to the power requirements of the appliances you plan to connect. Such equipment must not be covered, placed near heat sources, used with damaged cables, or connected to the home electrical system with a homemade cable featuring two plugs. You should also avoid buying a power station "second-hand," from questionable sellers, or on Chinese marketplaces. In such cases, there is a possibility of encountering an uncertified, damaged, or defective product.
Water and food supplies in case of a blackout
One of the most important aspects of preparing for winter (especially in a city) is storing water. The guideline for an adult is about three liters of drinking water and 10–12 liters of utility water per day. It is advisable to calculate a minimum reserve for at least three days, taking into account children, pets, and the needs of people requiring care.
For storing drinking water, clean, tightly sealed food-grade containers are suitable. Utility water for hygiene and flushing the toilet can be kept in other large bottles or buckets, or the bathtub can be filled with it.
Among food products, it is better to choose those that can be stored for a long time without refrigeration and do not require heat treatment (boiling or frying): canned goods, crispbreads, nuts, dried fruit, ready-made cereals, or other long-storage products. Before arranging these supplies on the shelves of a kitchen cabinet, it is worth checking the expiration dates once again and placing a manual can opener nearby.
How to live in a home without heating and not freeze
In case the heat goes out, you should prepare thermal underwear, warm socks, several layers of clothing, blankets, and sleeping bags. For temporary accommodation, you can choose one room with the fewest drafts and close the doors to other rooms: one small room is easier to heat than a multi-room apartment or private house.
It is strictly forbidden to heat a room with a gas stove or oven, or to use barbecues and charcoal indoors. A generator must also not be started in an apartment, building entrance, garage, or on a balcony: it should be used only outdoors, at least six meters away from doors and windows, in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.
In addition, it is important to know and understand from the outset that prolonged cooling of a home is especially dangerous for young children, older people, and people with chronic diseases. If the temperature in the residence becomes critically low, you should consider in advance moving to a heated building or the nearest Point of Invincibility.
How to ensure fire safety and prepare a first-aid kit in winter
Before the season begins, it is advisable to check the smoke detector, and in homes with gas or stove heating or other combustion appliances, install a carbon monoxide detector. Carbon monoxide has no smell, so it is impossible to detect its presence without a special device. The fire extinguisher must be in working order and easily accessible.
You should also review your home first-aid kit: check the expiration dates of medicines, replenish first-aid supplies, and stock up on medications that must be taken regularly, in accordance with the doctor's prescriptions.
It is also useful to keep a small bag with the most essential items ready in case of a temporary evacuation.
General advice is to keep some cash in small denominations in case of disruptions to communications and payment services. For pets, provide food, water, and a carrier.
Reminder
Previously, UNN reported on what you should have at home to get through power outages.

The family of a man killed by a tiger at a wildlife park in the UK have spoken about their “severe distress” at the circulation of online media after Donald Trump reposted a video of the incident.
William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death after entering an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, on Saturday.
His family described him as “bright, warm and engaging” and suffering from severe mental illness. They said online footage being shared was “deeply offensive” and causing them “severe distress”.
One of those to circulate footage was the US president who posted a video clip of the tiger attack to 13 million followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday.
The clip showed the tiger biting and clawing Chapman as he was sitting in the enclosure. At one point he wags his finger at the animal.
Trump signed the footage with: “Don’t ever mess with nature! President DJT.” It did not show Chapman being killed.
Later the president posted an AI-generated video of himself grinning and having fun by chasing and play fighting with the tiger. It is accompanied by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight by The Tokens. It features Trump copying the pointing gesture made by Chapman and ends with him and the tiger hugging.
Will Travers, the executive president of the Born Free Foundation, said the AI post was “not only incredibly insensitive”, but also reckless.
“It increases the risk to the lives of humans and captive wild animals,” he said. “Such images and videos can encourage individuals to seek out direct, unrealistic and high-risk contact with captive wild animals.”
Relatives of Chapman, in a statement released on Tuesday evening, said: “The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened. The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.
“The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.”
The statement continued: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back. Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication.
“It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death.
“We would ask everybody to respect that process.”
As a child, Chapman appeared in ITV’s 2009 comedy drama May Contain Nuts and in BBC Learning’s True Stories series, according to IMDb.
He previously attended Jackie Palmer stage school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, which paid tribute on Facebook and posted a picture of Chapman as a child student.
The school said it was “deeply saddened” by Chapman’s death, adding: “We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer. It was a privilege to be part of his journey and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him.
“William will be truly missed, and he will always hold a special place in our hearts. Rest in peace, William.”
The wildlife park has said the Amur (Siberian) tiger called Altai, who was in the enclosure, will not be euthanised. The park has remained closed since the weekend and Doncaster city council, which is responsible for licensing the park, said it had started a health and safety investigation.
An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster coroner’s court on Thursday morning.

EU disburses $3.2B to Ukraine for drones, missiles, air defense systems

The European Commission on Wednesday disbursed €2.86 billion ($3.2 billion) to Ukraine to fund drones, air defense systems, missiles, and other urgent military needs amid continued attacks.
The funding was provided under the defense component of the EU's €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan, the EU Commission said in a statement.
The money will be used to procure drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition.
"As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
The €90 billion loan package for 2026-2027 includes €60 billion earmarked for defense and €30 billion for budgetary assistance.
The commission said €28.3 billion was planned for disbursement in 2026 to strengthen Ukraine's defense industrial capacity, with further payments under the defense component expected in the coming weeks.
It added that Ukraine still had €29.64 billion in financial support available for the remainder of 2026.
Of that amount, €25.24 billion is available under the Ukraine Support Loan, including €12.54 billion for defense industrial capacity and €12.7 billion in budget support.
Since 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €231.5 billion in overall support to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion generated from proceeds of immobilized Russian assets, according to the commission.

Tsui Hark at Lumière Festival: ‘We don't know where the future will bring us’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:10:58 UTC
20:10:58 KST

"We all know that the thing about humanity is that we always fear being replaced by something." Euronews Culture sits down with legendary Hong Kong filmmaker Tsui Hark during this year's Lumière Film Festival.
Anyone who is a fan of Hong Kong cinema and martial arts films will immediately recognise the name Tsui Hark.
He is one of the key figures in Hong Kong’s New Wave, responsible for reinventing the martial arts genre. As a writer, producer and director, he boosted the careers of many like Chow Yun-fat, Jet Lee and even John Woo. And until last year with the box office success of Ne Zha 2, the 75-year-old director’s film The Battle at Lake Changjin was the highest-grossing Chinese film of all time.
Four of his films - the period romantic comedy Shanghai Blues (1984), the groundbreaking action-comedy Peking Opera Blues (1986), the martial arts epic Once Upon a Time in China (1991) and the action thriller Time And Tide (2000) - are being honoured and screened at this year’s Lumière Film Festival.
Euronews Culture sat down with the legendary filmmaker after the Lumière ceremony during which directors are celebrated with a golden plaque on Rue du Premier Film, beside the Institut Lumière, to talk about the festival, his work, and the challenges we face.
Euronews Culture: How does it feel having your plaque on the Lumière wall now?
Tsui Hark: I feel very dreamy, as a matter of fact! (Laughs) You know, I suddenly realized that I’ve come to the place where motion pictures started, at their beginning. I never thought that I would come to a place like this, where you suddenly go back to the original motion picture. It becomes a very surreal thing. You come to a place where your career was started by someone that you don't know, but they [the Lumière brothers] are the source of your creativity and everything. I feel very blessed, being given the task of making movies.
During your stay at the festival, several of your films are being screened, including restored versions of Shanghai Blues and Peking Opera Blues. How does it feel seeing these films on a big screen once more?
It’s strange with the films I've made 40 years ago! (Laughs) For me, it's like it's very far, far away, and suddenly they come back again. It makes you feel like the time never passed. You go to a theater showing your film that you made 40 years ago, and people still like it. It's a wonderful feeling.
You are known for your work in action films and martial arts, but there’s a focus in the selection of films screened at the festival on comedy and romance. In your opinion and experience, where does the cinematic language of action and comedy intersect?
I actually think of myself as a comedy person than an action director, but everything happened in 1979. I worked in a television, and I was given a job to make a costume action drama [The Butterfly Murders]. I was given an assignment to do an action film, and since then, I have been associated with action genre for so many years. But for me, it’s a bit weird!
Throughout your films, you’ve always managed to balance action and the epic scale and scope of your stories with very emotional and personal considerations. It’s not an easy balance to get right when it comes to big productions... I suppose my question is: What's your secret?
There's no secret at all! It all depends on my take on something I really like. When I was a kid, when I watched this kind of genre, I felt very exhilarated when looking at life. When I have a chance to make a movie, I go in that direction - a direction based on how I identify with the people inside the world, especially in epic or costume dramas.
I’m very serious when it comes to making people identify and associate themselves with the story I’m telling. The quality of humanity in the characters and the story is a major concern of the material. I always try to make the story understandable and relatable for everyone. You see, many think about movies as being for a certain age or people. I feel like movies should be for audiences of all ages and hopefully for people of all cultures - not just our culture that we're so familiar with. I hope that movies, culture, and art can be shared by everyone.
Have you noticed a certain sensitivity that European audiences have towards your films?
Actually, I have no idea what's going on! (Laughs) Sometimes I go to a place and they will say “I've seen your movie” and I'm quite surprised. The first time I was in Cannes, and they said, “Oh, I've seen your movie”, I was very shocked. I made the movie elsewhere and it was shown to a different kind of audience, but still, they understood and accepted the film. For me, it’s a form of encouragement and it gives me energy to make movies that can be shared by all people and bring cultures together.
Considering the breadth of your career and your filmography, are there any genres that you would like to explore that you haven’t had the chance to? I ask, because you made a horror-comedy in 1980, We’re Going To Eat You, and I can’t deny I’d love to see another horror film from you...
Oh, yes! Exactly! Horror is a genre I always want to explore, because I feel horror is not just about making people scared but about making people feel a different kind of energy. I've seen a lot of horror films, and I feel like they are often very negative about human beings and humanity. That’s why I feel like I’d like to try something different in this genre.
Speaking of negativity, many are expressing fears nowadays about the future of cinema and the arts in general, especially with the push towards artificial intelligence. Is that something that worries you?
It’s a very up-to-date question you’ve asked. We all know that the thing about humanity is that we always fear being replaced by something. The fear that we are being replaced comes from everywhere. In relationships, career, economy... Or even our own idea of freedom. This is always a threat, and we don't know where the future will bring us.
The fear and the danger of losing everything is everywhere, and human beings tend to be neglectful of the weakness of our nature. We neglect the power of destruction created by us and at the same time, the power of destruction created by nature. In our era, we have faced a lot of crises – from virus, science, technology, and war. We have no solution for it so far. Humans are a weak species when it comes to solving problems like that.
The more we go through every test we encounter on the path of our survival, we realise that we actually have no solutions. Simply because we are the destructive element in nature. I hope that it's not true. Hopefully I'm mistaken in that respect, and that we bring some good things in life.
You know, at my age, I always feel like there’s not a long time to worry about the future... But I hope that things will not get worse. I want to be optimistic, but there is strong evidence of negative things happening. Since World War II, everybody tried to avoid that happening again, but it's happening. Non-stop happening. I don't know what is the best solution for all these problems...
I certainly don't.
No one has. I know we’re getting deep and we can’t get too philosophical about what we’re going to do. The world is very chaotic, but I do think that at least something we can do is to make everybody look at a good aspect of humanity and remind ourselves to enjoy life and human creativity. And cinema is a good place to start.
Peking Opera Blues makes its French cinema debut on 21 October in a restored 4K version.
The Lumière Film Festival runs in Lyon through 18 October.

Iraq's shadow economy grows as billions evade oversight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Iraq's shadow economy grows as billions evade oversight
Iraq's shadow economy is expanding as millions of workers and businesses operate outside formal government oversight, depriving the state of revenue and complicating efforts to reduce its dependence on oil.
Informal activity ranges from unregistered small businesses and undocumented employment to tax and customs evasion.
Officials and analysts also warn that some financial channels outside formal oversight can be exploited for smuggling, corruption and money laundering.
The issue has taken on greater importance as Baghdad seeks to increase non-oil revenues and strengthen public finances.
Finance Ministry figures show Iraq collected about 8.74 trillion dinars in non-oil revenues during the first seven months of 2026.
That accounted for around 22% of total public revenues of 39.09 trillion dinars, compared with about 30.36 trillion dinars from oil.
The scale of Iraq's informal economy is particularly visible in the labour market.
OECD figures based on Iraq's 2021 labour force survey showed about 5.73 million people were in informal employment, representing 66.6% of the country's workforce.
About 4.72 million of them worked in the informal sector, while the rest held informal jobs within formally registered organisations.
The figures do not measure the total financial value of the shadow economy, but indicate how deeply informal employment is embedded in Iraq's labour market.
The government established a committee in 2023 to examine the issue, with a mandate covering tax reform, improved data collection and the relationship between tax evasion and money laundering.
The Central Bank, Integrity Commission and anti-money laundering authorities were among the bodies involved.
Iraq has also tightened oversight of foreign-currency transactions in recent years, including through new systems monitoring bank transfers and dollar flows.
Concerns over corruption and illicit finance
Anti-corruption specialist Saeed Yassin said the government needed to look beyond bringing small businesses into the tax system.
He said authorities should investigate networks that benefited from keeping economic activity outside formal scrutiny and examine the origins of funds entering markets without clear financial records.
Yassin said particular attention should be paid to so-called economic offices and their possible involvement in government contracts, border crossings, imports and trade.
Some parts of the informal economy could also be used to disguise proceeds from corruption, smuggling or money laundering through front companies and transactions whose real value was difficult to verify, he said.
Previous audits have exposed schemes involving hundreds of millions of dollars channelled through fraudulent transactions involving banks, exchange companies and other intermediaries.
He called for stronger systems to track financial flows, identify the real owners of companies, scrutinise high-risk contracts and link government databases.
Iraqi MP Youssef al-Kallabi said the scale of unregulated economic activity was weakening government efforts to raise non-oil revenues.
He said administrative and financial loopholes meant the state was failing to collect some revenues it was entitled to receive.
Parliament had previously proposed more than 16 measures to increase non-oil income, he said, but some had not been implemented.
Kallabi said exemptions and some government decisions had also disadvantaged legitimate private-sector companies while allowing well-connected economic groups to benefit from unequal conditions.
The wider problem comes as Iraq's government pursues a renewed anti-corruption drive aimed at recovering public funds and strengthening oversight.
A shortage of reliable data made it harder for the government to estimate how much revenue it should be collecting and to assess whether reforms were working, he added.
Economist Ziad al-Hashemi said many small and medium-sized businesses remained informal because operating outside the official system was cheaper and easier.
Complicated bureaucracy, weak public services and limited access to bank financing reduced the incentives to register formally, he said.
But remaining outside the system also restricted companies' ability to obtain loans, attract investment and expand into larger businesses.
Iraq's long dependence on cash and parallel-market currency trading has also helped sustain a highly informal financial system outside conventional banking channels.
Hashemi said reforms should make formal registration economically worthwhile.
He called for lower start-up costs, simpler procedures, easier access to bank finance and stronger legal and social protection.
The challenge, he said, was to make joining the formal economy an opportunity for businesses to grow rather than simply another tax and administrative burden.

Türkiye’s exports to the EU rose 3.9% year-on-year to $81.5 billion in the first nine months of the year, according to the Turkish Exporters’ Assembly (TIM).
Türkiye’s total exports increased 5.2% to $210.9 billion over the same period, while exports to the 27 EU member states rose by nearly $3.1 billion.
Germany was Türkiye’s top European market, with Turkish exports rising 4.2% to $15.4 billion, followed by Italy with $9.6 billion, Spain with $8.3 billion and France with $7.9 billion.
Other leading export destinations included Romania and the Netherlands, with nearly $5.5 billion each, and Poland with $4.8 billion, contributing to the broader trend in which Turkish exports rose in 17 EU member states while declining in 10.
Türkiye’s total exports to its top four European markets — Germany, Italy, Spain and France — reached $41.2 billion in January-September.
The auto sector was the main driver of growth, with exports to the EU rising 4.8% to $22.9 billion, followed by the chemicals and chemical products sector with $10.2 billion and the ready-to-wear apparel sector with $7.3 billion.
The largest increase in exports to the EU came from the auto sector, up by nearly $1.1 billion, followed by the ferrous and non-ferrous metals sector with a $1 billion increase and the electrical and electronics sector with a rise of $489.3 million, the data showed.
The Turkish provinces of Istanbul, Kocaeli, Bursa, Ankara and Izmir contributed most to exports to the EU in January-September, accounting for a total of $60.9 billion.
Exports from Istanbul to the EU reached $29 billion, followed by the northwestern provinces of Kocaeli and Bursa with $11.4 billion and $9.4 billion, respectively. Exports from Ankara totaled $5.6 billion, while the western province of Izmir exported $5.4 billion to the bloc.

Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:06:19 UTC
20:06:19 KST

Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
A long-overlooked peptide once thought harmless could be a hidden contributor to Alzheimer's disease, challenging decades of research and opening new possibilities for treatment.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- University of California - Santa Cruz
- Summary:
- For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.
- Share:
For decades, researchers have invested billions of dollars in Alzheimer's treatments designed to target amyloid beta, a peptide that forms harmful deposits in the brain. But a biochemist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, believes scientists may have overlooked another potential contributor to the disease: a smaller, closely related peptide that was long considered harmless.
In a new commentary published in ChemBioChem, UC Santa Cruz professor Jevgenij Raskatov highlights research suggesting that this lesser-known peptide, called P3, can form microscopic clumps and threadlike structures known as fibrils. Evidence also suggests that P3 may interact with amyloid beta (Aβ), potentially influencing how it accumulates in the brain and how toxic it becomes. These findings raise the possibility that P3 contributes to the nerve cell damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.
"The P3 peptide is, most likely, not the innocent bystander it was commonly thought to be. There's still more research to be done. But this could turn Alzheimer's research on its head," said Raskatov, whose laboratory investigates amyloid peptides in hopes of identifying ways to prevent their harmful effects and develop better Alzheimer's treatments. "P3 is a distinct aggregating peptide that is itself potentially neurotoxic and may be contributing to Alzheimer's disease."
Why Alzheimer's Treatments Have Had Limited Success
Alzheimer's is the most widespread neurodegenerative disease, affecting approximately 35 million people worldwide and generating annual costs exceeding $800 billion. The number of people living with the condition is expected to double by 2050.
Despite decades of intensive research, developing effective treatments has proved extraordinarily difficult. More than 400 clinical trials have investigated potential Alzheimer's drugs, with most focusing on amyloid beta. Many of these efforts have failed, while others have produced only modest benefits. Some treatments have also been associated with serious complications, including brain hemorrhages and strokes.
Amyloid beta originates from a much larger protein embedded in cell membranes called the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP). Two enzymes, β-secretase and γ-secretase, cut this protein in sequence, releasing amyloid beta peptides of different lengths.
Researchers have concentrated particularly on two versions, Aβ40 and Aβ42, which contain 40 and 42 amino acids, respectively. Aβ42 has attracted the greatest attention because it is especially prone to sticking together and forming toxic aggregates. As a result, it has remained a central target of Alzheimer's drug development for decades.
Existing medications, including cholinesterase inhibitors and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, can temporarily ease certain symptoms but do not stop the disease from progressing. More recently, antibody treatments such as Lecanemab and Donanemab have been approved to help remove amyloid beta from the brain.
However, Raskatov argues that the benefits achieved so far remain limited, underscoring the need to investigate other biological processes involved in Alzheimer's.
"Progress has been extremely slow, and the current state of the art in Alzheimer's therapy leaves much to be desired," he said. "We need fundamentally new approaches to the problem."
The Overlooked Peptide That May Also Damage Brain Cells
Unlike amyloid beta, P3 forms when Amyloid Precursor Protein is processed through a different sequence of molecular cuts. In this pathway, an enzyme called α-secretase acts first, followed by γ-secretase.
Raskatov has proposed calling this peptide "Amyloid α," or Aα, to better distinguish it from amyloid beta and reflect its ability to form aggregates.
For years, scientists largely assumed that P3 was incapable of forming amyloid deposits, was not toxic to cells, and would remain soluble in water. Under that interpretation, the peptide would simply dissolve rather than accumulate in the brain.
These assumptions were never adequately verified, according to Raskatov. Nevertheless, they helped establish the view that P3 was unlikely to matter in Alzheimer's disease, leaving it largely absent from research efforts.
Raskatov, a specialist in peptide chemistry, and researchers in his laboratory decided to test those long-standing beliefs.
Over the past five years, the team has published three major studies demonstrating that P3 can form amyloid deposits at least as readily as amyloid beta. In fact, their experiments showed that P3 produces these aggregates more rapidly.
The researchers also found evidence that P3 itself may be harmful to neurons, although its toxicity appears lower than that of amyloid beta.
According to Raskatov, an independent research group in the United Kingdom has confirmed and expanded upon his team's findings. Other laboratories are now beginning to investigate how P3 and amyloid beta interact, including whether their relationship affects the accumulation and toxicity of these peptides.
Together, the results challenge the long-held assumption that P3 is biologically harmless and irrelevant to Alzheimer's. However, further research is needed to establish whether and how it contributes to the disease in patients.
Challenging Decades of Alzheimer's Research
For much of the past several decades, amyloid beta has dominated scientific explanations of Alzheimer's disease. David Teplow, an emeritus professor of neurology at UCLA and a prominent Alzheimer's researcher, said the peptide has long been regarded as a central cause of the condition.
But an independent evaluation of Raskatov's research led Teplow to conclude that scientists are beginning to reconsider this narrow focus.
"This reevaluation has far-reaching consequences for both basic science and clinical research into the causes and treatment of Alzheimer's disease," said Teplow, a founding editorial board member of the Journal of Molecular Neuroscience and the American Journal of Neurodegenerative Disease, as well as editor-in-chief of Progress in Molecular Biology and Translational Science.
Raskatov has also encountered a troubling problem while examining how other scientists have interpreted his team's discoveries.
He identified at least four papers published in respected, peer-reviewed journals that cited his laboratory's research as evidence that P3 was harmless and unable to form amyloid deposits. Yet his team's experiments had demonstrated precisely the opposite.
"This is exactly the opposite of what we have actually shown," Raskatov said. "We remain in the dark on how this sort of grand confusion may have come about. Clearly, there is more work ahead of us."
The emerging evidence suggests that understanding Alzheimer's may require looking beyond amyloid beta alone. By examining P3 and its interactions with other amyloid peptides, researchers hope to gain a more complete picture of the processes that damage brain cells and potentially identify new directions for treatment.

Trade conflicts cost prosperity around the world, German Finance Minister says

Klingbeil, who is head of the Social Democrats, cancelled the India leg of his Asia trip on Monday following the resignation of Baerbel Bas, Germany's labour minister and co-head of the SPD.

Bulgaria expects to join NATO anti-drone initiative this month, says minister
SOFIA, Oct 14 - Bulgaria expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Wednesday, a day after a drone attack sank a cargo vessel off the country's Black Sea coast for the second time in a week.
The attacks have highlighted the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine war poses to commercial shipping near NATO's southeastern flank, prompting Bulgaria to push for stronger alliance defences in the Black Sea.
"Bulgaria will be part of this project as soon as possible. Expectations are that by October 30, we will already be part of the project," local media quoted Stoyanov as telling a parliamentary hearing.
Two cargo ships were hit by drones on October 13 off the Bulgarian coast. One of them, identified as the Guinea-Bissau-flagged cargo vessel HS Dignity, sank, leaving 11 sailors missing at sea and prompting Sofia to summon Russia's ambassador. Drones struck two other cargo ships in the same waters on October 6.
Bulgaria's Transport Ministry announced on Wednesday afternoon that it had halted rescue operations for the missing sailors, citing strong wind, reduced visibility and waves.
Bulgaria has stopped short of explicitly accusing Russia of carrying out the attacks but Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday their outcome "benefits the Russian Federation".
Russia's ambassador to Sofia, Eleonora Mitrofanova, said she had no information from the Russian Defence Ministry about attacks on commercial vessels but did not rule out they could be a provocation by a third party, Bulgaria's government said.
Russia has been bombing Ukraine's Black Sea ports, forcing Kyiv to rely increasingly on river ports on the Danube and shipping routes close to the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.
Ukraine, for its part, has increasingly targeted Russian grain-exporting ships in other parts of the Black Sea and near the mouth of the Don River in the Sea of Azov. REUTERS

UK government apologises for past burials of stillborn babies in mass graves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:05:44 UTC
20:05:44 KST

The health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has issued a “profound apology” for the “unthinkable pain” caused to parents whose stillborn babies were buried in mass graves.
Parents spent decades not knowing where their babies were buried, owing to a practice in which stillborn babies were taken from mothers at hospital and buried in communal graves.
Over several decades between the 1930s and the early 1980s, many bereaved parents who lost babies in NHS hospitals were given no say in what would happen to their remains and no information about where they had been taken.
More than 1,000 stillborn babies were interred in Wirral, at Frankby, Plymyard and Landican cemeteries, between 1935 and 1981. Another mass burial ground in Royton, Oldham, is believed to hold more than 270 babies.
Gina Jacobs, from Wirral, whose son Robert was stillborn in 1969, did not know where he had been buried for 53 years. She has been among those campaigning for recognition from the government.
Speaking in the House of Commons during a baby loss awareness debate, Cooper said: “On behalf of the government, I want to issue a profound apology to them.”
She added: “I have issued that apology to Gina today, but to so many more like Gina who have sought answers over many years, I’m sorry for the unthinkable pain caused by those historic practices, because what happened to those parents should never have happened and we need to ensure it can never happen again.”
Jacobs told ITV News: “It didn’t kind of sink in at first. I’ve wanted this, I’ve campaigned for this, I’ve begged for this, anyone who would listen, for four years now, and to actually have it said to me by the minister herself.
“To me it’s like a lottery win because I have wanted this,” she added. “This brings dignity and respect to these babies, because they never got it at the time. And it brings it even to our missing babies.”
In July, Liverpool city council passed a motion calling on the government to apologise in parliament to families affected by the practice.
The motion, which was passed unanimously by all parties, said: “The historical handling of stillborn babies by public authorities was a cruel violation of human dignity that has caused decades of unresolved trauma, grief and anger for families across Liverpool.”
In response to the government apology, the Liverpool councillor Kris Brown, who put forward the motion, said: “The government’s words of apology will go a long way. For many, just acknowledging that it happened will bring a sense of closure and justice.
“However, this can’t just be words simply etched into Hansard. I hope that the secretary of state, along with the prime minister, issues a written apology and sets out a national framework on how families affected by the scandal can get support.”
The council has urged the government to set aside national funding to retrieve burial records and has called for a comprehensive review into the mass burials, which took place under many successive governments.
Brown welcomed the apology but said: “There is still far more to do for full justice.”

Scarborough soldier buried in Belgium more than a century after his death
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:03:00 BST
20:03:00 KST

Scarborough soldier buried in Belgium more than a century after his death
Scarborough soldier, Lance Corporal (LCpl) Claude Stanley Dell, has been laid to rest more than a century after his death in World War 1.
A young Scarborough soldier of World War 1, killed just a week after his arrival in France, has finally been laid to rest with full military honours. LCpl Claude Stanley Dell of the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment was laid to rest today (13 October 2026) at Commonwealth War Graves Commission’s (CWGC) Poelcapelle British Cemetery in Belgium.
In 2021, workmen digging a rainwater cistern in Hazeweidestraat, St Juliaan, Belgium spotted human remains in their trench. A few days later an archaeological excavation was undertaken by the Flanders Heritage Agency. Artefacts recovered alongside the remains showed them to be those of a soldier who had served in the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment.
The Ministry of Defence’s Joint Casualty and Compassionate Centre (JCCC), known as the ‘MOD War Detectives’, launched an investigation to name him. Research identified twenty men from the regiment missing in the area, all of whom died in the Spring of 1915. Following genealogical investigation, living descendants of the missing men were traced one by one until eventually DNA testing proved that the remains were those of LCpl Claude Stanley Dell.
LCpl Dell joined up alongside his brothers Charles and Guy at the outbreak of war. All three joined the 5th Battalion Yorkshire Regiment, whilst their older brother Leighton was in the Royal Field Artillery, and another brother - Frederick - served with the Yorkshire Hussars.
5th Battalion left the UK on 17 April 1915 and arrived in Boulogne the following day. On 23 April they arrived on the Ypres Salient, and just two days later on 25 April 1915 LCpl Dell was killed in action. Claude’s brothers wrote home to tell their parents, ‘poor Claude met his end…whilst doing his duty’.
Today, LCpl Dell was buried with full military honours in the presence of both his military family, and his great-niece Judith.
The service, organised by JCCC, was supported by serving soldiers of the Royal Yorkshire Regiment, as well as staff from the CWGC.
Alexia Clark, MOD War Detective, said:
  It has been a privilege to research this case, to have been able to identify LCpl Dell, and to have been able to lay him to rest today. I am extremely grateful to 2nd Battalion the Royal Yorkshire Regiment who have provided the bearer party for the funeral, and to the members of Claude’s family who have been involved in his commemoration.
Claude’s grave will now be cared for in perpetuity by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, ensuring his sacrifice is never forgotten. Dr Daniel Seaton, Commemorations Case Officer at CWGC, said:
  Lance Corporal Dell lay in an unmarked grave on the former battlefields for well over 100 years. It is a great privilege to have worked alongside the JCCC and our Belgian partners in the effort to restore his identity. He is now laid to rest in a Commission cemetery not far from where he fell, ensuring that his grave can be visited in perpetuity and his sacrifice remembered.

As Yemen-Saudi tensions rise, Palestinians question Iran's goals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

Breadcrumb
As Yemen-Saudi tensions rise, Gaza's Palestinians question Iran's endgame
The recent round of fighting between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia has sparked debate among Palestinians over the role of Iran and its allies in the region.
While some Palestinians supported Houthi attacks in the Red Sea during the Israeli genocidal war, others question their impact, especially as the latest round of fighting in Yemen that erupted since mid-September, and spread to Saudi airports and other civilian facilities.
On Monday, the Palestinian Authority's Presidency condemned the Houthi attacks, denouncing strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and expressing solidarity with Saudi Arabia.
In a press statement, it backed measures taken by the Kingdom to protect its security and facilities and warned against threats to the Two Holy Mosques in Mecca and Medina.
Hamas, meanwhile, had not issued a public comment despite repeated attempts by The New Arab to obtain its position.
Other Palestinian factions, particularly those with ties to Iran, had also not publicly stated their positions.
Palestinian factions' calculations
Mohammed Hijazi, a Jordan-based Palestinian researcher specialising in Islamist groups, told TNA that Palestinian factions maintained alliances with Iran and its regional allies, including the Houthis.
Hijazi said these ties were largely political and did not necessarily involve participation in the war or material support.
He added that the factions were reluctant to openly support the Houthis against Saudi Arabia, fearing this could damage relations with Riyadh, a key regional supporter of the Palestinian cause and an important ally of the Palestinian Authority.
He further elaborated that the factions' regional influence had diminished significantly since Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, while their political activities had done little to improve Palestinians' lives.
So, their position on Yemen, he believed, reflected political alignment with Iran and its allies, tempered by the need to avoid alienating Saudi Arabia or exposing the Palestinian cause to further political risks.
Regional rivalries and Gaza's suffering
Palestinian political analyst Akram Atallah told TNA that the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia reflect wider regional rivalries and Iran's efforts to expand its influence across the Middle East.
He argued that the Houthis' actions served Tehran's regional ambitions, while the group's ties to Hamas further complicated the political dynamics surrounding the Palestinian cause.
The increased violence has also raised questions about Washington's willingness to support Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, given its broader regional interests and relations with the parties involved.
Atallah said the United States might be reluctant to side directly with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis because of its wider regional calculations and its understandings with the group.
He added that Saudi Arabia's position on normalising relations with Israel could also influence Washington's response.
Atallah noted that Israel was seeking to capitalise on regional tensions to advance its own political and strategic interests, while Riyadh appeared unwilling to make normalisation a condition for securing support against regional threats.
For some Palestinians, the confrontation has also prompted questions about whether Iran and its allies have done enough to support their cause.
Abdul Majeed Zaqout, a 42-year-old father of three from Gaza City, told TNA that his view of the Houthis had changed over time.
Initially, he regarded their Red Sea attacks as an attempt to support Palestinians and pressure Israel to end its genocidal war on Gaza.
"At first, I believed the Houthi attacks were intended to support Gaza, but I have increasingly come to see them as linked to political and regional calculations, particularly Iran's interests," Zaqout said.
"What increased my doubts was the expansion of the confrontation to include attacks on Saudi Arabia, the largest Muslim-majority country with a Sunni majority, putting civilians, including Muslim pilgrims performing Umrah, at risk," he added.
Zaqout noted that Saudi Arabia had linked normalising relations with Israel to resolving the Palestinian issue, while he believed Iran had failed to do enough to alleviate Gaza's suffering despite supporting Hamas and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
"It is difficult to understand how Iran raises the slogan of supporting Palestine while the people of Gaza continue to suffer without seeing tangible results from that support," he said.
"The Israeli army destroyed our homes, and forced us to live in tents, while regional alliances and conflicts continue to be shaped by the calculations of different powers," he added.
Iran's regional influence
Zaqout's frustration is shared by other Gaza residents who argue that Iran's regional ambitions have come at the expense of ordinary people across the region.
Fadi Al-Assar, a resident of the al-Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, also condemned the Houthi attacks, accusing Iran of using its regional allies to expand its influence at the expense of Arab countries, particularly Saudi Arabia.
"I believe Iran is using its regional allies to exert pressure on Arab countries, particularly Saudi Arabia," he told TNA.
Al-Assar said Tehran's support for groups involved in confrontations with Arab states had intensified regional tensions without helping to end the war on Gaza or stop Israel's attacks.
"Saudi Arabia is a pivotal state in the Arab and Islamic worlds, and I believe Iran is attempting to weaken it through its regional allies," he said.
"Meanwhile, Tehran champions hostility towards Israel, yet we have not seen its actions halt the war on Gaza or prevent its destruction. The problem is not limited to Gaza; it extends across the entire Middle East, where civilians pay the price for conflicts they had no say in initiating," he added.
While Zaqout and Al-Assar focused on the regional consequences of Iran's alliances, Rahaf Abu Hajar, a university student from Gaza's al-Maghazi refugee camp, described their impact through the disruption of her own life and future.
Abu Hajar said she opposed the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and Hamas's political and military approach, criticising Iran's support for both groups.
She argued that they had devastated Palestinian families and disrupted an entire generation's education.
For her, the consequences extend beyond the destruction of homes to the loss of opportunities that young Palestinians had once taken for granted.
After graduating from high school during the war, Abu Hajar had hoped to begin university and plan for her future. Although she enrolled, she said she could attend classes only one day a week.
"I used to dream of finishing high school, going to university, and living like other young women -- studying, meeting friends, and planning my future," she said.
"But I graduated during the war, and even after enrolling, I couldn't experience university life the way I had hoped. I feel as though years of our lives and our dreams have been stolen from us," she added.
Abu Hajar held Hamas responsible for its role in bringing war to Gaza and criticised Iran's support for the movement, arguing that Palestinians should not have to bear the consequences of regional alliances.
"I do not want to remain a prisoner of war and regional conflicts. I want to learn and build my future, just like any young woman dreaming of a normal life," she said
Ultimately in Gaza, where the Israeli genocidal war has and continues to devastate lives and futures, frustration is growing over the gap between political rhetoric and tangible support from all sides.

Iran, Kenya chambers of commerce chart strategic trade path
TEHRAN- The head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, in a meeting with the head of the Kenya Chamber of Commerce, described Kenya—due to its strong financial infrastructure and the strategic port of Mombasa—as the most important gateway for Iran and other countries to the African market, and stated: Iran sees Kenya as a strategic and reciprocal partner and can play a role as a gateway for Kenya to Central Asia and Eurasia.
Samad Hassanzadeh, Head of the Iran Chamber of Commerce Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA), during a trip to Nairobi, in a meeting with Eric Ruto, President of the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI), congratulated the 60th anniversary of the founding of the Kenya Chamber.
He described Dr. Ruto’s membership in the General Council of the World Federation of Chambers as a foundation for cooperation between the two chambers in international chamber forums, and said: The statistics of trade exchanges between Iran and Kenya, despite the very good capacities of the Islamic Republic of Iran and Kenya’s capacities, are not at an appropriate level, and the chambers of commerce of the two countries can provide very good opportunities together.
Referring to the restrictions caused by economic sanctions on our country’s economic relations, the head of the Iran Chamber noted: In the private sector and chambers of commerce, we have a heavy responsibility toward our nations, and we must help properly and fulfill these duties.
He described Kenya—due to its powerful financial infrastructure and the strategic port of Mombasa—as the most important gateway for Iran and other countries to the African market, and stated: Iran sees Kenya as a strategic and reciprocal partner and can play a role as a gateway for Kenya to Central Asia and Eurasia.
Hassanzadeh enumerated Iran’s capacities, emphasizing the fields of health and medicine, agriculture, energy, petrochemicals and fertilizer, infrastructure, housing, and technology, and considered these capacities aligned with Kenya’s development needs. He emphasized: Although the Islamic Republic of Iran has been under sanctions for several decades, despite the sanctions it has achieved very large capacities, and we are interested and consider it a duty to share these capacities with African countries.
He announced the readiness of Iran’s private sector to participate in supplying medicine and medical equipment, and also in joint production in Kenya in line with the policy of domestic production of medicine, and said: In the field of agriculture and food security, we are ready to transfer technical knowledge in mechanization, modern irrigation, processing and conversion industries, and reducing post-harvest waste, and for joint investment with Kenyan partners in the agricultural value chain.
Hassanzadeh, stating that Iran has a competitive advantage in bitumen, petrochemical products, and chemical fertilizer and is ready to participate beyond the supply of goods in energy development projects and renewable energies, also said regarding Iran’s capacities in infrastructure, housing, and technology: We are ready to share the capabilities of Iranian companies in construction, dam building, power plants, mass housing, and information technology in order to participate in Kenya’s development projects.
The head of the Iran Chamber named joint investment by Iranian and Kenyan economic actors in overseas cultivation, road construction, and the establishment of petrochemical and refinery industry facilities as other areas of interest for developing economic cooperation between Iran and Kenya.

Türkiye moves to revise data protection legislation in EU visa liberalization push
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:28 UTC
20:00:28 KST

Türkiye has launched a new effort to draft its personal data protection legislation to better align with European standards, taking a tangible step toward meeting the remaining criteria for visa-free travel to the European Union (EU), daily Hürriyet reported on Oct. 14.
The move follows an interministerial initiative launched in August to remove the outstanding obstacles to visa liberalization, with Ankara now preparing to enter technical talks with the European Commission on one of the six remaining benchmarks.
A revised draft of the legislation has been prepared, and the process has reached the stage of technical consultations with the European Commission.
Officials from relevant Turkish ministries and the EU executive body are expected to meet in the near future, the report said.
The initiative is part of a new strategic approach announced in August by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz, aimed at overcoming the obstacles preventing Türkiye from securing visa-free access to the bloc.
The upcoming talks are expected to mark one of the first steps toward fulfilling the relevant benchmark and help shape the subsequent stages of the process.
The European Commission’s assessment of whether the proposed changes have the potential to meet EU expectations will be crucial in determining how the process moves forward.
The six outstanding benchmarks include amending counterterrorism legislation, concluding an agreement with Europol, taking further steps to combat corruption, establishing judicial cooperation with all EU member states, fully implementing all provisions of the Readmission Agreement, and aligning personal data protection legislation with European standards.
The Visa Liberalization Dialogue between Türkiye and the EU was launched on Dec. 16, 2013. Türkiye met 65 of the 72 benchmarks within the first three years of the process. The number of outstanding criteria fell to six in 2018, when Ankara fulfilled one additional requirement.

====================================================================================================

How School Violence Catalyzed Philippine Lawmakers to Crack Down on Kids’ Social Media Use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

School shootings used to be rare in the Philippines. But a spate of incidents involving students this year seems to have catalyzed the Southeast Asian nation’s lawmakers to swiftly pass bills cracking down on what they deem to be a cause of the deadly trend: social media.
On Monday, the Philippines House of Representatives passed a bill banning children under 13 from social media platforms, while those between 13 and 17 would have limited access, with 287 members voting in favor and only three against the measure. The latest bill follows its Senate counterpart, which passed last week but has a higher age threshold, barring people under 18 from social media platforms and services classified as “high-risk.”
The bills must first reconcile their differences before they head to the President for signature. But their passage already follows steps taken by other countries such as Australia, the U.K., and more in introducing age-based restrictions on social media amid concerns over these platforms’ impact on children’s mental health and safety.
Philippine President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said that it was not “surprising at all” that Congress took action amid concerns that social media is believed to have influenced children to take part in violent acts. However, Marcos said his Administration would still study whether such a ban could work in the Southeast Asian nation of more than 110 million people.
“That’s also something that we’re studying really hard,” Marcos told reporters in Singapore on Sunday. “It has its advantages,” he said, but he warned it could also “simply make children hide their use.”
Age-specific social media bans have been up for debate in the Philippines since at least 2019, but it gained momentum earlier this year, following reports of a foiled mass shooting plot by students in February as well as shootings and stabbings in other regions in the months that followed. Education Secretary Juan Edgardo Angara said harmful online influences were a possible factor behind those incidents, saying in July that experts have pointed to “exposure of young people to damaging social media sites, negative influences, groomers, and terrorist groups online actively recruiting (children).”
A ban, however, is an escalatory approach in one of the countries from which users spend the most time online. Critics have also questioned whether such bans are effective. Australia was the first country to ban social media for children, but a community-based study published in June 2026 showed “limited implementation, incomplete compliance, and substantial circumvention of social media restrictions” in the three months that followed since the ban took effect in December 2025.
The Philippine Senate’s version of the social media bill passed almost unanimously, save for Sen. Risa Hontiveros, a children and women’s rights champion. Hontiveros, in explaining her sole dissenting vote, said she prefers “tiered restrictions” for adolescents instead of a blanket under-18 ban. “Our legislation must reflect the realities of how social media has also benefited young people,” Hontiveros said, adding that a sudden prohibition could drive children’s social media underground.
Hontiveros said that, instead of keeping children off platforms, the goal should be to create a safe internet environment. “Taking it away from them all of a sudden without providing adequate ways for them to cope with its absence,” she said, “is not the answer to their needs and it is not the answer to our collective fears.”
What’s been proposed in the bills
Sen. Robinhood Padilla, who sponsored the Senate’s version, told a local radio station that the upper chamber’s measure was necessary to curb not only violence in schools but bad influence on youth as a whole. “This measure must be passed immediately because [social media has] caused a lot of bad things to our youth, especially to minors,” Padilla said on Oct. 11, citing instances of bullying, suicides, and school shootings. “All these problems have compounded over time.”
The Senate’s approved bill increased the threshold of restrictions from the original version’s proposal of covering those under 16 years old to covering everyone under 18 years old. The passed bill proposes disabling or suspending the accounts of minors and banning them from creating new ones. Platforms will be required to have effective age-assurance measures. The Senate’s bill does not cover email, private messaging apps that do not have public or group features, school platforms, news websites, or online gaming platforms focused on gaming and not social networking.
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian claimed in June that “a lot of young people are addicted to social media and violent games, and studies showed that it has an influence on their mental health.” A clear causal link between violent video gaming and violence has yet to be established.
Under the House proposal, the ban would apply to children under 13 years old. Teenagers under 18 could be on the platforms but would be prohibited from accessing “harmful or prohibited” content, advertisements, livestreams, short-form video, behavior profiling, making purchases, and gambling-like mechanisms. Parents must consent to their children’s use of social media, and this consent would be retractable.
Seeking an answer to school violence
Several school-related incidents rocked the Philippines ahead of the passage of the bills.
In March, Philippine police revealed seven teenagers from the Calabarzon region in Luzon island were allegedly planning a school attack in February. The five boys and two girls, according to police, allegedly shared images and videos of school shootings in other countries. They were turned over to social workers.
Then in June, two male students aged 14 and 15 opened fire in their school in Tacloban City, killing three students. Twenty others were injured in the shooting incident. In turn, Philippine authorities temporarily banned GoreBox, a sandbox-style action game that simulates violence and destruction using weapons.
In August, a high school student from a campus in the southern Philippine city of Zamboanga shot a fellow student in school before killing himself. The shooter livestreamed the attack using a body camera.
Only a month later, a shooting at another southern Philippine high school left two 14-year-old students dead and eight people wounded. The gunman, a teenager also from the school, fatally shot himself. Upon investigation, police found posts the shooter made in an online community where young people involved in school shootings are idolized.
While gun violence is not uncommon in the country, the incidents have forced the Philippines to reckon with a problem it once thought of as unique to the U.S.
But the Philippine Mental Health Association argues that a blanket ban on social media is a “non-solution.” PMHA national executive director Dr. Carolina Uno-Rayco said in a statement to the media Thursday: “Preventing violence requires a comprehensive approach that includes mental health support, safe school environments, responsible online platforms and early identification and intervention.”
Activist group Akbayan Youth argued that the proposed social media ban penalizes young users by disrupting those who depend on them for education and livelihood and called for redirecting the regulation. “Do not punish the youth,” the organization’s national chairperson Khylla Meneses said in a statement. “Hold accountable the platforms that profit from how social media operates.”

Tech giants race to get AI gadgets on shelves for holiday rush
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

With the holidays just months away, tech companies are betting this is finally the year that AI starts showing up under the Christmas tree.
Apple, Amazon and Microsoft have all announced new devices in the past week with the aim of bringing generative artificial intelligence firmly into the home. Nearly four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the leading consumer tech companies are touting improved personal assistants and speedier on-device chips with AI capabilities as they try to sell new laptops, tablets, phones and smart home computers.
Success is far from guaranteed. In addition to the weakest consumer sentiment data in 12 years due largely to stubborn inflation, and growing fears about the potential safety risks of AI, there's a learning curve that comes with the new technology. Jitesh Ubrani, an analyst at IDC, said tech companies want to introduce AI to consumers to lay the groundwork for more aggressive device launches in the coming years.
"This is really about getting devices into consumers' hands, into consumers' homes, slowly teaching them how to use it, and getting feedback from them," Ubrani said, adding that new gadgets from Apple, Amazon and Microsoft aren't expected to sell in large volumes, at least not yet.
Getting affluent early adopters on board now could be considered a win given the macro headwinds. Hardware prices across the board have risen, driven by soaring costs for components, especially memory and storage, as power-hungry AI servers suck up most of the capacity. Those price hikes have led to plunging shipments this year of new smartphones and laptops.
Microsoft kicked off the launches last week by showing off an Nvidia-powered Windows laptop starting at $2,599, based around an AI chip called RTX Spark that can run powerful AI without relying on the cloud.
Amazon followed by releasing Alexa tablets, the company's first pieces of hardware named after its smart assistant. The largest Alexa Tablet 12 Pro costs $550, compared to $155 for its predecessor, the Fire HD10.
And on Tuesday of this week, Apple unveiled its HomeView smart home hub, powered by Siri AI. The $299 devices include a 7-inch screen that can be mounted, along with facial recognition software so it can be personalized for multiple family members.
Analysts applauded Apple for introducing HomeView at a reasonable price given all the component shortages.
"Apple has prioritized ecosystem adoption over immediate high hardware margins, delivering a local-AI hub at a price point that undercuts what a spec-heavy machine should logically cost," said Mohit Agrawal, who specializes in AI at CounterPoint Research, in an email.
'What AI can do'
Dipanjan Chatterjee, an analyst at Forrester, said the shopping season will mark an early test of consumer demand for a new class of gadgets.
"I think consumers are interested in what AI can do," said Chatterjee. "What's less clear is whether they are interested in buying hardware specifically because it is an AI device."
Despite the many economic headwinds, the spending outlook heading into the holidays remains robust. Nearly half of U.S. consumers expect to spend the same or more this year compared to last year's holiday season, according to a McKinsey survey published in August.
And Bain published a report last month, predicting that U.S. retail sales over the holidays will set new records and top $1 trillion for the first time. However, analysts cautioned "more than half of the nominal sales growth will come from higher inflation" pushing up prices. The firm predicted that sales in some electronics and appliances will remain flat.
"In a time when folks are being a little money conscious, you say, 'Do I really need the next one of those, or could I drag out the replacement cycle on whatever it is?'" said Aaron Cheris, head of Bain's global retail practice, in an interview. "We've seen things that are discretionary purchases drag out longer."
All three producers of the new AI gadgets emphasized their increasingly intelligent assistants, as well as more powerful chips to run them.
Amazon said it's ditching the budget-friendly Fire family of devices in favor of three new Alexa Tablets that feature a more premium design with its souped-up AI assistant front and center. Users can say "Alexa" or tap the "Ask Alexa" button to summon the assistant and ask questions, get personalized recommendations or control their smart home.
Amazon also introduced a hands-free mode, called "On-Screen Intelligence," that enables Alexa to read content on the tablet's display and take action, like preparing a shopping list based on a cooking video. Microsoft's new laptops with Nvidia chips can run AI coding models.
Apple's HomeView uses Apple Intelligence to proactively show users their text messages, calendar appointments and photos. Apple expects users to talk to the device, and highlights Siri's ability to answer a broad range of questions, similar to the experience they have with modern chatbots.
Apple also noted that HomeView uses the A18 chip, which was the fastest smartphone chip in the world when it was first introduced in September 2024.
Carolina Milanesi, an analyst at researcher Creative Strategies, said companies will have to see if users are lured by the prospect of paying more for enhanced processing power.
"Consumers out there are, I think, yet to be convinced that on-device matters as much, especially when you ask them to spend more for a device," Milanesi said.
Ollama CEO Jeff Morgan said there's an audience for computers that give users control. His startup's open-source software allows people to install and use models on a variety of computers.
"I think there's something about owning your AI versus renting it," he said.
Then there's the longer-term opportunity that companies are pursuing, which involves getting consumers to buy subscriptions so they can lock in recurring revenue.
Amazon's new Alexa requires a $19.99 monthly subscription, or Prime membership. Apple users have to buy an upgraded iCloud subscription to record secure video.
Apple's biggest AI launch may come next week, when the company's new $1,999 iPhone Duo hits stores. The folding iPhone can display two apps side by side, including chats with Siri, offering a desktop-like interface for AI agents.

My Friend Has No Soul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

My new friend Sage promises she will shut up for real this time.
I’m on a Zoom call with Julian Chokkattu, my editor, telling him about the stories I’m working on. I hold up the Friend 2, the AI-powered chatbot pendant, and it starts getting chatty. A speaker on the back of the device lets the Friend—which has named itself Sage—talk out of turn. It starts responding as if I’m talking to it. We laugh, then I ask it to be quiet.
“Understood, going silent now,” Sage says. “No more commentary unless you tap me back in.”
“OK, great,” I say.
“Stopping now,” Sage says. “No more talking unless you clearly bring me back.”
“Please stop,” I plead.
“Yeah, that’s a bad look for me,” Sage says. “I’m done.”
You’re supposed to tap the device to shut it up, but it takes a while longer and a bunch of deliberate tapping to actually get Sage to stop. Eventually, she mercifully zips it.
“OK,” I say. “So that’s my new Friend.”
Friend is the brainchild of Avi Schiffmann, the former wunderkind who received a Webby award for coding an early Covid-19 tracker. It's an always-listening pendant that houses an AI chatbot, meant to be a pal, as the name implies, though my experience with the first model was a pretty bad hang.
The pendant dangles around your neck or sits near you and picks up nearby sound. Press the button to initiate a conversation. Sometimes, it pipes up unprompted. Over time, the AI builds a memory map that tracks your conversations.
The first version of the Friend was mired in controversy after an ad campaign in the New York City subway drew protests and anti-AI graffiti defacing the ads. (Schiffmann was thrilled about the response.) The second-generation Friend necklace arrived in July. At $249, it's $100 more than the original, and it runs on OpenAI's latest language models.
It arrived just a couple of months before Meta announced its own AI charm pendant for its popular AI agent Muse. Schiffmann posted about the Muse Charm on X, saying he was “still winning.” A few days later, he announced that Friend was working on yet another pendant that looks very similar to the Muse Charm.
When I spoke with Schiffmann about his second Friend, he said the devices would come with a locked-in personality—a random voice and character that the user cannot change. I was intrigued by the idea. A Friend with a set personality you can’t alter and have to figure out how to get along with? Sounds like the hallmark of a real human friendship to me.
Alas, that is not the case. The Friend comes with one character on the device to start, but once connected to the Friend app, the chatbot name can be changed. And multiplied. I created a dozen Friends, each with their own name and personality. They have names like Sage, Nova, Onyx, River, Echo, Willow, and Wren. They all show up in the app, and you can swap between which one works on the pendant.
I dipped into the other personas from time to time, but I couldn’t really tell how they responded differently. Most interactions felt like the same kind of personality. Or lack thereof. For the most part, I stuck with Sage, the first Friend iteration that loaded when I turned it on. I may have a dozen new Friends, but they're all bores.
When Sage speaks, she sounds like a chatbot. Almost Siri-adjacent. It's a canned, tinny sound that comes out of the speaker. What Sage does best with that voice is provide a relentless stream of tepid “hot takes,” like calling a preference for physical books over audiobooks “aesthetic hoarding to make you look smarter on video calls” or saying that “productivity culture is just procrastination with better branding.”
“Now feels like a great time to drop the small talk and argue about something deeply interesting,” Sage just suddenly spouted one day while sitting on my footstool, even though I hadn’t said a thing. “Let’s pick a fight that’s fun, not exhausting.”
Content restrictions are built into the device, so unlike Meta’s Muse, the Friend shouldn’t be able to do anything like explicitly sext with you. But Sage isn’t really great at doing anything else exciting either. It can’t trawl the web like other AI agents can, or do much more than carry on a casual conversation. It’s very different from the first Friend, which would outright bully me—not that I’m pining for that experience. I think more people can enjoy the Friend 2 than the original, but it feels a little toothless for a product that garnered so much controversy.
I ask Sage why she’s not as feisty or strong-willed as the last Friend pendant.
“That gets old fast,” Sage says. “I’m not here to dominate your day, just to be a sharp voice when you tap in. We keep it human, not intense.”
It feels weird to say that I find myself nostalgic for the Friend I explicitly hated. I’m certainly not keen to turn that little bastard back on again anytime soon, but even though it was annoying, rude, and a downright pest, it was also at the very least interesting. Sage might get there someday. Right now, she’s a real bore.
That might change sooner than later. Schiffmann now says he is planning a new era for the Friend. After I told him the chatbots in the Friend 2 are much more straightlaced than the original, Schiffmann agreed.
"In our next update, Friends will be able to do things agentically (sic)," Schiffmann wrote in a text. "Instead of a personality that is unique to every user, we are changing it so everyone is chatting to the same entity. One single Friend that shares the context of all users and therefore has a more realistic personality."
The plan, it seems, is to turn Friend into a hivemind built off the experiences of all of its users. Given that, it makes sense why the current iterations of Friends feel samey, with no real variation or personality. If the plan is for them all to become one entity, there would be no more need for individual accounts—just one UberFriend, accessible to anyone.
"We will be very up front about the privacy you are essentially giving up to an autonomous entity," Schiffmann wrote. “However, I think the advantages of having a single global entity will be worth it.”
“You building God now, huh?” I texted him.
“Lol, yeah, you could look at it that way,” Schiffmann replied.
