Breville Eye Q Toaster Review: Neat Sensors, but Less-Than-Perfect Toast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

It's also pretty good looking as countertop appliances go, a bar that Breville's products tend to clear easily. The “dark noir” brushed steel is handsome, the controls intuitive, and the ceramic-coated top is clean and will likely stay that way over time, more so than a traditional stainless top.
Over the summer, I brought the Eye Q along for a couple of weeks of family time in New Hampshire, where we were often eight or more around the table, tweens to octogenarians. Most everyone was intrigued by the toaster, and encouragingly, nobody needed coaching on how to use it.
During the months I had it, it almost always did an acceptable job. It wasn't hard to get the toast right, but—and this is a big but—compared to a regular toaster, the quality of the toast it made was comparable, not superior. To generalize, especially if you compared front to back on a slice, or piece to piece, the Eye Q's toasting was a little uneven and the top of the toast tended to come out darker than the bottom. A noticeable thing, but nothing a polite person would complain about if you set a couple buttery slices in front of them.
On BLT day, I took my nephew Eli on as intern for the afternoon and had him toast seven consecutively darker batches of toast, one per setting, then line them up in order on a sheet pan. The lowest setting was very light, settings two and three were pretty identical, settings four and five were excellent, setting six was mysteriously lighter than setting four, and setting seven was very dark and a little burnt. Two-slot toasters aren't designed for seven back-to-back cycles of toasting, but it did well enough. Store-bought bagels didn't fare particularly well.
Back in Seattle, I unpacked a new Eye Q, and that one had a bad habit of making lighter shades darker than most people would appreciate, so Breville sent another one along to close out the testing. It worked fine, though it tended to get the edges a little toastier than the center; this seemed to be getting worse as testing wound down, so if you’re thinking about buying one of these, perhaps watch the comments for a couple months before pulling the trigger.

Nordic soldiers in Israeli army face growing war crimes scrutiny
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:58:40 UTC
19:58:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Nordic soldiers in Israeli army face growing war crimes scrutiny
Hundreds of citizens from Nordic countries are registered as serving in the Israeli military, according to Israeli army data, fuelling debate in Europe over the legal responsibility of nationals who fight in foreign conflicts.
Swedish broadcaster SVT reported this month that 346 people with Swedish, Danish, Norwegian or Finnish citizenship were registered in the Israeli army.
They included 150 Swedish citizens, 99 Danes, 62 Finns and 35 Norwegians.
SVT also interviewed a dual-national soldier, identified only as "David", who said he had taken part in fighting in Gaza.
The figures have renewed questions over whether European authorities should investigate citizens who serve in the Israeli military where there is specific evidence linking them to alleged violations of international law.
The issue extends far beyond the Nordic countries.
Israeli military data reported earlier this year indicates that tens of thousands of personnel hold at least one additional foreign nationality.
One dataset obtained through a freedom of information request showed 47,107 Israeli military personnel holding additional citizenships as of March 2025.
A separate count reported by Yedioth Ahronoth put the number at 50,632.
The figures included more than 12,000 US citizens, more than 6,000 French nationals, more than 3,000 each from Germany and Ukraine and more than 2,000 British nationals.
The data does not show how many served in Gaza, whether they were active soldiers or reservists, or whether they served in combat units.
That distinction is important because holding foreign nationality or serving in the Israeli military does not in itself establish involvement in a crime.
But legal complaints targeting particular soldiers have increasingly been filed in European and other jurisdictions over alleged conduct during the Gaza war.
Israel has longstanding programmes allowing people from abroad to join its military.
The Mahal programme allows eligible Jewish volunteers who are not Israeli citizens to carry out military service without permanently immigrating to Israel.
More than 500 people are currently serving through the programme, according to figures cited in the original report, with more than 400 joining annually.
Other programmes, such as Sar-El, have traditionally focused on civilian and logistical volunteering rather than enlistment in combat units.
The participation of foreign nationals has attracted greater scrutiny since the start of the Gaza war. The New Arab has previously documented the network of "lone soldier" programmes recruiting people from abroad to serve in the Israeli military.
John Graversgaard, a Danish researcher and writer, told The New Arab that authorities should apply the same standard to citizens serving in foreign militaries regardless of which country they fight for.
He said the relevant issue was whether an individual had participated in conduct that could violate international law.
Walid Daher of the Palestinian Forum in Denmark said responsibility should similarly be based on each individual's actions and role.
More than 50,000 with additional nationalities
Israeli military data obtained by investigative website Declassified UK through a freedom of information request showed that 43,194 members of the military held Israeli citizenship and one other nationality.
Another 3,913 had multiple citizenships, producing a total of 47,107 in the dataset.
Separately, Yedioth Ahronoth reported that an Israeli military database listed 50,632 personnel with at least one additional foreign citizenship.
The army said some people appeared in more than one category, accounting for differences between the figures.
Neither dataset distinguishes between active service and reserves or between combat and non-combat roles.
Among those listed were 12,135 US nationals, 6,127 French nationals and more than 3,000 people holding either German or Ukrainian citizenship.
More than 2,000 held British citizenship.
The numbers have increased pressure on European governments to clarify how they deal with nationals serving in foreign armed forces.
Legal cases move into European courts
Several countries have already seen criminal complaints involving individuals who served in the Israeli military.
Swedish police had received more than 700 reports relating to possible war crimes in Gaza by August 2025, according to the report.
Prosecutors said several investigations had been opened, although they did not say whether Swedish nationals serving in the Israeli army were suspects.
In France, rights groups filed a complaint in July 2025 against two French-Israeli soldiers over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
A similar complaint was filed in Germany in September 2025 against a soldier with links to Munich.
The allegations remain subject to investigation and have not resulted in final convictions.
In Britain, lawyers referred 10 British nationals who had served in the Israeli military to the Metropolitan Police in 2025, alleging involvement in war crimes.
The Metropolitan Police later reopened its investigation into several identifiable British nationals.
Other Israeli soldiers have faced complaints or investigations while travelling abroad. In 2025, Belgian police detained and questioned two Israeli soldiers following allegations relating to Gaza.
More recently, the Hind Rajab Foundation filed a criminal complaint in Portugal against an Israeli soldier, alleging war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Danish human rights lawyer Helia Ratz told The New Arab that European states should apply the same standards to all citizens who fight abroad.
He argued there was greater scrutiny of Europeans who had joined armed groups in Syria than of those who served in the Israeli military.
Individual responsibility
Legal experts and activists interviewed for the report stressed that foreign citizenship or military service alone does not establish criminal responsibility.
The central question is whether evidence links an individual to a specific act that could constitute a war crime or another international offence.
The figures therefore cannot show how many foreign nationals took part in combat in Gaza or whether any particular soldier committed an offence.
But the growing number of investigations has shifted the debate.
What was once largely discussed as a question of volunteering in a foreign military is increasingly becoming a question of individual accountability and whether European governments will investigate their own nationals when credible evidence of alleged international crimes is presented.

Iran, Pakistan deepen economic ties with focus on mining sector cooperation
TEHRAN- In a significant step toward strengthening bilateral economic relations, senior officials from Iran and Pakistan convened to explore avenues for expanding cooperation in the mining sector. The meeting between Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, Head of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran (TPO), and Asad Ahmad, CEO of the Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation, marked another milestone in the two neighboring countries' ongoing efforts to deepen their trade and economic partnership.
During the meeting, both sides reviewed solutions for expanding trade and economic relations while examining existing capacities to develop cooperation in the mining sector. Dehghan Dehnavi held comprehensive talks with Ahmad regarding areas for expanding trade cooperation and creating new opportunities for economic interactions between the two countries. The discussions also covered existing capacities for developing trade exchanges and strengthening bilateral cooperation in the mining sector, with both parties exchanging views on potential collaborative frameworks.
The two sides called for expanding bilateral interactions and utilizing shared opportunities to develop trade relations between Iran and Pakistan. Dehghan Dehnavi, announcing the readiness of the Trade Promotion Organization of Iran to support the expansion of trade cooperation with Pakistan, emphasized the importance of strengthening bilateral relations across various trade areas. The CEO of the Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation welcomed the development of cooperation and the creation of new capacities for expanding trade interactions between the two countries.
This latest meeting builds upon a series of high-level engagements between the two nations aimed at transforming their longstanding neighborly relationship into a robust economic partnership. In early August, Iran and Pakistan took a significant step toward deepening economic ties by signing a memorandum of understanding to expand trade cooperation during the 10th session of the Joint Trade Committee held in Islamabad. Both sides reaffirmed their mutual commitment to achieving the ambitious $10 billion target in bilateral trade and advancing toward a formal free trade agreement.
The final session of the committee was attended by Iran's Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, Seyyed Mohammad Atabak, and his Pakistani counterpart, Jam Kamal Khan. The MOU was signed following extensive deliberations covering a wide range of commercial cooperation areas, including joint border regions, maritime activities and shipping development, coordinated steps for a free trade agreement, establishment of joint free zones, and barter trade mechanisms.
Speaking at the signing ceremony, Minister Atabak described the negotiations as highly constructive, noting that Iran places no restrictions on increasing trade volume with Pakistan. "We call on the business communities of both countries to play their essential role in this direction," he stated, reinforcing Iran's principled policy of expanding cooperation with neighbors.
Dehghan Dehnavi, addressing a gathering of traders and economic activists from both countries, outlined Iran's strategic vision for bilateral trade relations. "One of the main priorities of Iran is the development of trade and economic relations with neighboring and aligned countries, which it pursues through a targeted program," he stated. "Pakistan, as a friendly neighboring country with good political and economic relations, holds great priority for Iran."
The TPO head highlighted Iran's unique position as a regional economic powerhouse, noting its population of approximately 90 million, exceptional energy resources, extensive mining and industrial capacities, technical and engineering services, and strategic geopolitical location with access to rail, road, and international maritime shipping networks. He pointed to Iran's numerous ports on the Caspian Sea, the Persian Gulf, and the Indian Ocean—particularly Chabahar—as vital nodes connecting neighboring countries to each other and to other continents, expressing Iran's willingness to utilize the capacities of Karachi and Gwadar ports to expand international interactions.
The mining sector cooperation discussions represent a natural extension of these broader economic initiatives. Iran's extensive mining and industrial capacities, combined with Pakistan's growing mineral development sector, present significant opportunities for joint ventures and knowledge sharing. The emphasis on private sector engagement, as demonstrated through the cooperation memorandum signed between the Iran Chamber of Commerce and Industries and the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry, further institutionalizes these collaborative efforts.
Dehghan Dehnavi noted that the volume of trade between Iran and Pakistan in 2025 stood at approximately $3 billion, with both countries targeting $10 billion by 2030. To achieve this goal, he emphasized the need for removing obstacles to trade development, including resolving transportation and customs problems, eliminating barriers related to financial transfers and banking matters, and strengthening border infrastructure.
The large Iranian trade delegation accompanying officials includes representatives from major Iranian companies in oil, gas, petrochemicals, food, agriculture, transportation, shipping, and knowledge-based products, all ready to negotiate and cooperate with Pakistani counterparts. With the recent MOU signed and implementation mechanisms being developed, both nations appear poised to translate their centuries-old brotherhood into tangible economic dividends benefiting the nearly 300 million people across their shared borders. The mining sector cooperation between the TPO and Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation stands as a promising component of this broader economic renaissance.

Colombia opens embassy in West Jerusalem despite city’s disputed international status
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:57:15 UTC
19:57:15 KST

Abderaouf Arnaout, Ikram Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Colombia opened an embassy in West Jerusalem on Wednesday, becoming the 10th country to establish an embassy in the contested city despite widespread international opposition to moves recognizing it as Israel’s capital.
The opening ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar, Colombian Foreign Minister Omar Bula Escobar and Moshe Lion, mayor of West Jerusalem, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
Lion said Colombia had become the 10th country to relocate its embassy to West Jerusalem.
The move follows the restoration of diplomatic relations between the two countries in August 2026, after Colombia severed ties with Israel in May 2024 under its previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem – occupied by Israel since 1967 – as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.
Israel annexed East Jerusalem in 1980, a move that has not been recognized internationally.
In Resolution 478, adopted in August 1980, the UN Security Council rejected Israel’s measures seeking to alter the character and status of Jerusalem and called on countries with diplomatic missions in the city to withdraw them.
Most countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv or surrounding areas rather than Jerusalem, reflecting the city’s contested status and the international position that its final status should be resolved through negotiations.
With Colombia’s move, the number of countries maintaining embassies in West Jerusalem rises to 10, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry.
They include the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Paraguay, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Nauru and Somaliland, which is recognized as independent only by Israel.

Saudi Aramco headquarters suffered extensive damage in Houthi attack, sources say
Oil giant Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran suffered extensive damage in an attack on Oct 13, with fire spreading across several floors, three people with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Operations at the complex in eastern Saudi Arabia have continued normally, but some employees have been asked to work from home, according to two of the sources.
A fourth person said some functions had been shifted to global offices, adding that the fire was still burning into the early hours of Oct 14.
The facility hosts an operations centre that helps the world’s largest oil company oversee onshore and offshore oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and thousands of kilometres of pipeline.
Saudi Arabia’s Energy Ministry said in a statement that the Oct 13 night attack, which came as fighting between Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified, had caused a limited fire, with no reported injuries or deaths.
Two of the sources said a fire started on the ninth floor of the south wing of the office block and spread between the sixth and 10th floors.
Another source added that the top three floors of the building, where the office of Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser is located, were severely damaged, with part of the ceiling caved in and windows and doors blown out.
Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.
The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack and vowed on Oct 14 to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.
The Iran-aligned group said it had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, without saying when.
The Houthis had threatened a “harsh and painful” response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesman Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.
Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Oct 10 that killed 13 people.
The Oct 10 ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country.
Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the Aramco complex.
The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details.
The authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country’s southern region.
Four people in Riyadh were injured by falling fragments from two Houthi missiles following their interception and destruction, Saudi Civil Defence said on Oct 14.
The debris caused limited damage to 15 homes in the capital, the Civil Defence spokesperson said, adding that the injured were two women, a man and a child.
The Houthis earlier on Oct 13 said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city’s outskirts.
Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company’s Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.
The coalition said in a statement on Oct 13 that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at “neutralising the capabilities of Houthis” to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways.
The Saudi Cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Oct 13 before the strike on Saudi Aramco, saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government to reverse the Houthis’ sudden gains in September, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.
A government offensive that began a week ago has pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, but the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz in October. REUTERS

does the paris of the impressionists still exist? alix urien finds it through her lens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:55:04 UTC
19:55:04 KST

does the paris of the impressionists still exist? alix urien finds it through her lens
french photographer alix urien revisits impressionism in circa 2020s, using movement, light and color to capture the fleeting beauty of contemporary paris and normandy.
[FEATURED]
FINDING IMPRESSIONISM IN CONTEMPORARY PARIS
Does the Paris of the great Impressionist painters still exist? French photographer and videographer Alix Urien believes the answer may lie in the way we look rather than in what we see. In her series Circa 2020s, created between Paris and Normandy, she transforms ordinary contemporary scenes into photographs and videos shaped by the light, color and fleeting sensations of nineteenth-century Impressionism. Rather than reproducing famous paintings through a camera lens, Urien explores the emotions that connect different generations, suggesting that while cities and societies evolve, certain human experiences remain remarkably unchanged.
‘Impressionism was an answer to a changing world,’ Urien tells designboom, recalling the industrialization, urban transformation and accelerating pace of life that accompanied the movement’s emergence. ‘They looked for the poetry in their everyday lives,’ she explains, finding inspiration in nature, intimate circles and familiar surroundings. A century after Claude Monet’s death in 1926, the photographer sees striking parallels between the nineteenth century and today, when technological change and an increasingly restless world make the simple act of observing feel almost radical.
PAINTING WITH MOVEMENT, LIGHT AND COLOR
Urien’s photographic process begins with reality: an ordinary moment unfolding before her lens. From there, she experiments with movement, captured directly through the camera, introducing a degree of unpredictability that recalls the spontaneity of an Impressionist brushstroke. ‘I’m drawn to the physicality and randomness of it, to the fact that I can never fully control the outcome,’ she explains. Rather than pursuing the precision usually associated with photography, she embraces uncertainty, allowing the image to move beyond documentation and toward something more sensory. The result occupies a space somewhere between a photograph and the memory of a scene.
Color plays an equally important role in her compositions. Drawing on color theory, Urien works with fragmented touches of light and color to emphasize the emotional atmosphere of an image. Yet her interest in Impressionism goes beyond aesthetics. Just as the arrival of photography challenged painters to reconsider their medium in the nineteenth century, she sees a parallel in the questions raised by artificial intelligence today. In response, she observes a renewed interest in experimental approaches to image-making, where personality and creative intuition matter more than technical perfection. For Urien, the camera becomes less a tool for reproducing reality than a means of interpreting how it feels.
SEVEN YEARS OF REDISCOVERING THE SAME CITY
Paris itself has become an ongoing subject of this exploration. After returning from London in 2019, Urien began discovering the French capital through a photographer’s eyes, finding a city that, despite its extraordinary density of history, could still feel like a small village. Hidden museums, overlooked corners and art shops revealed themselves alongside the changing character of its neighborhoods. Over seven years, she has returned to familiar places through different seasons and everyday encounters, observing how the same setting can take on an entirely different atmosphere from one moment to the next. Photography and video have become her ways of tracing these subtle transformations.
This fascination with the city’s evolving identity also informs Paris is for the Dreamers, her forthcoming photography book project, conceived somewhere between an artistic collection and a personal guide to the capital. ‘We all have our own idea of a Paris shaped by paintings or movies,’ Urien reflects, while emphasizing that the real city continues to evolve with its seasons, stories and inhabitants. Her work offers neither an exercise in nostalgia nor an attempt to preserve Paris as an open-air museum. Instead, it suggests that the world of the Impressionists has never entirely disappeared. It simply requires a different way of looking.
project info:
name: Circa 2020s
artist: Alix Urien | @hifromalix
location: Paris and Normandy, France

Türkiye-EU trade hits record $233B as Customs Union modernisation talks advance

10:52:05 UTC
19:52:05 KST

Türkiye and the European Union are making progress on updating their Customs Union agreement, with technical discussions covering e-commerce, public procurement, investment and agricultural products, Turkish trade minister Omer Bolat has said.
Speaking to reporters during a visit to Brussels, Bolat said negotiations were advancing on a “case-by-case basis”, despite the EU Council not yet formally authorising the European Commission to launch modernisation talks.
He said technical discussions with European counterparts were already under way, following the completion of a bilateral analysis and the passage of Türkiye’s new public procurement law in late July.
“We’re making progress on a case-by-case basis since the relevant issues have come up and authorities of the European Commission are conducting negotiations with us,” Bolat said.
He stressed that maintaining economic ties was as important for the EU as it was for Türkiye, noting that bilateral trade had increased elevenfold over the past three decades to reach a record $233 billion.
Industrial and digital trade
Bolat said Türkiye had spent the past year working to address concerns over restrictive provisions in the EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
He warned that some measures in the draft legislation could affect future investment and disrupt integrated supply chains, particularly in the electric vehicle and automotive sectors.
Ankara is maintaining communications with EU officials to convey its expectations and reduce the potential economic impact of the proposed rules, he added.
Bolat also said the EU was coordinating with Türkiye on preparations for digital trade legislation. Türkiye remains exempt from a newly implemented EU regulation imposing a €3 fee per package, he said.
He cautioned that political intervention by the European Parliament could have adverse consequences, adding that many European officials also supported including Türkiye in the “Made in EU” origin framework.
However, he noted that the EU comprises countries with differing economic interests, urging a “calm and level-headed” approach.
Bolat said he had made three official visits to Brussels over the past three months, following five visits last year, and expressed hope for positive developments in the talks.

Greek students organized a overnight camp-out and concert to press the conservative government for rent caps, increased housing subsidies, and the construction of new state-run dormitories.
Rent for small apartments has surged across Greece, where flat-sharing is uncommon, putting students in direct competition for limited housing with young couples, single-parent households and digital nomads.

‘art can be everywhere’: yinka ilori brings chairman to community center in london
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:50:57 UTC
19:50:57 KST

‘art can be everywhere’: yinka ilori brings chairman to community center in london
returning to islington for an exhibition during frieze london, the british-nigerian artist and designer considers how overlooked furniture can carry personal histories, build community, and challenge where art belongs.
[FEATURED]
chairman: yinka ilori explores the stories behind discarded chairs
Yinka Ilori brings ten years of chair–based work back to Islington, North London, where he grew up, with Chairman, an exhibition at the Walter Sickert Community Centre from October 14th–16th, 2026. Presented during Frieze London and UK Black History Month, the exhibition returns a body of work shaped by the neighborhood’s people, cultures, and everyday encounters to the community that helped inform it. Rather than treating chairs solely as functional objects or collectible designs, Ilori uses them to explore memory, identity, and the relationships that form around familiar things.
His interest in chairs began with a discarded object spotted from a London bus. ‘One moment that’s really stayed with me was spotting a discarded chair out of a bus window in London. It was about to be thrown away, but something about it caught my attention,’ he recalls during our interview. Seeing that chair made him think differently about unwanted furniture and what it could become .‘I started thinking about all the furniture we see on the streets, things people no longer want or think have had their day, and wondering what else they could become.’ That impulse to look again at what others overlook has remained at the core of Ilori’s practice. The designer collects and transforms existing chairs through color and pattern, giving familiar forms new identities without erasing their histories. ‘I’ve always looked at chairs a little differently. We all have them around us, but we don’t often stop to think about their stories. Who has sat on this chair? What’s their story? Where has it been? Why has someone left it behind? That’s what got me interested in collecting and making them in the first place.’
chairs as vessels for memory and identity
For the British-Nigerian artist and designer, the significance of a chair extends beyond its construction or appearance. It belongs to a shared vocabulary of everyday life, associated with domestic rituals, social encounters, and places where people gather. ‘Whether it’s gathering around the dinner table with your family, sitting in the barbershop, or learning in a classroom, chairs are part of so many everyday moments,’ he tells us. ‘I think that’s what makes them so special. They might seem like ordinary objects, but they hold so much memory, meaning and emotion.’ Because chairs are objects familiar to everyone, people can connect with Ilori’s work in different ways. Even when he changes their colors, shapes, and patterns, they remain recognizable. Visitors can relate to them through their own memories and experiences, without needing any knowledge of design. ‘You don’t need to know anything about design to connect with a chair. You just bring your own experiences to it, and that’s where the story begins,’ the artist explains.
Ilori’s first book, Chairman, published by ORO Editions in fall 2026, traces more than a decade of chair-based work through photography, archival material, studio documentation, essays, and interviews. Exploring how his British-Nigerian heritage and London upbringing shape his approach to furniture, the publication also considers how audiences bring their own experiences to the objects they encounter. Although his chairs draw on memories of growing up in Islington in a Nigerian household, Ilori leaves room for others to find their own stories in them. ‘I might be thinking about my childhood, while someone else sees a chair and thinks about their grandparents’ house or family dinners around the table,’ he reflects. ‘For me, it’s about being personal without being prescriptive. I can tell my story through the work, but leave enough space for someone else to find their own story in it.’
bringing art back to the community
 Bringing the exhibition to Islington gives the work a direct connection to the neighborhood where Ilori grew up. At the Walter Sickert Community Centre, his chairs return to the community that helped shape his practice, offering local residents a chance to connect with the work through their own memories and experiences. The choice of venue also reflects Ilori’s belief that art should be accessible beyond museums and galleries.
‘It means a lot to bring Chairman back to Islington because that’s where so much of my story began,’ Ilori shares with us. ‘Growing up in North London, I was surrounded by different people, cultures, buildings and ways of life. You take all of that in when you’re young, sometimes without even realising it, and it stays with you. I can see so much of that in my work today…’
For Ilori, the community center offers a setting that aligns with the social intentions behind his chairs. ‘I love the idea of someone who grew up around the corner coming in, seeing a chair and being reminded of a memory of their own.’ He sees the neighborhood as a repository of cultural knowledge, arguing that its histories deserve recognition beyond the conventional structures of museums and galleries. ‘To me the Walter Sickert Community Center is bigger than any traditional institution. The people living here have so much history and connection, that to me the community is already a museum and they are walking artifacts,’ Yinka Ilori adds.
‘I want to deconstruct the idea that you have to have your work displayed in these places to be seen. It’s important to bring art to the people and recognize that not everyone can go to a museum or gallery,’ he says. For Ilori, the timing offers a way to redirect attention toward a neighborhood that might otherwise sit outside the usual routes taken by art-world visitors. ‘Ultimately it’s about opening up the conversation around how people engage with art, which is why holding the exhibition during Frieze is so important. I want people to come away from the traditional areas and view art for more than just an allocated week; art can be everywhere.’
from visual spectacle to shared experience
Color and pattern give Ilori’s chairs an immediate presence, helping them stand out in public settings where people may not be actively looking for art. The designer is also interested in what happens after someone notices an object, whether that means stopping to look, taking a photograph, sitting nearby, or starting a conversation. ‘Color can completely change how a place feels, how you feel, and make you stop and notice something you might normally walk straight past,’ the British-Nigerian artist explains. Unlike a gallery visit, an encounter with a chair on a street or in a community setting may happen without planning or prior knowledge of the artist. ‘For me, that’s where the fun really starts. Maybe it makes someone smile, maybe they take a photo, or maybe it gets people talking. You never really know what will happen, and I love that. I want the work to catch people’s attention, but hopefully it also brings people together and leaves them with something to remember,’ he continues.
The designer wants people to engage with his chairs. A chair can be used as intended, but it can also spark curiosity and invite people to see it differently. ‘I don’t want people to feel that they can only look at my work from a distance. I want them to get curious, spend some time with it and make their own memories around it. Chairs are all about bringing people together, so seeing that happen in different ways is really special to me,’ Yinka Ilori concludes.
project info:
name: Chairman
artist: Yinka Ilori | @yinka_ilori
location: Walter Sickert Community Centre, Islington, London, UK
dates: October 14th–16th, 2026

Intelligence failures surrounding the October 7 massacre should not automatically lead to a premier's dismissal, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a radio interview with Army Radio on Wednesday, arguing that "nobody told [former US president George W.] Bush to go home after" the September 11 attacks.
Netanyahu compared Israel's intelligence failures to those preceding the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor and the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center in New York, arguing that those disasters had not automatically led to the removal of the countries' political leaders.
"There was blindness here," he admitted, "And I can tell you: There was also blindness at Pearl Harbor, when the Japanese bombed the United States. Yes, there was blindness. There was also blindness on September 11, at the Twin Towers. Nobody said: Okay, you have to go home. They didn’t say that to Roosevelt; they didn’t say that to President Bush."
Netanyahu defended his proposal to establish a "national" inquiry committee with equal representation for coalition and opposition members.
He argued that a government-appointed commission would lack public trust among opposition voters, while a state commission appointed through the existing judicial framework would be rejected by many of his own supporters. He also suggested modeling the investigation on the bipartisan US commission established after September 11.
Additionally, the prime minister doubled down on the position that had he been awakened and informed of the reported unusual Hamas activity on the night before October 7, he would have ordered military preparations and canceled the Nova music festival.
The prime minister insisted that Israel's security establishment had repeatedly assessed that Hamas was deterred and had not expected an imminent major attack from Gaza.
"The answer is no," he said when asked whether he had recognized the warning signs before the attack.
Netanyahu warns Iran against attacking Israel ahead of election
He also warned Iran that any attempt to attack Israel would trigger an unprecedented response.
"If Iran makes that mistake, [unclear word], and tries to attack us, it will encounter a response it cannot even imagine," Netanyahu said, responding to questions about possible Iranian military action ahead of Israel's October 27 election and the US midterm elections.
"We are prepared for all those scenarios. I hope we won’t have to resort to them, but I can say one thing: Israel will not allow - I will not allow - Iran to have nuclear weapons. As long as I am prime minister, Iran will not have nuclear weapons."
He said Israel had completed approximately 60% of its security objectives against the Iranian axis and suggested further operations could be necessary.
"Just a year ago, I’m saying this as emphatically as I possibly can, Iran was poised to destroy us. We removed a threat to the State of Israel. That is the most important thing," he said.
Asked whether Israel was coordinating with Saudi Arabia over recent Houthi attacks, Netanyahu declined to discuss specific countries or security cooperation.
He nevertheless claimed Israel's military successes had created opportunities for new regional alliances, saying countries both inside and outside the Middle East were increasingly interested in cooperation.
Netanyahu also pointed to what he described as an International Monetary Fund projection of 4.5% economic growth for Israel, arguing that the economy's performance demonstrated the success of his security and economic policies.
Netanyahu says election is 'extremely close,' pushes against smaller parties
The prime minister said he hoped the election would proceed as scheduled but warned that Israel's enemies could attempt attacks or rocket fire to create an impression of Israeli vulnerability.
Netanyahu also described the contest as extremely close.
"I’m worried because this election, right now, is tied," he said, adding that he had begun traveling across the country to encourage Likud supporters to vote.
Discussing the government he hopes to establish after the election, Netanyahu said his first preference was a right-wing coalition consisting of his existing political partners.
However, he did not completely rule out cooperation with opposition parties, including those associated with former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu said any potential coalition partner would have to accept his opposition to Palestinian statehood and support his government's security policies.
"If you accept our policies, of course we will talk with them," he said, while emphasizing that he intended to form a right-wing government first.
He criticized Eisenkot's positions during the war in Gaza, accusing him of supporting a premature end to military operations and withdrawal before Israel had achieved its objectives.
"I’m telling you that after October 7, I had to struggle, struggle against Gadi, who wanted to stop the war and withdraw. He said: We’ll come back after two years and see."
Netanyahu: Defense Ministry will remain in Likud's hands
Netanyahu also said Likud would keep the Defense Minister portfolio in a future government, while cautioning against distributing ministerial positions before the election results were known.
His statement came as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir continued his campaign to secure the portfolio for himself in a future Netanyahu-led government. Ben-Gvir has repeatedly affirmed he would demand the position of defense minister as a condition for joining Netanyahu's coalition.
The prime minister repeatedly warned right-wing voters against supporting smaller parties that might fail to enter the Knesset, arguing that such votes could undermine the chances of forming another government under his leadership.
He said he planned campaign stops in Kiryat Malachi, Kiryat Gat, Beersheba and Beit Shemesh on Wednesday to encourage turnout.
Netanyahu also defended his government's settlement policies, claiming it had established or legalized 104 communities and more than 100 farms. He pledged to continue pursuing security measures and settlement construction while criticizing the High Court of Justice's intervention in government decisions.

Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties, while intensified fighting along multiple front lines has cut off aid to around 800,000 people, humanitarian agencies said on Wednesday.
Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen's Red Sea coast are seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the Red Cross.
'Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure'
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in the country began in recent weeks, sparked by renewed fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, according to the United Nations' International Organization for Migration.
"Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure," ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anesthesia, oxygen and medicines.
Yemen's health services, battered by more than a decade of conflict, economic crisis, displacement and disease outbreaks, may have limited capacity to absorb a new surge in mass casualties if fighting intensifies further, the ICRC warned.
The fighting has also cut off life-saving humanitarian assistance for 800,000 people in Taiz - Yemen's third-largest city, which currently hosts the largest number of people fleeing the fighting - and other areas impacted by the conflict, the UN World Food Program said on Wednesday.
Some districts are now inaccessible because of fighting and road closures, the WFP said, adding that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted and remaining food in local markets may last only a short time.
"This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most," said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen, in a statement.

Ronen Bar files NIS 3 million defamation lawsuit against Netanyahu over shifting Oct. 7 blame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:50:08 UTC
19:50:08 KST

Former Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief Ronen Bar filed an NIS 3 million defamation lawsuit against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the Central District Court in Lod on Wednesday, alleging that the prime minister knowingly published false accusations about his conduct before the October 7 attack to shift responsibility onto him.
The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the October 27 elections, centers on a September 28 post on Netanyahu’s personal X/Twitter account accusing Bar of “failures and crimes.” Alongside compensation, Bar seeks a court-ordered correction or denial and legal costs, and says he will seek disclosure of relevant documents held by Netanyahu.
The lawsuit made serious allegations about what Netanyahu knew and how he acted in the years, months and hours preceding the attack. The court has not ruled on these allegations.
In the September 28 X post, Netanyahu accused Bar of recognizing warning signs but deciding not to call and alert him. Bar rejected that accusation, saying that the Shin Bet shared the available intelligence with Netanyahu’s military secretariat and that he instructed his staff to update the military secretariat before the attack began.
The lawsuit argues that the military secretariat was the official channel for updating Netanyahu and deciding whether to wake him. Bar also states that Netanyahu had not given him his personal phone number.
Responding Wednesday, Netanyahu dismissed that explanation, saying Bar could have reached him through other channels.
“Ronen, are you serious?” Netanyahu wrote on Telegram. “You had my secure phone number and could have called me immediately, as all the heads of the security establishment do.”
Netanyahu added that his Shin Bet guards, whom he described as Bar’s subordinates, could have reached him within minutes. “How many lives we could have saved if only you had called in time,” he wrote.
The distinction between information reaching the Prime Minister’s Office and reaching Netanyahu personally is central to the dispute.
The lawsuit emphasizes that Bar is not trying to evade responsibility for the Shin Bet’s intelligence failure, but is rather challenging accusations that he knowingly withheld information and chose not to take action to save lives.
“As the head of the service, I bear responsibility for the Shin Bet’s failure to provide the intelligence required regarding the October 7 attack and its timing,” Bar said in a statement issued on his behalf.
“Accordingly, I resigned from my position, bowing my head before the bereaved families.”
Lawsuit contradicts Netanyahu claims that Shin Bet concealed evidence
Bar’s departure followed a prolonged confrontation with Netanyahu over his dismissal and the agency’s independence. The government voted on March 20, 2025, to end his tenure, citing a breakdown in professional trust. Netanyahu maintained that the loss of trust stemmed from October 7; Bar argued that the move followed his resistance to improper demands and investigations involving people close to the prime minister.
The High Court of Justice froze the dismissal while considering petitions against it. On April 28, Bar announced that he would leave on June 15, and the government rescinded its dismissal decision the following day.
On May 21, the court nevertheless ruled, by a majority, that the dismissal decision had been unlawful. It found that Netanyahu had acted under a conflict of interest arising from investigations involving his associates, and that the government had bypassed the required advisory process, lacked an adequate factual basis, and failed to give Bar a proper opportunity to answer the allegations against him.
The investigations at the center of the conflict included “Qatargate”, which examined suspicions that figures close to Netanyahu promoted Qatari interests while working around the prime minister during the war. Qatar’s role as a mediator in hostage negotiations made the alleged relationships particularly sensitive. A separate investigation concerned the unauthorized transfer of classified military material to the German newspaper Bild.
In his April 2025 affidavit opposing his dismissal, Bar argued that the investigations posed a threat to Netanyahu’s personal and political interests. He also alleged that Netanyahu sought to use the Shin Bet’s powers against anti-government protesters. Netanyahu rejected Bar’s account and denied requesting unlawful surveillance of protest leaders.
The new lawsuit returns to those allegations, linking the attacks on Bar to his affidavit and describing the alleged efforts to deploy the agency against political protests as an attempt to use it as a “secret police” force.
During the dismissal proceedings, bereaved relatives also demanded accountability from Bar. At the April 8 hearing, bereaved father Itzik Bonzel, now a Likud candidate, challenged the court’s intervention, arguing that Bar’s acknowledged responsibility for the failure meant he should leave office.
The lawsuit details how, in the months leading up to October 7, Bar says he repeatedly warned Netanyahu about the possibility of escalation on multiple fronts, including Gaza, with particular concern ahead of the High Holy Days. He also presented proposals to target senior Hamas officials, which he says Netanyahu rejected or failed to advance.
Bar demands full disclosure of documents
Among the examples is a July 23, 2023, conversation in which Bar says he told Netanyahu: “I am giving you a strategic warning of war.” According to the filing, he also explicitly cautioned that the agency would not be able to provide a precise day and hour.
These were warnings of a deteriorating security situation, rather than intelligence identifying the date, scale, or operational plan of the October 7 attack; the lawsuit expressly acknowledges that the Shin Bet failed to identify those in advance.
The filing further alleges that Netanyahu pursued a policy of “quiet at any cost” in Gaza, directing the security establishment to postpone confrontations, keep Gaza as a secondary arena, and preserve Hamas as the governing authority.
Bar argues that this policy constrained offensive action against Hamas and allowed it to strengthen. He alleges that Netanyahu continued permitting Qatari money into Gaza despite warnings that funds were reaching Hamas’s military wing.
Netanyahu has presented a competing account, citing excerpts from security discussions and intelligence assessments to argue that Bar supported economic concessions and restraint toward Gaza and failed to warn him of an impending attack. In his April 2025 affidavit, Netanyahu cited a Shin Bet assessment from days before the massacre that suggested renewed understandings with Hamas could help preserve stability.
Bar argues that selected quotations obscure the broader record of his warnings and recommendations. His lawsuit also acknowledges that Netanyahu sometimes approved preparations for targeted killings in principle, including at an October 1, 2023, discussion, but alleges that he failed to issue the instructions needed to advance them.
Regarding the night of October 7, the lawsuit disputes Netanyahu’s claim that Bar held numerous conversations with then-IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi and then-military intelligence chief Aharon Haliva before deciding not to alert the prime minister. Bar says he did not speak to either man that night, although officials in their organizations exchanged information.
According to the lawsuit, Shin Bet personnel began updating their military counterparts at about 11 p.m. on October 6 and distributed an electronic alert at 3:03 a.m. concerning an unusual accumulation of possible indications of offensive Hamas activity.
The lawsuit acknowledged that the alert was assigned a lower level of urgency than it should have been. It also states that the Shin Bet did not anticipate a full-scale attack that night.
Bar said the intelligence officer in the prime minister’s military secretariat received updates overnight, including a follow-up call at 3:55 a.m. that drew attention to information already sent. He further says that, after an assessment ending around 5:15 a.m., he instructed his staff to update Netanyahu’s military secretary, Avi Gil, before the attack began.
The filing placed the subsequent call from Bar’s chief of staff to Gil at 6:15 a.m., while quoting Gil’s account that he was awakened at 6:12 a.m. Neither account establishes that Netanyahu himself received the information at those times.
The lawsuit also challenged Netanyahu’s accusations that Bar failed to alert local emergency response squads or evacuate the Nova music festival. Bar says he did not know the festival was taking place, and argues that the Shin Bet did not command the IDF or the local squads and was not responsible for licensing civilian events.
He further disputes Netanyahu’s argument that dispatching a small “Tequila” operational team demonstrated advance knowledge of the impending massacre. The lawsuit says such teams were regularly mobilized in response to possible attacks and that sending one did not mean the agency anticipated an assault on the scale of October 7.
The dispute has increasingly focused on access to the full documentary record. Netanyahu has released selected excerpts from security discussions, including in a 55-page account published in February as part of his response to the state comptroller. Bar alleges that the presentation omits context necessary to assess what was recommended and decided.
Separately, Gil has alleged that Netanyahu’s former chief of staff, Tzachi Braverman, sought to change the recorded time of a call on the morning of October 7. Braverman has denied wrongdoing. The allegation of altering a record is distinct from the dispute over selectively publishing excerpts.
On Tuesday, dozens of former hostages, bereaved relatives and other family members demanded that Netanyahu release the full protocols, original recordings and logs from security discussions before and on the morning of the attack, subject to military censorship and the law. Signatories included former hostages Yocheved Lifshitz and Ditza Heiman; Einav Zangauker, whose son Matan was abducted on October 7; and Hadas Kalderon, whose children Sahar and Erez and their father Ofer were also taken hostage.
Bar said he had waited three years for a state commission of inquiry to examine the Shin Bet’s actions alongside its failures, but had decided to sue in light of what he described as an ongoing campaign against him.
The filing argues that Netanyahu should not be protected by parliamentary immunity because, in Bar’s account, the publication was a planned personal and political attack rather than protected conduct in the performance of his duties.
“I call on the prime minister not to hide behind claims of immunity,” Bar said. “In the absence of a state commission of inquiry, the truth will be established in court.”

Israeli plan to reopen settler ‘Route 463’ threatens to isolate Ramallah
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:49:40 UTC
19:49:40 KST

Israeli plan to reopen settler ‘Route 463’ threatens to isolate Ramallah
The move to open Route 463 for Israeli settlers threatens to isolate Palestinian villages and severely fragment the Ramallah governorate.
The Israeli army is reportedly preparing to reopen Route 463 to settler traffic, a move that threatens to isolate eight Palestinian villages and two large residential neighbourhoods in the occupied West Bank.
The areas that would be most affected by the reopening of the road would be northern Ramallah and el-Bireh, a suburb of Ramallah city. It would separate the northern and southern parts of the Ramallah and el-Bireh Governorate.
The road extends for about 10km (6 miles) from el-Bireh and the Jalazone refugee camp in the east to Ein Qiniya in the west.
It was originally constructed in the mid-1990s to connect the Beit El settlement, north of Ramallah, to Dolev, another settlement to the west of the city.
Following the outbreak of the Second Intifada in 2000, the Israeli army barred both settlers and Palestinians from using the road for a period.
The reopening of the road is part of a 1.075-billion-Israeli-shekel ($355m) settler infrastructure budget, aimed at connecting settlements in the occupied West Bank, illegal under international law.
While there is no timeline for the reopening of Route 463, the far-right Israeli government is pushing for it to be implemented before Israeli elections on October 27. The law will bypass the Knesset in an apparent attempt to speed up the process.
Geographic fragmentation
The Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, a monitor affiliated with the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), warned that the plan falls under a “systematic policy to dismantle Palestinian geographic and demographic contiguity” in a governorate home to nearly 400,000 Palestinians across 80 communities.
If reopened, tens of thousands of Palestinians would be forced to use an old alternative road near the Jalazone camp, north of Beit El, which is already heavily congested and would be unable to accommodate any increase in traffic.
Jamal Juma, coordinator of the Popular Campaign to Resist the Wall and Settlements, a coalition of independent Palestinian civil society groups, said the reopening of the road will completely encircle the western side of Ramallah.
The villages affected will include Surda, at-Tira, and Wadi at-Tira to the north of Ramallah, and Ein Qiniya, Ras Karkar, Deir Ibzi, and Ein Arik to the west. The impacted zone would extend southwest to Beitunia and the Fruits Roundabout, southwest of Ramallah, connecting to the town of Safa and Route 443, a main artery between Jerusalem and Israel.
Road closures to the east have pushed the urban expansion of Ramallah, the administrative capital of Palestine, westwards over the past two decades, making one continuous urban block between the city and neighbouring areas such as Birzeit and Surda. Opening the road to settlers will impede this expansion, separating Ramallah from its surrounding villages.
Land confiscation fears
Turning a route used by the inhabitants of heavily populated West Bank villages into a “settler road” will likely be accompanied by more military checkpoints, watchtowers, and widespread land confiscations, Juma warned, all affecting Palestinians. There could also be more home demolitions and restricted access for farmers under the pretext of “settler security”.
Settler roads are a major component of a network that connects settlements and outposts while separating Palestinian communities. As of March 2026, settler roads occupy more than 3 percent of the occupied West Bank’s area, with many more swaths of Palestinian land affected by their presence.
The commission noted that out of 173 military and security orders issued between October 2023 and April 2026, 66 were dedicated to constructing settler roads. During the first half of 2026 alone, the Israeli occupation issued 40 military land seizure orders targeting 611 dunams – a dunam being 1,000 square metres – to build 16 security roads.
Violating signed agreements
The push to reopen the road follows a wave of pogroms across the occupied West Bank by settlers, in coordination with the Israeli military.
On September 8, settlers closed a roundabout near Ein Ayoub in the Ras Karkar area, pelting Palestinian vehicles with stones.
The attacks and the push for the reopening of the road coincide with a tightening of restrictions on Palestinian movement in the occupied West Bank since October 7, 2023, when Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began.
Munif Treish, the mayor of el-Bireh, told Al Jazeera that 95 percent of the road’s route falls within Area B, which according to the 1995 Oslo II Accords is under Palestinian civil administration and joint Israeli and Palestinian security control. Only a small section lies in Area C, which is under full Israeli control.
Treish said the reopening of the road would be a “clear violation” of agreements Israel has previously agreed to in the past with the PLO.
“The repurposing of the street for the benefit of settlers and the military constitutes an existential threat that paralyses urban expansion and serves settlement activities, harming the future of 250,000 Palestinians,” he said.
“The municipality will not allow it to be confiscated and diverted to serve settlements and will continue to pursue all legal avenues to prevent this.”

October 7 not just another day on the calendar, Bar Kalifa says

Palestinian child pushed into spitting on Israel hostage
Or believed that was the moment he would be killed.

"They tell him, 'Spit again.' And the child spits, and this time he enthusiastically improves his performance. Everyone around him applauds and tells him, 'Good boy, good boy.'"
"These are the people we fought against," Bar Kalifa concluded. "These are the people we will not return until we have destroyed them all. This is how a generation of murderers is educated and raised."

Trump did not invite OSCE observers to the U.S. midterm elections — The Hill

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:47:18 EEST

Trump did not invite OSCE observers to the U.S. midterm elections — The Hill
Kyiv • UNN
The Trump administration declined to invite OSCE observers to the midterm elections, breaking with a practice that had lasted more than 20 years. Democrats criticized the decision.
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration declined to invite observers from the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to monitor the midterm elections, breaking with a practice Washington had followed for more than 20 years. The decision drew criticism from Democrats and human rights organizations. The Hill reports, according to UNN.
Details
As the publication notes, Trump's decision puts the United States in the same camp as the isolated autocratic regimes of Belarus and Russia. These countries have also refused international observers, and their most recent elections have been widely condemned as fraudulent.
White House spokesperson Lauren Biss, explaining the absence of an invitation, said that the elections would be administered, conducted with the participation of, and observed by American citizens. The United States is one of the OSCE's 57 members.
The ODIHR and the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly called the administration's decision "regrettable" last month. OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons said the refusal represented a significant departure from the established democratic practice that had been in place for more than two decades.
Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen said that failing to invite international observers contradicted the principles of freedom, democracy, and electoral transparency. Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse called the absence of an OSCE mission "a warning signal for democracy." Democratic Congressman Steve Cohen also suggested that the administration might not want independent observation on Election Day.
Trump's critics, the publication writes, fear possible attempts to challenge or derail election results unfavorable to Republican candidates. State officials, predominantly Democrats, are also discussing possible actions by the federal government regarding elections, which are administered by the states in the United States.
Additional information
Election observation is carried out by the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR). Its mission has no enforcement mechanisms and does not determine the legitimacy of elections. The observers' task is to assess the electoral environment and prepare recommendations to bring the process into line with the OSCE's commitments to democratic standards.

Russia’s arrest of Japanese journalist: Why are tensions rising?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:46:55 UTC
19:46:55 KST

Russia’s arrest of Japanese journalist: Why are tensions rising?
Japanese journalist Imai Yuki arrested on Sakhalin for allegedly spying on Russian defence capabilities, says the FSB.
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist from Sakhalin Island after accusing him of spying and gathering information on its defence capabilities.
On Tuesday, Russian news agencies reported that the reporter, working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was arrested by the Federal Security Service (FSB) as he was preparing to leave the next day.
According to the TASS news agency, the FSB said the journalist, Imai Yuki, was arrested in the Sakhalin region and taken to Moscow after being accused in a “criminal case”.
The arrest of the Japanese citizen comes amid deteriorating relations between the two countries as Tokyo joined Western sanctions against Moscow due to the invasion of Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s August visit to Iturup Island, which is part of the Kuril Islands archipelago, drew sharp reactions from Japan.
The two countries have a longstanding territorial dispute over the Kuril Islands dating back more than a century.
Here’s what we know about the arrest:
Who is the arrested journalist and what is he accused of?
Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Maria Zakharova, during a press briefing on Tuesday, said Yuki was accused of espionage.
“Tokyo’s attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country’s security are regrettable. We cannot help but point out that today’s incident is not an isolated one,” Zakharova said.
“Given the overall decline in bilateral cooperation caused by the Japanese authorities’ anti-Russian policies since the start of the Second World War, as well as Tokyo’s reluctance to listen to Moscow’s concerns regarding Japan’s remilitarisation policy, which affects our legitimate security interests in the Far East, we are forced to note that this development will further darken the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations.”
Zakharova called on Tokyo to “come to its senses and change its approach, abandoning hostile steps towards Russia”.
According to Russia’s Interfax news agency, Yuki will be remanded until December 12 before the trial begins.
What has Japan said?
On Wednesday morning, Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said Tokyo had requested the “prompt provision of information” from Russian authorities over the arrest.
“As well as for humanitarian consideration and fair and impartial treatment,” he added.
Japanese media have also reported that the country’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs would summon the Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a protest over the arrest, but no official confirmation has been released so far.
The Hokkaido Shimbun, where Yuki worked, said it was still confirming details and added that it would “respond with the reporter’s safety as our top priority”.
What’s the history of Russia-Japan tensions over Sakhalin Island?
While Russia administers the Kuril Islands archipelago, Japan claims the four southernmost islands – Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan and the Habomai islets – calling them the Northern Territories.
The Kuril chain of islands sits between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula.
The dispute began in 1855, after Russia and Japan established their first diplomatic and trade treaty, which also drew the Russo-Japanese border in the Kuril Islands, with Iturup under Japanese control and the islands to the north under Russian control.
Russia took control of the Kuril Islands after the 1945 Yalta agreement, which was signed by United States President Franklin Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.
Following Japan’s surrender in the final weeks of World War II, Moscow seized the entire archipelago and expelled about 17,000 Japanese citizens.
In the 1951 San Francisco peace treaty, Japan renounced the Kurils but maintained that the four southernmost islands were part of its territory. However, Russia never signed the treaty.
Because of the ongoing dispute, Russia and Japan have never signed a peace treaty to end World War II.
What’s behind the recent rise in tensions?
In August, Putin visited Iturup on his first-ever trip to the disputed islands.
He was the second president to visit the islands after his predecessor, Dmitry Medvedev.
But Putin’s visit caused uproar, with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi calling it “absolutely unacceptable”.
Takaichi told reporters at the time that Putin’s visit had “worsened Japanese sentiment towards Russia”, adding that the chain of islands was a “unique territory of [Japan] historically and under international law”.
“I hope that the Russian side will take the gravity of this matter very seriously,” she said.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi also said the islands were “inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit”.
What is the status of Russia-Japan relations?
Relations between the two neighbouring countries are at a low point.
Russia has increased its military presence on the Kuril Islands over the past decade, with Iturup used as its primary military airbase in the region.
Moscow has also labelled Japan as an “unfriendly” country due to sanctions over the Ukraine war.
On the other hand, Takaichi’s cabinet last week approved additional sanctions against Moscow, including expanded export bans and asset freezes for those linked to the Russian military.

'Bomb selfie' exposes Israel negligence after deadly school trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:46:35 UTC
19:46:35 KST

Breadcrumb
'Bomb selfie' exposes Israeli negligence after deadly school trip
Israeli schoolchildren reportedly posed for selfies with an unexploded bomb, passed it between them and carried it in a backpack before it detonated, killing a 14-year-old boy and injuring 24 others during a school trip near the Lebanese border.
The incident on Monday has exposed serious questions over the Israeli authorities' failure to protect children from unexploded ordnance in an area devastated by years of war, with an initial investigation revealing that a nearby restricted zone had neither been physically sealed off nor clearly marked to prevent public access.
According to Israeli newspaper Haaretz, students from ORT Ma'alot religious high school discovered the munition while hiking near the border, with some handling the device and taking photographs with it before the deadly explosion.
"He was playing with the bomb," one student told Haaretz, describing the actions of his classmate who was killed.
"Some of the kids told him to leave it, but no one thought it contained explosives. We continued along the trail and stopped to pray at one point. After the prayer, he played with it again, put it back in his bag, and then there was a massive explosion."
The Israeli military alleged that the device was a cluster munition fired by Hezbollah during the war, although its origin has not been independently established.
The explosion occurred in the Manara mountain range, approximately 50 to 100 metres from the Lebanese border, according to Israeli newspaper Maariv.
The site was close to an Israeli military post that had been manned by combat engineering troops during the war and subjected to heavy Hezbollah fire.
Despite the area's proximity to military positions and the known danger posed by unexploded munitions, students were permitted to hike nearby.
Israeli authorities under fire over deadly negligence
Israel's education ministry said on Tuesday that it was investigating whether the students had strayed from their approved route before the explosion.
The ministry maintained that the planned route had been authorised and complied with restrictions imposed by the Jewish National Fund, also known as KKL-JNF, which manages the area.
"The planned route did not pass through the prohibited area," the ministry said.
It added that safety instructions issued before the trip explicitly prohibited students from touching unexploded ordnance or ammunition and required them to report any discoveries.
However, KKL-JNF officials told Haaretz that the dangerous area had been designated off-limits in May 2025 but remained physically accessible, without clear signs or barriers to prevent people from entering.
The organisation said it had informed the Education Ministry of the closure, although it lacked the authority to approve school trips or physically seal off the area.
Schools are required to submit planned routes to the ministry for approval before each excursion.
The ministry acknowledged knowing that KKL-JNF had closed a dangerous route along the Ramim Ridge and said it had approved an alternative route taking that restriction into account.
However, the approved route passed close to another area closed because of unexploded ordnance, where access remained unrestricted.
Investigators are now examining whether the students deviated from their approved route or whether the ministry itself incorrectly defined the route.
The revelations have raised questions not only about the supervision of the students but also about the decision to authorise school excursions near an active military frontier littered with unexploded weapons.
'Ignorance and negligence'
In a sharply critical commentary published by Haaretz, columnist Rogel Alpher condemned the extraordinary complacency of Israeli society and authorities in treating a heavily militarised border region as an ordinary recreational destination.
Alpher questioned how high school students could be permitted to hike along an authorised trail near the Lebanese border as though the past three years of war had never happened.
He described how the students reportedly passed the munition around, placed it in their bags, photographed themselves holding it and sent the images to their parents.
The behaviour, he argued, exposed failures extending beyond the children themselves to the adults and institutions responsible for their safety.
"At least some staff were aware of what was happening, yet they let it happen. They failed to grasp the extent of the danger. The impression is that they did not guide the students, nor had anyone guided them," Alpher wrote.
"This hike, like the ones Israelis take there during the holidays, reflects ignorance and negligence."
He also accused Israel's Education Ministry of failing to instil even a basic understanding of the dangers posed by unexploded ordnance, arguing that the incident reflected a broader detachment from the realities of Israel's continuing war on Lebanon.
Alpher questioned whether Israelis had failed to recognise that fighting was continuing across the border, where Israeli forces occupy parts of southern Lebanon and remain engaged in military operations.
He also linked the school trip to the Zionist conception of hiking as "a continuation of the battle by civilian means", in which walking across territory becomes a symbolic assertion of sovereignty and control.
The students' decision to treat an unexploded munition as a souvenir of war reflected a wider culture of complacency.
"The selfies show that the students knew it was a bomb. Perhaps they saw it as a war souvenir, a trophy of war," he wrote.
"Their tragic complacency is part of the broader complacency that surrounds this blind state," he added, accusing Israel's political, military and economic institutions of ignoring realities that could ultimately have devastating consequences.
War continues across the Lebanese border
The deadly incident has also drawn attention to the contrasting realities on either side of the Israel-Lebanon border, where unexploded ordnance continues to threaten civilian lives.
Dozens of towns and settlements in northern Israel were evacuated during the conflict, while areas affected by the fighting remain contaminated by unexploded munitions.
Across the border, Lebanese civilians continue to face the deadly consequences of Israeli bombardment, with unexploded Israeli ordnance threatening farmers and residents attempting to return to their homes.
The Israeli military continues to occupy parts of southern Lebanon, having expanded its invasion since fighting with Hezbollah resumed in March.
Israeli airstrikes, shelling and demolitions have continued in southern Lebanon despite a framework agreement signed between Beirut and Tel Aviv in June.
On Monday, Lebanon's Health Ministry said Israeli attacks over the past three years had killed 8,596 people and wounded 30,660, many of them civilians.
