(DHA Photo)
Turkish authorities on Oct. 14 appointed a state trustee to the pro-opposition news channel Halk TV, with the police raiding its headquarters and halting its live broadcasts.
Officers from the Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK) searched the building in Istanbul’s Zeytinburnu district for evidence, while riot police cordoned off the surrounding area.
A statement from the Istanbul Chief Prosecutor’s Office said an investigation was launched into Halk TV chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu over allegations of bid rigging, bribery and money laundering.
Detention warrants were issued against 17 suspects and 11 of them were taken into custody, the statement said.
Mahiroğlu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.
Citing financial records obtained from MASAK, confidential witness testimony and suspect statements, the prosecutors said an analysis of the financial data found that companies linked to Mahiroğlu as a shareholder or executive had a combined transaction volume of 30.35 billion Turkish Liras.
Prosecutors also alleged that Mahiroğlu had used his connections at the İzmir Municipality to facilitate the establishment of BUSTECH Vehicle Maintenance and Repair Services Inc., appointed individuals to run the company and secured illicit gains through transactions related to municipal tenders.
Authorities seized companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroğlu and placed them under the administration of government-appointed trustees, the prosecutor’s office said.
He had previously come under scrutiny over alleged interference in public procurement procedures. Prosecutors subsequently opened a separate investigation into him following statements by Turkish businessman Aziz İhsan Aktaş and further inquiries.
“Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted,” the channel wrote on X shortly before 7 a.m. (04:00 GMT).
Halk’s news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.
“Today is a dark day for Türkiye. The public’s right to information is being seized for political reasons,” said Mahiroğlu in a video on X in which he said seven of his family members were among those detained.
The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition New Party and press groups.
New Party leader Özgür Özel lashed out against a TV channel “watched by millions,” describing the action as “weak.”
The Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) co-chair Tülay Hatimoğulları called for the decision to be “immediately” reversed.
The Halk TV chair, meanwhile, held the opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP) leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu responsible for the operation.
Özel had resigned from the CHP and founded a new party in August after being removed from the party leadership through a court ruling that reinstated Kılıçdaroğlu as chairman.
Halk TV sided with Özel in the aftermath of the split, airing programs that sharply criticized Kılıçdaroğlu.
In an interview four days ago, Kılıçdaroğlu criticized Mahiroğlu for living abroad despite operating a television channel in Türkiye.
In response to Mahiroğlu’s allegations, the CHP said its commitment to the rule of law did not vary depending on the individuals or institutions involved.
“Halk TV must be allowed to continue broadcasting; you cannot put an end to its broadcasting operations. Legal scrutiny must be carried out, but restrictions imposed on press freedom are unacceptable,” the party said.

Comedian Russell Brand was a sexual predator: British prosecutors

Comedian Russell Brand was a sexual predator, say British prosecutors

LONDON – British actor and comedian Russell Brand, once one of Britain’s most high-profile broadcasters, was a ruthless sexual predator who raped or abused six women despite their protestations to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite, prosecutors said on Oct 14.
Brand, 51, the former husband of US singer Katy Perry, is on trial facing three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to six women from 1999 to 2009.
He denies all the accusations and will set out his defence in court at a later date.
“Today I feel blessed,” he said as he arrived at London’s Southwark Crown Court. “I feel of course concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved.”
Desire was indiscriminate, prosecutor tells court
Opening the case against him, prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said some of the six women who had made the allegations had protested against, while others had no opportunity to react to his advances. It had made no difference to Brand, she said.
“His desire, his strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious,” the prosecutor said.
Although he could be funny, charming and likeable when he wanted something, he also had a childlike expectation that his every desire should be met, she added.
“He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative and, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said.
The alleged offences took place over a decade as he progressed from gigs as a stand-up comedian to a TV presenter, actor and Hollywood movie star, she said.
Brand says never engaged in non-consensual activity
The first is alleged to have occurred in 1999 when he was performing in a show on the fringe of the Labour Party Conference in Bournemouth.
The first complainant, who had watched the show and had assumed Brand was gay, said he had raped her in her hotel room where she had invited him because she thought he was interested in a cause she had been talking to him about.
One of his co-performers at that show said Brand had bragged that he had wanted to bed 5,000 women in his lifetime, the prosecutor said.
In 2001, he is accused of trying to drag a woman into a toilet cubicle at MTV Europe where she worked. Three years later, a woman said he had dragged her into a toilet cubicle in a bar before orally raping her.
Around the same time in 2004 or 2005, a woman working at a media company said he indecently assaulted her at her office.
The fifth complainant, a fan, had consensual sex at his home in 2009 but then he anally raped her, the prosecutor said. The sixth complainant, who worked for Channel 4, alleges Brand had demanded a massage and then pressed his face into her groin area, in the same year.
When interviewed by police, Brand declined to answer questions but provided written statements in which he said he did not remember the incidents, had never engaged in non-consensual activity and accepted that he had had sex in toilet cubicles during parties, Karmy-Jones said.
Woman came forward after TV programme
The women involved did not know each other and had not taken the matter to the police at the time for various reasons, but came forward with complaints following a TV programme and a press report in 2023 in which anonymous allegations were made by other women, the prosecutor said.
Brand sat in the dock wearing a dark suit and thin, white scarf, staring forward intently.
His trial is expected to last about six weeks, has attracted huge media attention, with a second court opened to allow more journalists to attend and many outlets running daily podcasts.
The comedian, known for his flamboyant style and appearance, became famous in Britain before starring in a number of films including Get Him To The Greek in 2010, the same year he married Perry. They divorced in 2012.
More recently, Brand has mainly appeared in online broadcasts, with content often focused on US politics, religion and free speech. REUTERS

The proposed changes cover three pension schemes and the National Social Assistance Programme under the rural development ministry.
NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved the renaming of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) and several of its sub-schemes, including those named after former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.The Cabinet also approved the continuation of NSAP for five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31, with a total outlay of Rs 53,428 crore.Here are the approved name changes and details of the schemes:
National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana. Launched on August 15, 1995, the programme provides social security assistance to poor and vulnerable households.
Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vridhavastha Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly financial assistance to eligible elderly people from below poverty line (BPL) households.
Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vidhawa Pension Yojana. It provides financial assistance to eligible widows from BPL households.
Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly pension assistance to eligible persons with disabilities from BPL households.
National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh Yojana. The scheme provides financial assistance to eligible households following the death of the primary breadwinner.
Alse read: Diwali bonanza for railway staff: 78-day bonus cleared for 11.4 lakh employeesChanges to disability pensionAlongside the renaming, the Cabinet approved changes to the disability pension scheme. Monthly assistance will increase to Rs 375 for beneficiaries aged 0-79 years and Rs 625 for those aged 80 and above.The minimum benchmark disability requirement will be reduced from 80% to 40%, while the minimum age criterion will be removed, making individuals eligible for assistance from birth, subject to the scheme's other conditions.The Cabinet said the old-age and widow pension schemes, along with the family benefit scheme, would continue in their existing form.
A total of 3.20 crore beneficiaries across all 36 states and Union territories are expected to benefit from the approval.
Guidelines covering the revised eligibility criteria, beneficiary coverage and assistance under the disability pension scheme will be issued and implemented within three months.The programme was launched to fulfil the Central government's responsibility under Article 41 of the Constitution's Directive Principles of State Policy, which concerns public assistance in cases including old age, sickness and disability.Also read: IDBI Bank stake sale; Rs 53,428 crore welfare package- key decisions by Union cabinet

Western sanctions increase risk of satellite collisions — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:03:55 UTC
19:03:55 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The sanctions regime imposed by the European Union and the United States on Russia and other nations is increasing the risk of spacecraft collisions as satellite constellations expand, Yelena Pavlova, Chief Designer of a component of the Russian Automated Warning System on Hazardous Situations in Outer Space (ASPOS OKP), told TASS.
"Large low-Earth orbit satellite constellations are being expanded primarily by the Americans and the Chinese. While the Americans ensure collision safety for their own and European spacecraft (Starlink performed over 350,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers last year), they do not coordinate satellite trajectories with the Chinese or with the operators of the Rassvet satellites. This is a direct result of the sanctions policy pursued by the US and EU against 'unfriendly' Eastern states. Consequently, the simultaneous growth of these constellations significantly raises the probability of collisions due to the absence of universally accepted space traffic management rules," Pavlova noted.
According to her, the "layers" of the US military constellations Starshield and SDA pose a distinct threat. The US Space Command does not publish their orbital data, which also creates conditions for potential collisions with other space objects, the expert believes.

French students continue school blockades ahead of talks with government officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:02:23 UTC
19:02:23 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Nearly 200 high schools across France were expected to remain closed Wednesday amid continuing student blockades, as the government pledged proposals to improve university admissions. 
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told French broadcaster BFMTV that “96% of high schools are open,” with no disruptions reported in three-quarters of the country’s departments, a day after the fifth round of nationwide protests. 
Several schools remained blockaded in Paris, including Voltaire, Helene-Boucher, and the Balzac school complex. Balzac’s administration suspended in-person classes, citing access difficulties and safety concerns. 
Geffray said Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste would submit proposals to improve Parcoursup, France’s university admissions platform, to the prime minister by the end of October. 
He expressed openness “to adjustments, possibly substantial ones,” while questioning what would replace the platform if it were abolished. 
According to Geffray, fewer than 20% of the 90,000 contributions submitted to a government platform collecting students’ complaints concerned Parcoursup. 
He ruled out immediate changes to the baccalaureate, France’s school-leaving examination. 
“I’m not going to change the baccalaureate six months before a presidential election; we need to stop constantly reforming,” he said. 
Student representatives are scheduled to meet Geffray and Baptiste on Thursday afternoon as they press for €10 billion ($11 billion) in investment. 
Pierre Sourzat, president of the organization Les Lyceens!, told Franceinfo that students expected concrete measures after receiving “only crumbs.” 
Although organizers have not called for a sixth round of protests Thursday, the Union of High School Students urged demonstrators to maintain blockades. 
Union President Ryad Rani and other student representatives also called for participation in a “yellow vest” demonstration scheduled for Saturday. 
Meanwhile, classes resumed at Kleber High School in Strasbourg, where clashes between students and police had occurred in recent weeks. 
French President Emmanuel Macron has acknowledged the “legitimate anxieties” of young people amid nationwide high school protests, while condemning violence during demonstrations, government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said Wednesday. 
Bregeon said Macron believed young people’s concerns had been “politically exploited and transformed into urban violence.” 
The president denounced what he called “unacceptable scenes” of violence during demonstrations, particularly on Tuesday, she said. 
Macron has asked the government to provide “clear and concrete answers” in the coming weeks, including measures to protect teachers and an assessment of school buildings. 
The government has assigned 2,000 of the 3,000 substitute teachers it had pledged to deploy, Bregeon said. 
Geffray said earlier Wednesday that more than one-third of the 3,000 substitute teachers had already been deployed to work with students. 
Meanwhile, the justice minister released an updated tally of cases linked to urban violence during the student movement. 
Since the blockades began, 7,950 people have been taken into police custody, including 6,773 minors and 1,177 adults, according to the minister. 
Of those, 2,735 people have been prosecuted, while 2,225 have been offered alternatives to prosecution. 
A further 1,263 cases were dismissed, and 26 people were placed in pretrial detention, the minister said.

EIB plans to increase financial support for Ukraine – deputy secretary general
EIB Deputy Secretary General Mikołaj Dowgielewicz said this in comments to an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum.
“We are working very actively in Ukraine. For us, it has been one of the most important areas of activity for more than five years. Above all, we support critical infrastructure so that what has been destroyed can be rebuilt. We also support local communities, cities and infrastructure recovery to help society and the country function as normally as possible,” Dowgielewicz said.
He said supporting Ukraine through the winter remains a constant priority for the EIB: “We will do everything in our power to help Ukraine protect its critical infrastructure so it can get through this winter in the best possible condition.”
According to Dowgielewicz, the EIB works closely with the government, local authorities across Ukraine and financial institutions.
“We have signed agreements with many Ukrainian banks to support entrepreneurs. We lend to Ukrainian financial institutions so they, in turn, can provide credit to businesses. This is essential for sustaining economic activity, because the economy must function as much as possible,” he said.
He recalled that since the start of the full‑scale war, the EIB has allocated €4.5 billion to Ukraine, including €1.5 billion in 2025, as well as an additional support package of nearly €500 million announced in June 2026 for the housing sector, infrastructure and support for Ukrainian businesses.
Dowgielewicz expressed hope that the EU’s new multi‑year budget will include solid guarantees for continued financial support for Ukraine.
“We are working to convince EU governments to provide the necessary financing. If negotiations on the EU budget conclude successfully in the near future, we will make every effort to increase our support for Ukraine in the coming years,” he said.
As reported, the Cabinet of Ministers will allocate more than UAH 4.9 billion in EIB funds for community‑level recovery projects.

Despite Middle East war, Egypt remittances hit record $33.9bn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:01:21 UTC
19:01:21 KST

Breadcrumb
Despite Middle East war, Egypt remittances hit record $33.9bn
Remittances from Egyptians working abroad reached a record $33.9 billion in the first eight months of 2026, according to the Central Bank of Egypt.
The figure was 27.2% higher than the $26.6 billion recorded during the same period last year, an increase of about $7.3 billion.
The total between January and August has already exceeded the $29.6 billion received during the whole of 2024 and is approaching the $41.5 billion recorded across 2025.
Remittances reached about $4.2 billion in August alone, up 21.7% from $3.5 billion in the same month last year.
However, the monthly figure was about $300 million lower than in July, when inflows reached approximately $4.5 billion.
The latest figures continue a sharp recovery in money sent home by Egyptians overseas.
During the first eight months of 2025, remittances had risen 47.2% year-on-year, from $18.1 billion to $26.6 billion.
The increase followed a period in which Egypt's foreign currency shortage and a large gap between official and parallel exchange rates had pushed some overseas Egyptians away from formal banking channels.
Egypt moved to a more flexible exchange-rate regime in March 2024, allowing the value of the pound to be determined more closely by market forces.
The International Monetary Fund said remittances rose 62% year-on-year during the second quarter of 2024 and 85% in the third quarter after the official and parallel foreign exchange markets converged.
The currency shift formed part of a wider $8 billion IMF programme agreed in 2024.
For the whole of 2025, remittances reached $41.5 billion, up 40.5% from the previous year.
They totalled $36.5 billion during the 2024-25 financial year, according to Central Bank balance-of-payments figures.
The remittances surplus stood at $36.3 billion during that financial year, while Egypt's current-account deficit fell to $15.4 billion.
Remittances are a major source of foreign currency for Egypt, alongside exports, tourism, Suez Canal revenues and investment.
The Central Bank did not provide a breakdown of the countries from which the latest transfers were sent or the channels used to send them.

EU proposes delaying methane rules for oil and gas imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:01:15 UTC
19:01:15 KST

Concerns over Europe’s energy supplies have prompted the European Commission to seek a one-year postponement of new environmental requirements for foreign fuel suppliers, Reuters reported.
The rules, originally scheduled to take effect January 1, 2027, would require companies supplying oil and gas to the European Union to monitor and report methane emissions.
Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas and the second-largest contributor to climate change after carbon dioxide.
Under the proposed changes, importers would have until May 31, 2029, to demonstrate that their 2028 imports complied with EU methane monitoring and reporting requirements.
Suppliers outside the EU would be responsible for providing the necessary emissions information.
“This one-year postponement of the import-related rules is designed to help avoid further pressure on the security of supply of imported fossil fuels in the current geopolitical context,” the Commission said in a statement.
The proposal follows pressure from the United States and France, which have raised concerns about possible disruptions to Europe’s energy supplies.
The war in Iran has already affected global energy markets, increasing uncertainty about fuel availability ahead of winter.
In June, the United States, Europe’s largest supplier of liquefied natural gas, warned that the regulations could interfere with deliveries.
French President Emmanuel Macron also raised concerns in September, writing to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen about potential legal risks for European importers.
Supporters of the delay argue that foreign suppliers are not prepared to meet the requirements and could avoid the European market rather than risk financial penalties.
The postponement still requires approval from EU member states and the European Parliament.

EU warns of worsening energy costs as winter approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:01:09 UTC
19:01:09 KST

Millions of European households could face greater difficulty paying their heating bills in the coming months as fuel prices remain high, European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen warned.
Europe is not facing an energy supply shortage, but rising prices are placing significant pressure on household finances, he said.
Diesel prices have doubled since February, when U.S. strikes on Iran prompted Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz. Gas prices have increased by 140 percent.
“It is a very serious situation we are in. And unfortunately, it will only become more serious in the coming months,” Jørgensen said.
He noted that even during an average winter, 47 million Europeans struggle to heat their homes adequately, sometimes having to choose between heating and food.
Energy costs are expected to feature prominently at this week’s EU summit in Brussels.
The European Commission has already proposed targeted financial support for vulnerable households and businesses.
Other measures under consideration include joint energy purchases, releasing oil reserves and delaying parts of EU methane regulations.
Germany, Spain and Italy are pushing for a common windfall tax on energy companies’ unusually high profits.
Although the Commission does not plan to propose an EU-wide tax, Jørgensen said it could help individual countries introduce one.
He also encouraged governments to lower electricity taxes, as Denmark has done, saying this could reduce household energy bills by an average of 14 percent.
Jørgensen said Europe’s long-term response must focus on reducing fossil fuel imports and expanding domestic renewable energy production.
“We must not backtrack on the green agenda. We need to secure more green energy,” he said.

Into the fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

In August 2014, ISIS swept into Sinjar, a town in northern Iraq and home to many of the country’s Yazidis, a Kurdish-speaking ethnic and religious minority long subjected to persecution. Regarding the Yazidis as infidels, ISIS killed thousands and enslaved thousands of women and girls, in what is now widely recognised as genocide.
The short documentary Into the Fire follows Hana Khider, a Yazidi woman who heads an all-female de-mining team. Khider works for the Mines Advisory Group, one of the founding members of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, which shared the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize with its coordinator, Jody Williams. The perilous work of Khider’s crew consists of searching for and deactivating hidden explosives left by ISIS, some disguised as everyday objects, including children’s toys. Directed by the British filmmaker Orlando von Einsiedel, the film moves between Khider’s job and her life as a wife and mother, showing two sides of caring for one’s community and rebuilding after the trauma of the genocide.
The film is part of von Einsiedel’s five-part series produced in collaboration with the Nobel Prize and National Geographic, with each instalment focusing on the continuing influence of a different peace laureate.

MEDICLINICS ALL-IN-ONE CENTRALIZES HAND HYGIENE AT THE WASHBASIN
Mediclinics eliminates the clutter of wall-mounted dispensers, isolated faucets, and distant dryers with its All-in-One hand hygiene station. Integrating soap, water, and air into a single fixture right at the washbasin, the design simplifies handwashing while keeping water off the restroom floor. Combining these functions into one architectural form prevents unnecessary movement across the space, giving architects and designers a clean, minimal canvas to design contemporary bathrooms and occupants to use.
HIDDEN INFRASTRUCTURE AND TAILORED FINISHES
The company draws on over 50 years of manufacturing expertise to simplify modern washroom layouts. Unifying what is typically separate equipment, the All-in-One series functions as a single synchronized family. Crafted from durable solid brass, each automatic unit features a matching swan-neck profile that creates a continuous rhythm across the washbasin. Available in bright chrome, matte black, and custom PVD finishes, the system hides all plumbing and electrical infrastructure below the surface, leaving only three minimal spouts visible in the space.
FROM FRAGMENTED HARDWARE TO A UNIFIED FIXTURE
Operating through integrated infrared sensors, the All-in-One delivers a completely touch-free experience. Containing soap dispensing, rinsing, and high-speed drying within the washbasin perimeter eliminates water drips on surrounding floors and countertops to preserve clean, dry surfaces. ====================================================================================================

A drug-free trance can blur the line between self and surroundings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:58 UTC
19:00:58 KST

Practitioners of a drug-free trance technique describe it as profoundly changing how they experience their own minds and bodies, according to a small new study. When recalling a deep trance, participants reported fewer self-focused thoughts, blurred body boundaries, and a strong sense of oneness, along with more inner peace than during an ordinary meal. The findings were published in Neuroscience of Consciousness.
Psychologists generally divide our sense of self into two main components. The “narrative self” is the internal storyteller, consisting of the thoughts we have about our past, our future, and our personality traits. The “minimal self” is the immediate, wordless physical sensation of being anchored in a body and being the one who controls its movements.
Theorists have proposed that loosening our grip on a rigid, self-centered focus might open the door to lasting happiness. According to a 2011 theoretical paper co-authored by Michael Dambrun, one of the new study’s authors, moving beyond an everyday self-centered mindset paves the way for deeper emotional stability and peace of mind.
Later experiments provided evidence for this idea. For example, a 2016 study by Dambrun found that people who felt their physical boundaries dissolving during a body scan meditation reported greater happiness. A 2021 investigation mapped out how deep meditative states systematically break down specific parts of self-experience, such as where people feel physically located and whether they feel in control of their actions.
The new study extends this line of research to a practice called auto-induced cognitive trance. This is a learnable, drug-free state of awareness characterized by deep sensory immersion, spontaneous body movements, and vivid mental imagery. Practitioners use personal sounds and gestures to enter the trance without external aids. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2026, brain scans of a single practitioner showed her activity shifting toward an internal focus as she voluntarily entered a similar drug-free trance.
“For about a decade, our research has focused on the link between states of ‘self-transcendence’ (moments when the feeling of being a separate, self-centered individual fades) and the emergence of positive emotions and well-being,” said lead researcher Pierre De Oliveira of the Psy-DREPI laboratory at Université Bourgogne Europe in Dijon, France.
“So far, this link has mainly been studied in the context of meditation, a practice grounded in stillness and the attentive observation of one’s own thoughts,” De Oliveira told PsyPost. “We first wanted to know whether a very different route, a self-induced trance practice that is dynamic, bodily and expressive, would also alter the experience of self.”
To investigate this, the researchers interviewed 17 practitioners (13 women and four men, with an average age of 49) who had previously undergone specialized training in auto-induced cognitive trance. On average, they had trained about 15 months earlier and practiced several times a week in sessions lasting about 10 minutes.
The participants were asked to vividly recall and describe two distinct moments in a randomized order. One was an ordinary waking state, specifically the last time they had a meal. The other was one of their most intense and memorable episodes of deep cognitive trance.
During the interviews, the participants answered open-ended questions about what they were thinking and feeling, and they also completed quantitative ratings, scoring different aspects of their self-awareness and emotional states on scales from 0 to 100.
The results indicated a large shift in the participants’ narrative self during the trance. Mind wandering dropped dramatically, with thoughts about the future falling from 31.5 percent of the time in the ordinary state down to just 2.7 percent in the trance state. Present-focused thoughts also dropped, from 63.5 to 37.0 percent of the time, with one participant explaining they were fully present in the trance rather than in the room.
Participants also felt much less like the authors of their own thoughts and feelings, with ratings dropping from 67.4 to 12.1. However, the feeling of being an observer of those thoughts did not change significantly. Time perception was also sharply altered: the feeling that time was present in their mind dropped from 64.3 to 7.0, and 11 of the 17 participants could not even estimate how fast time passed during the trance.
The minimal self also underwent profound changes. In their ordinary state, participants generally felt located in their head or upper torso and reported a high sense of bodily control. During the trance, this feeling of motor agency plummeted from 83.8 to 10.4, as movements and vocalizations were described as spontaneous or irresistible.
Dissociation refers to feeling detached from one’s own body, actions, or surroundings, and in clinical settings it can signal psychological distress. “What we found particularly interesting were participants’ accounts of a nonpathological form of dissociation,” De Oliveira explained. “Several participants described a body that moved and made sounds on its own, without any sense of deciding to do so, while a part of themselves watched the scene unfold.”
“They felt both like spectators of the experience and carried along by it, in a kind of willing surrender,” De Oliveira said. “For several of them, however, this surrender remained partial. They described this observing part as a kind of brake on whatever might emerge, one that both limited how deep the trance could go and allowed them to keep some degree of control.”
“Unlike the dissociation seen in clinical settings, this experience is self-induced, and many participants spontaneously mentioned that they could come out of it whenever they wished,” he added.
Additionally, the physical boundaries separating the practitioners from their environment seemed to melt away. The perceived distinctness of their bodily boundaries dropped from 83.8 in the everyday state to 36.5 in the trance state. At the same time, their feelings of oneness with their surroundings rose from 28.4 to 75.9. In contrast, participants’ sense of being their body and of being at the center of the scene did not differ meaningfully between the two conditions, although their sense of self became less tied to one specific point, dropping from 85.7 to 50.4.
These shifts in self-awareness were accompanied by higher well-being ratings. Overall happiness scores rose from 50.5 during the meal to 74.2 during the trance. The difference came mainly from the “inner peace” dimension, which jumped from 44.3 to 74.7; contentment also rose, but that difference was not statistically significant.
The researchers then checked whether the self-related changes tracked happiness during the trance. Only two correlations were statistically significant: participants who felt less at the center of the scene, or whose sense of self was less tied to one specific point, tended to report greater happiness. Weaker, nonsignificant links appeared for softened body boundaries and oneness, and changes to the narrative self, such as reduced mind wandering, showed no reliable association.
The overall pattern, softened body boundaries alongside greater well-being, is in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that immersive virtual exposure to spacious natural environments reduced perceived body boundaries, and that this, in turn, was linked to greater selflessness and positive emotions. In the new study, however, the specific correlation between boundary changes and happiness was not statistically significant, and the 2023 study examined virtual reality nature exposure in students rather than trance states in trained practitioners.
Altered states do not always feel good. The new findings stand in some tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which found that while most people who had experienced non-drug altered states described positive effects, about 13 percent reported moderate or greater suffering afterward. That earlier study surveyed a broad population experiencing varied states, whereas the current study examined a small group of trained practitioners.
“The main misinterpretation to avoid would be to conclude that trance makes people happier or that it is a form of therapy,” De Oliveira cautioned. “Our participants were recalling a past experience, and our study can neither establish cause and effect nor tell us whether any such effects carry over into everyday life.”
“Second, these experiences are not always pleasant and may not suit everyone,” he continued. “Some participants described moments of fear or oppressive sensations, and research on meditation shows that alterations in the sense of self can also be experienced as destabilizing.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a very small sample of 17 individuals, most of whom were highly educated women, many working in health professions.
“These results should nonetheless be read cautiously,” De Oliveira noted. “This was a pilot study with a small sample, which tends to overestimate the size of effects. In terms of practical significance, our data at this stage describe the intensity of a transient nonordinary state of consciousness, not a lasting benefit.”
Another limitation relates to the study’s reliance on retrospective recall. Asking participants to remember past events can sometimes introduce memory distortions, especially when describing emotionally intense or hard-to-explain experiences. Participants also chose one of their most intense and memorable trance experiences, which was compared against an ordinary meal, a contrast that could magnify the differences between conditions. Recalling a meal might also have drawn participants’ attention to their bodily sensations, making the everyday state seem more body-centered than usual.
The participants’ common training could also have shaped what they reported. All of them were trained by the TranceScience Research Institute, with which one of the study’s co-authors is affiliated.
“All our participants had been trained by the same institute and likely shared common expectations about what trance would feel like,” De Oliveira said. “These expectations may have shaped their accounts, and our study cannot separate them from the effects of the practice itself. This is why we believe it is important for research to examine more closely the psychological and social processes underlying these practices: practitioners’ expectations and dispositions, the setting in which the practice is taught, and how these experiences are later integrated into everyday life.”
The cross-sectional design of the study means the researchers cannot determine if practicing these trance states leads to permanent trait changes in a person’s baseline well-being. It remains to be seen whether regular engagement with these practices translates to lasting psychological flexibility in everyday life.
“Our long-term question concerns regular practice: can these self-transcendent experiences, repeated session after session, have lasting effects on the sense of self?” De Oliveira said. “Our hypothesis, drawn from research on meditation, is that these transient states could gradually loosen the way people perceive themselves. They would come to experience themselves a little less as a fixed, separate entity and a little more as connected to their surroundings.”
“According to our model, this less self-centered way of functioning would foster a form of inner peace, because people would be less driven by the need to protect the self,” he explained. “But this process is not automatic; it probably depends on how people integrate these experiences and on the story they build around them afterward. The same experience of dissolving boundaries can become a source of openness or, on the contrary, of destabilization, depending in part on the meaning given to it.”
“It is genuinely exciting to be able to study, within a scientific framework, practices that remain largely unexplored,” De Oliveira concluded. “We would also like to thank the participants, who agreed to put into words experiences that are often hard to describe.”
The study, “From the attenuation of self-boundaries to inner peace: how nonordinary states of consciousness modulates self-experience and subjective well-being,” was authored by Pierre De Oliveira, Hélène Meunier, Audrey Breton, and Michael Dambrun.

Russian airstrikes killed six people across Ukraine overnight into Wednesday, according to Ukrainian authorities reported by the news agency AFP on Wednesday morning.
In the capital city of Kyiv, two people died when an airstrike hit an apartment building in the Desnyanskyi district, Ukraine’s emergency service reported. A third person died in an attack in the Holosiivskyi district.
Ukrainian military authorities reported that airstrikes in the central region of Dnipropetrovsk killed two people and wounded six others.
One more person was killed in the Zaporizhzhia region in the southeastern part of the country.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the overnight strikes were extensive and caused power outages across the city on Wednesday morning.

The Ukrainian energy company DTEK also reported blackouts on Wednesday morning in Kyiv, home to roughly 3 million people. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that 600,000 people in the capital lost electricity after the strikes, according to Reuters.
The strikes on energy infrastructure took place after U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire.
Zelenskyy said Russia’s attacks on power facilities defied Trump’s statement.
“The attack was deliberate and demonstrative in its scope. Russia has never before shown such blatant disrespect toward the United States,” Zelenskyy wrote on the social media platform X.
AFP reported that ballistic missile strikes were also reported Wednesday morning in the Kharkiv and Zhytomyr regions.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces hit seven Ukrainian energy infrastructure facilities and a data center overnight into Wednesday, according to Reuters. The ministry said the targeted sites were helping the Ukrainian military.
The Russian ministry also stated Wednesday morning that it neutralized 902 drones over Russian regions during the night.
According to the governor of the Saratov region, a Ukrainian drone strike killed one person in the city of Balakovo.

Signal failure disrupts Copenhagen-Næstved trains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:47 UTC
19:00:47 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Denmark’s minister for homeland security and emergency preparedness, Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, says there is a clear need to talk with members of the Danish parliament about how to protect the country against cyberattacks.
Bech-Nielsen belongs to SF (Socialistisk Folkeparti), the Socialist People’s Party, which is a left-wing and green political party in Denmark. She spoke about the situation to the Danish broadcaster TV 2.
“The serious threat assessment and recent events are the reason why I have summoned the parties to a discussion of what initiatives can be set in motion,” she said.
The minister called the political parties in the Danish parliament, to discuss what specific steps Denmark should take to make its digital systems safer. The statement did not say when this meeting will take place.
Her comments came right after Sund & Bælt, the state-owned company in charge of major Danish bridge and tunnel links, announced on Tuesday afternoon that its construction site at Rødbyhavn was hit by what it called a cyber incident.
“Our contractor, FLC, has informed us that they have been subjected to a cyber incident,” said Jens Villemoes, the head of press at Sund & Bælt, in a statement published on the company’s website. FLC stands for Femern Link Contractors, the consortium hired to build the tunnel.
The local newspaper Lolland-Falsters Folketidende described the event as a hacker attack. According to the newspaper, the problems meant that workers were ordered not to connect to Wi-Fi, turn on their computers, or open emails from the contractor.
Large parts of the computer network were shut down. The security guards could not use their digital access systems, and employees were unable to log their working hours in the normal way.
The problems also spread to work on the water. Several ships had to stop moving because they lost access to their digital tools and data. According to the newspaper, these issues first began during the night leading up to Monday.
Bech-Nielsen had actually called for the political meeting before the problems hit the Femern project. That decision came after a recent leak of Danish CPR numbers, which are the personal identification numbers assigned to all citizens in Denmark.
The minister said it is still too early to draw final conclusions about the latest incident, but noted that “the authorities are investigating” it.
Border checks between Denmark and Germany extended for another six months
Travelers entering the country may continue to face inspections until May 17, 2027, as authorities maintain that security threats remain serious.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, informed the European Commission of the decision Wednesday, according to a statement from the Justice Ministry.
The temporary controls were previously scheduled to expire November 11, following a four-month extension announced in June.
Denmark’s decision comes despite the general principle of open borders under the Schengen Agreement, which allows people to travel between participating European countries without routine border checks.
However, regulations introduced in 2024 allow countries to extend existing border controls when the security threats that originally justified them remain in place.
Wammen said Denmark continues to face threats involving terrorism and sabotage.
“The security situation at home is serious, and we continue to see a terror and sabotage threat directed at Denmark,” he said in the ministry’s statement.
He also referred to recent developments in Ceuta, a Spanish territory in North Africa, as an example of how quickly movements of people across borders can change.
“The overall picture emphasizes how important it is for the security and safety of Danes to have control over the checks at the border,” Wammen said.
Under the extended measures, people crossing from Germany into Denmark may be stopped by authorities and asked to provide documentation confirming their right to enter or remain in the country.
Reports of AI-generated child abuse material rise sharply in Denmark
Save the Children received 4,069 reports of suspected artificial intelligence-generated sexual abuse material involving children and young people during the first six months of 2026, according to figures obtained by Kristeligt Dagblad.
The international children’s rights organization recorded 6,558 reports throughout 2025, compared with 2,770 in 2024, an increase of approximately 140 percent.
The figures reflect reports submitted by people who believe they have encountered such material online, rather than confirmed cases.
Lea Wermelin, justice spokesperson for Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, expressed concern about the growing numbers.
“The technology makes it much easier to make, but we must never get used to it just being something encountered online,” she told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Pernille Spitz, Save the Children’s head of protection against abuse, warned that greater exposure to such content could make it appear more acceptable.
“The more of it there is, and the easier it is to come across, the more legitimate it may seem,” Spitz said.
Save the Children’s reporting service, AnmeldDet, reviews submissions from the public and assesses whether they should be forwarded to authorities.
During 2026, the service has referred 377 reports to police.
Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, known as NSK, told Kristeligt Dagblad that it could not determine what proportion of child sexual abuse material involved artificial intelligence.
However, the agency said it believed AI was increasingly being used to produce such content.
Denmark amended its criminal code in 2025 to make realistic AI-generated child sexual abuse material punishable by law.
Denmark restricts land registry searches after 17 million queries in days
An unusually high volume of requests for publicly available property information has prompted authorities to introduce new safeguards following disruptions to a government database.
The Danish Court Administration said 17.2 million searches were recorded in the Digital Land Registration System over several days, compared with fewer than two million in a typical week.
The activity was discovered after the system experienced repeated disruptions during week 41.
Rikke Holler, president of the Land Registration Court, emphasized that the searches were legal and involved only information available without logging in through MitID, Denmark’s digital identification system.
“It is the number of lookups that gives cause for attention,” Holler said.
The system provides limited public information about properties, cooperative housing and vehicles.
Authorities have not identified what caused the surge in activity.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a member of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, said he had informed the Danish Parliament about the incident.
Although the searches were permitted, Wammen said their unusual volume warranted serious attention.
The Danish Court Administration warned that publicly available information could potentially be used to make fraud attempts appear more convincing.
It also referred to a recent leak involving 8.8 million CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
Wammen urged people never to share passwords or confidential information through phone calls or emails, even when someone contacting them knows details they consider private.
The Land Registration Court has introduced additional limits on searches to maintain system stability.
Officials did not specify the measures but reported that the number of queries had decreased following their introduction.
Danish agriculture group threatens legal action over temporary pig farm permit freeze
A proposed one-year suspension of permits for new conventional pig farms and expansions of existing facilities has raised questions about the government’s legal authority and potential compensation claims.
Landbrug & Fødevarer, the Danish Agriculture and Food Council, warned in a consultation response that the measure could lead to lawsuits over financial losses.
“If the amendment to the executive order is implemented, a number of lawsuits regarding liability for compensation for economic losses as a result of the regulation must be expected,” the organization stated.
Christian Fink Hansen, the council’s pig sector director, called for an assessment of the proposal’s economic impact on businesses.
He warned that the industry could otherwise be forced to pursue compensation claims in court.
The suspension is scheduled to take effect October 26, but applications submitted since September 23 must already be assessed under the proposed rules.
Several legal experts have questioned whether Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen, of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, has authority to impose the restrictions.
Two experts cited by Dagbladet Information disputed the legal basis for an immediate suspension, while another supported the minister’s position.
Rabjerg Madsen has rejected those concerns, citing assessments by lawyers from his ministry and the Justice Ministry.
“I am completely at ease. I do not make an amendment to an executive order without an assessment of the legal basis having been carried out,” he said in September.
Although the government’s June platform proposed introducing the measure through legislation, Rabjerg Madsen instead used an executive order, which does not require parliamentary approval.
The government says the suspension will remain in place while it clarifies future production rules through negotiations involving the pig industry, which began September 30.
Full train service between Fredericia and Odense to resume Monday
Full train service between Fredericia and Odense will resume on Monday, Banedanmark announced on Wednesday.
Banedanmark, which operates, maintains and develops Denmark’s state-owned railway network, announced the resumption in a post on the social media platform X.
Earlier on Wednesday, railway operator DSB said in a preliminary announcement that fewer trains would run on the route through Sunday, October 18.

International trains, InterCityLyn express services and InterCity trains have continued to run as normal, but at reduced speeds on parts of the route between Odense and Middelfart or Fredericia.

A signal fault near Kildebrønde in eastern Zealand is disrupting train services between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved via Køge.
On Wednesday morning, DSB said passengers should expect longer travel times until 1 p.m. But about an hour before that deadline, the railway operator announced that disruptions would continue until 7 p.m., according to its website.
Banedanmark, which operates and maintains Denmark’s state-owned railway network, told DSB that repair work would not take place until Wednesday night, leading into Thursday.
However, a solution has been found that will allow trains to run normally on the affected section after 7 p.m., even though the fault will not yet have been repaired.
Some trains that usually run via Køge Nord are being diverted through Roskilde instead. These services will not stop between Copenhagen Central Station and Ringsted.
Additional replacement buses were introduced between Køge and Næstved on Wednesday morning to ease pressure on train services. The buses stopped running at noon, and DSB is advising passengers to take the S-train from Copenhagen toward Køge. Trains between Køge and Næstved are running once an hour.
Banedanmark told the Danish news agency Ritzau that a severed cable caused the signal fault. DSB advises passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public transport journey planner, before setting off.
Meanwhile, fewer trains are running between Odense and Fredericia through Sunday, October 18, according to DSB. The date is provisional, and services could return to normal earlier or later than expected.
All regional trains on the route have been replaced by buses since Friday, following a fire in a railway relay hut near Aarup in western Funen.
International trains, as well as InterCityLyn and InterCity services, are running as normal, but at reduced speeds on some sections of the route.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.
